title: Neural Codes, Noise, and Memory: A Guide to Three Papers
text:
Contents
These three neuroscience papers study how groups of nerve cells represent information used in memory, eye control, and navigation. The guide connects mathematical models of stored values with eye-movement recordings from monkeys and recordings of spatial activity in rodents and bats. Begin with the reading path for the setting, contribution, and limits of each study, followed by the background and step-by-step calculations. Part III connects these neural memory questions to physical electronic storage and selected neuromorphic advances through 30 October 2026. Part IV explains the simulations, methods, and tools behind the original studies. Part introductions identify the source and role of each chapter contribution.

title: Neural Codes, Noise, and Memory: A Guide to Three Papers
text:
Front matter

What the three papers establish
These neuroscience papers study memory, eye control, and navigation. Their settings are mathematical models of stored values, eye-movement and neural recordings from macaque monkeys, and recordings of location-dependent neural activity in rodents and bats. This reading guide explains each study’s question, methods, findings, and limits.
Mathematical tools connect neural signals to the papers’ predictions
Before Part I, explain the mathematical tools behind all three papers: feedback and Fisher information for memory; covariance and filtering for eye drift; Gaussian spatial maps, crossings and peak geometry for place fields. Keep physical meanings, assumptions and exact versus limiting results visible.
Exam review: connect mechanisms, measurements and results
Return after studying the three papers to reconstruct their arguments, locate a formula, read its symbols and check its assumptions. Core results are visible; supporting results remain in closed notes.



Part I: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models
In a model neural circuit, a pattern of firing rates across many nerve cells can represent a remembered angle. Random spike timing can change that angle while activity persists. The central source, Burak and Fiete (2012), derives how quickly accuracy can be lost and how well the value can be read. Chapters 1 and 2 establish the background. Chapters 3 and 5 develop the central diffusion and information results. Chapters 4 and 6 explain long-delay behavior and readout. Expanded examples and marked checks of printed formulas are guide-derived.

Chapter 1: Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value
Introduce the question and steady-state equation in the 2012 paper, then explain eye mechanics, the neural model brought forward from Methods, spike statistics, and a preview of its simulations.
Chapter 2: Stable representations can accumulate error
Explain the continuous family of states in the 2012 Results, then provide eye mechanics and the random-spreading background needed to understand how persistent activity can accumulate error.
Chapter 3: Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor
Starting from the neural model in Chapter 1, derive the weak-fluctuation approximation and follow small disturbances through the circuit to calculate diffusion of a stored value.
Chapter 4: Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays
Follow the paper’s diffusion section through Figures 1 and 2, then use the supporting text to explain how boundaries, angular wraparound, state-dependent diffusion, and systematic drift affect longer delays.
Chapter 5: Spike information limits memory stability
A neuron receiving spikes from a memory circuit has access to information about the stored value. This chapter sets a bound on estimation error under the model’s assumptions and derives the constraint that spike information places on the circuit’s memory stability.
Chapter 6: Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed
Reading spikes from a memory circuit takes time, during which its stored value can keep changing. This chapter calculates how much longer observation can help recover the value present at a recall cue, and explains why it cannot recover every earlier random displacement.



Part II: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code
These studies connect neural activity to eye control in monkeys and location in rodents and bats. Ben-Shushan et al. (2022) supply the central shared-drive inference and a possible integrator explanation in Chapters 7 to 9. Mainali et al. (2025) supply the spatial model, field-size predictions, and supporting shape tests in Chapters 10 to 12. Chapter 13 is a guide-derived comparison of those results with Burak and Fiete (2012). The eye chapters begin with recordings and then test a possible neural source. The place chapters begin with a spatial input model and then test its field statistics.

Chapter 7: Eye drift points to a shared neural drive
Even when a monkey looks at a stationary spot, its eyes drift slightly. This chapter explains how paired measurements of eye angle and the firing of neurons that command eye muscles support a shared neural source of that drift, before considering a particular circuit mechanism.
Chapter 8: Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise
Eye movements recorded during steady gaze in monkeys look different over short and long time intervals. This chapter uses their timing to distinguish fluctuations around a fixed command from accumulated changes in the command, while accounting for eye-position measurement error.
Chapter 9: A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift
A circuit that stores the intended eye angle is one possible source of fixational drift. This chapter follows the proposed model from interacting neurons through motor neurons and muscles to eye motion, and explains how delayed visual feedback can limit that motion.
Chapter 10: Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale
Hippocampal place cells fire more at particular locations as an animal moves. This chapter introduces the rodent and bat recordings, then shows how a smooth random input that exceeds a firing threshold can produce several separate active regions for one cell.
Chapter 11: High peaks explain size laws across dimensions
A place cell’s active regions can have different sizes on a route, across a floor, or in a flight volume. This chapter derives why the spatial model predicts different field-size distributions in one, two, and three dimensions, and identifies the high-threshold approximation used in that derivation.
Chapter 12: Holes and measurements test the spatial explanation
Recordings show where a hippocampal cell is active as an animal moves through an environment. This chapter tests the spatial model against the shapes and arrangement of those regions, then asks what agreement can reveal about the inputs and connections that produce them.
Chapter 13: Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests
The three papers address different links between nerve-cell activity and behavior: retaining a value, producing eye movement, and representing location. This chapter compares what the models and recordings establish, and separates supported connections from further questions about how a complete neural circuit would work.



Part III: Neural memory in electronic hardware
Electronic circuits store connection settings, changing states and values represented by networks. Von Neumann (1958) motivates the comparison. Chapter 14 identifies physical states and weights; Chapter 15 follows feedback through electronic architectures. Chapter 16 compares stability and noise with the neural model of Burak and Fiete (2012). Chapter 17 examines selected hardware results through October 30, 2026. Chapter 18 develops guide-derived experiments and readout tests connected to all three papers.

Chapter 14: A stored weight and a remembered value are different states
A silicon circuit can keep a connection strength unchanged while losing the angle it was asked to remember. It can also keep that angle while its individual electrical signals change. To compare electronic memory with the neural memory in Part I, we first need to identify what information each physical quantity represents. This chapter separates the connection settings, the changing state of each artificial neuron, and the value represented by their joint activity. That separation will let us ask what feedback actually preserves.
Chapter 15: Electronic feedback circuits store and transform neural-like states
Compare electronic circuits and neuromorphic networks with neural models of persistent activity, eye control, and spatial representation. Identify what each architecture stores, how its components interact, how noise and readout affect its state, and what each cited result establishes.
Chapter 16: Discrete restoration and continuous random wandering produce different memory errors
A circuit can remain active for seconds even when its individual voltages decay in milliseconds. The explanation is feedback: activity supplies new input before old input disappears. But long-lived activity does not by itself identify what is being preserved. This chapter first explains how feedback extends a time scale, then distinguishes a restoring discrete memory from a freely changing continuous one. Measured silicon circuits show why this distinction matters beyond a mathematical model.
Chapter 17: Neuromorphic chips choose where physics performs the calculation
Suppose we want to study how a noisy network retains an angle. One machine can calculate every state update as arithmetic. Another can let capacitor voltages perform part of the dynamics. A third can use material conductances to multiply inputs by stored weights. The scientific choice is which physical effects we want to control, measure, or exploit. This chapter compares these implementations and then examines recent demonstrations of memory and learning.
Chapter 18: Memory experiments must separate device error from network dynamics
The earlier stability comparison followed the response to one disturbance. A memory experiment instead repeats a cue and observes what happens as disturbances continue over time. After an angle cue, the estimate may be wrong because the state wandered, because unequal connections pull it toward another angle, or because the observer reads it poorly. This chapter separates mean motion from trial-to-trial spread, relates spread to circuit noise and asks what the output reveals about the state. Its tests and reduced models are proposed tools, not results demonstrated on every platform in the preceding chapter.



Part IV: Simulations connect model assumptions to measurable outcomes
Burak and Fiete (2012) test memory diffusion in spiking networks. Ben-Shushan et al. (2022) connect a simulated neural command to eye motion. Mainali et al. (2025) generate spatial maps and compare their fields with recordings. This Part explains the methods, measurements, and software behind those studies, then gives a guide-derived route for checking a reproduction.

Chapter 19: Network simulations test how random spikes move a stored value
To compare a simulated memory trace with Burak and Fiete’s (2012) theory, the numerical update and the measurement of the stored value must match the model. The foundation chapter explains the spike-update cycle, and the long-delay chapter interprets its diffusion tests. Here the additional task is to recover the published network settings, distinguish a numerical position measurement from the theoretical coordinate, and identify choices left open for an independent reproduction.
Chapter 20: Eye simulations connect a noisy neural command to measured motion
A reproduction of Ben-Shushan et al. (2022) must distinguish the recording analysis from the simulated eye-control pathway. The circuit chapter explains why a noisy internal command is a possible source of drift. Here the added detail is how the published parameters, spike generator, update intervals, saved samples, and MATLAB files determine the numerical experiment, and which code or data gaps limit reproduction. The pathway below gives the mechanism needed to interpret those choices.
Chapter 21: Random spatial maps test the statistics of place fields
To reproduce Mainali et al.’s (2025) place-field comparisons, we need the rules for generating and fitting model maps, and for measuring both model and recorded maps. The spatial-model chapter explains the statistical assumptions, and the tests chapter interprets the evidence. Here the additional detail is the Python map-generation procedure, filter and boundary conventions, fitted summaries, field detectors, and access to code and recordings. Position is the independent variable; each generated map is fixed during analysis, so these computations do not simulate a remembered position changing over time.
Chapter 22: Reproduction depends on the model, numerical method, and measurement
A simulated eye trace can look convincing while answering the wrong question. It may use different spike statistics, a different muscle response, or a different definition of displacement from the experiment. Beyond the paper-specific methods in the preceding chapters, a reproduction needs checks that its software, resolution, and saved run record preserve the intended comparison. This chapter explains how to choose those checks and distinguish the authors’ program from an independent implementation or a smaller teaching model.



Appendices

Glossary
These short definitions support lookup after the explanations and examples in the main chapters.
References
Entries follow their first use in the reading path and chapters. The paper’s supporting information shares its main article entry. The author’s mathematical notes are listed separately because the guide also uses them for the excursion derivation.

Variable neural signals must support reliable behavior

The subject is neuroscience: how groups of nerve cells represent information used in memory, eye control, and navigation. The three papers examine mathematical models that store a quantity such as an angle, eye movements and neural activity recorded in macaque monkeys, and location-dependent neural activity recorded in rodents and bats. They ask how activity can retain a value, how an internal fluctuation can move the eyes, and why a cell can respond at several separate locations.
A remembered direction must remain useful after its cue disappears. The eyes must hold an angle while an animal looks at a target. A moving animal must keep track of where it is. These tasks depend on groups of neurons, the brain’s signaling cells, whose electrical signals are brief and variable. Computational and systems neuroscience studies how these cells and their interactions support such behavior. Mathematical models connect assumptions about cells and their interactions to predictions. Recordings test those predictions against neural activity and movement.

title: What the three papers establish
section: Persistent activity can still lose memory accuracy
text:
Persistent activity can still lose memory accuracy
Burak and Fiete (2012) study short-term memory for a continuous quantity, such as a direction or eye angle. A proposed mechanism is that interacting neurons keep activity going after the original input ends. Yet the remembered value can change while the activity persists. The problem is to explain how the properties of the cells and their connections set the rate of this loss of accuracy.

The authors analyze a network with a continuous family of persistent activity patterns, each representing a different value. Each cell sends signals at random times. They use an approximation for small fluctuations to derive how these signals move the stored value, compare the calculation with network simulations, and relate the motion to the best accuracy possible when estimating the stored value from those signals. 

Their central result is the lower bound \(D\ge 1/(2\tau^2J)\): uncertainty in reading the network’s current value limits how slowly that value can wander. Here \(D\) measures how quickly the represented value spreads, \(J\) is the internal spike information rate, and \(\tau\) is the synaptic decay time. Under the model’s assumptions, at short times near a chosen state the variance of memory displacement grows approximately as \(2Dt\), where \(t\) is elapsed storage time; boundaries can change that behavior over longer delays. Reading for longer also has diminishing benefit because the state continues moving during observation. This gives a benchmark for evaluating proposed memory circuits and their recall errors. It applies to the analyzed family of continuous-state memory models, with the required noise assumptions and no external signal anchoring the value. Chapters 3–6 develop the diffusion calculation, its long-delay behavior, the information bound, and the limits of readout.1

title: What the three papers establish
section: Eye drift points to a shared neural source
text:
Eye drift points to a shared neural source


Even while gaze is held on a stationary target, the eyes move smoothly and irregularly between brief, rapid movements. This smooth motion is called fixational drift. It changes the image reaching the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. Understanding its source is therefore part of understanding the visual signals the brain receives. Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022) ask whether the motion begins mainly in muscles or in neural commands sent to them.  
They reanalyze recordings from 57 neurons that send commands to eye muscles in two macaques, paired with precise eye-position measurements. They first calibrate the relation between each cell’s activity and larger eye movements. They then use it during fixation to compare the movement predicted from one cell with the measured movement. A separate circuit model tests whether a wandering stored eye-position command could explain the movement’s amplitude and time dependence.


For 350-millisecond intervals, their analysis estimates that about 82% of horizontal displacement variance comes from a common source before the final motor neurons, assuming the fitted movement relation also holds during fixation and the relevant noise contributions do not vary together. Writing \(Y\) for measured displacement and \(X\) for a single neuron’s displacement prediction, the estimated shared fraction of measured displacement variance is \(\chi\simeq\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(Y)\), after matching their calibrated gains. The reported \(0.82\pm0.07\) is the weighted estimate across cells, not an individual cell’s fraction. This supports a central neural contribution to drift. The memory-circuit model provides a possible explanation of that contribution, linking an internal storage error to observable behavior. The recordings do not uniquely locate the noise inside that memory circuit. Chapters 7–9 separate the shared-drive inference, the timing of drift, and the proposed circuit mechanism.2

title: What the three papers establish
section: Smooth random maps explain the variety of place fields
text:
Smooth random maps explain the variety of place fields


A place cell in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory and navigation, becomes more active in particular locations. Each connected region of elevated activity is a place field. Small environments encouraged a picture of one smooth field per cell. Larger environments reveal multiple fields with widely varying sizes and shapes. Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025) ask whether one statistical account can explain this variety across species and spatial dimensions.  
Their model gives each cell a smooth, mean-centered random input \(h(x)\) at position \(x\) and firing rate \(F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+\), where \(z(x)=h(x)/\sigma_h\), \(\sigma_h\) is the input standard deviation, \(q\) is a dimensionless threshold, \(a\) is a positive gain, and \([u]_+=\max(u,0)\). Activity is positive where the normalized input exceeds the threshold. The authors derive predictions for the resulting regions, simulate the model, and compare it with existing rodent and bat recordings from one-, two- and three-dimensional environments. Parameters fitted to field sizes and their spatial arrangement also support further tests of field shapes and connectedness.


The model explains different size distributions across dimensions and predicts additional features, such as multiple peaks within a field and inactive holes surrounded by activity. This makes irregular spatial responses quantitatively understandable and supports a common statistical description across the examined settings. Such statistics can arise when cells combine many inputs through largely random connections. The study does not directly measure those connections. Chapters 10–12 develop the spatial model, its size and shape predictions, and the tests and circuit interpretation. They distinguish exact predictions, limiting approximations and empirical comparisons.3  




The three contributions therefore have different meanings: a mathematical constraint on memory models, evidence about the source of eye movement, and a statistical explanation of spatial activity. Together they show how a representation can be described, maintained and related to behavior. Combining all three in one biological circuit remains a further research question, developed in Chapter 13.

title: What the three papers establish
section: Electronic implementations make memory mechanisms testable
text:
Electronic implementations make memory mechanisms testable

Part III asks how the neural memory mechanisms can be implemented in electronic circuits. The setting is neuromorphic computing, where engineered systems implement computations inspired by neural organization and dynamics. The chapters distinguish connection weights from changing neural states, explain how feedback affects retention, and examine selected hardware research through October 30, 2026. They end with a proposed experiment that separates systematic drift, random spreading, and readout error. This extension is a comparison of mechanisms and evidence. The original papers remain the foundation of Parts I and II.

section: Simulations separate the model from the evidence used to test it
text:
Simulations separate the model from the evidence used to test it
Part IV follows the computational methods in Burak and Fiete (2012), Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), and Mainali et al. (2025). It distinguishes simulated neural trajectories, recorded-data analysis, and generated spatial maps. Each chapter identifies the model states, numerical procedure, measurements, available code, and limits on reproducing the published figures. The final chapter compares tools and explains resolution and repeatability checks. These are explanations of the sources, not a claim that the guide reran their full simulations.
Part introductions identify the paper behind each chapter’s result using author and year. Central marks a main finding of that paper. Supporting marks an analysis used to establish or qualify it. Background supplies needed concepts. Guide-derived marks expanded explanations, comparisons, or proposed tests developed here. A result can be central in its own paper while serving as supporting evidence in another argument.

title: What the three papers establish
section: Starting knowledge and reading paths
text:
Starting knowledge and reading paths

The guide assumes undergraduate calculus, basic probability, and linear algebra, including expected value, variance, standard deviation and probability density. Before Part I, the mathematical-tools chapter introduces the tools behind all three papers: neural feedback and information, covariance and filtering of eye signals, and spatial random fields with crossing and peak calculations. The later chapters develop the full derivations and the remaining tools in context. 


Before Part I: read the mathematical tools for all three papers, with optional folded calculations.
Chapters 1–2: establish neural signals and variability, then persistence and accumulated error.





Chapters 3–6: derive memory diffusion, its long-delay behavior, the information bound, and readout.





Chapters 7–9: follow the eye study from shared-drive evidence through timing to a circuit model.




Chapters 10–12: develop spatial maps, their size predictions, and tests of their shapes and possible origins.



Chapter 13: connect the results and compare related work.


For a path focused on particular papers: 

Memory and eye drift: follow chapters 1 through 9 in order.



Place fields: start with tuning curves, population codes, and rate maps, then variable spike counts, and fixed spatial maps versus values that change over time. Continue with chapters 10–12. This short route supplies the shared foundations without requiring the eye-mechanics or memory-readout calculations.


The Glossary gives short definitions for lookup after their first explanation. The References section gives full source details. The original paper figures are discussed by number and can be inspected in the linked PDFs.
After the foundations, the guide map shows the three paper questions together.
On a first reading, follow the main text, figures, assumptions, and results. The expandable notes preserve longer calculations and extensions. Open one when you want to check the steps behind a result. The explanations needed for the next section remain in the main text.

title: What the three papers establish
section: Neural mechanisms and mathematical derivations answer different questions
text:
Neural mechanisms and mathematical derivations answer different questions

Chapters 3–6 explain how interacting neurons can retain a value while random spike timing changes it. Their treatment of the Burak and Fiete appendix separates three parts of each substantial topic: 


Neural mechanism: which cells and signals interact, what changes, and which features are assumptions of the model. For readout, this part also states what an observer can measure and which value it must estimate.




Mathematical derivation: the general tool, its conditions, and the calculation after neural quantities are assigned to the symbols.



Interpretation: what the result predicts about memory or readout, and what its assumptions leave unresolved.


An equation that specifies how a cell responds belongs to the model. A derivation works out what follows from that choice. 

For example, a spike can disturb several cells’ activity. The circuit’s interactions remove some changes, while others leave the represented angle displaced. Linear algebra calculates which part survives. Probability gives the spread of that displacement. The result then predicts how quickly memory errors accumulate in this model. The mathematical tools also apply to other systems, but this neural prediction depends on the circuit and spike statistics used in the calculation. 
The same distinction matters for readout. A calculation of the best possible estimate sets a benchmark under specified access to neural signals. Establishing that an animal’s neurons implement the assumed computation requires separate evidence.

For a first conceptual pass, read the mechanism, inspect the displayed result and its variables, then read the interpretation. Follow the mathematical derivation when you want to understand why the result holds or calculate with it. Assumptions remain part of both readings. 

The PNAS appendix supplies both neural-model choices and mathematical arguments. This map links its seven sections to the guide’s explanations. Page links open the local copy. The guide sometimes uses an equivalent teaching derivation and identifies source inconsistencies beside the affected calculation.

title: What the three papers establish
section: How to interpret the calculations and evidence
text:
How to interpret the calculations and evidence

Examples chosen for the guide distinguish independent from shared fluctuations, complete from limited access to neural signals, and exact formulas from approximations for rare fields. Their numbers are checked separately from the published experimental measurements. A teaching reconstruction is labeled when its simplified model differs from the paper’s full model. 

The guide explains how to interpret the experiments and their figures. It does not rerun the original animal recordings, data processing, or full neural-network simulations. A successful numerical check of a probability identity is different from an independent reproduction of a paper’s empirical result. Related work is selected to clarify the assumptions and alternatives rather than to claim an exhaustive literature search. 
The following map is a guide-derived comparison of the source papers’ contributions. Read each paper’s column downward: the mathematical prediction, numerical comparison, and animal-data comparison answer different questions.456




Table 2: Guide-derived map of the three source papers’ evidence. Each column follows a separate study; the table does not claim a jointly tested circuit.





Step in the evidence
Burak and Fiete (2012)
Ben-Shushan et al. (2022)
Mainali et al. (2025)




Physical system and question
A proposed neural circuit maintaining a continuous value after a cue ends. How quickly does its accuracy deteriorate?
Motor-neuron activity and eye motion during macaque fixation. Where does the shared motion originate?
Place-cell responses in rodent and bat environments. Why do field sizes and shapes vary?


Actors, variables, and interactions
Fixed neural connections turn outgoing spike effects into new firing rates. Spikes renew activation and disturb the represented value. Connection-matrix explanation.
Two neural populations produce command \(E_{\mathrm{OI}}\). Motor spikes, muscles, and delayed feedback connect it to actual eye angle \(E\). The two angles are different signals.
Cell \(i\) receives smooth Gaussian input \(h_i(\mathbf x)\) at position \(\mathbf x\). Activity occurs above a threshold; the spatial map is fixed during analysis.


Derived prediction
Spike fluctuations produce memory diffusion. An information bound limits stability under the model assumptions.
Shared and private fluctuations imply displacement-covariance relations. Filtering a diffusing command predicts the time dependence of eye motion.
Covariance, threshold, and dimension determine field statistics, with exact results and high-threshold approximations kept separate.


Simulation comparison
Stochastic ring and two-population networks test theoretical memory diffusion. These are model tests, not animal-data validation.
A noisy integrator and motor pathway test whether the proposed mechanism can produce the observed motion and analysis results.
Generated spatial maps test analytical approximations and provide finite-threshold comparisons with recorded field statistics.


Empirical comparison
This study does not directly test the bound against animal recordings.
Paired single-neuron and eye recordings support a substantial shared source upstream of the final motor neurons, under the inference assumptions.
Existing rodent and bat recordings test field sizes, arrangements, shapes, and connectedness. Parameters fitted to summaries remain distinct from additional comparisons.


What remains unknown
Whether a biological memory circuit meets the assumptions or approaches the bound.
Whether the shared source is specifically the modeled integrator. A successful model does not uniquely locate it.
Which connections, learning rules, and dynamics generate the spatial inputs. A statistical fit does not establish a memory circuit.







Throughout the guide, \(D\) denotes the diffusion coefficient, which sets how quickly uncertainty spreads. In the basic one-dimensional model, \(D\) is constant, neither direction is favored, and no boundary limits the motion. Its mean squared displacement (MSD), the average squared change in the represented coordinate after elapsed time \(t\), is \(2Dt\). Chapter 2 explains this model and its assumptions.
The other recurring symbols are:

\(d\): spatial dimension.
\(\theta\): the represented coordinate in the memory chapters.
\(q\): the normalized threshold in the place-field chapters, called \(\theta\) in that paper.
\(C\): the spatial covariance in the place-field chapters.

section: The original papers
text:
The original papers
The copies are the published versions. Supporting information is linked separately.


Burak and Fiete (2012): Paper PDF and 20-page supporting information PDF. Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650. Published DOI. The local main PDF uses the six-page Early Edition layout, so PDF page locators run from 1 to 6.




Ben-Shushan, Shaham, Joshua, and Burak (2022): Paper PDF, supplementary notes and figures PDF, and open peer review PDF. Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. Published DOI. Ben-Shushan and Shaham contributed equally.




Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025): Paper and STAR Methods PDF and supplementary figures and Methods S1–S4 PDF. Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities. Neuron, 113(7), 1110–1120.e3. Published DOI. The main PDF has a cover before the article. Guide citations distinguish printed and PDF page numbers when needed.


The supporting-information copies preserve their original formulas. The guide identifies apparent inconsistencies in several printed intermediate equations beside the affected calculations and follows an explicitly shown derivation. Such observations are independent mathematical checks, not author-confirmed corrections.

title: Mathematical tools connect neural signals to the papers’ predictions
text:
Connection weights determine how neurons sustain activity
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated images may contain incorrect or missing labels, arrows, formulas and numbers. Use the chapter text and paper links as the source for the explanation.
The three papers ask different questions about neural activity. How accurately can a circuit retain a value? What do fluctuations in neural recordings reveal about eye movement? Why do place cells have fields of different sizes and shapes? Each question needs a mathematical tool whose variables correspond to a physical part of the system.
This chapter introduces those tools before their use in Parts I and II. It assumes calculus, linear algebra and basic probability, including expected value, variance, standard deviation and probability density. The main text explains the physical meanings and conclusions; folded calculations supply the longer steps. The reading paths are:
For a quick return to the complete arguments, use the Exam review: reasoning chains, formulas, symbol keys and exact locations.
A single neural signal is brief, so retaining a value requires something to carry its effect forward. A spike is a brief electrical event emitted by a neuron. Its firing rate is the expected number of spikes per unit time. A rate gives an expectation; it does not specify an evenly spaced sequence of spikes.
In Burak and Fiete’s (2012) model, a spike leaves a longer-lasting effect on the cells receiving it. The synaptic activation \(s_j\) tracks the remaining effect of neuron \(j\)’s outgoing spikes. Each spike increases \(s_j\) by one, and between spikes it decays with time constant \(\tau\), measured in seconds. The changing activation therefore carries the effect of earlier spikes into the present.1
How does that effect change another cell’s activity? The connection matrix \(W\) lists the strengths and signs of all the modeled neural connections: \(W_{ij}\) converts neuron \(j\)’s activation into input to neuron \(i\). For \(N\) neurons it is an \(N\times N\) matrix. Rows identify receiving cells; columns identify sending cells. Each receiver adds its weighted inputs and a constant background input:
\[ g_i=\sum_jW_{ij}s_j+b_i, \qquad r_i=\phi(g_i). \]
Here \(g_i\) is the total input, \(b_i\) is its constant bias, and \(r_i\) is the firing rate in spikes per second. The function \(\phi\) converts total input into a nonnegative rate. Activations are dimensionless in this one-unit-per-spike convention, so \(W_{ij}\) has input units per activation unit and \(b_i\) has the same units as \(g_i\). A positive weight raises input, a negative weight lowers it, and zero means no direct influence in the model. These signs raise or lower firing when \(\phi\) increases with input.
The equations describe a complete feedback cycle:
Consider two mutually inhibiting populations. If population 1 becomes more active, it inhibits population 2 more strongly. Population 2 then fires less and inhibits population 1 less strongly. With the paper’s particular balance of weights, decay and rate response, the circuit restores changes in the total activation while leaving a change in the activation difference in place. That difference stores the value. Arbitrary mutual inhibition does not guarantee this balance.
If \(W=0\) in this model, rates become the constants \(\phi(b_i)\). Any difference due to the initial synaptic activations then decays toward the bias-determined state. Connections allow the present activity to influence what happens next; their arrangement determines whether the circuit preserves a useful pattern. The weights stay fixed during storage. The remembered value is carried by changing neural activity, rather than by changing the weights. Chapter 1 gives the full spike and activation equations; Chapter 3 calculates which disturbances those interactions remove and which leave a lasting memory change.
In the model without spike fluctuations, a fixed point is an activity pattern whose activations have zero rate of change. The tuned memory circuit has a continuous family of these patterns, each labeled by a represented value \(\theta\). Small disturbances away from the family relax toward a member of it, which may differ from the original member. A shift along the family changes the represented value without being restored. The direction along the family is its neutral tangent: a small displacement in that direction neither grows nor decays under the local noise-free dynamics.
Near one fixed pattern, the network’s linear response matrix \(K\) describes how a small activation disturbance \(\delta\mathbf s\) changes: \(d(\delta\mathbf s)/dt\simeq K\delta\mathbf s\). A small change \(\delta s_j\) in cell \(j\)’s activation contributes \(K_{ij}\delta s_j\) to the rate of change of cell \(i\)’s activation. If a right eigenvector \(\mathbf z\) satisfies \(K\mathbf z=\lambda\mathbf z\), a disturbance initially in that direction evolves as \(e^{\lambda t}\mathbf z\). The eigenvalue \(\lambda\) has units of inverse time. A negative real eigenvalue gives decay; zero gives a neutral direction. For complex eigenvalues, the sign of the real part controls growth or decay, while the imaginary part describes oscillation; real disturbances use the real and imaginary components together. Write \(\bar{\mathbf s}(\theta)\) for the noise-free activations at value \(\theta\). Their derivative \(\mathbf u=d\bar{\mathbf s}/d\theta\) is the neutral tangent and satisfies \(K\mathbf u=0\).
The network can return to the family along a tilted path. Let \(\delta\theta\) be the lasting change in represented value. The left zero eigenvector \(\mathbf v\) satisfies \(\mathbf v^TK=0\) and is normalized so that \(\mathbf v^T\mathbf u=1\). It extracts the lasting coordinate change from a small disturbance: \(\delta\theta=\mathbf v^T\delta\mathbf s\). The first condition makes \(\mathbf v^T\delta\mathbf s\) constant during the noise-free linear return; the second makes a change along \(\mathbf u\) read out in units of \(\theta\). It need not point along \(\mathbf u\): unlike a perpendicular projection, it incorporates the circuit’s return path. Chapter 3 derives it for the neural model.
Random spike counts also need a bridge to the continuous noise used later. Many weak, sufficiently independent contributions to a receiver can sum to an approximately Gaussian fluctuation. Matching its mean and variance specifies the proposed approximation’s scale; those two moments alone do not prove that the fluctuation is Gaussian. The network limit also requires an appropriate population and time-scale separation. Chapter 3 states how this approximation is used.

title: Mathematical tools connect neural signals to the papers’ predictions
text:
A spike from cell \(j\) increases \(s_j\).
Receiving cell \(i\) gets an input change \(W_{ij}\), which can change its firing rate.
Its later spikes change other cells’ inputs, including paths that return to the original cell.




Example: feedback preserves a difference while correcting the total activity


Use the two-unit model with \(W_{12}=W_{21}=-1\), zero self-weights, equal biases \(b>0\), and \(\phi(g)=g/\tau\) where both inputs are positive. Replacing spike events by their mean rate gives \(\dot s_i=-s_i/\tau+r_i\). Substitution gives
\[ \tau\dot s_1=b-s_1-s_2, \qquad \tau\dot s_2=b-s_1-s_2. \]
For total activation \(S=s_1+s_2\) and difference \(\theta_s=s_1-s_2\),
\[ \dot S=\frac{2(b-S)}{\tau},\qquad \dot\theta_s=0. \]
An equal increase in both activations raises \(S\) above \(b\), and the circuit drives it back down. A difference between the activations persists. For the illustrative choice \(b=20\), the states \((s_1,s_2)=(12,8)\) and \((8,12)\) both have the required total but store different values, \(4\) and \(-4\). The weights and transfer rule are as in the paper’s mutual-inhibition model; the calculation uses mean rates without random spikes. It does not imply that every inhibitory pair stores a continuous value. Both steady rates are positive only for \(|\theta_s|<b\).








Example: a disturbance can move sideways while it decays


Let \(x\) be a coordinate along a line of fixed states and \(y\) a disturbance away from it; take both as dimensionless activation coordinates. Consider \(\dot x=ay\), \(\dot y=-by\), with \(b>0\) and \(a\) and \(b\) in inverse seconds. The response matrix and two directions are
\[ K=\begin{pmatrix}0&a\\0&-b\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf u=\binom{1}{0},\qquad \mathbf v=\binom{1}{a/b}. \]
\(K\mathbf u=0\), \(\mathbf v^TK=0\), and \(\mathbf v^T\mathbf u=1\). Starting at \((x_0,y_0)\), the disturbance \(y\) decays as \(y_0e^{-bt}\), but it also changes \(x\). Integrating \(\dot x\) gives \(x(\infty)=x_0+(a/b)y_0\). Thus \(\mathbf v^T(x_0,y_0)^T\) gives the final position on the fixed line. A perpendicular projection would give \(x_0\) and miss that shift. The model is an illustration; it is not a fitted neural circuit.





Example: averaging independent spike counts


Suppose \(N\) independent cells each have a fixed rate \(r\) for a window of length \(h\), and their counts \(n_j\) are Poisson with mean and variance \(rh\). The average count \(\bar n=N^{-1}\sum_jn_j\) has mean \(rh\) and variance \(rh/N\). As \(N\) grows, the suitably centered and scaled average approaches a Gaussian distribution by the central limit theorem. No individual count has to be Gaussian. In a recurrent network, rates and inputs interact; applying a Gaussian approximation to their aggregate requires the paper’s additional weak-input assumptions. A single cell’s count over an interval made arbitrarily short remains a jump count.

title: Mathematical tools connect neural signals to the papers’ predictions
section: Fisher information measures how clearly spikes distinguish nearby values
text:
Fisher information measures how clearly spikes distinguish nearby values
Suppose a circuit currently represents an angle near \(30^\circ\). A receiving cell sees spikes rather than an angle label. If \(30^\circ\) and \(31^\circ\) produce almost identical probabilities of spike patterns, a short observation gives little evidence about which value is represented. If their spike probabilities differ strongly, the distinction is easier.
Fisher information, abbreviated FI, measures how sensitively the probabilities of observations change with a small change in the value being estimated. It describes local precision: the distinction between nearby values. A large FI at one angle does not resolve ambiguity between distant angles that happen to produce the same activity pattern. It is not a count of stored bits or of different memories.
A tuning curve \(\bar r_i(\theta)\) gives neuron \(i\)’s expected firing rate at represented value \(\theta\). The bar here denotes the model’s steady rate in the absence of noise. Its slope \(\bar r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\) measures sensitivity to a small value change. To turn sensitivity into a measure of precision, we must also specify how the spikes fluctuate.
For this calculation, hold \(\theta\) approximately fixed during a brief observation of length \(h\) seconds. Assume positive rates and independent Poisson spike counts conditional on that value. Under this spike model, count mean and variance are both \(h\bar r_i\). A small angle change \(\delta\theta\) changes the expected count by approximately \(h\bar r_i'\delta\theta\). The count sensitivity \(h\bar r_i'\) is the change in expected spike count per unit change in \(\theta\). The rate sensitivity \(\bar r_i'\) is the change in expected firing rate per unit change in \(\theta\). Let \(I_{h,i}(\theta)\) be the information supplied by cell \(i\) in that observation. Comparing the squared count sensitivity with the count variance gives
\[ I_{h,i}(\theta)=\frac{(h\bar r_i')^2}{h\bar r_i} =h\frac{(\bar r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}. \]
For this Poisson model the ratio is exactly the single-cell Fisher information. Let \(I_h(\theta)\) be the total information in the spike counts from all cells, and \(J(\theta)\) be that information per unit observation time. Independent contributions add:
\[ I_h(\theta)=hJ(\theta),\qquad J(\theta)=\sum_i\frac{(\bar r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}. \]
The internal Fisher information rate \(J\) is the information per unit observation time in these spikes about the circuit’s current represented value. “Internal” means that the value is maintained by the circuit; a present external stimulus is not needed. If \(\theta\) is measured in degrees, \(I_h\) has units \(\mathrm{degree}^{-2}\) and \(J\) has units \(\mathrm{degree}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). The paper uses this rate in Eq. 3.2
The numerator measures how strongly expected firing changes with the value. The denominator reflects Poisson spike variability: sensitivity must be judged relative to count noise. Increasing every rate also changes the slopes, so the denominator alone does not imply that higher firing always lowers information.


Example: equal firing rates can provide different angle precision


Take two illustrative cells, each firing at 20 spikes per second at the current angle. Their local slopes are 2 and 10 spikes per second per degree. In a 0.1-second observation, each has mean count 2 and count variance 2. Their expected count changes per degree are 0.2 and 1. Their information contributions are
\[ I_{h,1}=\frac{0.2^2}{2}=0.02\,\mathrm{degree}^{-2}, \qquad I_{h,2}=\frac{1^2}{2}=0.5\,\mathrm{degree}^{-2}. \]
The steeper response gives 25 times the local information despite the equal rates and count noise. If these two cells’ counts are independent at the given angle, their joint information is \(0.52\,\mathrm{degree}^{-2}\). These are chosen local response curves, not measured cells or a constructed recurrent network.


The derivation in Chapter 5 connects this count calculation to the likelihood and formal definition of FI. Shared spike fluctuations require a joint probability model; they cannot generally be handled by adding these single-cell terms.

title: Mathematical tools connect neural signals to the papers’ predictions
section: Information limits how slowly a neural memory can spread
text:
Information limits how slowly a neural memory can spread
The same uncertain spikes that tell a receiving cell about the value also renew activity inside the memory circuit. Synaptic effects fade, so the network must carry the value forward through those new events. This links the precision of the signals to the persistence of the memory.
One statistical benchmark concerns reading a value that is effectively fixed during observation. Let \(\hat\theta\) be an estimate computed from the spikes. An estimate is locally unbiased when its mean agrees with the true value to first order near the value under study. For smooth probability models satisfying the differentiation conditions explained in Chapter 5, the Cramér Rao bound gives a lower limit on the variance of such an estimate:
\[ \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\geq\frac{1}{I_h(\theta)} =\frac{1}{hJ(\theta)}. \]
The bound does not promise that every finite sample admits an estimate achieving it. Chapter 5 gives its derivation and conditions.
A second quantity describes what happens while the circuit stores the value. With zero mean drift and approximately constant coefficients, the displacement variance grows as \(\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\theta(0)]\simeq2Dt\). Here \(t\) is storage time and \(D\) is the diffusion coefficient: half the variance growth per unit time. The paper’s weights are tuned so that, without noise, a continuous range of represented values can persist as stationary activity patterns. Other activity disturbances relax toward those patterns. Burak and Fiete (2012) prove, for these networks in the weak-fluctuation approximation with a common synaptic time constant \(\tau\) and conditionally independent Poisson spike generation,
\[ \boxed{D(\theta)\geq\frac{1}{2\tau^2J(\theta)}.} \]
Low information in the spikes forces a high minimum rate of memory spreading. Larger information lowers that minimum; the network’s connections and dynamics determine whether it reaches the limit. The factor \(\tau^2\) makes the units consistent: if \(J\) is inverse angle squared per second, the bound has angle squared per second, as \(D\) must.3
The physical interpretation is that maintaining activity acts like repeatedly estimating the circuit’s own state from its spikes. This motivates the bound. It does not replace the dynamical proof: the state can move while spikes are collected, and the circuit’s feedback is itself noisy. Chapter 5 derives the bound from the network equations and states its equality conditions.
When a circuit represents several values, a single number cannot describe every possible change in them. The information-rate matrix \(J\) describes how well the spikes distinguish small changes in each direction in that space. For a change \(\delta\boldsymbol\theta\), the quadratic form \(\delta\boldsymbol\theta^TJ\delta\boldsymbol\theta\) measures its local distinguishability per unit observation time. For a brief window of length \(h\) in which the state is effectively fixed, multiplying by \(h\) gives a dimensionless measure. A direction that produces no change in the expected rates has zero information in this Poisson model. Individual diagonal entries can be positive even when a combination of values is invisible.


Example: two values can be visible separately but ambiguous together


Suppose both coordinates are measured in degrees and all modeled firing rates depend on them only through their sum. At a given state, take their information-rate matrix to be
\[ J=j\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad j>0, \quad [j]=\mathrm{degree}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}. \]
Changing either coordinate alone changes that sum. Increasing one by an amount and decreasing the other by the same amount leaves it unchanged. Indeed \(J(1,-1)^T=0\): this direction is invisible to those rates, and \(J\) has no ordinary inverse. The multi-coordinate bound in Chapter 5 uses \(J^{-1}\) only when the relevant directions are distinguishable. Its matrix inequality means that the corresponding scalar inequality holds for every linear combination of coordinates. For any matrix \(Q\) and vector \(\mathbf z\), \(\mathbf z^TQ^TQ\mathbf z=\lVert Q\mathbf z\rVert^2\ge0\); this is the nonnegative quantity used in that proof.


Finally, \(J\) measures information about the current value \(\theta(t)\), while diffusion describes its departure from the initial value \(\theta(0)\). The current angle can be easy to read even after it has wandered far from the angle originally supplied by the cue. The eye paper asks how such internal fluctuations could appear in recordings and physical movement. That requires a model of shared signals and of the muscles that filter them.

title: Mathematical tools connect neural signals to the papers’ predictions
section: Covariance tests which fluctuations are shared
text:
Covariance tests which fluctuations are shared
If one neuron’s spikes predict some eye movement, is the neuron passing on a common command or adding its own noise? Both can make its activity vary. Comparing the prediction with measured movement helps separate the part they share from fluctuations present in only one signal.
The covariance of \(X\) and \(Y\) measures how their deviations from their own means vary together. Positive covariance means that deviations tend to have the same sign. The correlation coefficient \(\rho\) scales that covariance by both signals’ standard deviations. Private noise in either signal can reduce this scaled measure even if the common source has not changed.


Mathematical definitions: covariance and correlation


\[ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb EX)(Y-\mathbb EY)],\qquad \rho=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}. \]
Here \(\sigma_X\) and \(\sigma_Y\) are the standard deviations of \(X\) and \(Y\). Covariance has the product of the signals’ units. Correlation is dimensionless and lies between \(-1\) and \(1\) when both variances are finite and positive.


Consider a teaching model, with all signals measured in degrees:
\[ X=aS+\eta_x,\qquad Y=bS+\eta_y. \]
Here \(S\) is a shared displacement command, \(X\) a cell’s displacement prediction, and \(Y\) measured displacement. The dimensionless gains \(a,b\) multiply the common command to give its contribution to each signal. This \(b\) is a gain, not the bias \(b_i\) in the memory model. The private contributions \(\eta_x,\eta_y\) vary independently of one another and of \(S\). Let \(\chi_Y\) be the fraction of the variance of measured displacement \(Y\) contributed by the shared command \(bS\). Thus only the shared command survives in the covariance:
\[ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=ab\operatorname{Var}(S),\qquad \chi_Y=\frac{b^2\operatorname{Var}(S)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =\frac ba\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}. \]
The last equality requires \(a\ne0\). Correlation alone does not give a shared variance fraction. That interpretation requires a model of the shared and private contributions and a calibrated gain. The gain ratio \(b/a\) converts the covariance to the shared contribution to \(Y\)’s variance. The eye study obtains an eye-position prediction from each cell’s spikes by inverting a movement-to-firing fit calibrated on larger movements. Its variance estimate assumes this calibration also applies during drift and gives the shared component the same displacement scale in prediction and measurement. A calibration error can change the inferred fraction. Private noise in \(X\) lowers correlation by increasing \(\sigma_X\), the standard deviation of \(X\), even when the shared command dominates \(Y\).


Example: a weak correlation can accompany mostly shared movement


Choose unit gains and independent contributions with variances \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=1\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\eta_x)=24\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(\eta_y)=0.25\), all in deg\(^2\). Then \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=25\), \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=1.25\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1\) deg\(^2\). Consequently
\[ \rho=\frac1{\sqrt{25\times1.25}}\simeq0.18, \qquad \chi_Y=\frac1{1.25}=0.80. \]
The prediction has large private noise, while measured movement has little. These chosen numbers illustrate the mechanism; they are not experimental estimates.


The 2022 analysis uses this logic for 350 ms displacements, assuming that calibration from larger movements still holds during drift. It also neglects a small covariance between the two private contributions, of order \(1/N_m\), where \(N_m\) is the number of motor neurons in its population model. These are assumptions to check, not consequences of the covariance definition.4 Many independent private contributions can average down in actual movement while remaining large in a single cell’s prediction. Shared fluctuations survive that averaging; the paper’s separate population bound tests whether independent motor noise alone could explain the observations.5

title: Mathematical tools connect neural signals to the papers’ predictions
section: Filtering changes how noise appears in eye motion
text:
Filtering changes how noise appears in eye motion
Muscles take time to respond to neural commands. Could their response turn rapidly changing noise into the smooth, continuing motion seen during fixation? The answer depends on whether the input merely fluctuates or accumulates changes.
A causal filter determines present output from present and past input. For a linear response that does not change with time, its impulse response \(h(u)\) gives the surviving response after a unit impulse \(u\) seconds ago. Here \(h\) is a function of time, not the observation duration \(h\) used in the spike-count calculation. The convolution adds these responses over the input history:
\[ E(t)=\int_0^\infty h(u)U(t-u)\,du. \]
For a simple response, \(h(u)=e^{-u/\tau}/\tau\) for \(u\ge0\). Input \(U\) and output \(E\) are angles in degrees; \(h\) has units s\(^{-1}\) and response time \(\tau\) is in seconds. This \(\tau\) describes the eye’s response. It is a different physical quantity from the synaptic decay time also denoted by \(\tau\) in the memory model, and their values need not be equal. Equivalently, \(\tau\dot E=U-E\): the command’s mismatch with current position drives velocity. This is a low pass filter: it suppresses rapid changes relative to slow changes.
White noise idealizes fluctuations uncorrelated at distinct times; in continuous time its intensity specifies variability of integrated input, rather than an ordinary finite pointwise variance. Passing it through this decaying filter produces a stationary position after initial transients: mean and variance stay constant and covariance depends only on time separation. Its mean squared displacement \(M(\ell)=\mathbb E[(E(t+\ell)-E(t))^2]\) approaches a plateau. The lag \(\ell\) is the separation between readings, not the clock time \(t\).6
A diffusing position command instead accumulates independent changes with displacement variance \(2D\ell\), where \(D\) has units deg\(^2\)/s. Filtering smooths its motion without stopping that accumulation. In the simple model below, short lag MSD grows as \(\ell^2\) and long lag MSD grows linearly. Position is not stationary; its increments have statistics independent of \(t\) once the initial velocity transient has decayed.


Example: the same filter separates fluctuating and accumulating input


For centered white input with \(\mathbb E[U(t)U(t')]=A\delta(t-t')\), intensity \(A\) has units deg\(^2\) s. The Dirac delta \(\delta\) is an instantaneous unit-area impulse; here it expresses the covariance concentrated at equal times. Write \(C_E(\ell)=\mathbb E[E(t)E(t+\ell)]\) for the covariance of the centered output at lag \(\ell\). Overlap of the two impulse responses gives
\[ C_E(\ell)=A\int_0^\infty h(u)h(u+\ell)\,du =\frac{A}{2\tau}e^{-\ell/\tau},\qquad M_{\rm white}(\ell)=2[C_E(0)-C_E(\ell)]. \]
Thus \(M_{\rm white}=(A/\tau)(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})\), approaching \(A/\tau\). For a Brownian position input with diffusivity \(D\), the same filter gives stationary velocity covariance \(C_v(s)=(D/\tau)e^{-|s|/\tau}\) after the initial velocity transient. Velocities at two times share some of the same past Brownian increments; their exponentially weighted overlap gives this covariance. The eye-timing derivation calculates the overlap. Integrating velocity over the displacement interval gives
\[ M_{\rm diffusion}(\ell)=2\int_0^\ell(\ell-s)C_v(s)\,ds =2D[\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})]. \]
Expansion at \(\ell\ll\tau\) gives \((D/\tau)\ell^2\): velocity barely changes across that interval. For \(\ell\gg\tau\), it approaches \(2D(\ell-\tau)\), with continuing growth. White input instead has linear short lag MSD in this single exponential example. The input and filter together determine short lag behavior.


These calculations use one response time as a teaching simplification. The 2022 model includes two muscle response times and visual feedback. Its conclusions concern the measured lag range; smooth movement alone does not identify diffusion, and short lag behavior also depends on measurement error. The eye-drift and timing chapters retain the full analysis.7

title: Mathematical tools connect neural signals to the papers’ predictions
section: Random fields describe a fixed spatial map
text:
Random fields describe a fixed spatial map
Why does a cell stay active over a stretch of track, rather than change its response independently at every position? Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025) describe the cell’s combined input as a spatial map \(h(x)\). This is a new use of \(h\), distinct from the eye filter’s impulse response. Nearby values depend on one another. A distribution of such maps can predict field sizes without predicting where a particular cell’s fields will occur.8
A random field assigns random values to positions; a Gaussian random field requires the values at every finite set of positions to form a jointly Gaussian vector. It is also called a Gaussian process, including when positions have more than one coordinate. A jointly Gaussian vector has Gaussian distributions for all its linear combinations. Gaussian distributions at individual positions alone do not impose this joint rule.
For jointly Gaussian variables, zero covariance implies independence. This special rule will let us separate a map’s height and slope in the crossing calculation. Zero covariance does not generally imply independence.


Example: zero covariance needs a joint Gaussian assumption


Let \(X\) and \(Z\) be independent standard Gaussian variables and set \(Y=\rho X+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,Z\), with \(-1<\rho<1\). The pair is jointly Gaussian and has covariance \(\rho\). At \(\rho=0\), \(Y=Z\) is independent of \(X\).
For a contrast, let \(Y=X^2-1\). Its covariance with \(X\) is \(\mathbb E[X^3-X]=0\), yet knowing \(X\) determines \(Y\). This pair is not jointly Gaussian. The Gaussian rule cannot be applied merely because two quantities have zero covariance.


Once a map is drawn, it stays fixed while the animal traverses it. Revisiting a position evaluates the same map value, rather than drawing a fresh input. The randomness describes possible maps, not changes with time during a visit.
The spatial covariance \(C(x,y)\) measures how deviations of input from its mean at two positions vary together across possible maps. Mean and covariance determine the Gaussian law. For a field, stationarity means that shifting all positions leaves its probability law unchanged. The mean is then a constant \(\mu\) and covariance depends on separation: \(C(x,y)=C(y-x)\). This does not make an individual map flat. For a field, isotropy means there is no preferred direction in its statistics. Stationarity alone does not require isotropy.
Normalize the input using its standard deviation \(\sigma_0\), and express the firing threshold \(h_{\mathrm{th}}\) in the same units:
\[ z(x)=\frac{h(x)-\mu}{\sigma_0},\qquad q=\frac{h_{\mathrm{th}}-\mu}{\sigma_0},\qquad F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+. \]
Here \([u]_+=\max(u,0)\) and \(a>0\) converts dimensionless input excess into firing rate. The excursion set \(A_q=\{x:z(x)>q\}\) is the active part of the map. Each connected piece is one field. Two peaks can belong to the same field if an active path connects them.
Field widths also depend on how quickly the input changes over distance. The paper’s correlation length compares typical input height with typical spatial slope. For a differentiable stationary map along a line, write \(z'=dz/dx\) for the spatial rate of change of the normalized input; \(C(0)\) is the input variance and \(C''(0)\) is the second derivative of spatial covariance with respect to separation, evaluated at zero. Then
\[ \ell_c=\sqrt{-\frac{C(0)}{C''(0)}},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(z')=\ell_c^{-2}. \]
It has distance units. For \(C(r)=\sigma_0^2e^{-r^2/(2\ell_c^2)}\), increasing \(\ell_c\) stretches the map. More generally it describes local covariance curvature, without fixing distant spatial relationships. In an isotropic map the same scale applies along every direction.9
Gaussian values do not guarantee smooth maps. Crossing calculations need differentiable sample maps and a nonsingular covariance matrix for height and slope: those variables must not obey an exact linear constraint. Peak calculations additionally need second derivatives and enough regularity for a local quadratic approximation. For example, the corner at zero in \(C(r)\propto e^{-|r|/b}\) prevents its use for the differentiable crossing calculation below.

title: Mathematical tools connect neural signals to the papers’ predictions
section: Crossings and peak geometry predict field counts and sizes
text:
Crossings and peak geometry predict field counts and sizes
On a track, a field begins where the input crosses upward through threshold. An upcrossing is a crossing of \(z=q\) with positive spatial slope. At a randomly selected position, conditioning on \(z=q\) asks about slopes at that height. For a continuous height, an exact value has probability zero. Where the height density is positive and regular, the conditional mean can be understood as the limit of means for a narrowing band around \(q\); equivalently it is calculated from the conditional density. It is not a ratio of probabilities of two zero-probability events.
To count crossings, imagine a narrow band of height \(2\varepsilon\) around the threshold. A curve crossing upward with slope \(v\) spends approximately \(2\varepsilon/v\) of track length in that band. A steeper crossing therefore contributes less occupied length, so multiplying by its slope corrects for that shorter stay. Averaging gives the mean number of upcrossings per unit distance: the input’s probability density at the threshold times its mean positive slope conditional on being there. Write \(\nu_+(q)\) for that number per unit distance, \(p_z(q)\) for the normalized input’s density at threshold \(q\), and \(z'=dz/dx\) for its slope along the track; \((z')_+=\max(z',0)\) keeps only positive slopes. The scale \(\ell_c\) is the correlation length defined above.
\[ \nu_+(q)=p_z(q)\,\mathbb E[(z')_+\mid z=q] =\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\ell_c}. \]
The Kac–Rice formula counts crossings by combining the input density at threshold with conditional slope. The displayed result applies to the smooth stationary Gaussian model. The result is exact under these assumptions at any threshold.10


Derivation: height and slope give the crossing density


In a narrow height band of width \(2\varepsilon\) around \(q\), an upward crossing with slope \(v\) occupies distance approximately \(2\varepsilon/v\). Weighting that distance by \(v/(2\varepsilon)\) counts one crossing. Averaging gives \(\nu_+=\int_0^\infty v\,p_{z,z'}(q,v)\,dv\).
Stationarity gives \(\operatorname{Cov}(z,z')=0\). Joint Gaussianity makes height and slope independent, with \(z\sim N(0,1)\) and \(z'\sim N(0,\ell_c^{-2})\). Thus \(p_z(q)=e^{-q^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\) and \(\mathbb E[(z')_+]=1/(\ell_c\sqrt{2\pi})\), giving the displayed result.


On a finite track of length \(L\), a field can already be active at the left endpoint. Counting all active components that intersect the track gives \(\mathbb E[N_L]=L\nu_+(q)+\Pr[z(0)>q]\). Discarding clipped boundary fields changes this convention. The later place field chapter follows this correction explicitly.
Counts do not determine the size distribution. At high positive \(q\), fields counted once each typically surround isolated high peaks. This sampling gives each field equal weight, rather than selecting fields by the amount of space they occupy. A smooth isotropic Gaussian field becomes approximately a downward quadratic near such a peak. If its height exceeds threshold by \(\epsilon\), the active radius grows as \(\sqrt{\epsilon}\) at fixed \(q\) and \(\ell_c\). Length, area and volume therefore grow as \(\epsilon^{d/2}\) in spatial dimension \(d\).11
The Hessian \(H\) is the matrix of second spatial derivatives of the input map. At a point with zero gradient, a small spatial displacement \(\mathbf x\) changes the normalized input by approximately \(\tfrac12\mathbf x^TH\mathbf x\). Its eigenvectors give principal spatial directions, and the eigenvalues give curvature in those directions. Negative curvature in every direction describes a nondegenerate local peak; mixed signs describe a saddle. A zero eigenvalue needs further analysis.


Example: curvature distinguishes a peak from a saddle


For dimensionless input \(z\) and coordinates \(x,y\) in metres, suppose near a critical point
\[ z(x,y)\simeq z(0,0)-(1\,\mathrm{m}^{-2})x^2-(4\,\mathrm{m}^{-2})y^2, \qquad H=\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&-8\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}. \]
Moving along either axis lowers the input, faster along \(y\), so the point is a peak. Reversing the sign of the \(y^2\) term changes the second eigenvalue to \(+8\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\): input rises along \(y\) but falls along \(x\), giving a saddle. In two dimensions, \(\det(-H)\) is positive for the peak and negative for this saddle. The place-size chapter applies the quadratic approximation to a random map; the topology chapter uses the signs to count changes in connected regions and holes.


The Gaussian model also supplies the statistics of the peak excess. For fields selected this way in the high threshold limit, \(U=q\epsilon\) approaches an exponential distribution of mean one: the chance that \(U>u\) approaches \(e^{-u}\) for \(u\ge0\). Combining that excess law with the geometry gives the size distribution.12
The geometric conversion changes the density as well as the units. A change of variables preserves the probability of each event while expressing it in a new variable. Let \(X\) be a random quantity and \(x\) a possible value. If \(U=g(X)\) for a smooth, strictly increasing function \(g\), a small interval \(dx\) around \(x\) corresponds to \(du=g'(x)dx\). Hence \(p_X(x)=p_U(g(x))g'(x)\): the derivative accounts for how the transformation stretches or compresses intervals. The density itself is not a probability at one exact value. For a decreasing transformation use the absolute derivative; a nonmonotonic transformation may have several branches.


Example: an exponential variable gives a Rayleigh-shaped density


Let \(U\) have density \(e^{-u}\) for \(u\ge0\) and define the dimensionless size \(X=\sqrt U\). The event \(X\le x\) is the same event as \(U\le x^2\), for \(x\ge0\). Therefore
\[ \Pr(X\le x)=1-e^{-x^2},\qquad p_X(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\Pr(X\le x)=2x e^{-x^2}. \]
The factor \(2x\) also follows from \(u=x^2\) and \(du/dx=2x\). Both expressions assign the same probability to corresponding intervals. The place-field calculation uses the same step with \(U=\beta s^{2/d}\); its random field size \(s\) has physical size units and \(\beta\) supplies the required units.


The result is three different limiting size laws. The 1D length law is a Rayleigh distribution: the chance of a length exceeding \(S\) is \(\exp(-\beta S^2)\) for a positive scale constant \(\beta\). The corresponding chance is \(\exp(-\beta S)\) for area in 2D, an exponential distribution, and \(\exp(-\beta S^{2/3})\) for volume in 3D. Because size \(S\) has units distance\(^d\), \(\beta\) has units inverse distance squared in every dimension; its geometric factor changes with dimension. Thus the same spatial mechanism can give different length, area and volume histograms.


Example: the same peak excess gives different size laws


For a stationary isotropic Gaussian field, conditioning on height \(b\) gives mean second derivative \(-b/\ell_c^2\) along each unit direction, with fluctuations that do not grow with \(b\). Thus typical high peaks concentrate around a quadratic shape. Here \(x\) is displacement from the peak, taken as the origin; \(\epsilon\) is the peak height above threshold \(q\); \(\ell_c\) is the correlation length; and \(r_*\) is the approximate radius where input falls back to threshold:
\[ z(x)-q\simeq\epsilon-\frac{q\|x\|^2}{2\ell_c^2},\qquad r_*\simeq\ell_c\sqrt{2\epsilon/q}. \]
For typical high fields the scaled excess \(U=q\epsilon\) approaches an exponential distribution of mean one. Writing size as \(s=v_dr_*^d\), with \(v_1=2\), \(v_2=\pi\), \(v_3=4\pi/3\), converts the size event \(s>S\) into \(U>\beta S^{2/d}\). Therefore
\[ \Pr(s>S)\simeq\exp[-\beta S^{2/d}],\qquad \beta=\frac{q^2}{2\ell_c^2v_d^{2/d}}. \]
Geometry changes the distribution even though the scaled peak excess has the same limiting law.


These size laws are high threshold limits, not exact laws at finite \(q\). At lower thresholds fields can have several peaks or irregular shapes. The detailed chapter checks the approximation against finite threshold calculations.

text:
Table 1: Choose the physical question before choosing an equation.





Question and system
Reasoning chain
What the result establishes




Memory: Burak and Fiete (2012). A modeled recurrent neural circuit retains a continuous value after its cue ends.
Spikes renew synaptic activity → fixed connections sustain a family of activity patterns → some noise survives relaxation as a value change → Fisher information constrains how small that change can be.
A lower bound links memory diffusion to spike precision and synaptic decay. Simulated networks test the theory; this paper does not fit animal memory errors.


Eye drift: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022). Motor-neuron spikes and horizontal fixation movements were recorded in macaque monkeys.
Calibrate spikes into predicted displacement → compare predicted and measured movement → separate shared variance from private noise → test how muscles filter candidate noise sources.
The recordings support a large shared contribution; the model explains how a diffusing command can produce smooth motion. They do not uniquely locate the source in one circuit.


Place fields: Mainali et al. (2025). Spatial firing patterns in rodents and bats are compared with a statistical model.
Draw a correlated Gaussian spatial map → apply a threshold → count crossings and active regions → use high-peak geometry for sizes → compare dimension, slices and holes.
One model predicts several spatial statistics. Crossing formulas can be exact within the Gaussian model; the universal size laws require a high-threshold limit.










Firing rate: \(r_i\) in the memory model, \(f\) or \(\lambda\) in the eye model, and \(F(x)\) in the place-field model. All are expected spike counts per unit time, in spikes/s or Hz.
Coordinate: \(\theta\) labels the current value represented by the memory circuit; \(E\) is the true physical eye angle in degrees; \(x,y\) are physical positions in the place-field model, scalar on a track or vectors in space. The memory coordinate has the chosen model’s units, for example radians; place-field positions have distance units. Each coordinate keeps the physical meaning and units of its own model.
Indices and counts: \(i,j\) label cells in neural weight and rate arrays; E1 instead uses \(j\) to label spikes, and P11 uses \(j\) for geometric dimension. \(N\) is a dimensionless count: neurons in M1–M16 and E7, but fields in P5 and P12. \(N_m\) specifically counts motor neurons.
Time and response times: time intervals and decay times have seconds as units. \(t\) is time in the temporal models; \(\tau\), \(\tau_s\), \(\tau_f\) and \(\tau_\pm\) label particular response or decay times. Their biological roles differ and are specified locally. P9 instead uses \(t\) as a coordinate along a spatial line.
Diffusion coefficient: \(D\) in the 2012 and 2022 models has units of the evolving coordinate squared per second. The unfiltered diffusing coordinate has displacement variance \(2Dt\) for constant \(D\) without drift or boundaries; a filtered eye output need not have that MSD at short lags. Here \(d\), used for spatial dimension, is a different quantity.
Information rate: \(J\), where used in the memory model and the eye scaling estimate, is information per second about the represented coordinate, in inverse coordinate units squared per second. The main argument uses scalar \(D,J\); M5 and M11 use matrices.
Estimates and arrays: a hat marks an estimate or prediction, as in \(\hat\theta\) or \(\widehat E\); the row identifies its observations. Bold symbols denote vectors or matrices, and a superscript \(T\) transposes an array.



\(r\): a firing rate in the memory model; the velocity coefficient in the eye calibration equation E1. Eye firing rates there use \(f\) or \(\lambda\).
\(W\): connection weights in the memory model, a Brownian process in E6, and random input weights \(W_i\) in P2.
\(h\): a counting-window duration in memory calculations, an eye-response kernel \(h(u)\), or the spatial input map \(h(x)\).
\(C\): shared displacement in E3; \(C_E\) is eye-position covariance; \(C(x,y)\) is spatial input covariance. Covariance units are the product of the input variables’ units, while displacement has angle units.
\(s\): synaptic activation \(s_i\), a time lag or integration time in some temporal calculations, or field size in the place-field model.
\(\chi\): the shared movement-variance fraction in E3; \(\chi_d\) is the signed Euler-characteristic count in P11–P12.
\(\sigma\) and \(V\): the place-field chapters use \(\sigma\) for distance scale \(\ell_c\), whereas \(\sigma_0\) is input standard deviation and the eye model’s \(\sigma_m\) is measurement-error standard deviation. \(V\) denotes error variance in memory rows, but environment size in P12.
