title: Exam review: connect mechanisms, measurements and results
section: Feedback sustains activity while noisy spikes move the remembered value
text:
Feedback sustains activity while noisy spikes move the remembered value
Burak and Fiete (2012): continuous memory in a modeled neural circuit. The stored value is a coordinate of a persistent neural activity pattern. Fixed recurrent connections sustain that pattern. Random spikes disturb it; the circuit removes some disturbances, while others leave the value displaced. The derivation follows that surviving displacement and asks how its variance relates to how clearly the spikes distinguish nearby values.
Recall the chain: feedback mechanism (M1) → surviving displacement (M3) → spike information (M7) → diffusion bound and equality (M8–M9) → readout (M13). Long-delay storage error and total recall error are M6 and M14 in the additional results below.
Primes on rate and input tuning curves denote derivatives with respect to the represented value. In M9, \(\phi'\) differentiates the transfer function with respect to its input. The shared key below defines recurring symbols; rows list only additions and exceptions. Diffusion and Fisher information are scalars in the main argument; M5 gives their matrix generalization for several stored coordinates.

Memory-specific additions. Use the common notation for rates, coordinates, time units, \(D\) and \(J\). These additions apply to both memory tables; a row states any further change or extra symbol.

\(W_{ij}\) sends activation from cell \(j\) to receiver \(i\).
\(\Theta\): the initial represented value. \(h\): short counting window; \(T\): storage delay; \(L\): observation duration after the recall cue. The source writes readout duration as \(\Delta T\).
\(s_i\): outgoing activation of cell \(i\), dimensionless with one unit added per spike. Bars in \(\bar s_i\) and \(\bar r_i\) denote noise-free steady values.
\(\bar r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\): tuning slope, in rate units per coordinate unit.
\(g_i\): total input; \(b_i\): constant bias (same input units). \(W\) is an \(N\times N\) matrix in input units per activation unit. \(\phi(g)\) converts input into rate; \(\phi'\) differentiates with respect to input.
\(\tau\): synaptic activation decay time.
\(K\): \(N\times N\) linear response matrix (s\(^{-1}\)). \(\mathbf u=\partial\bar{\mathbf s}/\partial\theta\): tangent \(N\)-vector (activation/coordinate). \(\mathbf v\): normalized left zero vector; \(v_i\) measures the retained coordinate shift per activation unit from cell \(i\).
\(V\) with a subscript denotes error variance (coordinate units squared); the subscript identifies the estimate being assessed.

The state is effectively fixed during this short count calculation, and finite-sample attainment is not guaranteed.

The same noisy spikes convey the value and renew the activity carrying it. At fixed \(J\) and synaptic time \(\tau\), tuning the network cannot reduce diffusion below this bound in the stated model. It assumes the tuned continuous family, weak independent conditional spike noise, a common decay time and no external anchoring signal.

The retained effect of each cell’s spike noise must match the information its spikes provide. Suitable symmetric exponential networks reach the lower bound under the same tuned-model assumptions. M13. Diffusion-aware readout · central\(V_{\rm ideal}(L)=\sqrt{\dfrac{2D}{J}}\coth(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L)\)\(V_{\rm ideal}(\infty)=\sqrt{2D/J}\)\(L^*=1/\sqrt{2DJ}\le\tau\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(V_{\rm ideal}(L)\): variance of error in reading the cue-time state; \(V_{\rm ideal}(\infty)\) is its long-observation limit.• \(L^*=1/\sqrt{2DJ}\): characteristic approach time (s), not a finite optimum.• \(P=1/V_{\rm ideal}\): Gaussian precision, in inverse coordinate units squared.• \(\coth z=(e^{2z}+1)/(e^{2z}-1)\); the argument here is dimensionless.• \(D,J\) are held locally constant in this Gaussian readout calculation.
Accounting for motion makes more observation keep helping, toward a finite limit. \(L^*\) is a characteristic saturation time, not a hard deadline. This is an ideal observer within the local Gaussian readout model; it does not show a biological decoder implementing the rule.

Paper location: Open cited PDF page. SI, IV. Internal Fisher Information, Eq. S43, PDF p. 9, displays the joint product-Poisson likelihood with observation duration \(\delta t\) and counts \(n_i\). Main Eq. 9, PDF p. 5, states the Poisson spike model. Equal mean and variance and the rare-event derivation are worked out in the guide, not separately displayed source results.Guide location: Chapter 1, §1.4, A variable spike count at a fixed rate.Origin: Paper count model with guide aliases \(K_i,h,\lambda_i\); the count moments and elementary derivation are exact properties of that model when the state is held fixed.Derivation route: Independent rare events in short subdivisions give the Poisson count law over a duration \(h\). Its first two moments give equal count mean and variance. Here \(\bar r_i\) is the steady tuning curve at value \(\theta\).


M4. Symmetric connections · supporting\(2D=\dfrac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2}{\tau^2(\sum_i\bar r_i' g_i')^2}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(g_i\) is evaluated at a steady state here; \(g_i'=dg_i/d\theta\) has input units per coordinate unit.• \(W_{ij}=W_{ji}\) is pairwise connection symmetry. Primes are first derivatives.
For this special connectivity, tuning and input slopes determine diffusion without separately solving for \(\mathbf v\). The numerator contains squared input slopes, as in the published correction. The general projection formula does not require symmetric weights.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. SI, II. The Coefficient of Diffusion, Eqs. S16-S18, PDF p. 4: S18 displays the squared input slope in the numerator and the full formula. Main Eq. 2, PDF p. 2, omits that square in the supplied Early Edition PDF. The guide links the 2017 author correction for main Eq. 2.Guide location: Chapter 3, §3.4, Symmetric weights express diffusion through tuning curves.Origin: Corrected source expression, directly supported by SI S18. It uses symmetric weights, the tuned continuous family and the same leading weak-noise assumptions.Derivation route: If \(W_{ij}=W_{ji}\), differentiate the fixed-state equations to find \(v_i\propto g_i'\), then normalize by \(\mathbf v^T\mathbf u=1\). Primes mean derivatives with respect to memory value \(\theta\).


M5. More than one stored coordinate · supporting\(2D_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i v_i^\alpha\bar r_i v_i^\beta\)\(J_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i(\partial_\alpha\bar r_i)(\partial_\beta\bar r_i)/\bar r_i\)\(2D\succeq\tau^{-2}J^{-1}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(m\): number of stored coordinates; \(\boldsymbol\theta\) is an \(m\)-vector. Indices \(\alpha,\beta=1,\ldots,m\) label coordinates.• \(\mathbf u^\beta=\partial\bar{\mathbf s}/\partial\theta_\beta\) and \(\mathbf v^\alpha\): matching right and left \(N\)-vectors, with activation/coordinate and coordinate/activation units.• \(\partial_\alpha\bar r_i\): rate slope in coordinate \(\alpha\); \(\delta_{\alpha\beta}\) is one for equal indices and zero otherwise.• Here \(D,J\) are \(m\times m\) matrices. \(D_{\alpha\beta}\) has coordinate-\(\alpha\) times coordinate-\(\beta\)/s units; \(J_{\alpha\beta}\) has inverse coordinate-\(\alpha\) times inverse coordinate-\(\beta\)/s units. \(J\) must be invertible.• \(A\succeq B\) means \(A-B\) has a nonnegative quadratic form in every direction.
The diagonal entries give spreading in each coordinate. Off-diagonal entries give coupled changes in two stored coordinates, even when the elementary spike noises are independent. The weak-noise and local-state assumptions remain. The matrix inequality means every linear combination of coordinate changes obeys its variance bound, including coupled directions.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. SI: S21 defines \(D\) on PDF p. 5; S22-S24 give tangents, normalization and the displayed diffusion tensor on p. 6. S44 displays the information matrix on p. 10. S52 displays the matrix bound on p. 11; S53-S56 prove it on p. 12. Information matrix; matrix bound; proof.Guide location: Chapter 3, §3.3, Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient; Chapter 5, §5.2, Spike information sets a lower bound on memory diffusion, matrix derivation.Origin: Paper diffusion and information matrices and paper matrix inequality; guide proof uses an equivalent nonnegative residual matrix. The ordinary inverse needs nonsingular \(J\).Derivation route: Choose a tangent for each stored coordinate and left vectors satisfying \(\sum_i v_i^\alpha u_i^\beta=\delta_{\alpha\beta}\). Project the same spike noise onto each pair of coordinates. Applying the same normalization in matrix form gives the bound when the information matrix \(J\) is invertible.


M6. Accumulated storage error · supporting\(\partial_t p=\partial_\theta^2[D(\theta)p]\)\(\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\Theta]=2Dt\)\(p(\theta,t)=\dfrac{e^{-(\theta-\Theta)^2/(4Dt)}}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(p(\theta,t)\): density across trials, in inverse coordinate units. The Gaussian and \(2Dt\) formulas use constant \(D\).• \(\mathbb E[D(\theta)]\): trial-averaged diffusion coefficient.• For the circle example the coordinate is an angle in radians and error is wrapped to \([-\pi,\pi)\); its limiting MSD is \(\pi^2/3\) rad\(^2\).
The remembered value spreads even while neural activity persists. With state-dependent \(D\), variance instead grows at rate \(2\mathbb E[D(\theta)]\). Boundaries, angular wrapping and systematic drift require their own treatment; a linear MSD need not continue forever. For constant angular diffusion on a circle, wrapped error eventually becomes uniform and its MSD tends to \(\pi^2/3\) in radian-squared units; the plateau does not mean noise stopped.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. SI, III. Diffusive Dynamics Along the Attractor: S28-S30, PDF p. 7, give the density equation, point initial condition and Gaussian with variance \(2Dt\). S31 (p. 7) and S32 (p. 8) give the wrapped density and angular-error moment. The limit \(\pi^2/3\) and the moment-rate identity \(d\operatorname{Var}/dt=2\mathbb E[D]\) are exact guide deductions under the displayed diffusion model and suitable boundary conditions, not separately displayed source formulas.Guide location: Chapter 4, §4.1, Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion.Origin: Paper diffusion equation and constant-\(D\) line solution; guide derives the circle’s uniform-error limit and the general variance-rate identity. These assume zero systematic drift and the appropriate boundary rules.Derivation route: Combine small Itô diffusion increments, with no systematic drift, into a probability evolution equation. The Gaussian and \(2Dt\) formulas additionally require constant \(D\), a point initial value \(\Theta\) and an unbounded coordinate.


M10. Controlled changes of circuit parameters · supporting\(J\propto N,\quad D\propto N^{-1}\)\(J\mapsto cJ,\quad D\mapsto D/c\)\(D\propto\tau^{-2}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(c>0\): dimensionless multiplier of each rate tuning curve and its slope; distinct from preferred-value vector \(\mathbf c\) in M11.• Each proportionality describes the controlled change specified in the derivation, with the other properties kept fixed.
More comparable neurons can reduce independent noise, and longer synaptic effects can reduce the lasting shift per spike. The stated rate-to-diffusion scaling needs an equality-achieving network or preserved tuning/input geometry. Changing rate or decay time without the corresponding circuit adjustment need not preserve the stored-state family.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Main, Diffusive Drift due to Ongoing Neural Noise, paragraph following Eq. 2, PDF p. 2, states the network-size, firing-rate and decay-time comparisons. SI I, PDF pp. 1-2, gives population replication and \(1/N\) weight scaling, including S6 for a ring. The explicit proportionality powers and \(J\mapsto cJ\), \(D\mapsto D/c\) are guide algebra from corrected Eq. 2 and Eq. 3 under the listed constraints, not a separately displayed source equation.Guide location: Chapter 5, §5.3, Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed.Origin: Guide-derived scaling relationships supporting paper comparisons. The rate-to-diffusion scaling needs equality in the bound or preserved tuning/input geometry; changing \(\tau\) here holds rate tuning fixed by adjusting the circuit.Derivation route: Replicate a population of \(N\) neurons with the same tuning distribution and weights scaled as \(1/N\). Count the sums in the symmetric diffusion formula. A uniform rate multiplier \(c>0\) also multiplies tuning slopes. For the time comparison, hold rate tuning and its input relation fixed.


M11. Tuning width depends on dimension · supporting\(J_{\alpha\alpha}\propto\rho a w^{d-2}\)\(D_{\alpha\alpha}\propto w^{2-d}\quad\text{at equality}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(d\): number of stored spatial coordinates; \(\alpha\) labels one of them. Here \(D,J\) are \(d\times d\) matrices with the coordinate-wise units given in M5.• \(\boldsymbol\theta,\mathbf c\): represented and preferred positions, both \(d\)-vectors in coordinate units. \(\mathbf c\) is not multiplier \(c\) in M10.• \(w>0\): tuning width (coordinate units).• \(a\): fixed peak rate (spikes/s); \(f\): fixed dimensionless radial tuning shape, whose argument \((\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w\) is dimensionless.• \(\rho\): preferred-position density, in coordinate\(^{-d}\) units.
Under these fixed resources, narrower tuning helps in one dimension and broader tuning helps in three; the leading width power vanishes in two. The diffusion statement additionally assumes an equality-achieving network. Holding total spike rate fixed would be a different comparison. This is the guide’s reconstruction of the paper’s width argument.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Main, discussion of internal information and tuning width, PDF p. 4, states that narrower curves help in 1D and broader curves in 3D and cites sensory coding work (ref. 31). The displayed \(w^{d-2}\) and \(w^{2-d}\) power laws and the integral derivation are guide reconstructions under fixed peak rate, uniform center density, radial shape and equality in the matrix bound. They are not formulas displayed in this paper.Guide location: Chapter 5, §5.3, Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed, tuning-width integral.Origin: Guide-derived scaling laws explaining a paper argument under explicit resource and symmetry assumptions; the diffusion power additionally assumes a circuit that attains the information bound.Derivation route: Use tuning \(a f[(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w]\) with uniform preferred-value density \(\rho\), fixed peak rate \(a\), radial shape \(f\) and width \(w\). The information integral gains \(w^d\) from recruited cells and \(w^{-2}\) from squared slopes.


M12. Equal-weight readout · supporting\(V_{\rm naive}(L)=\dfrac1{JL}+\dfrac{2DL}{3}\)\(L_{\rm naive}^*=\sqrt{\dfrac3{2DJ}}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(V_{\rm naive}(L)\): error variance for the cue-time state under equal observation weights; \(L_{\rm naive}^*\) minimizes it (s).• In covariance \(2D\min(t,s)\), both \(t\) and \(s\) are elapsed observation times (s); this \(s\) is not activation.• \(D,J\) are held locally constant, and state-motion and observation noises are separate in the Gaussian readout model.
Collecting more spikes first helps, then hurts because later spikes represent a state that has moved further from the cue state. \(V\) is readout error variance under the local Gaussian observation model, with constant \(D,J\) and separate state-motion and observation noise.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. SI VI, Naive estimator, S76-S79, PDF p. 15, gives the equal-weight estimator, Brownian time covariance and displayed variance. S80 on p. 15 gives the optimal duration; S81 on p. 16 gives its minimum variance. The double covariance integral in the guide exposes the cross-time terms absent from the printed S77 sum-of-squares line.Guide location: Chapter 6, §6.2, Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long.Origin: Paper Gaussian-readout result; guide derives S79 explicitly through the covariance integral. This variance concerns reading the cue state, before adding storage error.Derivation route: Average observations for duration \(L\) after the readout cue. Count noise averages to \(1/(JL)\); integrating Brownian covariance \(2D\min(t,s)\) over the observation square gives \(2DL/3\). Differentiate to find the optimum.


M14. Storage plus partial readout · supporting\(V_{\rm recall}=2DT+V_{\rm readout}\)\(J_{\rm obs}=\alpha J\)\(L_{\rm obs}^*=L^*/\sqrt\alpha\)\(V_{\rm ideal,obs}(\infty)=\sqrt{2D/(\alpha J)}\)\(V_{\rm recall}(T,L)\ge2DT+\sqrt{2D/J}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(0<\alpha\le1\): probability of observing each spike independently, or a verified information fraction; distinct from the coordinate index in M5.• \(J_{\rm obs}\): observed information rate, with the same units as \(J\).• \(L^*\) and \(L_{\rm obs}^*\): full- and partial-access characteristic readout times (s).• \(V_{\rm recall}\): error variance about the original value; \(V_{\rm readout}\): error variance in reading the cue-time state.• \(V_{\rm ideal,obs}(\infty)\): ideal partial-access limiting readout variance. The final displayed lower bound is the full-access benchmark, \(\alpha=1\).
Missing spikes reduces readout information while the full circuit keeps diffusing at the same \(D\). Reading becomes slower and less precise. A selected fraction of neurons need not carry the same fraction of information; \(\alpha J\) follows from random spike thinning or a verified information fraction. With full spike access, the ideal total-error limit is \(2DT+\sqrt{2D/J}\); it equals \(2D(T+\tau)\) only at equality in the information bound. Why printed Eq. 6 needs this qualification.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. SI VI, S57, PDF p. 12, gives storage-plus-readout error addition. The Incomplete readout paragraph, S82 and Fig. S2, PDF p. 16, replace \(J\) by \(\alpha J\) and give the time/variance factors. The source’s S83 on p. 16 and main Eq. 6 on p. 4 print a stronger lower bound whose direction does not follow. The row’s full-access \(2DT+\sqrt{2D/J}\) lower limit is guide algebra from S57 and S75, not a displayed corrected source equation. Error addition; finite ideal variance.Guide location: Chapter 6, §6.1, Storage loss and readout error add under specific assumptions; §6.4, Limited access can make observation slower; §6.6, Readout saturates, and one printed error bound needs qualification.Origin: Paper error decomposition and partial-access relationships, plus guide derivation of the full-access total-error bound. Error addition needs local unbiasedness and independent future noise. \(2D(T+\tau)\) is this asymptotic expression only when the information-diffusion bound is attained, not a general lower bound.Derivation route: Storage for delay \(T\) adds independent error when readout is locally unbiased and future noise is independent of storage history. Independently retain each spike with probability \(\alpha\); substitute the thinned rates into the FI formula.


M15. A rate response time changes the bound · extension\(\tau_m\dot r_i=-r_i+\phi(g_i)\)\(D\ge\dfrac{1}{2(\tau+\tau_m)^2J}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(\tau_m\): firing-rate response time (s), distinct from synaptic decay \(\tau\).• \(\dot r_i\): time derivative of rate (spikes/s\(^2\)); \(\phi(g_i)\) is the target rate at the present input.
Slower intrinsic rate response can also carry memory between spikes. The two times add for this specified two-stage model, with the same Poisson drive and stable transverse directions. Replacing \(\tau\) by a sum of arbitrary biological response times is not justified.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. SI VII, More than one time constant, S84, PDF p. 17, displays the rate equation; S85-S90 on pp. 17-18 develops the linear modes; S91-S92 on p. 18 display diffusion and its bound. Source S85 prints a positive rate-decay block, although differentiating S84 gives the negative block used in the guide. Rate model.Guide location: Chapter 6, §6.5, Time scales and noise laws change the bound and its equality condition, two-time-constant derivation.Origin: Paper two-stage extension for symmetric weights; the displayed bound is S92 divided by two. The guide repairs the sign of the intermediate linear rate-decay block from the source’s own rate equation.Derivation route: Keep synaptic activation decay \(\tau\) and add a firing-rate response time \(\tau_m\). Linearize both sets of variables and normalize the left mode against their combined tangent. In the symmetric model the diffusion denominator gains \((\tau+\tau_m)^2\) in place of \(\tau^2\).


M16. Noise law changes the equality condition · extension\(J=\sum_i(\bar r_i')^2/q_n\)\(2D=q_n\sum_i v_i^2\)\(2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(q_n>0\): common additive Gaussian noise intensity, activation units squared/s, or s\(^{-1}\) with unit-spike activation. A noise increment has variance \(q_n\,dt\); the rate average over \(h\) has noise variance \(q_n/h\) (s\(^{-2}\)).• Here \(J\) is information per second in Gaussian rate observations. The coordinate, projection and time units are unchanged.• This \(q_n\) is unrelated to the dimensionless place-field threshold \(q\).
The information–diffusion relation survives this matched noise model, but equality now needs \(v_i\propto\bar r_i'\). In the symmetric model a linear transfer rule is sufficient. An optimal transfer rule therefore depends on how neurons fluctuate. The noise intensity \(q_n\) is unrelated to the place-field threshold \(q\).
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. SI VII, White Gaussian noise, S93-S95, PDF p. 19, changes the noise law and states that a linear transfer rule attains equality. The row’s explicit \(q_n\) normalization and the matched formulas for \(J\) and \(D\) are guide reconstructions, not equations printed in that exact form: the supplied S94-S95 omit noise/time factors. The guide chapter writes this noise strength as \(q\); the table renames it \(q_n\) to avoid the spatial-threshold alias.Guide location: Chapter 6, §6.5, Time scales and noise laws change the bound and its equality condition, Gaussian-noise reconstruction.Origin: Guide-derived matched Gaussian-noise formulas explaining the paper extension while keeping units explicit. The information-diffusion inequality follows by the same normalized projection proof; symmetric linear transfer is a sufficient equality class.Derivation route: Replace Poisson fluctuations by independent additive Gaussian noise with constant intensity \(q_n>0\); a rate observation averaged for \(h\) has noise variance \(q_n/h\). Repeat the likelihood and projection calculations with this same noise law.











Recall check: why can persistent activity still lose the original value?


The circuit can restore the shape of its activity pattern without restoring its original coordinate along the family of patterns. The left projection weights measure the displacement that remains. Fisher information concerns reading the present value from spikes; diffusion concerns how that present value has departed from the original cue. A decoder can therefore read the present state precisely while the original memory is already inaccurate.

title: Exam review: connect mechanisms, measurements and results
section: Covariance identifies a shared component of eye movement
text:
Covariance identifies a shared component of eye movement
Ben-Shushan et al. (2022): horizontal eye drift during fixation in macaque monkeys. A recorded motor neuron’s spikes are converted into a prediction in degrees. Comparing that prediction with actual displacement asks how much variation they share. A second argument asks whether independent motor noise, after muscle filtering, could explain the measured mean squared displacement (MSD).
Recall the chain: calibrate the spike-to-movement filter (E1) → estimate the shared variance fraction (E3) → compare filtered stationary noise with an accumulating command (E5–E6). E6 is a simplified guide calculation, not the paper’s full circuit model. The separate population bound (E2) challenges independent motor noise alone; it is in the additional results below.
The time lag in an MSD is the separation between two readings. The eye response time in E6 is different from the synaptic decay time in the 2012 theory. Measurement correction and parameter scaling remain available below the core argument.

Eye-specific additions. Use the common notation for firing rates, angle units, time, \(D\) and estimate hats. These additions apply to both eye tables; filter normalization and particular response times are specified in their rows.

\(\ell\): time separation between two readings; \(u\): integration lag. A dot differentiates with respect to time.
\(\widehat E\): angle predicted from spikes; \(E_{\rm obs}\): measured angle.
\(M(\ell)=\mathbb E[(E(t+\ell)-E(t))^2]\): mean squared displacement (MSD), in degrees\(^2\). \(C_E(\ell)\): covariance of centered eye position at lag \(\ell\), also in degrees\(^2\).
\(h\): causal response kernel. Its units depend on the input normalization in E1 or E5; it is not the spatial input map in the place-field model.
\(R_i\): correlation between cell \(i\)’s displacement prediction and measured displacement over the same 350 ms intervals, dimensionless. \(R\) omits the cell index.





Table 4: Covariance identifies a shared component of eye movement. Core argument.





formula and symbols
decoding
location and derivation




E1. From spikes to eye position · method\(m\ddot x+r\dot x+kx=f\)\(h_0(u)=\dfrac{\tau_+\tau_-}{m(\tau_+-\tau_-)}(e^{-u/\tau_+}-e^{-u/\tau_-}),\ u>0\)\(\widehat E(t)=E_T+\sum_j h(t-t_j)\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(f\): firing rate (spikes/s); \(x=E-E_T\): position offset from fitted threshold angle \(E_T\) (degrees).• \(k\): position coefficient (spikes/(s degree)); \(r\): velocity coefficient (spikes/degree), not firing rate; \(m\): acceleration coefficient (spikes s/degree).• \(t_j\): time of spike \(j\); \(\Delta t\): fitted neural lead (both s); \(p\): Laplace frequency (s\(^{-1}\)).• \(\tau_+,\tau_-\): distinct positive slow and fast response times (s).• \(h_0,h\): causal position responses before and after the delay, in degrees/spike; each vanishes before its effective input.
Each recorded spike at \(t_j\) contributes a calibrated position response in degrees. Coefficients \(k,r,m\) couple firing to position, velocity and acceleration; \(r\) here is not a firing rate. The two distinct positive decay times describe the fitted response. This predicts movement from one cell, rather than claiming that one cell controls the eye by itself.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main Methods ‘OMN firing rate estimators’ Eqs. 2–3 and ‘Model inversion’ Eqs. 4–7, PDF p. 9. Factoring the polynomial and checking impulse weights are expanded in the guide.Guide location: Chapter 7, section 7.4, A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell’s spikesOrigin: Paper calibration method; guide expands the factorization, normalization, and physical units.Derivation route: Invert the fitted rate–movement equation for \(x=E-E_T\). Factor \(mp^2+rp+k=m(p+1/\tau_+)(p+1/\tau_-)\); each root supplies a decay. Set \(h_0=0\) for \(u<0\) and restore the fitted delay by \(h(u)=h_0(u-\Delta t)\).


E3. Shared movement fraction · central\(X=C+\epsilon,\quad Y=C+\eta\)\(\chi\simeq\dfrac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}\)\(\chi\simeq R\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)/\operatorname{Var}(Y)}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(X,Y\): spike-predicted and measured displacements over 350 ms (degrees).• \(C\): shared upstream displacement; \(\epsilon\): private prediction error; \(\eta\): other measured-displacement contributions (all degrees). Here \(C\) is not a covariance function.• \(\chi=\operatorname{Var}(C)/\operatorname{Var}(Y)\): dimensionless shared fraction; \(\widehat\chi\) is its weighted estimate.• The reported \(0.82\pm0.07\) uses propagated weighted estimation error, not between-animal spread.
Weak single-cell correlation can coexist with a large common contribution to movement. The paper reports \(\widehat\chi=0.82\pm0.07\) at 350 ms. This requires transferable gain calibration and nearly uncorrelated private contributions; the recorded cell creates a neglected order-\(1/N_m\) covariance. Locating the shared source upstream also uses the biological independence premise.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main Methods ‘Estimated contribution of central source to measured eye position’, Eqs. 11–15 and weighted estimation Eqs. 16–17, PDF p. 10; measured result Fig. 2e–f, PDF p. 4.Guide location: Chapter 7, section 7.6, Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement varianceOrigin: Paper central estimate under unit calibration gain and nearly uncorrelated contributions; not a unique circuit identification.Derivation route: \(X\) is spike-predicted displacement and \(Y\) is measured displacement, both calibrated in degrees. Expand their covariance: it retains the shared component variance \(\operatorname{Var}(C)\) when the other covariances are negligible.


E5. Filtered white noise · supporting\(C_E(\ell)=A\int_0^\infty h(u)h(u+\ell)\,du\)\(M(\ell)=2[C_E(0)-C_E(\ell)]\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(\xi\): white input in a chosen input unit \(U\); \(A\) is its intensity, defined by \(\mathbb E[\xi(t)\xi(t')]=A\delta(t-t')\), with units \(U^2\) s.• For this normalization \(h\) has units degrees/(\(U\) s). \(E\) is centered and stationary in this calculation.• \(A\) here is noise intensity, not the visual-feedback gain used elsewhere.
If filter overlap decays to zero, MSD tends to the finite plateau \(2C_E(0)\). Muscle filtering can smooth private motor noise, but cannot make this stationary position noise accumulate displacement variance indefinitely. Eye MSD instead keeps growing over the observed range.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main Methods ‘MSD curve of low-pass filtered white noise’, Eqs. 20–22, PDF p. 10; related private-OMN comparison Fig. 3, PDF p. 6.Guide location: Chapter 8, section 8.2, The MSD plateaus for filtered white noise but grows for filtered diffusionOrigin: Paper stationary filtered-noise result; a decaying kernel gives a finite MSD plateau.Derivation route: Convolve white input of intensity \(A\) with a stable response \(h\), then average the product at two times. For a centered stationary position, expand the squared displacement.


E6. Filtered accumulating command · guide derivation\(\tau_f\dot E+E=B,\quad dB=\sqrt{2D}\,dW\)\(M(\ell)=2D[\ell-\tau_f(1-e^{-\ell/\tau_f})]\)\(M\sim D\ell^2/\tau_f\ (\ell\ll\tau_f)\)\(M\sim2D(\ell-\tau_f)\ (\ell\gg\tau_f)\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(B\): accumulating Brownian position command (degrees).• \(\tau_f\): the single eye-response time (s), written \(\tau\) in the detailed chapter; distinct from the 2012 synaptic time.• \(W\): standard Brownian process with increment variance \(dt\) and units sqrt(s), not a connection weight.• \(v=\dot E\): eye velocity (degrees/s); \(C_v(s)\): stationary velocity covariance (degrees\(^2\)/s\(^2\)), where \(s\) is a time lag.
The eye can move smoothly while its internal position command diffuses. Increasing \(\tau_f\) reduces short-lag motion; increasing \(D\) raises the entire curve. The synaptic time \(\tau\) from 2012 is a different parameter. This simplified calculation illustrates the 2022 interpretation; the paper uses two muscle times and feedback, and does not uniquely identify the circuit.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Guide derivation, not a displayed paper equation. Related context: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main Fig. 3 and discussion of diffusion versus muscle filtering, PDF pp. 5–6; stationary white-noise comparison Eqs. 20–22, PDF p. 10. The paper’s full model instead has two muscle times and feedback, Methods Eqs. 23–34, PDF p. 11.Guide location: Chapter 8, section 8.2, The MSD plateaus for filtered white noise but grows for filtered diffusionOrigin: Guide teaching derivation using a one-time-constant filter; not the paper’s full circuit formula.Derivation route: A Brownian position command \(B\) drives a one-time-constant eye response \(\tau_f\). After velocity transients, \(C_v(s)=(D/\tau_f)e^{-\|s\|/\tau_f}\). Integrate it as \(M=2\int_0^\ell(\ell-s)C_v(s)\,ds\).









More eye results: the independent-noise bound, measurement error, and parameter scaling






Table 5: Covariance identifies a shared component of eye movement. Further results, tests and model extensions.





formula and symbols
decoding
location and derivation




E2. Independent-noise limit · supporting\(\sum_{i=1}^{N_m}R_i^2\le1\)\(\langle R_i^2\rangle\le1/N_m\)Extra symbols and notes:• Angle brackets denote a motor-population mean; a representative sample estimates it with sampling uncertainty.• \(R_i^2\): explained variance fraction after best linear rescaling. Predictors and measured displacement are standardized to zero mean and unit variance for the proof.
If independent motor fluctuations alone supplied the movement, the average cell could explain only a small fraction of its variance. The measured mean correlation gives \(\langle R^2\rangle\ge0.17^2\simeq0.029\), challenging that explanation for a population of thousands. Applying the bound to sampled cells requires a representative average.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Supplementary Notes ‘The explanatory power of a single OMN’, Eqs. S1–S2, supplement 1 PDF p. 2; related main ‘Central source’ discussion PDF p. 3. Guide supplies the residual-variance proof.Guide location: Chapter 7, section 7.5, The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise aloneOrigin: Paper independent-noise bound; guide proof under independence and representative sampling.Derivation route: Standardize independent single-cell predictors and measured displacement. Subtract their best linear prediction; its residual variance \(1-\sum_iR_i^2\) cannot be negative. Here \(R_i\) is the displacement correlation and \(N_m\) is motor population size.


E4. Measurement offset · method\(M_{\rm obs}(\ell)=M(\ell)+2\sigma_m^2,\quad\ell>0\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(\nu(t)\): position-reading error (degrees); \(\sigma_m^2\): variance of one reading error (degrees\(^2\)).• \(M_{\rm obs}\): MSD from measured angles \(E_{\rm obs}\), with the same units as \(M\). Displacement error uses two readings.
Independent position-reading error raises every positive-lag MSD by a constant, which can dominate the smallest movements. At zero lag it cancels exactly. Temporally correlated measurement error needs a lag-dependent correction instead.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main Methods ‘Removal of measurement noise’, Eqs. 18–19, PDF p. 10; supporting noise plateau and fixed-coil control in Extended Data Fig. 2, supplement 1 PDF p. 8.Guide location: Chapter 8, section 8.1, Independent measurement error adds a constant offset to the MSDOrigin: Paper measurement correction assuming temporally independent errors independent of true movement.Derivation route: For measured position \(E_{\rm obs}=E+\nu\), expand its squared displacement. Independent errors at the two times each contribute variance \(\sigma_m^2\); movement–error cross terms vanish. \(M(\ell)=\mathbb E[(E(t+\ell)-E(t))^2]\).


E7. Firing variability and sensitivity set a noise scale · supporting estimate\(J\simeq Na^2/\lambda_0\)\(D\propto\dfrac{\mathrm{CV}^2\lambda_0}{Na^2\tau_s^2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{N\lambda_0 b^2\tau_s^2}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(N\): number of comparable integrator neurons, rather than motor count \(N_m\).• \(\lambda,\lambda_0\): rate and typical mean rate (spikes/s).• \(a=d\lambda/dE\): absolute slope (spikes/(s degree)); \(b=a/\lambda_0\): fractional slope (degree\(^{-1}\)). These are not the place-field gain.• \(J\): Poisson information rate about angle (s\(^{-1}\) degree\(^{-2}\)).• \(\mathrm{CV}\): interspike-interval standard deviation divided by its mean, dimensionless; \(\tau_s\): synaptic decay time (s).• The paper calls \(k_0\) position sensitivity but leaves its absolute/fractional normalization unclear.
Within this estimate, more regular spikes, more comparable cells or longer synaptic decay \(\tau_s\) reduce diffusion. Increasing rate helps at fixed fractional slope but raises the scale at fixed absolute slope. The paper’s Eq. 1 leaves slope normalization unclear. This simpler Poisson-based scale comparison is not an exact formula for its full saturating, sub-Poisson network.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Guide Poisson/renewal scale comparison. Related paper expression: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main Eq. 1 and parameter discussion, PDF p. 6; sub-Poisson construction in Methods ‘Sub-Poisson spike trains’, PDF p. 11. The paper prints inverse lambda_0 dependence without clarifying the slope normalization.Guide location: Chapter 9, section 9.2, Spike regularity and circuit parameters set the model’s drift scaleOrigin: Guide supporting scale estimate and paper Eq. 1 comparison; not an exact equation for the full saturating, sub-Poisson network.Derivation route: In a comparable population of \(N\) cells, write mean firing \(\lambda_0\), absolute position slope \(a=d\lambda/dE\) and fractional slope \(b=a/\lambda_0\). Long-window renewal count variance supplies the squared interval coefficient of variation, \(\mathrm{CV}^2\); project that noise with fixed network geometry.











Recall check: why does weak single-cell correlation not imply a small shared contribution?


Private spike noise can make one cell’s prediction much noisier than the movement. Correlation divides covariance by both signals’ standard deviations, so the noisy predictor lowers it. The calibrated shared-fraction estimate instead divides covariance by measured displacement variance. This interpretation needs the gain and noise assumptions; locating the source upstream also needs a biological premise about private motor-neuron variability.

title: Exam review: connect mechanisms, measurements and results
section: Thresholded Gaussian input links spatial structure to place-field statistics
text:
Thresholded Gaussian input links spatial structure to place-field statistics
Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025): place fields in rodent and bat recordings, compared with a spatial statistical model. A cell’s input is a correlated Gaussian map over position. Once drawn, that map stays fixed during traversal. Thresholding it makes connected active regions. Crossings determine 1D counts and mean lengths; isolated high peaks supply the limiting size laws in different dimensions. Slices and holes test spatial structure beyond a size histogram.
Recall the chain: input map and threshold (P1) → exact crossings and mean-length constraints (P3–P4) → high-threshold size law (P6). Slice and topology tests (P9 and P11) probe spatial structure further; they are in the additional results below.
The map varies over space, unlike the memory coordinate that diffuses over time. The local distance scale is written as \(\ell_c\) here; the place-field chapters call the same scale \(\sigma\). It is distinct from input standard deviation \(\sigma_0\).

Place-field-specific additions. Use the common notation for physical position, firing rate and the distinction between spatial and temporal variables. These additions apply to both place-field tables.

\(d\): spatial dimension, 1, 2 or 3. Positions are in \(\mathbb R^d\).
\(h(x)\): fixed Gaussian input map; \(\mu\): constant input mean; \(\sigma_0\): input standard deviation; \(h_{\rm th}\): absolute firing threshold (all in input units).
\(z=(h-\mu)/\sigma_0\): normalized input; \(q=(h_{\rm th}-\mu)/\sigma_0\): normalized threshold; \(\epsilon\): peak excess above \(q\) (all dimensionless).
\(a\): gain converting normalized excess into firing rate (Hz). It is not the eye model’s tuning slope.
\(C(x,y)\), or \(C(y-x)\) for a stationary map: covariance of unnormalized input, in input units squared. It is not the eye model’s shared displacement \(C\). Spatial primes differentiate with respect to distance.
\(\ell_c\): local distance scale, written \(\sigma\) in the place-field chapters; distinct from input standard deviation \(\sigma_0\).
\(Q(q)=\Pr(Z>q)\) for a standard normal scalar \(Z\): dimensionless Gaussian upper-tail probability. \(\nu_+(q)\): upcrossing density (distance\(^{-1}\)).
\(s\): complete-field size (length, area or volume, with distance\(^d\) units); \(S\): nonnegative cutoff in the same units.
\(v_d\): dimensionless unit-ball volume, with \(v_1=2\), \(v_2=\pi\) and \(v_3=4\pi/3\). \(\beta\): size-law coefficient, in inverse distance squared in every dimension.





Table 6: Thresholded Gaussian input links spatial structure to place-field statistics. Core argument.





formula and symbols
decoding
location and derivation




P1. Active spatial regions · model\(z=(h-\mu)/\sigma_0\)\(q=(h_{\rm th}-\mu)/\sigma_0\)\(F=a[z-q]_+\)\(\ell_c=\sqrt{-C(0)/C''(0)}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \([u]_+=\max(u,0)\) retains positive excess and sets negative excess to zero; \(u=z-q\) is dimensionless.• \(C''(0)\): second spatial covariance derivative along a unit direction (input units squared/distance\(^2\)). The normalized covariance is \(C/C(0)\).
A field is one connected region where \(z>q\). The sampled map stays fixed during traversal. Raising threshold removes active space; increasing \(\ell_c\) stretches the local spatial scale. Here \(\ell_c\) is the distance scale called \(\sigma\) in later place chapters, not input standard deviation \(\sigma_0\).
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), STAR Methods ‘Model details’, Eqs. 2–3, main PDF pp. 13–14; local spatial scale Eq. 4, main PDF p. 14. The guide makes the removable constant mean and rate gain explicit. Supplement Methods S1, PDF p. 9, defines the spatial Gaussian process.Guide location: Chapter 10, section 10.1, Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fieldsOrigin: Paper spatial Gaussian threshold model and local scale, with explicit guide normalization.Derivation route: Normalize a stationary Gaussian input map \(h\) with mean \(\mu\), standard deviation \(\sigma_0\) and covariance \(C\). Threshold at \(q\); gain \(a\) converts excess into firing. Differentiating covariance gives \(\operatorname{Var}(z')=\ell_c^{-2}\).


P3. Crossing density and finite-track count · exact\(\nu_+(q)=\dfrac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\ell_c}\)\(\mathbb E[N_L]=L\nu_+(q)+Q(q)\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(L\): track length (distance); \(N_L\): count of connected active intervals intersecting \([0,L]\), including clipped intervals.• \(z'\): spatial derivative (distance\(^{-1}\)); height density times the mean positive part of slope gives a count per distance.
This counts active components intersecting the track, including clipped boundary fields. It is exact for a sufficiently smooth stationary nondegenerate Gaussian map at any threshold. Higher \(q\) reduces counts when \(q>0\); larger \(\ell_c\) reduces crossings per unit length at fixed \(q\).
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), supplement Methods S3 ‘Field statistics in 1D’, Eqs. S9–S10, PDF p. 11; crossing density Eqs. S11–S13, PDF p. 12. The finite-track endpoint term is also in main STAR Methods Eq. 8, PDF p. 15. The guide explains the counting identity explicitly.Guide location: Chapter 10, section 10.2, Upcrossings count fields, with an endpoint correctionOrigin: Exact paper crossing and expected Euler-characteristic results; guide explains the endpoint field convention.Derivation route: Kac–Rice multiplies height density at \(q\) by mean positive part of the spatial slope there. Stationary Gaussian height and slope are independent. Add \(Q(q)=\Pr(Z>q)\), \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), for a field already active at the left end of a track of length \(L\).


P4. Means identify threshold and scale · exact\(\mu_s=Q(q)/\nu_+\)\(\mu_g=[1-Q(q)]/\nu_+\)\(q=Q^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{\mu_s}{\mu_s+\mu_g}\right)\)\(\ell_c=\dfrac{\mu_s+\mu_g}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(\mu_s,\mu_g\): stationary mean complete-field and complete-gap lengths (distance), measured per field or gap rather than per occupied position.• \(Q^{-1}\): inverse Gaussian upper-tail function, dimensionless.• These are not finite clipped-track ratios; \(\mu_s\) is distinct from input mean \(\mu\).
Two measured means constrain two model parameters before testing the full length histograms. These are stationary complete-field and complete-gap means. Finite-track clipping or selection of only cells with fields must be handled before treating sample means as these quantities.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), supplement Methods S3, Eqs. S14–S15 for mean field/gap lengths, PDF p. 12; related main STAR Methods ‘Parameter inference in 1D environments’, PDF p. 14. The explicit inversion for q and ell_c is guide algebra from those means.Guide location: Chapter 10, section 10.3, Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scaleOrigin: Paper exact stationary 1D means; guide derives the explicit parameter inversion.Derivation route: Divide active and inactive spatial fractions by the same upcrossing density to obtain mean field length \(\mu_s\) and gap length \(\mu_g\). The ratio \(\mu_s/(\mu_s+\mu_g)\) gives active fraction; invert the Gaussian upper tail and crossing scale.


P6. Universal size laws · central approximation\(\Pr(s>S)\simeq e^{-\beta S^{2/d}}\)\(\beta=\dfrac{q^2}{2\ell_c^2v_d^{2/d}}\)\((v_1,v_2,v_3)=(2,\pi,4\pi/3)\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(U=q\epsilon\): dimensionless scaled excess tending to a mean-one exponential variable.• \(r_*\): approximate field radius (distance), not a firing rate.• Each field is sampled once, rather than weighted by occupied volume.
The same input mechanism gives Rayleigh lengths in 1D, exponential areas in 2D and a Weibull volume law with exponent \(2/3\) in 3D. Each field has equal sampling weight. These are high-threshold limits; multi-peak fields and finite thresholds can change the distribution.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), main Eq. 1, PDF p. 3; supplement Methods S4, local parabola/full-width Eqs. S22–S23, PDF p. 14, and scaled peak excess Eqs. S24–S25, PDF p. 15. The guide reconstructs the geometric beta with the sqrt(2) width factor missing from printed S23 and the corrected negative quadratic term before S25.Guide location: Chapter 11, section 11.2, Geometry gives different size laws in each dimensionOrigin: Paper central high-threshold size law; guide derives and checks the leading geometric constant and corrects printed algebra.Derivation route: For a smooth stationary isotropic Gaussian map at large positive \(q\), a typical counted field surrounds one nearly quadratic peak: radius \(r_*\simeq\ell_c\sqrt{2\epsilon/q}\) for peak excess \(\epsilon\). The scaled excess \(q\epsilon\) tends to a unit-mean exponential law. Substitute size \(s=v_dr_*^d\).









More place-field results: wiring, counts and gaps, peaks, moments, slices, boundary slopes, and topology






Table 7: Thresholded Gaussian input links spatial structure to place-field statistics. Further results, tests and model extensions.

decoding
location and derivation




P2. Random inputs create spatial covariance · supporting\(h(x)=\sum_i W_i u_i(x)\)\(C(x,y)=v_W\sum_i u_i(x)u_i(y)\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(i\): input-cell index; \(u_i(x)\): fixed input firing profile (Hz).• \(W_i\): zero-mean random weight (input units/Hz); \(v_W=\operatorname{Var}(W_i)\): weight variance (input units squared/Hz\(^2\)). These are not Brownian quantities.• Covariance is over choices of weights. The Gaussian limit requires many active terms with no dominant input; spatial properties also depend on the fixed profiles.
The same input cell contributes at nearby positions, creating spatial covariance. Broader input profiles can broaden fields; changing weight variance instead changes input amplitude and hence effective threshold if the absolute threshold stays fixed. Random weights alone do not guarantee smooth, stationary or isotropic maps.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), supplement Methods S2 ‘Derivation of Gaussian process input to CA1 cells’, Eqs. S2–S5, PDF p. 10, and heterogeneous-profile Eqs. S6–S8, PDF p. 11. The covariance formula is Eq. S4; guide expands its cancellation of cross terms.Guide location: Chapter 12, section 12.3, Random input weights can generate Gaussian mapsOrigin: Paper supporting input-generation model; guide expands the covariance calculation and conditions for a Gaussian limit.Derivation route: Use fixed input profiles \(u_i(x)\) and independent random weights with mean zero and variance \(v_W\). Average over weight choices; cross terms vanish. Many individually small contributions permit a Gaussian limit.


P5. Rare field locations and gaps · limiting approximation\(N_L\approx\mathrm{Poisson}(\nu_+L)\)\(\Pr(G>g)\simeq e^{-\nu_+g}\)\(\mathbb E[N\mid N\ge1]=\lambda/(1-e^{-\lambda})\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(L\): track length; \(G\): inactive gap length; \(g\): nonnegative gap cutoff (all distance units).• \(N_L\): rare-field count on that track; \(N\): unconditioned field count; \(\lambda\): unconditioned Poisson mean count, dimensionless rather than a firing rate.• The survival law concerns large gaps in the rare-field limit; the conditioned mean excludes zero-field cells.
The model predicts whole count and gap distributions beyond their means. Smoothness and stationarity alone do not imply independence. The bulk count omits finite-track boundary effects; excluding zero-field cells also raises the observed mean and must be accounted for in fitting.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), supplement Methods S3 ‘Distributions in the high threshold regime’, PDF p. 13, gives limiting Poisson counts/exponential gaps; main STAR Methods Eq. 5, PDF p. 14, gives the zero-truncation mean used in the 2D fit. Guide states the extra weak-dependence condition and separates it from exact crossing density.Guide location: Chapter 10, section 10.3, Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scaleOrigin: Paper limiting rare-event distributions and Poisson selection correction; not an exact finite-threshold field-count law.Derivation route: At high threshold, well-separated rare excursions can approach independent locations if spatial correlations decay sufficiently. Their spacing is then approximately exponential, and short field widths make gaps \(G\) approach the same scale. Conditioning a Poisson count with mean \(\lambda\) on at least one field gives the last expression.


P7. Peak firing and field size · supporting approximation\(F_{\max}=a\epsilon\)\(F_{\max}\simeq\dfrac{aq}{2\ell_c^2}(s/v_d)^{2/d}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(F_{\max}\): peak rate (Hz); \(r_*\): approximate field radius (distance).• \(s^{1/d}\): linear-size measure (distance); for a 1D full width, \(v_1=2\).
Higher peaks create wider fields, with limiting exponent two against linear size \(s^{1/d}\). The exponent against area or volume differs. Finite-threshold data and simulations have smaller fitted exponents, so the limiting square law is not an exact empirical relation.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), supplement Methods S4, Eqs. S22–S23 and following peak-amplitude discussion, PDF pp. 14–15; empirical/model comparisons main Fig. 3C–D, PDF p. 7, and shape progression Fig. 5, PDF p. 9. Guide corrects the full-width factor and writes the explicit rate-size equation.Guide location: Chapter 11, section 11.1, Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolicOrigin: Paper high-threshold peak-size prediction, expanded in the guide; not an exact empirical square law.Derivation route: Use the same high-peak parabola: \(\epsilon\simeq q r_*^2/(2\ell_c^2)\) and \(s=v_dr_*^d\). Firing above threshold is \(a\epsilon\) at the peak.


P8. Size moments and shape · supporting approximation\(\mathbb E[s^k]\simeq\Gamma(1+kd/2)\beta^{-kd/2}\)\(\mu_s\simeq\Gamma(1+d/2)\beta^{-d/2}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(k\ge0\): dimensionless moment order, not the eye coefficient.• \(\mu_s=\mathbb E[s]\): mean field size (distance\(^d\)). This limiting mean differs from the exact 1D mean in P4.• \(u=\beta s^{2/d}\): dimensionless integration variable; \(\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du\) for dimensionless \(t>0\). The moment has distance\(^{dk}\) units.
After the mean fixes size scale, higher moment ratios test the predicted shape. No extra shape fit is needed in the limiting law. These moments inherit its high-threshold assumption and describe complete fields rather than fields selected by occupied volume.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), supplement Methods S3, paragraph before Eq. S18, PDF p. 13, states the mean Gamma(1+d/2) beta^(−d/2); main Eq. 1, PDF p. 3, supplies the size density. The guide derives arbitrary nonnegative moments and corrects the multiplication/division error in printed S18.Guide location: Chapter 11, section 11.2, Geometry gives different size laws in each dimensionOrigin: Paper limiting mean plus guide general-moment derivation, inheriting the high-threshold approximation.Derivation route: Differentiate the size survival law to obtain its density; set \(u=\beta s^{2/d}\) in the moment integral. Here \(k\ge0\) and \(\Gamma\) is the gamma function, defined by its integral in the linked derivation.


P9. Slices retain Gaussian structure · central test\(h_{\rm line}(t)=h(x_0+t\mathbf e)\)\(C_{\rm line}(t,t')=C[(t-t')\mathbf e]\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(x_0\): point on the sampling line (position vector, distance units); \(\mathbf e\): dimensionless unit direction.• \(t,t'\): signed spatial coordinates along the line (distance), not times.• \(h_{\rm line}\) and \(C_{\rm line}\): restricted input and covariance, with the same units as \(h,C\). The original map dimension \(d\) differs from the slice dimension.
At high threshold, line-slice lengths approach a Rayleigh law and plane-slice areas an exponential law, even within a 3D map. Slice components have different sampling weights from complete fields; larger objects are more likely to be intersected. A chosen central cut through each field is a different sampling rule.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), main Fig. 2C–D and H–J, PDF p. 5, and Results ‘Statistics of place fields in two- and three-dimensional environments’, PDF pp. 3,6; alternative spherical model and slice comparison Fig. S2, supplement PDF pp. 3–4. The Gaussian restriction equation is an explicit guide explanation, not a numbered paper equation.Guide location: Chapter 11, section 11.3, Slices test spatial structure beyond field volumeOrigin: Paper central slice test; guide states the exact Gaussian restriction property, with limiting size laws applied to the slice dimension.Derivation route: Restrict a jointly Gaussian map to points on a line with unit direction \(\mathbf e\), or to a plane. The retained joint distributions remain Gaussian with the restricted covariance. Under isotropy they retain the local scale \(\ell_c\).


P10. Boundary slopes · exact\(p_{\uparrow}(v)=\ell_c^2v\,e^{-\ell_c^2v^2/2},\quad v>0\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(v=z'(x)>0\): normalized input slope at an upcrossing (distance\(^{-1}\)).• \(p_{\uparrow}(v)\): density of slopes selected at upcrossings; \(p_{z'}(v)\): derivative density at an ordinary spatial point (both have distance units).• \(w\): positive slope integration variable (distance\(^{-1}\)); \(av\): rate slope (Hz/distance). This \(v\) is not eye velocity or unit-ball volume \(v_d\).
Steep slopes are sampled more often at crossings. This Rayleigh law is independent of \(q\) under the smooth stationary Gaussian model, without a high-threshold approximation. Firing-rate slope is \(av\), so its scale also depends on the rate gain \(a\).
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), main Results prediction and Fig. 3E, PDF pp. 6–7; STAR Methods ‘Boundary slopes’, PDF p. 15, describes the 0.1 m finite-difference measurement. The slope-weighted Kac–Rice density and its normalization are derived explicitly in the guide; no numbered paper equation gives this density.Guide location: Chapter 11, section 11.4, Why slopes at field boundaries are RayleighOrigin: Paper boundary-slope prediction; guide exact density derivation under smooth stationary Gaussian assumptions, without a high-threshold limit.Derivation route: Select an upcrossing rather than a uniformly chosen position. Its slope density is proportional to \(v p_{z'}(v)\); normalize over positive slopes. Here \(v=z'\) is the normalized input slope at a boundary.


P11. Components and holes · exact\(\eta_1=\dfrac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\ell_c}\)\(\eta_2=\dfrac{qe^{-q^2/2}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\ell_c^2}\)\(\eta_3=\dfrac{(q^2-1)e^{-q^2/2}}{(2\pi)^2\ell_c^3}\)\(\mathbb E[\chi_d]=Q(q)+\sum_{j=1}^d\binom dj L^j\eta_j\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(L\): side length of the box (distance); \(j=1,\ldots,d\): dimension of the contributing interior, face or edge.• \(\eta_j\): signed Euler-characteristic contribution per \(j\)-dimensional measure (distance\(^{-j}\)), not a positive field density.• \(\chi_d\): Euler characteristic of the active set in the closed box, a dimensionless signed count; unrelated to eye fraction \(\chi\). The sum retains real boundary terms.
Here \(\chi_d\) is Euler characteristic, unrelated to the eye variance fraction \(\chi\). It counts components minus holes in 2D, and components minus tunnels plus cavities in 3D. These formulas retain boundary contributions for a smooth stationary isotropic nondegenerate Gaussian map; they are not periodic-box formulas or general field counts.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), main STAR Methods ‘Euler characteristics’, Eqs. 8–10, PDF p. 15; comparisons Fig. 3F–H, PDF p. 7. The guide obtains eta_j by a signed critical-point Kac–Rice calculation and derives box face factors, relying on the underlying Morse/kinematic theorem.Guide location: Chapter 12, section 12.1, Holes distinguish maps with the same field countOrigin: Paper exact expected topology formulas; guide derivation of signed densities and boundary factors. Not an exact component-count formula at general threshold.Derivation route: Count spatial critical points with signs: maxima create components, while other critical points join regions or alter holes. The signed Kac–Rice calculation gives \(\eta_j\); faces and edges supply the coefficients for a closed box of side \(L\), in \(d=1,2,3\).


P12. Rare-field count in higher dimensions · supporting approximation\(\mathbb E[N]\simeq\dfrac{Vq^{d-1}e^{-q^2/2}}{(2\pi)^{(d+1)/2}\ell_c^d}\)Extra symbols and notes:• \(N\): number of connected active fields, not neurons; \(V\): environment length, area or volume (distance\(^d\)).• \(\chi_d\): signed Euler-characteristic count from P11; it approaches \(N\) only for isolated simple blobs at high threshold. The bulk formula omits boundary terms.
This predicts how field count changes with threshold, spatial scale and dimension in a large region at high threshold. It drops boundary terms and holes; the exact Euler-characteristic formula must not be used as an exact component count at ordinary thresholds.
Paper location: Open cited PDF page. Mainali et al. (2025), supplement Methods S3 ‘Field statistics in higher dimensions’, Eq. S16, PDF p. 13; related exact Euler-characteristic Eqs. 8–10, main PDF p. 15. Guide keeps the leading volume term and high-q polynomial power explicitly.Guide location: Chapter 12, section 12.1, Holes distinguish maps with the same field countOrigin: Paper supporting high-threshold, volume-dominated component-count approximation; not an exact count at ordinary thresholds.Derivation route: At high \(q\), isolated components usually have one peak and no holes, so their count approaches Euler characteristic. Retain the leading volume term and leading power of \(q\) in the preceding formula; \(V\) is environment length, area or volume.











Recall check: why do exact crossing counts not make the size law exact?


The crossing calculation averages height and slope at threshold under the smooth stationary Gaussian model. It does not require high threshold. The universal size argument additionally replaces a typical field by an isolated nearly quadratic high peak and uses the limiting peak-excess distribution. At finite threshold a field can have several peaks or an irregular shape. The extra approximation has to be checked, even when the crossing formula is exact.

title: Exam review: connect mechanisms, measurements and results
section: Different quantities answer different questions
text:
Different quantities answer different questions
Before giving a result, check which of these questions it answers:

Activity, stored value or estimate? Neural activations form the circuit state; a coordinate identifies the represented value; a decoder computes an estimate from observations. Persistent activity alone does not guarantee accurate memory. M1, M3, M13.
Present-state precision or storage loss? Fisher information measures a local distinction in present spike probabilities. Diffusion measures accumulated movement of the stored value. M7–M8.
Correlation or a causal variance fraction? A shared-fraction interpretation needs calibrated gains and a noise model. Correlation alone does not supply it. E3.
Internal command or observed movement? Muscle response and feedback change how internal fluctuations appear in eye motion. E5–E6.
Temporal noise or a fixed spatial map? The 2012 and 2022 arguments concern evolving signals. The 2025 spatial randomness describes an ensemble of possible maps, not fresh input at each revisit. M6, P1.
Exact model identity or limiting approximation? Gaussian crossing and topology formulas have their stated exact model scope. Universal field-size laws need a high threshold; nearly independent field locations need sufficiently decaying spatial dependence as well. P3, P6, P4 and its supporting rare-event result.

title: Part I: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models
text:
Chapters in this part
Unreviewed draft diagram. This AI-generated image may contain incorrect or missing labels, arrows, formulas and numbers. Use the Part text and paper links as the source for the explanation.
[Paper] In the model of Burak and Fiete (2012), Results and Eq. 1, PDF p. 2, each value \(\theta\) has a noise-free sustained pattern satisfying \(\bar s_i(\theta)=\tau\phi(\sum_j W_{ij}\bar s_j(\theta)+b_i)=\tau\bar r_i(\theta)\). Here \(\bar s_i\) is neuron \(i\)’s steady synaptic activation, \(\bar r_i\) its steady firing rate, \(W_{ij}\) the connection from neuron \(j\) to \(i\), \(b_i\) a constant input, \(\phi\) the input-to-rate rule, and \(\tau\) the synaptic decay time. Bars indicate noise-free steady values.
[Paper] Random spike timing moves the represented value. For intervals long enough for transient disturbances to relax but short enough for the local diffusion coefficient \(D\) to remain approximately constant, with negligible systematic drift and boundary effects, the mean squared displacement is approximately \(2Dt\). With symmetric weights the authors’ corrected formula is \(2D=\sum_i\bar r_i(\bar g_i')^2/[\tau^2(\sum_i\bar r_i'\bar g_i')^2]\), where \(\bar g_i=\sum_jW_{ij}\bar s_j+b_i\) is the steady input to neuron \(i\). The internal Fisher information rate is \(J(\theta)=\sum_i[\bar r_i'(\theta)]^2/\bar r_i(\theta)\) for positive firing rates and conditionally independent Poisson spikes. The authors establish \(D\geq1/(2\tau^2J)\) for their model. A prime denotes differentiation with respect to \(\theta\). These results link the neural circuit’s noise to the precision of its spike signals (diffusion and information, PDF pp. 2–3).
[Paper] Let \(T\) be the storage delay and \(L\) the duration of observing spikes after the recall cue. In the paper’s local, unbounded, constant-\(D\), constant-\(J\) Gaussian readout approximation, with independent future fluctuations and a locally unbiased estimate, the ideal observer with access to all network spikes has initial-value error variance \(2DT+\sqrt{2D/J}\,\coth(\sqrt{2DJ}L)\). An observer who equally weights spikes has variance \(2DT+1/(JL)+2DL/3\). Here \(\coth z=(e^{2z}+1)/(e^{2z}-1)\). The term \(2DT\) is storage error; the remaining term is readout error for the state at the cue. As \(L\) increases, the ideal readout term approaches \(\sqrt{2D/J}\), while the equal-weight observer eventually worsens because it treats an evolving state as fixed. The main readout results, PDF p. 4, and supporting text section VI, PDF pp. 12–16, are developed in Chapter 6.
[Interpretation] A network can keep firing without keeping the original angle exactly. This Part follows that distinction from the model’s physical components to its predictions about error. Chapters 1–2 prepare the neural and mathematical background; Chapters 3–4 follow noise and diffusion; Chapter 5 explains the information bound; Chapter 6 follows the readout calculation.
How to read the labels. [Paper] marks an author claim or result, paraphrased here and linked to the relevant article or supporting-text passage. [Interpretation] marks this guide’s explanation of what a result or mechanism means. [Guide derivation] identifies steps filled in or rearranged for teaching; it does not imply that the authors wrote those exact steps. title: Part I: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models
text:
Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value: Introduce the question and steady-state equation in the 2012 paper, then explain eye mechanics, the neural model brought forward from Methods, spike statistics, and a preview of its simulations.
Stable representations can accumulate error: Explain the continuous family of states in the 2012 Results, then provide eye mechanics and the random-spreading background needed to understand how persistent activity can accumulate error.
Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor: Starting from the neural model in Chapter 1, derive the weak-fluctuation approximation and follow small disturbances through the circuit to calculate diffusion of a stored value.
Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays: Follow the paper’s diffusion section through Figures 1 and 2, then use the supporting text to explain how boundaries, angular wraparound, state-dependent diffusion, and systematic drift affect longer delays.
Spike information limits memory stability: A neuron receiving spikes from a memory circuit has access to information about the stored value. This chapter sets a bound on estimation error under the model’s assumptions and derives the constraint that spike information places on the circuit’s memory stability.
Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed: Reading spikes from a memory circuit takes time, during which its stored value can keep changing. This chapter calculates how much longer observation can help recover the value present at a recall cue, and explains why it cannot recover every earlier random displacement.

title: 1  Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value
text:
1.1 Repeated spikes maintain eye muscle tension
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated images may contain incorrect or missing labels, arrows, formulas and numbers. Use the chapter text and paper links as the source for the explanation.
[Paper: Introduction and Results, pp. 1–2] Burak and Fiete (2012) ask how accurately a network of interacting neurons can retain a continuous value, such as an eye position or a direction, when its neurons emit spikes at variable times. The paper takes a continuous attractor model as its starting point. Its contribution is to calculate how spike variability makes the stored value wander, and how that wandering is related to the information available in the network’s spikes. For an effectively constant local diffusion coefficient \(D\) and negligible systematic drift, the represented value has mean squared displacement approximately \(2Dt\) over a suitable time interval \(t\). The paper’s information–diffusion inequality is \(D\ge 1/(2\tau^2J)\), where \(J\) is the internal Fisher information rate in the network’s spikes and \(\tau\) is the common synaptic decay time. These are results for the authors’ specified noisy continuous-attractor model, not universal bounds on every memory circuit. Read the introduction and Results setup.
[Interpretation] Imagine the network holding an eye angle \(\theta\) after a cue disappears. Neuron \(i\) emits spikes at a firing rate \(r_i\), the expected number of spikes per unit time. Each spike increases its outgoing synaptic activation \(s_i\), which then decays. The weighted activations from the network determine each neuron’s input and thus its firing rate. This feedback can maintain an activity pattern that represents the angle.
[Guide derivation: preview of the paper’s bound] At a fixed represented value \(\theta\), write \(\bar r_i\) for cell \(i\)’s noise-free steady firing rate and \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\) for its slope. Let \(v_i\) measure the lasting change in \(\theta\) caused by one unit of activation disturbance in cell \(i\) after the other disturbances relax. A unit change in \(\theta\) changes the steady activations by \(\tau r_i'\); the projection must therefore obey \(\sum_i\tau v_i r_i'=1\). The steady-state relation used here is derived just below.
Conditional Poisson spike fluctuations have variance \(\bar r_i\,dt\) over a short interval \(dt\). Their independent contributions give \(2D=\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i\). For positive rates, a Poisson count \(n_i\) in a fixed-state window \(h\) has mean \(h\bar r_i\). Differentiating its log probability \(\log p(n_i\mid\theta)=n_i\log(h\bar r_i)-h\bar r_i-\log(n_i!)\) gives the score \(S_i=(r_i'/\bar r_i)(n_i-h\bar r_i)\). Since the count variance is \(h\bar r_i\), \(E[S_i^2]=h(r_i')^2/\bar r_i\). Independent counts add, so the internal information per unit time is \(J=\sum_i(r_i')^2/\bar r_i\). Cauchy–Schwarz applied to the two vectors with entries \(v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}\) and \(r_i'/\sqrt{\bar r_i}\) then gives
\[ \frac{1}{\tau^2} =\left(\sum_i v_i r_i'\right)^2 \leq\left(\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i\right) \left(\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}\right) =2DJ. \]
For \(J>0\), rearranging gives \(D\geq1/(2\tau^2J)\). This preview assumes the stable continuous family, weak fluctuations, a common synaptic time constant and independent Poisson spike generation conditional on the current rates. Chapters 3 and 5 derive the lasting-shift weights and information rate instead of taking them as starting points.
[Paper: Results setup, Eq. 1, p. 2] In the idealized noise-free model, each value \(\theta\) corresponds to a persistent pattern across the neurons. For neuron \(i\), \(\bar s_i(\theta)\) is its steady synaptic activation and \(\bar r_i(\theta)\) its steady firing rate. The bar means a steady value in the noise-free model; it does not mean a time average of a noisy trajectory. The paper states the condition for this family of states as
\[ \bar s_i(\theta)=\tau\phi\!\left(\sum_j W_{ij}\bar s_j(\theta)+b_i\right)=\tau\bar r_i(\theta).\qquad\text{(Burak and Fiete, Eq. 1)} \]
Here \(W_{ij}\) is the strength with which neuron \(j\) affects neuron \(i\), \(b_i\) is a constant input to neuron \(i\), \(\phi\) converts its total input into a firing rate, and \(\tau\) is the synaptic decay time. The sum collects input from the network. The equation says that, at each steady state, activation lost by decay is balanced by the activation supplied by firing. The next sections explain these quantities and how the model obtains this balance; the original Eq. 1 precedes the paper’s analysis of noise.
[Guide derivation: steady states] The relation follows from balancing decay against the mean effect of new spikes. Over a short interval \(dt\), neuron \(i\)’s activation changes by \(ds_i=-s_i\,dt/\tau+dN_i\), where \(dN_i\) counts its new spikes. At the current state, the expected spike count is \(E[dN_i\mid\mathbf s]=\phi(g_i)dt\) to leading order, with input \(g_i=\sum_j W_{ij}s_j+b_i\). Thus the deterministic rate of change obtained by averaging the spike increment at that state is
\[ \frac{E[ds_i\mid\mathbf s]}{dt}=-\frac{s_i}{\tau}+\phi\!\left(\sum_jW_{ij}s_j+b_i\right). \]
At a noise-free steady state the right-hand side is zero. Multiplying by \(\tau\) gives \(\bar s_i=\tau\phi(\sum_jW_{ij}\bar s_j+b_i)=\tau\bar r_i\), which is Eq. 1. This is a conditional local drift calculation; it does not replace the average of a nonlinear function by the function of the average across noisy trials. The detailed spike and input equations follow in this chapter.
[Interpretation] A family of steady patterns gives the network different values it can hold. It does not by itself guarantee that noisy spikes leave the chosen value unchanged. Chapter 2 explains this distinction. This chapter first gives the eye and neuron background needed to read the model, then brings forward the model equations from the paper’s Methods and explains the spike statistics. A simulation example previews the later test of the diffusion result, and a final section connects the statistics to the eye paper.
[Background: eye muscles and neurons] For the eye to stay directed at a target, its muscles must keep exerting force after the movement command ends. The following anatomy and mechanics prepare us for the neural model; Burak and Fiete (2012) do not derive them.
A neuron communicates through brief electrical events called spikes. A firing rate is the expected number of spikes per unit time. A rate of 20 hertz means an average of 20 spikes per second under the specified conditions, rather than a promise of one spike every 50 milliseconds.
Anatomy: muscles turn the eyeball. In humans and macaques, the eyeball rotates within the bony eye socket, or orbit. The six extraocular muscles attach to the outside of the eyeball and control its orientation. The medial rectus pulls it toward the nose; the lateral rectus pulls it away. The superior and inferior rectus and the two oblique muscles contribute to vertical movement and rotation about the line of sight. Their actions depend on the eye’s orientation.1
Ocular motoneurons (OMNs) are neurons that activate these muscles through long nerve fibres. Their cell bodies lie in brainstem groups, and these fibres travel through three cranial nerves. The abducens nerve, VI, supplies the lateral rectus; the trochlear nerve, IV, supplies the superior oblique; the oculomotor nerve, III, supplies the other four. For horizontal gaze, changing the relative pull of the medial and lateral rectus rotates the eye. A force’s turning effect is its torque. Opposing torques can balance even while the muscles remain under tension.2
Repeated spikes maintain tension. Each motor spike affects muscle force for longer than the electrical event lasts. Repeated activation and the combined action of many muscle fibres give a smoother force than a sequence of isolated eye movements. Tonic firing means sustained firing during the holding period. It need not be perfectly periodic. During a rapid repositioning movement, called a saccade, a brief strong drive moves the eye; a sustained position-dependent drive then holds the new angle. This is the pulse-and-step description: the step means continuing drive, not one more spike.34
The mechanical properties contribute in different ways:
[Interpretation: holding the eye] Mechanical damping smooths movement; sustained neural drive selects the angle around which the eye is held. Inertia cannot preserve a stationary gaze against an unbalanced elastic pull.
So far we have followed the output from motor neurons to muscles. The next step is a model of how neurons act on one another and sustain a signal.

Elasticity creates restoring forces when muscles and surrounding tissues are stretched. At an off-centre gaze angle, active muscle torque must balance the restoring tendency.
Viscosity resists motion and dissipates mechanical energy. It damps rapid changes but supplies no holding torque once velocity is zero.
Inertia is resistance to a change in angular velocity. It matters during acceleration, not as a force holding a stationary eye. In primate eye movements, elastic and viscous effects dominate inertia.5
