title: 1  Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value
section: 1.2 Recurrent spikes renew decaying synaptic activity
text:
1.2 Recurrent spikes renew decaying synaptic activity
[Interpretation] How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than a spike lasts? In the paper’s model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually. Incoming activations determine new firing rates. The resulting spikes renew those activations. This feedback can support activity after the external stimulus has ended.
[Background] Neurons affect one another through connections called synapses. In the models used here, inputs have two contrasting effects:

An excitatory input increases a receiving neuron’s tendency to fire.
An inhibitory input reduces it.

[Interpretation] The effect of a spike can last beyond the spike itself because synaptic input decays over time. When neurons send signals back into the same population, the circuit has recurrent connectivity. Such feedback can maintain activity after an external signal disappears.
[Paper] Burak and Fiete (2012) specify the following interacting-neuron model in Materials and Methods, Eqs. 7–9, PDF p. 5. The model assumes fixed connection weights, constant input biases and a common synaptic decay time. In full, its three rules are \(\dot s_i=-s_i/\tau+\sum_\alpha\delta(t-t_i^\alpha)\), \(g_i=\sum_jW_{ij}s_j+b_i\), and \(r_i=\phi(g_i)\). Here \(s_i\) is the effect of spikes from neuron \(i\), \(t_i^\alpha\) are their times, \(g_i\) is total input, \(W_{ij}\) is the effect of neuron \(j\) on neuron \(i\), \(b_i\) is the fixed bias, and \(\phi\) converts input to the firing rate \(r_i\). Spikes follow the model’s conditional Poisson rule, explained in the spike-count section. Each equation and its meaning follow immediately below.6
[Interpretation] These equations describe synaptic activity; muscle motion is a later part of the pathway.
[Paper] Equation 7. The synaptic activation \(s_i\) tracks the decaying effect of neuron \(i\)’s outgoing spikes on receiving cells. The dot means \(\dot s_i=ds_i/dt\), and \(\tau\) is the decay time in seconds. The index \(\alpha\) numbers the spikes of neuron \(i\), with spike \(\alpha\) occurring at time \(t_i^\alpha\). The Dirac delta \(\delta(t-t_i^\alpha)\) represents an instantaneous unit pulse at that spike time; its integral across that time is one. The paper writes the activation dynamics, PDF p. 5, as
\[ \dot s_i+\frac{s_i}{\tau}=\sum_\alpha\delta(t-t_i^\alpha). \]
[Interpretation] Between spikes, the right-hand side is zero and activation decays. Integrating through one spike gives a one-unit increase in \(s_i\). Read Eq. 7 as a balance: spikes add activation, while the term \(s_i/\tau\) removes it. Original Eq. 7, PDF p. 5.
[Guide derivation] Equivalent count form. Let \(N_i(t)\) count neuron \(i\)’s spikes up to time \(t\). Integrating the pulse train counts the spikes, so the same dynamics can be written as
\[ ds_i=-\frac{s_i}{\tau}\,dt+dN_i(t). \]
Equivalently, if its spikes occur at times \(t_i^\alpha\),
\[ s_i(t)=\sum_{t_i^\alpha\le t}\exp[-(t-t_i^\alpha)/\tau] \]
once the contribution from any activation present at the starting time has decayed. The sum includes a spike at time \(t\), so it gives the activation immediately after that spike. Here \(s_i\) is dimensionless in the convention that each spike adds one unit.
[Example] For five illustrative spike times, the plot shows the events and the activation they leave behind.







Figure 1.3: Each spike adds one activation unit, which then decays with a 50 ms time constant. Closely spaced spikes add to the activation left by earlier spikes. The five spike times are an illustrative input, and the activation is calculated exactly from Burak and Fiete (2012), Eq. 7.




[Interpretation: activation and connections] The activation retains a decaying contribution from earlier spikes, so a spike train and its activation trace are different objects.
The connection-matrix explanation establishes why the model needs these interactions.
[Paper] From activation to new spikes: Equations 8 and 9. The total input \(g_i\) to neuron \(i\) combines the activation arriving from other cells with a constant input bias \(b_i\). The fixed connection weight \(W_{ij}\) says how the activation of neuron \(j\) affects the input to neuron \(i\) (Eqs. 8–9, PDF p. 5):
\[ g_i=\sum_jW_{ij}s_j+b_i.\qquad\text{(Burak and Fiete, Eq. 8)} \]
[Paper] The neural transfer function \(\phi\) converts total input into a nonnegative firing rate \(r_i\), in spikes per second. This is Eq. 9, PDF p. 5:
\[ r_i=\phi(g_i).\qquad\text{(Burak and Fiete, Eq. 9)} \]
[Interpretation] These equations specify how the input sets the rate; they do not prescribe each spike’s time.


[Example] Increasing input might increase firing linearly over some input range, or exponentially. The paper allows general connectivity and transfer functions at first (Model, Eqs. 7–9, p. 5).7  

[Interpretation: recurrent feedback] A spike from cell \(j\) raises \(s_j\) by one and therefore changes the input to cell \(i\) by \(W_{ij}\). That contribution then decays over time \(\tau\). For an increasing transfer function, a positive weight raises the receiving cell’s rate and a negative weight lowers it. The resulting new spikes affect other cells in turn. Thus the weights set where a disturbance goes, the transfer function sets the rate response, and \(\tau\) sets how long each synaptic contribution lasts. The input \(g_i\) is in the model’s input units. It is not specified as a measured membrane voltage. 
Together, Eqs. 7–9 describe one feedback cycle: spikes change synaptic activation, weighted activation changes input, and input changes the rate of new spikes. The next question is how the resulting pattern of rates can represent an eye angle or location.

title: 1  Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value
section: 1.3 Patterns of firing rates represent a value
text:
1.3 Patterns of firing rates represent a value
[Background] A tuning curve gives a neuron’s expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable. The linear eye-tuning example here draws on the 2022 eye paper; it is not an equation from the 2012 article. For eye angle \(\theta\), a simple local model is \(r_i(\theta)=r_{i,0}+k_i\theta\). Neuron \(i\) has baseline rate \(r_{i,0}\) in spikes per second and slope \(k_i\) in spikes per second per degree. This rate baseline is different from the input bias \(b_i\) in Eq. 8. The linear expression can describe an active range, but it must be modified where it would predict negative firing. The eye paper includes a firing threshold and terms for movement as well as position.8
[Paper] The 2012 model represents a value by a pattern across neurons; see its Results setup and Fig. 1, PDF p. 2. Cells can have different tuning curves. The vector
\[ \mathbf r(\theta)=\bigl(r_1(\theta),\ldots,r_N(\theta)\bigr) \]


is a population code: the pattern across \(N\) neurons carries information about \(\theta\). The position of a cell in this vector is a neuron identity, rather than a location in physical space. Reading a value from observed spikes is decoding. Establishing a population pattern from an input is encoding. The 2012 paper asks how accurately the network can maintain such a pattern using its own noisy activity.  

[Background] Spatial tuning gives a second example. This discussion draws on Mainali and colleagues (2025), not on the 2012 memory model. In the hippocampus, a brain structure involved in memory and navigation, a place cell fires strongly in one or more localized regions of an environment. A connected region of elevated spatial firing is a place field. One neuron can have several fields. A rate map estimates the rate at each position by dividing the spikes recorded there by the time spent there. Sparse visits, smoothing, and firing cutoffs therefore affect the estimated map and its fields. A field in a model’s expected rate and a field extracted from finite recordings are related objects with different measurement uncertainties.9 
[Background] The hippocampal areas CA3 and CA1 contain place cells, but their connections differ:

CA3 supplies major input to CA1 and has substantial recurrent excitation.
CA1 also receives input from entorhinal cortex and has much less local recurrent excitation.

[Background] A grid cell, found in entorhinal cortex, has repeated spatial fields that often form an approximately hexagonal pattern in a two-dimensional arena. These repeated grid fields and a place cell’s irregular multiple fields should be kept distinct. A model explaining CA1’s output maps need not identify where the animal’s position estimate is maintained.10

title: 1  Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value
section: 1.4 A variable spike count at a fixed rate
text:
1.4 A variable spike count at a fixed rate
[Paper] A tuning curve describes expected activity, but a brief spike observation can differ each time the same value is represented. The 2012 model, Materials and Methods, PDF p. 5, uses a Poisson rule for spike generation: conditional on the current network state, neuron \(i\) emits a spike in a sufficiently short interval \(dt\) with probability \(r_i(t)dt+o(dt)\). Spike generation is independent between neurons conditional on their current rates. The rate itself changes with the recurrent input, so this rule does not make complete spike trains independent.
[Background] For a predetermined rate function, a Poisson process has independent spike counts in disjoint intervals; in a short interval, the probability of a spike is approximately the rate multiplied by the interval’s duration. In the recurrent model, the rate depends on network activity; the qualification about whole spike trains appears below.
[Guide derivation] For a constant rate \(r\), the Poisson assumption gives the following law for the number \(K\) of spikes in an interval of length \(\Delta t\):
\[ \Pr(K=k)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}, \qquad \lambda=r\Delta t, \qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots . \]
[Guide derivation: the count law] Divide the interval into \(n\) independent short bins, each with spike probability \(\lambda/n\), where \(\lambda=r\Delta t\). For fixed \(k\), the chance of spikes in exactly \(k\) bins is \(\binom nk(\lambda/n)^k(1-\lambda/n)^{n-k}\). As \(n\) grows, \(\binom nk/n^k\to1/k!\) and \((1-\lambda/n)^{n-k}\to e^{-\lambda}\), giving the displayed Poisson formula. The longer derivation below shows these limits and the mean and variance step by step.
[Interpretation] Here \(\lambda\) is an expected count, so it has no units. For this distribution,
\[ \mathbb E[K]=\lambda, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=\lambda. \]

Derivation: where the Poisson count formula and its variance come from
[Guide derivation] From random spike times to a count. Hold the rate \(r\) fixed over the observation of length \(\Delta t\). Divide that observation into \(n\) short bins of width \(\delta t=\Delta t/n\). Approximate each bin by one independent spike-or-no-spike trial, with spike probability
\[ p=r\delta t=\frac{\lambda}{n},\qquad \lambda=r\Delta t. \]
Take \(n\) large enough that \(p<1\). This construction assumes a constant chance of a spike per unit time and independence between nonoverlapping bins. In the continuous-time limit, the chance of two or more spikes in one bin becomes negligible compared with its width. These are assumptions of the Poisson model, not properties of every recorded neuron.11
A particular pattern with spikes in exactly \(k\) bins and silence in the other \(n-k\) bins has probability \(p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\). There are
\[ \binom nk=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{k!} \]
ways to choose the occupied bins. The numerator chooses them in order; dividing by \(k!=1\cdot2\cdots k\) removes the repeated counting of the same set in different orders. For \(k=0\), there is one empty set and \(0!=1\). Adding the probabilities of all these patterns gives
\[ \begin{aligned} \Pr(K_n=k) &=\binom nk\left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^k \left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n-k}\\ &=\frac{\lambda^k}{k!} \left[\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\left(1-\frac{j}{n}\right)\right] \left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n-k}. \end{aligned} \]
Here \(K_n\) is the count in the finite-bin construction. Keep the observation duration, \(\lambda\), and the integer \(k\) fixed while making the bins finer. The finite product tends to one. The remaining factor tends to
\[ \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n-k} =e^{-\lambda}. \]
For example, its logarithm is \((n-k)\log(1-\lambda/n)\), which tends to \(-\lambda\) because \(\log(1-u)/u\to-1\) as \(u\to0\). Exponentiating gives the displayed limit. The limiting count \(K\) therefore obeys
\[ \boxed{\Pr(K=k)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}.} \]
The exponential comes from requiring silence in all the unoccupied bins. The factor \(\lambda^k\) comes from the \(k\) spike probabilities together with the number of possible bin locations, and \(k!\) corrects repeated counting. In particular, \(e^{-\lambda}\) is the probability of no spikes. A positive expected count can therefore coexist with a silent observation.
[Guide derivation] From the count formula to its mean and variance. Shifting the summation index by one gives
\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[K] &=e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}\\ &=\lambda e^{-\lambda}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^j}{j!} =\lambda, \end{aligned} \]
where the last sum is \(e^\lambda\). Shifting by two similarly gives
\[ \mathbb E[K(K-1)] =e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k=2}^{\infty} \frac{\lambda^k}{(k-2)!} =\lambda^2e^{-\lambda}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^j}{j!} =\lambda^2. \]
Since \(K^2=K(K-1)+K\),
\[ \mathbb E[K^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=\mathbb E[K^2]-\mathbb E[K]^2=\lambda. \]


[Interpretation] The count variance grows with rate, while its size relative to the mean falls. Its relative standard deviation is \(\sqrt\lambda/\lambda=1/\sqrt\lambda\). This is why collecting more independent spikes can improve a rate estimate. It also means that increasing a firing-rate scale does not keep absolute noise amplitude fixed. Comparisons between networks must specify which quantities are held constant.12 

Example: an apparently silent cell and an informative population

[Example] Suppose the expected rate is 20 spikes per second and an observation lasts 50 ms. The expected count is \(20\times0.05=1\). The probability of seeing no spike is \(e^{-1}=0.368\). A silent interval is therefore common even though the expected rate is positive. 
Now suppose 20 conditionally independent cells each have that rate. Their total count is Poisson with mean 20 and standard deviation \(\sqrt{20}=4.47\). The total rate estimate has a relative standard deviation of about 22.4%, compared with 100% for one cell. Population averaging helps because the independent count variances add while the mean signal adds directly. If a common varying input makes several cells’ firing rates rise and fall together, that shared variation will not disappear in the same way.

The two count distributions can be compared on the same rate per cell scale. 







Figure 1.4: Analytic teaching construction for the chapter’s 20 Hz, 50 ms example. The count is Poisson with mean 1 for one cell and mean 20 for 20 conditionally independent cells. Both panels plot the rate per cell \(K/(N\Delta t)\), so both estimates have mean 20 Hz. Their standard deviations are 20 Hz and 4.47 Hz. Each stem is a probability at one possible estimate, rather than a continuous density. Only estimates through 100 Hz are drawn. The independence condition concerns fixed modeled rates, not complete recurrent spike trains.




Dividing the pooled rate estimate by 20 keeps the expected rate per cell fixed, while independent averaging reduces its relative spread. See Poisson count likelihood, SI Eq. S43, p. 9.


[Interpretation] For a predetermined rate function \(r(t)\), the time-varying Poisson model has a count parameter \(\lambda=\int r(t)\,dt\) over the observation. In a recurrent network, however, \(r(t)\) itself depends on earlier spikes. The whole-interval count need not then be Poisson. The useful independence statement is local and conditional: given the current modeled state, the elementary spike-generation noise is independent across cells in the basic 2012 model. The changing state can still produce correlations across time and across neurons. This qualification prevents treating a recurrent Poisson network as a collection of independent complete spike trains. 

[Background] Two other measurements describe different aspects of variability: 

The coefficient of variation, or CV, of interspike intervals, the times between successive spikes, is their standard deviation divided by their mean. A homogeneous Poisson process has exponential intervals and CV equal to one. More regular firing can have CV below one, as in the ocular motor neurons analyzed in 2022.
The count variance divided by mean count is the Fano factor. Its value also depends on the counting interval.

[Interpretation] CV and Fano factor cannot be substituted for one another without additional assumptions.

section: 1.5 Network simulations test whether spike noise moves a stored value
text:
1.5 Network simulations test whether spike noise moves a stored value
[Paper] Can a network keep firing while losing the value it represents? Burak and Fiete (2012) test this by following the spikes and synaptic activations generated by Eqs. 7–9. In two different simulated networks, the represented value wanders while the neural activity persists. The simulation measurements agree with diffusion predicted from each network’s noise-free activity, without fitting a free diffusion parameter. At short times, their prediction is \(\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\theta(0)]\simeq2Dt\), where \(\theta\) labels the represented value and \(D\) is the local diffusion coefficient; this assumes negligible systematic drift and an appropriate time window after fast disturbances relax. The ring and two-unit settings and the measurements are given below. They describe the result in Diffusive Drift, PDF p. 2, show Fig. 2, p. 3, and specify Network Simulations, p. 6.13
[Guide derivation] The update rule below reconstructs the stated simulation method. It shows how the simulated spikes generate changes in the stored value that can be compared with the paper’s theoretical prediction.
[Interpretation] The simulated system. The computer stores one changing activation \(s_i\) for each neuron. It calculates each input \(g_i\) and rate \(r_i\) from the current activations. The connections \(W_{ij}\), input biases \(b_i\), decay time \(\tau\) and transfer function \(\phi\) stay fixed during a run. Constant bias remains present, but no continuing stimulus fixes the remembered value. The model follows recurrent neural activity; it does not calculate muscle forces, membrane-voltage waveforms or learning of connections. This describes the procedure specified under Network Simulations, PDF p. 6.
[Paper] In the ring example, 1,024 neurons are ordered by their preferred angle, the represented angle at which each neuron’s expected firing rate is highest. An activity bump is a localized peak of firing rates across these neurons; its position represents the stored angle. For neuron \(i\), let \(\theta_i=2\pi i/N\) with \(N=1024\). The inhibitory connection from neuron \(j\) to neuron \(i\) is \(W_{ij}=w(\theta_i-\theta_j)\); write \(\delta=\theta_i-\theta_j\) for the difference in preferred angles. The connection profile is
\[ w(\delta)=e^{\cos\delta-1}-e^{0.3(\cos\delta-1)}. \]
The authors use common bias \(b=-2\) and synaptic time constant \(\tau=10\) ms. They compare two firing rules, \(\tau\phi(g)=10e^g\) and \(\tau\phi(g)=0.2[1+\tanh(g+4)]\). They initialize synaptic activations uniformly between 0 and 0.01, then simulate 100 trials of 1,000 s each, with 0.1 ms steps. The plotted theory uses the noise-free steady-state tuning curves, rather than a diffusion coefficient fitted to the noisy trajectory (Fig. 2 and Network Simulations, PDF pp. 3 and 6).
[Interpretation: ring dynamics] The ring describes the ordering of preferred angles, not an anatomical circle of cells. Nearby preferred angles have weak mutual inhibition, while the active group suppresses competing activity farther away. The chosen connection profile and firing rule sustain a localized pattern. Random spike timing can move its peak even while the pattern persists.
How neurons depend on one another. A spike in cell \(j\) increases \(s_j\) by one. Every receiving cell \(i\) then gets an input change \(W_{ij}\), which changes its rate through \(\phi\). Its later spikes feed back into the network. Independent random spike draws at given rates do not make the neurons’ activity independent: earlier spikes change the rates used for later draws.
[Guide derivation] The following update reconstructs one step of the ring simulation, of duration \(h\), from the stated method:

Calculate \(g_i\) and \(r_i\) from all current activations.
Draw a spike indicator \(X_i\): it is one with probability \(r_i h\) and zero otherwise, independently across cells conditional on those current rates.
Reduce the old activation by its decay over the step and add the generated spike:

\[ s_i(t+h)\approx s_i(t)\left(1-\frac{h}{\tau}\right)+X_i. \]
The next step uses these updated activations. This Euler update approximates continuous decay by the current rate of change times the step duration. The one-spike draw requires \(r_i h\) to be small. The authors use \(h=0.1\) ms and \(\tau=10\) ms. Their two-population example requires a spike-count rule suitable for aggregate population activity; the one-spike restriction above belongs to the ring implementation. The simulation chapter gives the full settings and numerical cautions.
[Background] Before comparing simulated motion with theory, we need a measure of how far the represented value moves. Let \(x(t)\) be that value at absolute time \(t\), and let \(\ell\) be the time between two observations, called the lag. The displacement is \(\Delta x=x(t+\ell)-x(t)\). The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the average of \((\Delta x)^2\) over intervals with the same lag. The average can use different starting times along a recording, repeated trials, or both; which intervals can be combined depends on whether their movement statistics are comparable. Squaring prevents leftward and rightward changes from cancelling.
[Interpretation: reading the MSD] For an angle measured in degrees, MSD has units degrees squared. An MSD plot puts lag on the horizontal axis and MSD on the vertical axis. Lag is a duration, not the clock time at which an interval starts. If the statistics change during a trial, the MSD can depend on that starting time as well as on lag.
A straight MSD curve on ordinary axes means that the average squared displacement grows at a constant rate over that range. The zero-mean diffusion model taught in the next chapter gives \(\operatorname{MSD}(\ell)=2D\ell\), where the diffusion coefficient \(D\) is half the rate of displacement-variance growth. The MSD slope is \(2D\) in degrees squared per second. On axes that plot logarithms, a relation \(\operatorname{MSD}\propto\ell^\beta\) has slope \(\beta\): diffusion has slope one, while constant-velocity motion has slope two. A slope alone does not identify the neural cause. Bias, smoothing by muscles, boundaries and the range of lags measured can change the curve.
[Paper] What is measured and compared. At each step, the ring’s angle is read from the preferred angle of the neuron with the highest instantaneous rate. The authors measure how much that angle changes over different time intervals and average the squared changes. They independently calculate the predicted spreading from the same network’s steady activity in the absence of noise. In Figure 2C–D, simulation points agree with these theoretical curves without fitting a free diffusion parameter. The paper also compares the prediction with the bound \(D\ge 1/(2\tau^2J)\), where \(J\) is the internal spike Fisher information rate. The symmetric exponential-transfer example reaches this bound, while the sigmoidal example’s predicted diffusion coefficient lies above its own information bound. Error bars show the standard error over 100 trials. Over short intervals \(t\), the mean squared angle change grows approximately as \(E[(\theta(t)-\theta(0))^2]\simeq 2Dt\), where \(D\) is the model’s local diffusion coefficient. This approximation assumes negligible systematic drift and an interval long enough for transient disturbances to relax but short enough that the local diffusion coefficient stays nearly constant. Over long intervals, wrapping angle differences into a single turn limits the plotted error.
[Interpretation] That flattening does not mean the original angle has been recovered.
[Paper] Figure 2E–G repeats the test with two mutually inhibiting units, which can represent two groups of neurons. Their difference in firing rates represents the stored value. The two-unit model has \(W_{11}=W_{22}=0\), \(W_{12}=W_{21}=-1\), common input \(b=5000\), \(\tau=100\) ms, and linear transfer \(\tau\phi(g)=g\) over its active range. Its steady rates satisfy \(2\tau\bar r_1=b+\theta\) and \(2\tau\bar r_2=b-\theta\). Thus \(\theta=\tau(\bar r_1-\bar r_2)\) labels the persistent state. For this coordinate the paper obtains \(D=b/(2\tau)\), so its short-time prediction is \(\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\theta(0)]\simeq bt/\tau\). The simulation uses 0.4 ms steps over 200 s; the reported displacement statistic averages squared changes of \(r_1-r_2\) over starting times. Writing \(\Delta r=r_1-r_2\), the activation-difference coordinate \(\theta=\tau\Delta r\) gives \(\operatorname{Var}[\Delta r(t)-\Delta r(0)]=\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\theta(0)]/\tau^2\simeq bt/\tau^3\). Thus its rate-difference diffusion coefficient is \(D_{\Delta r}=D_\theta/\tau^2=b/(2\tau^3)\) within the linear active range and the local diffusion regime. Agreement in this second design checks that the prediction is not specific to the ring’s symmetry.
[Interpretation: model and data] Relation to biological data. Figure 2 compares theory with simulated data. It does not fit the memory errors of a recorded animal. The paper motivates persistent activity and variable spiking using earlier experiments, and proposes tests using measured tuning curves. It also notes that eye-position neurons can spike more regularly than a Poisson process, so the Poisson formula cannot be applied directly to those recordings. The 2022 eye-drift study supplies a separate comparison with recorded neural activity and eye motion. Here the established result is narrower: the specified interacting network models produce the memory spreading predicted by the theory.14
The next section explains how measured changes can distinguish shared neural variation from a directional bias when the output is an eye movement.

section: 1.6 Shared neural signals and a biased command leave different signs in eye motion
text:
1.6 Shared neural signals and a biased command leave different signs in eye motion
[Background] This section prepares the covariance and motion analysis in Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022); it is not a result of the 2012 paper. During fixation, a monkey tries to keep looking at a stationary target, yet its eye moves slightly. A changing command from the brain can make many motor neurons change their firing together. Their spikes act on the eye muscles, which turn the eye. An individual motor neuron also adds spike variability of its own. The 2022 paper asks how much of the observed movement follows a shared neural command, and whether that command itself wanders over time.15

[Interpretation] Covariance asks which recorded changes occur together. Displacement statistics ask how far the eye moves and how that movement grows with elapsed time. Neither measurement by itself identifies the neural circuit responsible. 

The shared-signal explanation establishes the covariance and gain model.
[Interpretation] A shared command can survive averaging across neurons. If a common input raises the firing of many motor neurons that pull the eye in the same direction, their effects add. Independent extra and missing spikes partly cancel when those neurons act together.
[Background] Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022) compare measured eye displacement with a displacement predicted from one neuron’s spikes, after converting both to degrees.
[Interpretation] That prediction is an analysis of a recording, not an extra command sent to the muscles. A relationship between the two is evidence to test against a model of shared input and private noise. It does not mean that the one recorded cell causes all the movement. 
[Interpretation] Covariance measures whether two signals tend to be above their own averages together or on opposite sides of those averages. Positive covariance between the two displacements means that above-average changes in the neural prediction tend to accompany above-average changes in eye position. The correlation coefficient, written \(\rho\), expresses this shared variation relative to the spread of each signal. Extra private noise can lower \(\rho\) even when the shared drive has not weakened. The eye-drift calculation explains why a modest correlation need not mean a small shared contribution to movement.

Mathematical definitions: covariance, variance and correlation
[Guide derivation] Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be the two displacements, in degrees, across repeated intervals of the same duration. Subtracting each average leaves its fluctuation. Their covariance is
\[ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])]. \]
Here it has units degrees squared. In general its units are the product of the two signals’ units. Variance is \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,X)\). Expanding the square of a centered sum or difference gives
\[ \operatorname{Var}(X\pm Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)\pm2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y). \]
For nonzero variances, correlation is
\[ \rho_{XY}=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. \]


It is dimensionless and lies between \(-1\) and \(1\). Independence gives zero covariance when these moments exist. Zero covariance alone does not imply independence.  
To see the physical roles, write \(X=g_X S+\epsilon_X\) and \(Y=g_Y S+\epsilon_Y\). Here \(S\) is a shared displacement signal in degrees, the dimensionless gains \(g_X,g_Y\) multiply its contribution in each recording, and \(\epsilon_X,\epsilon_Y\) are private contributions in degrees. If all three random contributions are independent,
\[ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=g_Xg_Y\operatorname{Var}(S),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=g_X^2\operatorname{Var}(S)+\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_X). \]
Increasing private variance increases the denominator of \(\rho\) without increasing the covariance. Changing a gain changes the measured covariance even if the shared source is unchanged. This simple construction explains the need for calibration and explicit noise assumptions. It is not the paper’s full inference model.

[Interpretation] Random wandering differs from a persistent directional error. Apply the displacement measure above to horizontal eye angle \(x(t)\) in degrees, using a lag \(\ell\) in seconds. A random change in the maintained command can move the eye left in one interval and right in another. The average displacement can then be close to zero while individual displacements are large. A persistent imbalance in the command can instead make the average displacement grow in one direction. Muscles smooth the command before it becomes eye movement, so the timescale of the observation also matters.
[Interpretation] The MSD of this eye displacement has units degrees squared. Its two contributions are
\[ \mathbb E[(\Delta x)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(\Delta x)+\mathbb E[\Delta x]^2. \]

[Interpretation] A larger MSD can mean stronger random movement, a larger directional bias, or both. Measuring the mean displacement separately prevents mistaking bias for increased noise. 

Derivation: separating spread from mean displacement
[Guide derivation] Write \(\mu=\mathbb E[\Delta x]\) and \(\eta=\Delta x-\mu\), so \(\mathbb E[\eta]=0\). Squaring and averaging gives
\[ \mathbb E[(\mu+\eta)^2]=\mu^2+2\mu\mathbb E[\eta]+\mathbb E[\eta^2] =\mu^2+\operatorname{Var}(\Delta x). \]
The cross term vanishes because the fluctuations are measured relative to their own mean. This identity needs finite second moments, but no diffusion assumption.

[Interpretation] What changes the physical movement? The model must say which part of the pathway a parameter controls:

Random changes in the stored command: more frequent or larger lasting changes make the stored angle spread faster. The next chapter explains why the diffusion coefficient \(D\) depends on spike variability and the circuit’s response to each spike.



A persistent directional imbalance: this changes the mean displacement. In a constant-velocity approximation, doubling that velocity doubles the mean displacement at a fixed lag and quadruples its squared contribution to MSD.



The gain from command to eye angle: multiplying the command’s contribution to each displacement by a gain \(G\) multiplies that contribution’s variance and MSD by \(G^2\), with the input fluctuations held fixed. Any noise added after that gain needs to be counted separately. A fitted tuning slope, which describes rate as a function of angle, is not by itself a causal muscle gain.
Muscle response time: a slower response smooths rapid command changes more strongly. It changes the short-lag shape of the MSD curve, not just its height. The timing chapter separates this smoothing from growth of noise inside the memory circuit.


[Interpretation] Measurement error is a separate contribution: it changes recorded positions without moving the eye. Independent zero-mean position errors, each of variance \(\sigma_m^2\) and independent of true motion, add \(2\sigma_m^2\) to displacement MSD at nonzero lags. Thus an upward shift in the observed curve need not be a physical increase in movement. The measurement-noise calculation shows the conditions needed to remove it. 
The next chapter follows the proposed source upstream: how a circuit can keep a pattern of activity while random spikes change the angle that pattern represents.

text:
2.1 Results setup: stable activity with a vulnerable stored value
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated images may contain incorrect or missing labels, arrows, formulas and numbers. Use the chapter text and paper links as the source for the explanation.
[Paper: Results setup, p. 2] The 2012 paper begins its analysis with a continuous family of steady neural activity patterns, described by Eq. 1 in Chapter 1. For neuron \(i\), the family obeys \(\bar s_i(\theta)=\tau\phi(\sum_jW_{ij}\bar s_j(\theta)+b_i)=\tau\bar r_i(\theta)\). Here \(\theta\) is the represented value; \(\bar s_i\) and \(\bar r_i\) are steady activation and firing rate; \(W_{ij}\) couples neuron \(j\) to neuron \(i\); \(b_i\) is fixed input; \(\phi\) maps input to rate; and \(\tau\) is the common activation decay time. Each pattern represents a different value. Spike variability disturbs the activity, and the paper asks how the represented value changes as the network responds. Read the Results setup and Fig. 1.
[Interpretation] We first explain the geometry of the persistent states and use a small example to distinguish recovery of activity from preservation of the stored value. The eye mechanics that follow provide biological background. We then introduce the random spreading used in the paper and distinguish it from a spatial map that varies across position.
[Interpretation] Imagine a group of neurons maintaining a pattern that represents an eye angle after a movement command has ended. This explains the setup of the paper’s Results, Eq. 1 and Fig. 1, PDF p. 2. Random spikes disturb that pattern. Recurrent input can correct some disturbances by changing the cells’ firing back toward a persistent pattern. But if a disturbance produces the pattern for a different angle, an ideal memory circuit has no record of which angle was originally intended. Keeping a pattern stable is therefore different from keeping the stored value correct.
[Background] A circuit’s current activities are its state. A dynamical equation specifies how that state changes. A fixed point is a state where the deterministic rate of change is zero, as introduced in the mathematical-tools chapter. It is stable in a direction if a small disturbance in that direction decays.
[Paper] Burak and Fiete model a continuous quantity using a family of persistent states, Results, PDF p. 2. In their Eq. 1, \(\bar s_i(\theta)=\tau\bar r_i(\theta)=\tau\phi(\sum_j W_{ij}\bar s_j(\theta)+b_i)\). For each value \(\theta\), firing replenishes activation at the rate it decays, so the pattern can persist without a cue. The bar denotes the ideal steady state without spike noise. Noisy activation usually lies near, rather than exactly on, this family. The authors assign it the coordinate \(\theta\) of the fixed point it would reach if noise were turned off and deterministic dynamics continued.
[Interpretation] A continuous attractor is a continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and a neutral direction along it. Neutral means that there is no restoring force along that direction in the ideal deterministic model. The family is an attractor manifold. Its dimension counts independent coordinates represented on it, rather than neurons in the circuit. A line attractor has one represented coordinate. A ring can represent a periodic coordinate such as heading.1
[Example] The two-cell model below is a guide construction. The difference between its firing rates represents the angle. Raising both rates equally leaves that difference unchanged. The model’s feedback removes the common increase. Raising one rate while lowering the other changes the represented angle. That second change persists. The calculation makes these two responses explicit. It is not a fitted biological circuit.
[Paper] The authors simulate a two-unit mutual-inhibition network in Fig. 2E–G, PDF p. 3; they specify its dynamics in Network Simulations, p. 6. The weights are \(W_{11}=W_{22}=0\) and \(W_{12}=W_{21}=-1\), both units receive the fixed input \(b=5000\), the activation time constant is \(\tau=100\) ms, and the transfer rule is \(\tau\phi(g)=g\) in the active range. The steady family satisfies \(2\tau(\bar r_1,\bar r_2)=(b+\theta,b-\theta)\), so \(\theta=\tau(\bar r_1-\bar r_2)\). The predicted local diffusion coefficient for \(\theta\) is \(D=b/(2\tau)\); simulated firing-rate differences show the corresponding random spreading. This is a numerical test of the model prediction, not a fit to biological recordings.
[Guide derivation: the two-unit diffusion] In this linear active range, \(\theta=s_1-s_2=\tau(r_1-r_2)\): subtracting the two activation equations cancels their deterministic drift. Conditional on the present state, independent Poisson spikes from the two units give the variance of their difference over \(dt\) as \((\bar r_1+\bar r_2)dt\). Along the steady family, the two displayed rate equations give \(\bar r_1+\bar r_2=b/\tau\). Therefore
\[ \operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\theta(0)]\simeq\frac{b}{\tau}t=2Dt, \qquad D=\frac{b}{2\tau}. \]
The local approximation assumes the active linear regime and neglects boundary effects. For the plotted rate difference rather than \(\theta\), the diffusion coefficient is divided by \(\tau^2\), because \(r_1-r_2=\theta/\tau\).
[Guide derivation] This network has the same geometry as the example above. Over its positive linear firing range, its rate dynamics reproduce the example with common-mode decay rate \(a=2/\tau\), where \(\tau\) is the synaptic decay time. The difference between the rates remains neutral. The network chapter uses synaptic activations to describe this network and gives the conversion between its coordinate and the angle used here. This small network illustrates one possible memory mechanism; the gaze-holding circuit also needs the motor and muscle stages described below.

title: 2  Stable representations can accumulate error
text:
Example: two disturbances to the same stored angle

[Example] Consider a teaching model with two activities \(r_1,r_2\) in spikes per second. Let \(b=40\) spikes per second and let \(k=2\) spikes per second per degree. A stored angle \(\theta\) corresponds to 
\[ r_1=b+k\theta,\qquad r_2=b-k\theta. \]
The fixed points lie on the line \(r_1+r_2=2b\). Restrict attention to angles where both rates remain positive. Define the deviation in their mean activity and the represented angle as
\[ x=\frac{r_1+r_2}{2}-b, \qquad \theta=\frac{r_1-r_2}{2k}. \]
Suppose each activity changes according to
\[ \dot r_1=-a x,\qquad \dot r_2=-a x, \]
where \(a>0\) has units inverse seconds. Adding and subtracting these equations gives
\[ \dot x=-a x,\qquad \dot\theta=0. \]
The first equation has solution \(x(t)=x(0)e^{-at}\), so disturbances in the common activity decay. The second equation retains any angle set by the initial state.
[Interpretation] Increasing \(a\) shortens the recovery time \(1/a\) for the common activity disturbance. It does not correct the angle error, because \(\dot\theta\) is still zero. At fixed rate disturbance, a larger tuning slope \(k\) gives a smaller decoded angle change through division by \(2k\). Changing \(k\) in an actual circuit may also change its dynamics.
At \(\theta=5\) degrees, the rates are \((50,30)\). Compare two disturbances from this same state:

A disturbance of \((+3,+3)\) changes the rates to \((53,33)\). It creates \(x=3\) but leaves the represented angle at 5 degrees. The restoring dynamics return to \((50,30)\).
A disturbance of \((+3,-3)\) gives \((53,27)\), with \(x=0\) and angle \(26/(2\times2)=6.5\) degrees. This state lies on the fixed-point line, so there is no restoring response.

In the second case, the circuit remains coherent while holding the wrong angle.


The two changes occupy different directions in the activity plane. The solid arrow in the figure is the restoring motion produced by the model. The dashed arrow shows the imposed disturbance along the fixed-point line, rather than a deterministic restoring flow.  






Figure 2.2: A common activity disturbance returns to the initial angle, while an along-line disturbance persists as a changed angle. The solid arrow is deterministic recovery. The dashed arrow is an imposed disturbance. This is the guide’s two-activity construction, not experimental data.



[Interpretation] In a larger network, the lasting change depends on its connection weights and cannot always be found by an ordinary perpendicular projection. The network calculation derives the correct projection from the network’s linearized dynamics.

section: 2.2 Sustained muscle tension holds the eye against elastic restoring forces
text:
2.2 Sustained muscle tension holds the eye against elastic restoring forces
[Background] Eye mechanics and the experiments described here give biological context. The folded mechanical calculation is a guide model, not a derivation from the 2012 paper. The eye anatomy and motor pathway explain why holding an angle needs continuing muscle force. We now separate two questions: how that force balances the eye’s elastic pull, and how the brain maintains the command that produces it. The folded calculation answers the mechanical question; the experiments below test the neural one.

Mechanical calculation: what holds an angle, and what only slows its change
[Guide derivation] For a small angular range, a teaching approximation treats the eye as a rotating mass with a spring and viscous resistance. Let \(\phi\) be angle in radians measured from the position where the passive forces balance. Let \(I\) be the rotational inertia, \(B>0\) the viscous resistance, \(K>0\) the angular stiffness, and \(\tau_m(t)\) the net active muscle torque. The angular force balance is
\[ I\ddot\phi+B\dot\phi+K\phi=\tau_m(t). \]
The terms are torques: \(I\) multiplies angular acceleration, \(B\) multiplies angular velocity, and \(K\) multiplies displacement. This is a guide approximation, not the full model of eye mechanics in Ben-Shushan et al. (2022). Real muscle force is nonlinear and depends on activation and movement history.2
At a held angle, \(\dot\phi=\ddot\phi=0\), so
\[ \tau_m=K\phi. \]
The steady angle therefore depends on active torque and stiffness. At fixed torque, doubling \(K\) halves the angle in this linear model. Increasing \(I\) or \(B\) cannot replace the torque required to hold that angle.
If the active torque is removed, neglecting the relatively small inertial term gives
\[ B\dot\phi+K\phi=0,\qquad \phi(t)=\phi(0)e^{-t/\tau_p},\qquad \tau_p=\frac{B}{K}. \]
Greater viscous resistance slows the return; greater stiffness speeds it up at fixed \(B\). Neither creates a choice of indefinitely held angles. Actual eye mechanics include several relaxation times, so \(\tau_p\) is an effective timescale in this simplified calculation.

[Background: neural holding] The brain maintains the holding command. The oculomotor integrator converts movement commands into a maintained eye-position signal. This signal sustains the motor output after a saccade. The name refers to accumulating an eye-velocity command over time into a position signal. In monkeys, Cannon and Robinson (1987) reversibly disrupted brainstem regions involved in this function. Horizontal gaze then drifted back with a time constant of about 0.2 s, compared with more than 20 s before disruption in darkness. The muscles alone did not provide the original persistence.3
Visual feedback can correct gaze errors, and signals from the inner ear help compensate for head motion. Holding can nevertheless continue in darkness, so immediate visual correction is not the whole mechanism. Plasticity is a lasting, experience-dependent change in neural responses or connections. It can adjust how well the holding circuit is calibrated. Major et al. (2004) altered visual feedback in goldfish and trained their gaze holding toward drift or instability over tens of minutes to hours; normal feedback could reverse the change. That is a change in neural control over a longer timescale, distinct from the immediate elastic and viscous response of the tissues. The experiment did not identify the exact cellular learning rule.45
[Interpretation] The attractor model above isolates the neural question of how a circuit can preserve an activity pattern while losing the angle that pattern was supposed to hold. The next section connects those lasting changes to random spreading.

title: 2  Stable representations can accumulate error
section: 2.3 Independent steps with equal duration and variance give linear variance growth
text:
2.3 Independent steps with equal duration and variance give linear variance growth

[Paper] Each extra or missing spike changes synaptic input. After the circuit has corrected the disturbances it can remove, a small change in the represented angle may remain. The authors relate these lasting changes to spreading in Diffusive Drift, PDF p. 2, and supporting text, section III, PDF pp. 6–9. Repeating this process makes trials that began at the same angle gradually spread apart. For negligible systematic drift and a nearly constant local diffusion coefficient \(D\), their short-time result is \(E[(\theta(t)-\theta(0))^2]\simeq2Dt\). The interval must also be long enough for rapidly restoring disturbances to decay. The formula describes local random spreading; at long times, boundaries and changes in \(D\) can alter it.
[Guide derivation] We first model these lasting changes as independent, with no preferred direction and a constant variance per unit time. These are assumptions about the surviving changes, not about complete spike trains. 
[Background] Brownian motion \(W(t)\) models the accumulated effect of many small fluctuations. It starts at zero, has continuous paths and independent Gaussian increments with mean zero, and satisfies \(\operatorname{Var}[W(t)-W(s)]=t-s\) for \(t\geq s\). The independence concerns changes over disjoint time intervals. A physical network need only approach this description over the time and noise scales relevant to the calculation.
[Guide derivation: independent steps] Divide time into intervals of length \(\Delta t\). Let \(\xi_j\) be the change in the represented coordinate during interval \(j\). The calculation assumes:

Increments are independent.
Each increment has mean zero.
Each increment has variance \(2D\Delta t\), where \(D\) has units coordinate squared per time.

Let \(\theta_n\) be the represented value after \(n\) intervals and \(\theta_0\) its starting value. After \(n\) intervals,
\[ \theta_n-\theta_0=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\xi_j, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\theta_n-\theta_0) =\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(\xi_j) =2Dn\Delta t. \]
Writing \(t=n\Delta t\) gives linear variance growth \(2Dt\). The continuous approximation expresses this accumulated change through Brownian motion.

Mathematical model: Brownian motion
In this continuous diffusion approximation,
\[ \theta(t)=\theta(0)+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \mathbb E[(\theta(t)-\theta(0))^2]=2Dt. \]

[Interpretation] The diffusion coefficient \(D\) measures half the rate at which the variance of the stored angle grows. With independent, zero-mean increments of constant variance per unit time,
\[ \operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\theta(0)]=2Dt. \]

[Interpretation] Here \(D\) has units degrees squared per second when \(\theta\) is in degrees. More frequent retained disturbances, or larger ones at the same frequency, increase \(D\). At a fixed delay, doubling \(D\) doubles error variance and multiplies its standard deviation by \(\sqrt{2}\). A single memory trajectory can turn back even while the spread across trials grows. The network calculation obtains \(D\) from the spike variability and the lasting effect of each cell’s disturbance. 
[Background] The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the expected squared change across a lag. In the zero-mean diffusion just defined, MSD is \(2Dt\). A root mean squared displacement is its square root, \(\sqrt{2Dt}\), and has the same units as the represented coordinate. In several dimensions, adding independent coordinate contributions gives an overall MSD of \(2dDt\) only when each of the \(d\) coordinates has the same diffusion coefficient. A paper that defines its diffusion parameter as the entire two-dimensional MSD slope uses a different convention.
[Background] A systematic drift is a nonzero mean velocity. The eye paper’s term “fixational drift” names the eye’s slow motion between saccades, which can be largely random; it does not imply a nonzero mean velocity.

Example: why the noise grows slower than a fixed bias

[Example] Take an illustrative angular diffusion coefficient \(D=0.02\) degrees squared per second. At 0.35 s its variance is \(0.014\) degrees squared and its root mean squared displacement is 0.118 degrees, or about 7.10 arcminutes. At 1 s the root mean squared displacement is 0.20 degrees. 
If there is also a constant bias velocity \(v=0.10\) degrees per second, then
\[ \theta(t)-\theta(0)=vt+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \operatorname{MSD}(t)=v^2t^2+2Dt. \]
The deterministic and random contributions are equal at \(t=2D/v^2=4\) seconds. Their equal contributions there are each \(0.16\) degrees squared. At longer times the bias dominates this unbounded model even though it was small over a short observation. A theory of random diffusion must account separately for this systematic drift.
Sample paths show the irregular motion. Exact displacement scales show how its spread differs from a fixed bias.







Figure 2.3: Simulated Brownian teaching paths and analytic displacement scales for \(D=0.02\) degrees squared per second and \(v=0.10\) degrees per second. The upper paths have zero drift and start at zero. The dashed envelope is the exact root mean squared displacement, not a boundary on individual paths. Below, \(\sqrt{2Dt}\) and \(vt\) are equal at 4 s, when each is 0.40 degrees. Their squares are the separate contributions to the biased model’s MSD. The coordinate is unbounded, and these chosen values are not estimates from animal recordings.




A constant bias grows linearly, so it eventually exceeds the square root growth of the random displacement scale. See Gaussian displacement density, SI Eq. S30, p. 7.


[Interpretation] A later memory state contains earlier accumulated errors as well as new ones. Observing it twice therefore does not give two independent copies of the original memory. The covariance calculation below quantifies the shared history used in the readout chapter. 

Mathematical detail: why two times share accumulated noise
[Guide derivation] Two times along a Brownian path are correlated even though its increments are independent. For \(0\leq s\leq t\), write \(W(t)=W(s)+[W(t)-W(s)]\). The bracketed increment is independent of \(W(s)\) and has mean zero, giving
\[ \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t)) =\operatorname{Var}(W(s))=s, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t))=\min(s,t). \]
The same argument gives covariance \(2D\min(s,t)\) for a diffusing coordinate started at a fixed value. This identity is the intermediate step needed to compute the error from averaging a memory that moves during readout. It also helps explain why smoothing a diffusive input is different from smoothing a stationary noise source.


[Interpretation] A finite range, a periodic coordinate, external feedback, or a position-dependent diffusion coefficient changes long-time behavior. For example, ordinary squared angular distance on a ring cannot keep growing linearly forever. The basic \(2Dt\) result is local or unbounded unless those conditions are treated separately.

section: 2.4 A fixed spatial map differs from a value that wanders over time
text:
2.4 A fixed spatial map differs from a value that wanders over time
[Interpretation: time and space] The memory and eye papers study fluctuations that accumulate as time passes. This comparison connects the 2012 question to Mainali and colleagues’ 2025 place-field model; it is not a result jointly established by the papers. The place-field paper instead starts with a random function of physical position. Once drawn for a cell and an environment, that function is fixed while the animal moves through the map. Revisiting a place evaluates the same expected-rate function, although the actual spikes can still vary from visit to visit.

These two kinds of randomness can occur together. A circuit may maintain a position estimate with time-dependent noise, while downstream cells respond to position through irregular but repeatable tuning curves. Observing irregular spatial maps does not tell us how fast the maintained position drifts. Conversely, finding diffusion of a stored value does not determine the shapes of individual place fields. The following chapters develop the dynamical calculation first, then the experiment that tests a possible consequence, and finally the spatial statistics.6 

The three questions can now be placed beside the kind of variation each paper studies. 







Figure 2.4: Memory loss and eye drift concern changes over time. Place-field statistics concern variation across a fixed spatial map. The eye pathway shows the proposed changing-command mechanism. Original guide schematic based on the three papers, with illustrative traces rather than recorded data.




[Interpretation] The rows compare different questions. They do not establish one circuit connecting all three papers.

title: 3  Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor
text:
3.1 Many weak inputs allow a continuous approximation to spike noise
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated images may contain incorrect or missing labels, arrows, formulas and numbers. Use the chapter text and paper links as the source for the explanation.
[Paper section: “Diffusive Drift due to Ongoing Neural Noise”] Main article, pp. 2–3. This chapter intersperses the supporting derivation with the paper’s diffusion result; the next chapter examines its simulation tests and long-delay implications.
[Paper] A network can keep firing after a stimulus disappears and still lose the value that the stimulus supplied. Burak and Fiete study this distinction in a network whose stable activity patterns form a continuous set. They ask how random spikes move the represented value along that set. For negligible systematic drift, after transients have relaxed and before the local diffusion coefficient \(D\) changes appreciably, their result gives \(\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\Theta]\simeq2Dt\), where \(\theta\) is the represented value and \(\Theta\) its initial value (main article, p. 2).1
[Background] The article states its diffusion result in the main text and derives it in the supporting text. We start with the spike model from Chapter 1, replace the accumulated fluctuations by continuous noise under the authors’ assumptions, and follow one disturbance through the circuit’s return flow. The part of that disturbance that survives changes the remembered value. Adding many such changes gives the diffusion coefficient. We then examine symmetric connections and a two-cell example. The next chapter extends the calculation to longer delays.
Sources: Burak and Fiete (2012), paper and Supporting Information (SI).
[Interpretation] Here the physical network state is the vector of synaptic activations \(\mathbf s=(s_1,\ldots,s_N)\); firing rates follow from that state through the input and transfer function. The memory coordinate is \(\theta\), and its initial value is \(\Theta\). “Stored value” and “represented value” refer to this same coordinate, rather than to the whole activation vector. An observer’s estimate \(\widehat\theta\), obtained from a finite spike sample, can differ from \(\theta\).
[Paper] Noise generally puts \(\mathbf s\) slightly away from the attractor. To assign it a memory coordinate, imagine turning off further noise and following the deterministic return flow. The fixed point reached by this flow is the paper’s instantaneous attractor state; \(\theta\) labels that point. This local definition assumes that nearby states return to a unique point on the continuous family. It uses the circuit’s return dynamics, which can differ from a perpendicular geometric projection. Original definition and Figure 1A, p. 2.
[Background] A bar denotes a noise free steady state, so \(\bar r_i(\theta)\) is neuron \(i\)’s steady firing rate at memory value \(\theta\), and \(\bar s_i=\tau\bar r_i\). The common synaptic time constant is \(\tau\). A one dimensional diffusion coefficient \(D\) has units of memory coordinate squared per time, with the convention \(\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\Theta]=2Dt\) when \(D\) is constant and boundaries do not matter.
[Paper: random and systematic drift] Noise can cause both random wandering and a systematic tendency to move in one direction. The main diffusion calculation assumes that the network is tuned so that systematic drift is absent or negligible. We return to the consequences of relaxing this assumption in Chapter 4. Paper, p. 2.
[Paper: short-time diffusion and Eq. 2] The paper first states the result it will derive: for short times near a chosen state, with negligible systematic drift, the mean squared change in the represented value grows approximately as \(2D(\theta)t\). For symmetric weights, its corrected expression is
\[ 2D(\theta)=\frac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2}{\tau^2[\sum_i r_i'g_i']^2}. \]
Here \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\) describes how neuron \(i\)’s steady firing rate changes with the represented value. Likewise \(g_i'=d\bar g_i/d\theta\) describes the change in its steady total input; \(\tau\) is the synaptic decay time. The formula is local in \(\theta\) and assumes a stable continuous family, weak fluctuations, symmetric weights, and Poisson spike generation independent across neurons conditional on the current rates. The time window must be long enough for stable disturbances to relax and many small contributions to accumulate, but short enough that the local coefficients change little. It is shown in the form given by the authors’ 2017 correction. The original article prints an uncorrected version. The derivation below explains why spike-rate variability and the rate and input slopes enter this expression; the symmetric-weight section derives it explicitly.
[Guide derivation: the diffusion result] The calculation needs one direction along the family of steady patterns and one rule for projecting a disturbance onto the final memory value. The tangent is \(u_i=d\bar s_i/d\theta=\tau r_i'\). Let \(K\) be the linearized return matrix, with \(K_{ij}=-\delta_{ij}/\tau+\phi'(\bar g_i)W_{ij}\). Here \(W_{ij}\) weights neuron \(j\)’s input to neuron \(i\), \(\phi'(\bar g_i)\) is the firing-rate change per unit input at the steady input \(\bar g_i\), and \(\delta_{ij}\) is one when \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. The left zero vector \(\mathbf v\) satisfies \(\mathbf v^TK=0\) and is normalized by \(\mathbf v^T\mathbf u=1\). Its component \(v_i\) is the lasting memory shift caused by a unit activation perturbation in neuron \(i\).
A local spike fluctuation in neuron \(i\) has variance \(\bar r_i\,dt\). Projecting independent fluctuations through \(\mathbf v\) gives \(d\theta=\sum_i v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}\,dB_i\) and \(E[(d\theta)^2]=(\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i)dt=2D\,dt\), with independent Brownian increments \(dB_i\) of variance \(dt\). Thus the general projection result is \(2D=\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i\).
To find \(\mathbf v\) when \(W\) is symmetric, differentiate the steady-rate and input equations: \(\mathbf r'=\operatorname{diag}[\phi'(\bar g_i)]\mathbf g'\) and \(\mathbf g'=\tau W\mathbf r'\). Hence
\[ K^T\mathbf g'=-\frac{\mathbf g'}{\tau}+W^T\mathbf r'=0, \qquad v_i=\frac{g_i'}{\tau\sum_jr_j'g_j'}. \]
The second equality uses \(\mathbf v^T\mathbf u=1\) and assumes a nonzero normalization. Substituting these \(v_i\) into \(2D=\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i\) gives the corrected formula above. This is the local weak-noise calculation; the following sections derive the Gaussian approximation, return matrix and projection step in more detail, and retain the full symmetry calculation beside the example.
[Interpretation] \(D\) measures how quickly the remembered value spreads across repeated noisy realizations. Increasing \(D\) makes the loss of precision faster; a persistent population activity pattern can therefore coexist with a drifting memory.
[Paper] In the weak-fluctuation limit, the authors approximate the summed effects of many spikes by Gaussian noise. In the guide’s Brownian notation, their local noisy activation equation is
\[ ds_i=\left[-\frac{s_i}{\tau}+\phi(g_i)\right]dt+\sqrt{r_i}\,dB_i, \qquad r_i=\phi(g_i),\quad g_i=\sum_jW_{ij}s_j+b_i. \]
\(s_i\) is neuron \(i\)’s synaptic activation, \(\tau\) its decay time, \(g_i\) its total input, and \(r_i\) its firing rate. \(W_{ij}\) weights the activation sent from neuron \(j\) to \(i\), \(b_i\) is its constant input, and \(\phi\) maps total input to firing rate. \(dB_i\) is a Brownian increment with mean zero and variance \(dt\), independent across neurons in this approximation. This is a continuous approximation to the effects of many small spike contributions, not a claim that an individual spike count is continuous. The assumptions and population-size argument appear in Materials and Methods, Eqs. 10–11, PDF pp. 5–6, and supporting text, section I, Eqs. S1–S6, PDF pp. 1–2. The following steps derive this teaching notation.
[Interpretation] Chapter 1 established the spike, activation and firing-rate model, Eqs. 7–9. The connection-matrix explanation establishes the feedback role of those connections. Here we calculate how random spike timing makes activation fluctuate. The connections are tuned to a continuous family of steady patterns, and the Gaussian approximation assumes small fluctuations in each neuron’s total input.
[Guide derivation] To see what the approximation replaces, start from \(ds_i=-s_i\,dt/\tau+dN_i\). The elementary spike-generation noise is independent across neurons conditional on the present rates. The count and Brownian steps below expand the authors’ argument; the individual spike process itself remains discrete.
[Guide derivation] Conditioned on the present rates, the spike-count increments have the following leading-order infinitesimal mean and covariance. This does not assert independence of finite-interval counts when recurrent feedback changes the rates. Let \(\delta_{ij}\) be one when \(i=j\) and zero otherwise:
\[ E[dN_i\mid r_i]=r_i\,dt, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(dN_i,dN_j\mid\mathbf r) =\delta_{ij}r_i\,dt. \]
[Guide derivation] Write \(dM_i=dN_i-r_i\,dt\) for the spike count minus its conditional mean: the surplus or deficit of spikes in this interval. Splitting the count into its mean and this fluctuation gives
\[ ds_i=\left[-\frac{s_i}{\tau}+\phi(g_i)\right]dt+dM_i, \qquad E[dM_i\mid\mathbf r]=0, \quad E[dM_i dM_j\mid\mathbf r]=\delta_{ij}r_i\,dt. \]
[Interpretation] The split into a mean and a fluctuation leaves the individual spike events unchanged. Each spike raises \(s_i\) by one, and \(s_i\) decays between spikes. In the paper’s weak fluctuation approximation, many individually small spike contributions produce only small changes in each neuron’s total input. Their summed fluctuation can then be represented by Gaussian noise with the same leading mean and covariance. Many suitably independent contributions justify the approximately Gaussian sum; matching mean and covariance alone would not establish its distribution. The approximation describes a summed input on a scale where many small contributions matter. A single neuron’s count in an infinitesimal interval remains a discrete spike count.
[Guide derivation] Each receiving cell sees a weighted sum \(g_i=\sum_j W_{ij}s_j+b_i\). With fixed weights, the random part of its input increment is \(\sum_jW_{ij}\,dM_j\). Conditional independence gives its leading covariance with the corresponding increment of receiver \(k\):
\[ \operatorname{Cov}(dg_i,dg_k\mid\mathbf r) =\sum_jW_{ij}W_{kj}r_j\,dt. \]
[Interpretation] The same presynaptic fluctuation can affect both receivers, so their summed inputs can be correlated even when spike generation is conditionally independent. In the weak-fluctuation limit, the paper approximates the summed and synaptically smoothed input as Gaussian. It can represent that approximation using a separate Gaussian drive for each activation variable: multiplying those drives by \(W\) gives the input covariance above.
[Guide derivation] Let \(F_i(\mathbf s)\) be the mean rate of change of neuron \(i\)’s activation. Let \(B_i\) be independent standard Brownian motions. The increment \(dB_i=B_i(t+dt)-B_i(t)\) has mean zero and variance \(dt\). Multiplying it by \(\sqrt{r_i}\) gives the same leading variance \(r_i\,dt\) as the centered spike count. The Gaussian representation of the activation equation is
\[ ds_i=F_i(\mathbf s)dt+\sqrt{r_i}\,dB_i, \qquad F_i(\mathbf s)=-s_i/\tau+\phi\!\left(\sum_jW_{ij}s_j+b_i\right), \]
[Interpretation] The noise coefficient has units \(\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}\), so its product with \(dB_i\) is a dimensionless activation increment. The Brownian drives are a representation of the approximated summed-input dynamics; they are not a claim that an individual neuron’s discrete spike path or its isolated synaptic activation is Gaussian. The supplement derives the equivalent input equations after making the Gaussian approximation (SI Eqs. S2–S5, p. 2).2
[Paper] The supplement makes this limit concrete by replacing each population with \(n\) equivalent neurons and dividing each connection weight by \(n\). A summed input has a mean proportional to \(n/n=1\), while its variance is proportional to \(n/n^2=1/n\). Increasing population size therefore keeps the mean dynamics fixed and reduces input fluctuations. For a ring network, a neuron’s preferred angle is an angle where its tuning curve peaks. Increasing the density of equally spaced preferred angles and scaling weights as \(1/N\) serves the same purpose. The paper’s formulas give the leading terms in this large population limit, rather than exact finite network identities.3
[Paper] Setting noise to zero gives the deterministic rate dynamics \(\dot{\mathbf s}=\mathbf F(\mathbf s)\). The continuous family of fixed points satisfies main Eq. 1, p. 2:
\[ 0=-\frac{\bar s_i(\theta)}{\tau} +\phi[\bar g_i(\theta)], \qquad \bar s_i(\theta)=\tau\bar r_i(\theta). \]
[Interpretation] In the noise free dynamics, recurrent firing balances synaptic decay at each fixed point. The network must be tuned to possess this family. An arbitrary recurrent network will generally have isolated fixed points rather than a whole line or ring of them.

title: 3  Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor
text:
Example: how many small spike inputs approach a Gaussian


[Example] Suppose \(n\) cells fire independently at the same constant rate \(r\) during an interval \(h\), and each spike adds \(1/n\) to a receiving cell’s input. The total number of spikes is Poisson with mean \(nrh\), so the summed input has mean \(rh\) and variance \(rh/n\). When \(nrh\) is large, the standardized total count is approximately Gaussian: no single spike supplies a large share of the summed input. Increasing \(n\) keeps the mean input fixed while shrinking its fluctuations.
This example holds the rates fixed during the interval. In a recurrent network the rates change with the state, so the approximation must also use intervals short enough for the rates to change little. Synaptic activation sums and smooths spike effects over its decay time \(\tau\). The approximation does not say that each cell produces many spikes in every infinitesimal interval.

title: 3  Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor
section: 3.2 The network’s return flow determines the lasting memory change
text:
3.2 The network’s return flow determines the lasting memory change
[Paper] The authors write \(s_i=\bar s_i(\theta)+\delta s_i\) and linearize around the steady pattern. The perturbation obeys \(\delta\dot s_i=\sum_jK_{ij}\delta s_j+\xi_i\), with \(K_{ij}=-\delta_{ij}/\tau+\phi'(\bar g_i)W_{ij}\). Here \(\xi_i\) is spike noise, \(\delta_{ij}\) is one when \(i=j\) and zero otherwise, \(\tau\) is the activation decay time, and \(W_{ij}\) weights activation from neuron \(j\) to \(i\). The derivative \(\phi'(\bar g_i)\) is the change in neuron \(i\)’s firing rate per unit change in its input, evaluated at its steady input \(\bar g_i\). The component that survives after the stable disturbances decay is a displacement along the family of fixed patterns. See supporting text, Eqs. S7–S13, PDF p. 3; the steps below expand the calculation.
[Interpretation] A spike perturbs many aspects of a network’s state. Most of those changes decay as the state returns to the attractor. To calculate memory loss, we need the lasting change: the displacement to a different fixed point. We assume a smooth continuous family with one neutral memory direction, while all other local modes decay. The disturbance must be small enough that the first order response describes the return flow.
[Guide derivation] The supplement’s Eq. S7 writes \(s_i=\bar s_i(\theta)+\delta s_i\). Fix the reference value \(\theta\) while analyzing a small change, so \(\bar s_i\) does not change with time and \(\dot s_i=\delta\dot s_i\). Ignoring noise for a moment, substitute this expression into the deterministic activation equation:
\[ \delta\dot s_i=-\frac{\bar s_i+\delta s_i}{\tau} +\phi\!\left(\bar g_i+\sum_jW_{ij}\delta s_j\right), \qquad \bar g_i=\sum_jW_{ij}\bar s_j+b_i. \]
The change in input to neuron \(i\) is \(\sum_jW_{ij}\delta s_j\). A linearization keeps terms proportional to a small perturbation and drops terms quadratic or higher in it. Taylor expansion of the transfer function gives
\[ \phi\!\left(\bar g_i+\sum_j W_{ij}\delta s_j\right) \simeq\phi(\bar g_i)+\phi'(\bar g_i)\sum_jW_{ij}\delta s_j. \]

[Guide derivation] Substitute this expansion into the previous equation. The terms \(-\bar s_i/\tau+\phi(\bar g_i)\) cancel because the reference pattern is a fixed point. What remains is
\[ \delta\dot s_i=-\frac{\delta s_i}{\tau} +\phi'(\bar g_i)\sum_jW_{ij}\delta s_j. \]
Thus the first term makes a disturbance decay, and the second passes it through the network. Writing \(-\delta s_i/\tau\) as \(-\sum_j\delta_{ij}\delta s_j/\tau\) gives the paper’s matrix \(K\). Restoring the leading Gaussian noise gives the following Brownian form of S8 and S9. Here \(R\) is the diagonal matrix of spike-count variance rates at the fixed point: 
\[ d\delta\mathbf s=K\delta\mathbf s\,dt+R^{1/2}d\mathbf B, \qquad K_{ij}=-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\tau}+\phi'(\bar g_i)W_{ij}, \qquad R=\operatorname{diag}(\bar r_i). \]
[Paper] In the authors’ notation, \(\delta\dot s_i=\sum_jK_{ij}\delta s_j+\xi_i\), with \(K_{ij}=-\delta_{ij}/\tau+\phi'(\bar g_i)W_{ij}\). Their noise covariance is \(\langle\xi_i(t)\xi_j(t')\rangle=\delta_{ij}\delta(t-t')\bar r_i\). This is the linearization and noise rule in S8–S10, p. 3; the display above writes the same leading fluctuations as Brownian increments.4
[Interpretation: network response] The Brownian increment above is an equivalent leading local notation, with noise strengths evaluated at the fixed point. The entries of \(K\) have units of inverse time.
\(K_{ij}\) says how a small change in neuron \(j\)’s activation changes the rate at which neuron \(i\)’s activation evolves, near the reference state. The term \(-\delta_{ij}/\tau\) removes a disturbance as synaptic activation fades. The term \(\phi'(\bar g_i)W_{ij}\) describes recurrent renewal: the connection converts a change in cell \(j\)’s activation into input to cell \(i\), and the local slope of the transfer function converts that input into a rate change. A steeper slope makes this response stronger. Whether a disturbance decays, persists, or grows depends on the combined feedback through the whole network. A stronger connection alone does not establish better memory.
[Guide derivation] To see how the matrix controls time, temporarily switch off the noise and consider a disturbance in a right eigenvector direction \(\mathbf z\), with \(K\mathbf z=\lambda\mathbf z\). If it starts at \(c\mathbf z\), the linear equation gives \(\delta\mathbf s(t)=c e^{\lambda t}\mathbf z\). A negative real eigenvalue makes that component decay; a zero eigenvalue leaves it unchanged. Complex eigenvalues describe oscillating combinations, which decay when their real parts are negative. The attractor calculation assumes all directions away from its neutral tangent decay. Even if the matrix is not diagonalizable, stable components can have transient polynomial factors but still decay when their eigenvalues have negative real parts.
[Paper] The tangent to the fixed-pattern family is \(u_i=d\bar s_i/d\theta=\tau\phi'(\bar g_i)\,d\bar g_i/d\theta\). It is a right zero mode, \(K\mathbf u=0\): a small displacement along this direction changes the represented value without being restored by the noise-free linear dynamics. This is supporting text, Eq. S11, PDF p. 3. The derivative steps below explain why.
[Guide derivation] Moving a little along the fixed point family changes the activation by
\[ \delta\mathbf s\simeq\mathbf u\,\delta\theta, \qquad u_i=\frac{d\bar s_i}{d\theta}=\tau\frac{d\bar r_i}{d\theta}. \]
Differentiate the fixed point equation \(\mathbf F[\bar{\mathbf s}(\theta)]=0\). The chain rule gives
\[ K\mathbf u=0. \]

[Interpretation] Thus \(\mathbf u\) is a right zero eigenvector: a state direction that the linear dynamics neither restores nor amplifies. It is the tangent to the attractor. The other modes must decay for this local family to be attracting. 

[Paper] The left vector \(\mathbf v\) is chosen so \(\mathbf v^T K=0\) and \(\mathbf v^T\mathbf u=1\). It extracts the lasting coordinate displacement: for a small perturbation \(\delta\mathbf s\), \(\delta\theta=\mathbf v^T\delta\mathbf s\). Its components weight the different neurons’ contributions. These are supporting text, Eqs. S12–S13, PDF p. 3. The tilted two-variable example below is a guide construction.
[Interpretation] To extract the lasting memory displacement from a general perturbation, recall the left zero eigenvector, a vector \(\mathbf v\) satisfying 
\[ \mathbf v^T K=0, \qquad \mathbf v^T\mathbf u=1. \]
[Guide derivation] The normalization makes \(\mathbf v^T(\mathbf u\,\delta\theta)=\delta\theta\). If a stable mode \(\mathbf z\) satisfies \(K\mathbf z=\lambda\mathbf z\) with \(\lambda\ne0\), then
\[ 0=\mathbf v^T K\mathbf z=\lambda\mathbf v^T\mathbf z, \]


so \(\mathbf v^T\mathbf z=0\). The left vector discards every decaying mode (SI Eqs. S12–S13, p. 3). More generally, \(\mathbf v^T K=0\) makes \(\mathbf v^T\delta\mathbf s\) constant during the noise-free linear return, even when stable modes are not a complete eigenvector basis. Once those modes decay, this constant is the remaining coordinate change. Consequently the surviving part of a small perturbation is  
\[ \delta\mathbf s_{\mathrm{surviving}} =\mathbf u\,(\mathbf v^T\delta\mathbf s). \]
[Interpretation] This generally differs from a perpendicular geometric projection. Decay can be tilted relative to the tangent. Even symmetric synaptic weights do not usually make \(K\) symmetric, because \(\phi'(\bar g_i)\) multiplies different rows by different amounts.

Example: a disturbance that slides while it decays.
[Example] To see the distinction without a neural simulation, let \(x\) and \(y\) be dimensionless state coordinates and consider the local system
\[ \dot x=ay,\qquad \dot y=-\lambda y,\quad\lambda>0, \qquad [a]=[\lambda]=\mathrm{s}^{-1}. \]
Every point with \(y=0\) is fixed. Starting from \((x_0,y_0)\) gives \(y(t)=y_0e^{-\lambda t}\) and
\[ x(\infty)=x_0+\frac{a}{\lambda}y_0. \]


The response matrix and its neutral vectors are
\[ K=\begin{pmatrix}0&a\\0&-\lambda\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\a/\lambda\end{pmatrix}. \]
The right vector \(\mathbf u\) points along the fixed-point line. The left vector \(\mathbf v\) reads out the final shift: \(\mathbf v^T(x_0,y_0)=x_0+(a/\lambda)y_0\). The decaying eigenvector is \(\mathbf z=(-a/\lambda,1)^T\), with \(K\mathbf z=-\lambda\mathbf z\) and \(\mathbf v^T\mathbf z=0\). A vertical perturbation changes the final memory whenever \(a\ne0\). A perpendicular projection would miss that change. This is a teaching example of the projection geometry, not an additional network used in the paper.  







Figure 3.2: Original guide construction of the tilted decay example, with dimensionless coordinates and \(a/\lambda=1/2\). After an imposed jump from \((0,0)\) to \((0,2)\), the state relaxes toward \((1,0)\). Successive time marks crowd toward that endpoint. This illustrates the left and right zero vector construction in Burak and Fiete (2012), Supporting Text, Section II, pp. 3–4, Eqs. S10–S16. It is not a paper network simulation.




As \(y\) decays, \(x\) changes by one. The left vector extracts that lasting shift.
