title: 3  Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor
section: 3.3 Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient
text:
3.3 Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient
[Paper] Projecting spike fluctuations onto the lasting memory change gives the general local result (supporting text, Eqs. S14–S15, PDF p. 3):
\[ 2D(\theta)=\sum_i v_i(\theta)^2\bar r_i(\theta). \]
Here \(\bar r_i\) is neuron \(i\)’s steady firing rate and \(v_i\) is the lasting shift in the memory coordinate caused by a unit perturbation of its synaptic activation after the other disturbances decay. The rate \(\bar r_i\) supplies the local Poisson spike-count variance; \(v_i^2\) weights how strongly it shifts the stored value. The assumptions include weak fluctuations and independent spike generation conditional on the current rates. The main article’s diffusion discussion, PDF p. 2, states its role in memory loss; the steps below derive it.
[Interpretation] We can now calculate how much random displacement remains after the stable components have relaxed. Each cell’s random spikes disturb its outgoing synaptic activation. The circuit’s return flow determines the lasting shift in memory. This calculation uses the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions, with rates and return flow evaluated near one fixed point.
[Guide derivation] Recall the projection vector \(\mathbf v\) derived above: a small disturbance \(\delta\mathbf s\) leaves a coordinate shift \(\delta\theta=\sum_i v_i\delta s_i\) after the other components decay. Thus \(v_i\) is the lasting change in the represented value per unit change in neuron \(i\)’s synaptic activation, in this local linear model. These projection coefficients describe the whole circuit’s response; they are distinct from its connection weights \(W_{ij}\).
The variance of a linear combination of independent noise increments is the sum of their variances multiplied by squared weights. Let \(K\) be the matrix of the linearized return dynamics, \(R\) the diagonal matrix with entries \(R_{ii}=\bar r_i\), and \(d\mathbf B\) the vector of independent Brownian increments. Multiplying the linear stochastic equation by \(\mathbf v^T\) removes its deterministic return term because \(\mathbf v^TK=0\), leaving
\[ d\theta=\mathbf v^T R^{1/2}d\mathbf B =\sum_i v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}\,dB_i. \]
Here \(\delta_{ij}\) equals one if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. The independent Brownian increments have covariance \(E[dB_i dB_j]=\delta_{ij}dt\), so
\[ E[(d\theta)^2] =\sum_{ij}v_iv_j\sqrt{\bar r_i\bar r_j}\,E[dB_i dB_j] =\left(\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i\right)dt. \]

Matching this to \(2D\,dt\) yields the general local result (SI Eqs. S14–S15, p. 3) 
\[ \boxed{2D(\theta)=\sum_i v_i(\theta)^2\bar r_i(\theta).} \]
[Interpretation: local diffusion] For one memory coordinate, each neuron’s contribution combines its spike variability, \(\bar r_i\), with the squared effect of one activation fluctuation on the final memory, \(v_i^2\). The formula does not say that neurons with high rates necessarily damage memory more: changing rates can also change the tuning curves and the projection coefficients. Those changes must be included in a comparison.5
The result is local in state and leading order in weak noise. The time interval must satisfy two conditions:

It must be long enough for the approximation based on many spike contributions to apply.
It must be short enough that the coefficients do not change substantially as the memory moves.

These conditions justify a local spreading rate.
[Paper] For several memory coordinates \(\theta_\alpha\), the authors define their local displacement covariances by \(\langle\Delta\theta_\alpha\Delta\theta_\beta\rangle=2D_{\alpha\beta}\Delta t\) and obtain \(2D_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i v_i^\alpha\bar r_i v_i^\beta\). Here \(\mathbf v^\alpha\) extracts the lasting change of coordinate \(\alpha\), and \(\bar r_i\) sets neuron \(i\)’s local Poisson noise strength. This result and its conditions are in supporting text, Eqs. S21–S27, PDF pp. 5–6. The paired-vector example that follows is added by the guide.
[Guide derivation] For several memory coordinates \(\theta_\alpha\), choose tangent vectors \(u_i^\alpha=\partial\bar s_i/\partial\theta_\alpha\) and left zero vectors \(\mathbf v^\alpha\) satisfying \((\mathbf v^\alpha)^T K=0\) and \(\sum_i v_i^\alpha u_i^\beta=\delta_{\alpha\beta}\). A unit change of coordinate \(\beta\) moves the activation along \(\mathbf u^\beta\). The projection vector \(\mathbf v^\alpha\) extracts one unit when \(\alpha=\beta\) and zero when the two coordinates differ. It also discards the decaying activity components. Thus \(\sum_i v_i^\alpha\delta s_i\) gives the lasting local change in coordinate \(\alpha\). The same covariance calculation gives
\[ 2D_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i v_i^\alpha\bar r_i v_i^\beta. \]
[Interpretation] In this local approximation, the diffusion tensor is the matrix of displacement covariances divided by twice the elapsed time over a short interval. Its diagonal entries describe spreading in individual coordinates. Its other entries describe how coordinate displacements vary together. Even independently generated spike-count fluctuations can generate coupled motion of the represented coordinates.6


Example: reading two coordinates from tilted directions


[Example] Suppose two coordinate changes alter two activities along \(\mathbf u^1=(1,0)^T\) and \(\mathbf u^2=(1,1)^T\). A change by \(a\) in the first coordinate and \(b\) in the second gives the combined activity change \((a+b,b)^T\). The corresponding projection vectors are \(\mathbf v^1=(1,-1)^T\) and \(\mathbf v^2=(0,1)^T\): their dot products with the combined change give \(a\) and \(b\), respectively. For example, \(\mathbf v^1\) removes the contribution of the second coordinate because \((\mathbf v^1)^T\mathbf u^2=0\). This is a geometric example of the paired vectors; it does not specify a biological circuit.


Systematic drift requires a separate check in the next chapter.

section: 3.4 Symmetric weights express diffusion through tuning curves
text:
3.4 Symmetric weights express diffusion through tuning curves
[Paper] For symmetric weights \(W_{ij}=W_{ji}\), the corrected result is \(2D=\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2/[\tau^2(\sum_i r_i'g_i')^2]\), where \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\) and \(g_i'=d\bar g_i/d\theta\) are the response and input slopes along the memory family. This is main article, Eq. 2, PDF p. 2, with the authors’ 2017 correction; supporting text, Eqs. S16–S18, PDF p. 4, derives it. The derivation below supplies the intermediate steps.

[Interpretation] The general formula uses the projection vector \(\mathbf v\) derived from the network’s dynamics. The distinct matrix \(W\) contains the connection weights: \(W_{ij}\) describes the effect of neuron \(j\)’s synaptic activation on neuron \(i\)’s input. If each pair has equal connection weights in opposite directions, \(W_{ij}=W_{ji}\), can we express \(\mathbf v\) through the tuning curves and neural transfer function? Equal connection weights do not require equal firing responses. We retain the common synaptic time constant, a stable continuous family, and the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions. 
[Guide derivation] The chain rule relates the slope of a response curve to the slope of its input curve. Here let \(g_i'=d\bar g_i/d\theta\) and \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\). Differentiating the fixed point identities gives
\[ r_i'=\phi'(\bar g_i)g_i', \qquad \mathbf g'=\tau W\mathbf r'. \]
With symmetric \(W\), the transpose of the linearized matrix satisfies
\[ K^T\mathbf g' =-\mathbf g'/\tau+W\operatorname{diag}[\phi'(\bar g_i)]\mathbf g' =-\mathbf g'/\tau+W\mathbf r'=0. \]

Therefore \(\mathbf v\) is proportional to \(\mathbf g'\). Its normalization is 
\[ v_i=\frac{g_i'}{\tau\sum_jr_j'g_j'}, \]
because \(u_i=\tau r_i'\). Substituting into the noise projection gives
\[ \boxed{ 2D(\theta)= \frac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2} {\tau^2[\sum_i r_i'g_i']^2}. } \]

[Interpretation] The input slopes \(g_i'\) now determine the projection coefficients, so the diffusion coefficient can be calculated from the tuning curves and transfer function. This follows from SI Eq. S18, p. 4, with \(\bar g_i=\phi^{-1}(\bar r_i)\) wherever the transfer function is invertible over the relevant range. The supplied Early Edition main Eq. 2, p. 2 omits the square on \(g_i'\) in the numerator. Burak and Fiete’s published correction (2017) confirms the squared expression shown here, which also follows from the projection calculation and SI S18. The guide’s checks of other printed formulas remain separate from that correction. The result requires: 

Symmetric weights.
A stable continuous family.
The noise assumptions already introduced.

[Interpretation] The result does not require translation symmetry, in which shifting an activity pattern along the represented coordinate leaves the network dynamics unchanged in form.7

Example: opposite firing changes with constant diffusion.
[Example] Take two mutually inhibiting cells with \(W_{12}=W_{21}=-1\), zero self weights, equal biases \(b\), and \(\phi(g)=g/\tau\) over the positive input range. Its fixed points obey
\[ \bar s_1=\frac{b+\theta}{2},\qquad \bar s_2=\frac{b-\theta}{2},\qquad |\theta|<b. \]
Here \(b\) is an activation bias and \(\theta=s_1-s_2\) is an activation difference. These have different units from the rate baseline and angle in the earlier two-cell example. Writing that example’s baseline as \(b_{\mathrm{rate}}\) and its angle as \(\theta_{\mathrm{angle}}\), the conversion is \(b=2\tau b_{\mathrm{rate}}\) and \(\theta=2\tau k\theta_{\mathrm{angle}}\). The sum \(s_1+s_2\) relaxes to \(b\) at rate \(2/\tau\), while the difference is neutral. Here \(\mathbf u=(1/2,-1/2)^T\), \(\mathbf v=(1,-1)^T\), and
\[ 2D=\bar r_1+\bar r_2=b/\tau. \]
The boxed tuning-curve formula gives the same result. Here \(\bar g_1=(b+\theta)/2\) and \(\bar g_2=(b-\theta)/2\), so \(g_1'=1/2\), \(g_2'=-1/2\) and \(r_i'=g_i'/\tau\). Thus \(\sum_i r_i'g_i'=1/(2\tau)\) and the boxed formula reduces to \(2D=\bar r_1+\bar r_2\).



Although the two firing rates change with the stored value, their summed spike variability is constant. Therefore this network has constant local diffusion throughout its valid range. Near an endpoint, a negative linear rate would be impossible. A physical implementation must alter the transfer rule, and the interior formula alone does not describe that boundary. This model underlies the mutual inhibition example in Fig. 2E–G, p. 3.8   
The plot uses \(b=20\) activation units and \(\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}\).







Figure 3.3: For the chapter’s two mutually inhibiting cells, b = 20 activation units and tau = 0.1 s give opposite changes in the two rates. Their sum remains 200 spikes/s, so local D remains 100 coordinate units squared/s. Open endpoints mark the excluded boundaries. The linear interior model does not determine boundary behavior. These curves are calculated examples, not simulation data.





The dashed rate sum in the upper plot stays fixed, so the lower plot has the same \(D\) at every interior value of \(\theta\).

title: 4  Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays
text:
4.1 Figures distinguish memory motion from readout error and test diffusion
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated images may contain incorrect or missing labels, arrows, formulas and numbers. Use the chapter text and paper links as the source for the explanation.
[Interpretation] A rate of random spreading measured near one stored value does not yet tell us how memory error behaves after a long wait. The value may approach a boundary, wrap around an angular range, or reach a region where the spreading rate differs. A consistent movement of the average value would also change the error without being captured by the rate of random spreading alone.
[Paper section: “Diffusive Drift due to Ongoing Neural Noise”] The main article, pp. 2–3, predicts that short-time memory displacement has variance approximately \(2Dt\) and compares this prediction with two simulated network designs. Here \(D\) is the diffusion coefficient and \(t\) is elapsed time; the relation uses a locally constant \(D\) and negligible systematic drift. Figure 1 also separates this storage error from the error of reading the current state from noisy spikes. The supporting text extends the calculation to long delays and distinguishes spreading from systematic drift.
[Background] Here \(\theta\) is the current stored value and \(\Theta\) its common initial value across trials. The local diffusion coefficient \(D(\theta)\) comes from the weak spike fluctuations derived in the preceding chapter, after stable disturbances have relaxed. For constant \(D\), displacement variance is \(2Dt\) before boundaries matter and when there is no systematic drift.
[Paper] In Fig. 1, PDF p. 2, noise moves the represented value \(\theta(t)\) away from its initial value \(\Theta\) while the activity pattern persists. Its short-time variance is \(2Dt\), whereas an unbiased estimate of the current value from a short sample of duration \(h\) has variance at least \(1/(Jh)\), where \(J\) is the internal Fisher information rate. The two errors answer different questions: how the state moved, and how accurately its present position can be read. Fig. 2, PDF p. 3, compares the calculated spreading with simulated ring and mutual-inhibition networks; under the model assumptions, the predictions match the simulated trajectories without a free diffusion parameter. Materials and Methods, PDF p. 6, specifies the simulations.
[Interpretation: Figure 1] Figure 1A, p. 2 illustrates the coordinate assigned by the return flow in Chapter 3. The green state returns to the black attractor point under noise free dynamics. Comparing the endpoints before and after one noisy interval isolates the retained memory change. The tilted two variable example shows why the return path matters.
In Fig. 1B, an activity bump is a localized peak of population firing rates across the neurons’ preferred angles. The figure separates two sources of error:
The information calculation measures this second uncertainty and relates it to diffusion. The readout chapter then follows observation of the moving state.1
[Paper] Figure 2, p. 3, tests the diffusion calculation in two designs (original figure, PDF p. 3). In the ring, \(W_{ij}=f(\vartheta_i-\vartheta_j)\) depends on the difference between neurons’ preferred angles \(\vartheta_i\) and \(\vartheta_j\), with \(f(\delta)=e^{\cos\delta-1}-e^{0.3(\cos\delta-1)}\). The authors simulate \(N=1024\) neurons, constant bias \(b=-2\) and \(\tau=10\) ms, using 100 trials of 1,000 s with 0.1 ms steps. Their two transfer rules are \(\tau\phi(g)=10e^g\) and \(\tau\phi(g)=0.2[1+\tanh(g+4)]\), where \(g\) is a neuron’s total input and \(\phi\) maps input to firing rate. Both simulations agree with their respective diffusion predictions. The second design uses two mutually inhibiting units without rotational symmetry: \(W_{12}=W_{21}=-1\), \(W_{11}=W_{22}=0\), common input \(b=5000\), \(\tau=100\) ms and \(\tau\phi(g)=g\) in the active range. For the memory coordinate \(\theta=\tau(\bar r_1-\bar r_2)\), the predicted diffusion coefficient is \(D=b/(2\tau)\). Its simulated rate-difference spreading also agrees with the calculation. The individual panels and their measurements are described below.
[Guide derivation: two-unit diffusion] The steady rates satisfy \(\bar r_1+\bar r_2=b/\tau\). Independent Poisson spike fluctuations in the activation difference \(\theta\) have variance \((\bar r_1+\bar r_2)dt\) in an interval \(dt\). Therefore \(\operatorname{Var}[\Delta\theta]\simeq(b/\tau)dt=2Ddt\), which gives \(D=b/(2\tau)\) in the local active region.
[Interpretation: Figure 2] This gives the finite ring a rotational symmetry: shifting the activity pattern by a whole number of neuron positions leaves its dynamics unchanged in form.
Panel B shows the exponential-transfer simulation with 1,024 neurons. Its inset compares activity patterns 10 seconds apart. The horizontal axis orders neurons around the ring; the solid curves show their firing rates, with peaks near 85 Hz. Vertical marks show the spikes emitted in a 10 ms window at each snapshot. The peak moves between snapshots. The main trace follows the represented angle through time, rather than overall activity amplitude. The pattern can persist while its position, and therefore the remembered value, changes.
Panels C and D test different parts of the prediction:
Panel E replaces the ring with two mutually inhibiting units, which can also represent two neural populations. Equal opposing weights and a linear firing rule support a continuous range of rate differences. That difference represents a nonperiodic stored value, rather than an angle that wraps around.
In F the two rates vary in opposite directions. The vertical axis uses \(\mathrm{ms}^{-1}\): one spike per millisecond is 1,000 spikes per second. The large plotted rates can describe the summed activity of each population. They should not be read as ordinary rates of two individual biological neurons.
Panel G asks how far their rate difference changes over a lag. For each lag, the authors square that change and average over starting times in the 200-second simulation. Its vertical axis therefore has units \((\mathrm{ms}^{-1})^2\), while its horizontal axis is lag in seconds. Circles are those measurements; the solid line is the diffusion prediction from Eq. 2. The simulation chapter writes out the measured quantity and its unit conversion. This second design matters because the projection argument does not require rotational symmetry. These are simulations checking the model calculation. They are not direct measurements of memory noise in an animal.2
[Interpretation] Figure 2D shows why the short-time diffusion rate is not the whole long-delay story. The next section derives the effect of angular wrapping and considers state-dependent diffusion.

During storage, the bump’s location has moved away from its initial value \(\Theta\).
At the later time, an observer has additional uncertainty about the bump’s current location because it sees only a finite sample of spikes.

Figure 4.2: Noise-free return flow defines the memory coordinate. The second panel separates movement of that coordinate from uncertainty when reading it. Original Figure 1 from Burak and Fiete (2012), reproduced as an exact artwork excerpt. PDF page 2. Open image at full size.












Panel C compares simulated mean squared angular displacements with the prediction from the tuning curves and transfer function. The gray exponential case and black sigmoidal, or S-shaped, case have different transfer functions, shown in its inset. Circles are simulation measurements; solid lines are the diffusion prediction from Eq. 2. The dashed information bound is a lower limit for the sigmoidal case, not a separate fitted trajectory. A model can lie above its information bound while still agreeing with the derived diffusion formula. Error bars in C and D show the standard error of the mean (SEM): uncertainty in the mean MSD estimated from 100 trials, rather than the spread of individual trial values. In C they are smaller than the symbols.



Panel D follows angular error to longer intervals. Its theoretical curve inserts the predicted diffusion coefficient into the wrapped-angle mean squared error formula, SI Eq. S32. It therefore includes the effect of periodic boundaries rather than extending the short-lag straight line indefinitely. Its flattening uses angular wrapping, not a disappearance of noise. The expected limiting value with the caption’s error convention is \(\pi^2/3\). For a uniform wrapped error \(x\) on \([-\pi,\pi)\), the guide calculates \(E[x^2]=(1/2\pi)\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2dx=\pi^2/3\). The long-delay calculation shows how the wrapped density approaches this limit.

title: 4  Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays
section: 4.2 Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion
text:
4.2 Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion
[Paper] To follow memory over longer delays, the authors evolve the probability density \(p(\theta,t)\) of the represented value. With no systematic drift it satisfies \(\partial_t p=\partial_\theta^2[D(\theta)p]\), starting from \(p(\theta,0)=\delta(\theta-\Theta)\). Here \(\theta\) is the value represented at time \(t\), \(\Theta\) is the value shared by the trials at time zero, and \(D(\theta)\) is the local diffusion coefficient: in a short suitable interval \(dt\) the displacement variance is approximately \(2D(\theta)dt\). The symbol \(\delta\) denotes a point mass at the initial value. For constant \(D\) on an unbounded line the density is Gaussian with variance \(2Dt\); on a ring it is wrapped around the angular range and approaches a uniform density. These results are in supporting text, section III, Eqs. S28–S32, PDF p. 7, with state-dependent cases on pp. 8–9. The guide expands their derivations below.
[Interpretation] Spike fluctuations keep shifting the stored value after the cue has ended. The local diffusion coefficient describes the variance of those shifts after stable disturbances have relaxed. It does not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever: boundaries and variation of \(D\) can change the long time behavior. The derivation first permits \(D\) to vary with the memory state; the line and circle examples then keep \(D\) constant to compare different boundaries.
[Guide derivation] Let \(p(\theta,t)\) be the density of the memory coordinate across repeated trials initialized at \(\Theta\). The Itô convention evaluates a state-dependent noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment. A density equation tracks how small random increments redistribute probability. The calculation below first obtains that equation for a general state-dependent \(D\). Constant \(D\) then gives the line and circle solutions.
[Paper] In the zero-drift diffusion approximation, this density evolves according to the Fokker Planck equation: This is SI Eqs. S28–S29, p. 7.
\[ \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} =\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}[D(\theta)p], \qquad p(\theta,0)=\delta(\theta-\Theta). \]
[Guide derivation: the density equation] To pass from random increments to this equation, choose any smooth function \(F(\theta)\). In a short interval \(dt\), the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment \(2D(\theta)dt\). Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives
\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta] &=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta] +\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\ &=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt). \end{aligned} \]
The higher-order terms vanish faster than \(dt\) in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by \(dt\) gives
\[ \frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta =\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta. \]
Take \(F\) to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from \(F\) onto the product \(Dp\). Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth \(F\), it gives the density equation displayed above.
[Interpretation] Here the Dirac delta denotes a point mass: initially all probability is at \(\Theta\). It differs from the earlier zero-or-one symbol \(\delta_{ij}\).
[Paper] For constant \(D\) on an unbounded line, the Gaussian solution is SI Eq. S30, p. 7:
\[ p(\theta,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}} \exp\left[-\frac{(\theta-\Theta)^2}{4Dt}\right]. \]
[Paper] The unbounded Gaussian has variance \(2Dt\). For an angular coordinate the authors wrap it onto a circle by adding all turns \(k\in\mathbb Z\):
\[ p_{\rm ring}(\theta,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(\theta-\Theta+2\pi k)^2}{4Dt}\right]. \]
This is SI Eq. S31, p. 7. At long times the density approaches \(1/(2\pi)\); individual paths continue moving even though the circular density becomes uniform.
[Guide derivation] Let \(x\) be the angular error in radians. If errors are reported in \([-\pi,\pi)\), their limiting mean squared value is
\[ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2dx=\frac{\pi^2}{3}. \]

[Interpretation] The flattening of a ring network’s error curve can therefore occur while its local noise mechanism remains unchanged. It reflects the bounded way angular error is reported.3 
[Example] For \(D=0.5\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}\), the guide’s plots show how the density and squared error change with delay.







Figure 4.4: With the same constant D = 0.5 rad²/s, wrapped Gaussian error densities widen toward 1/(2π). The unbounded line has mean squared error 2Dt. Reporting angular error in \([-\pi,\pi)\) instead gives a mean squared error that approaches π²/3. The flattening comes from the bounded error convention while local diffusion stays constant. All curves are analytic teaching calculations, not paper simulation data.




[Interpretation] As the wrapped density approaches uniform, its mean squared error approaches \(\pi^2/3\). The unbounded line error keeps growing.
[Paper] For zero-drift diffusion with a state-dependent \(D(\theta)\), the supplement obtains \(\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\Theta]=2D(\Theta)t+D(\Theta)D''(\Theta)t^2+\cdots\) at short times, where \(D''\) is the second derivative with respect to the represented value. The first term is the local diffusion result; curvature in \(D\) produces the displayed next correction. The supplement then gives a mutual-excitation example and tests it in simulation (Eqs. S33–S41, PDF pp. 8–9; Fig. S1, PDF p. 10). The guide shows the moment calculation and identifies an apparent factor discrepancy in the printed example.
[Guide derivation] When \(D\) varies with state, the zero drift stochastic equation is \(d\theta=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dB\) with the Itô convention. Here \(dB\) is a Brownian increment of mean zero and variance \(dt\). Under conditions that remove boundary terms, the density equation gives
\[ \frac{d}{dt}E[\theta]=0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}(\theta)=2E[D(\theta)]. \]


[Guide derivation] To obtain these identities, multiply the density equation by \(\theta\) or \((\theta-\Theta)^2\), integrate over \(\theta\), and integrate by parts twice. The second derivatives of these functions are respectively zero and two, giving the two identities. A similar calculation for the smooth function \(D\) gives \(dE[D]/dt=E[DD'']\). Expanding at \(t=0\) therefore yields  
\[ \operatorname{Var}(\theta) =2D(\Theta)t+D(\Theta)D''(\Theta)t^2+O(t^3). \]
[Paper] This is SI Eq. S37, p. 8.4
[Paper] In this Poisson model, the rate of random spreading can change as the stored value changes, because the current firing rates set the spike-count variability. The supplement illustrates this dependence with mutual excitation, \(W_{12}=W_{21}=1\), biases \((b_0,-b_0)\), and the same linear transfer rule. The fixed activation states are \((\theta+b_0/2,\theta-b_0/2)\), and the transfer rule is \(\phi(g)=g/\tau\). The supplement prints \(D(\theta)=\theta/(2\tau)\) in Eq. S40 and a variance \(\Theta t/(2\tau)\) in Eq. S41 (supporting text, Eqs. S38–S41, PDF p. 9). With the stated convention \(\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)=2Dt\), these two printed expressions differ by a factor of two. The guide independently checks this discrepancy below; it is not an author-issued correction.
[Guide derivation] For this example the tangent and left projection vectors are \(\mathbf u=(1,1)^T\) and \(\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T\).




[Interpretation] Here \(\theta\) is an activation coordinate, not an angle, and both steady rates are positive only when \(\theta>|b_0|/2\). When both activations rise together, each cell raises the other’s firing enough to replace the extra synaptic decay. This common increase persists and changes the stored value. A disturbance in their difference instead decays toward the difference set by the biases. Larger \(\theta\) raises both firing rates and hence both Poisson count variances. Because the projection weights stay fixed in this example, more of that variability remains as memory error.    
[Guide derivation] For the mutual excitation network, substituting \(v_1=v_2=1/2\) into the diffusion formula gives
\[ 2D=\frac{1}{4}(\bar r_1+\bar r_2)=\frac{\theta}{2\tau}, \qquad D=\frac{\theta}{4\tau}. \]
[Interpretation] A state dependent \(D\) need not produce a nonlinear increase of variance with time. If \(D\) is linear in \(\theta\), then \(E[D(\theta)]=D(E[\theta])=D(\Theta)\), so the variance remains linear while the process stays within the model’s valid domain. The implied variance for this network is \(\Theta t/(2\tau)\), agreeing with SI Eq. S41, p. 9 and the slope tested in Fig. S1, p. 10. SI Eq. S40 instead prints \(D=\theta/(2\tau)\). Under the convention used throughout this guide, that displayed value differs by a factor of two from the direct projection and S41. This is the guide’s independent check, not an author-issued correction.5


Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S1








Figure 4.5: Mutual excitation produces a wandering state and approximately linear variance growth in the plotted simulation. Original Figure S1 from Burak and Fiete (2012), reproduced as an exact artwork excerpt. PDF page 10. Open image at full size.

section: 4.3 A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift
text:
4.3 A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift
[Paper] Systematic motion is a nonzero mean displacement, distinct from trial-to-trial spreading. To estimate a possible noise-induced drift, the supplement compares Itô and Stratonovich interpretations of \(d\theta=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dB\). The Itô version with no written drift has zero mean increment, whereas the Stratonovich version has mean increment approximately \(\tfrac12 D'(\theta_0)\,dt\) when started at \(\theta_0\). The authors offer this difference as a scale estimate, not an exact derivation of the microscopic neural process (supporting text, Eqs. S19–S20, PDF pp. 4–5). The explicit convention conversion below is a guide derivation.
[Guide derivation] For state dependent \(D\), where the coefficient is evaluated affects the process. The Stratonovich convention uses midpoint evaluation in its limiting increments. With the same written coefficient and zero written drift, it describes a different process from the Itô equation. If noise is stronger at larger values, a positive step samples stronger noise at its midpoint and a negative step samples weaker noise. Their average no longer cancels. Converting to Itô form expresses this effect as a drift \(D'/2\). The supplement uses the difference to estimate a possible scale of noise induced drift, not to identify the exact drift of every neural network.
[Guide derivation: midpoint evaluation] Write \(b(\theta)=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\) in a region where \(D\) is positive and smooth. A Stratonovich step uses \(\Delta\theta=b(\theta+\Delta\theta/2)\Delta W\). Expand about the starting value and use \(\Delta\theta\simeq b\Delta W\) in the correction:
\[ \Delta\theta\simeq b\Delta W+\frac{b'}2\Delta\theta\Delta W \simeq b\Delta W+\frac{bb'}2(\Delta W)^2. \]
Since \(E[\Delta W]=0\) and \(E[(\Delta W)^2]=\Delta t\), the added mean step is \(bb'\Delta t/2\). Differentiating \(b^2=2D\) gives \(bb'=D'\), so the mean velocity is \(D'/2\). The squared-increment term contributes to the limit as the time steps shrink. If \(D\) is constant, the correction vanishes. This expansion explains the convention change. It does not determine which convention a microscopic neural process produces.
[Interpretation] Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction. Both can occur, and the derivation of \(D\) alone does not settle the second question.



[Paper] The paper assumes that the network is tuned to eliminate systematic drift, meaning a nonzero mean velocity along the attractor. A deterministic mismatch in weights can create such a velocity. In addition, state dependent noise and curved network dynamics can create a small mean motion even if the noise free model has an exact continuous attractor. The supplement explains that deriving the exact mean motion requires the microscopic jump process, beyond the leading variance calculation (SI “Systematic drift,” pp. 4–5).6   
[Interpretation: random and systematic drift] With \(D\) of order \(1/N\), random displacement over \(dt\) is of order \(\sqrt{dt/N}\), while such a mean displacement is of order \(dt/N\).
The variance calculation captures the leading random term. Small changes to weights or biases might cancel the mean drift. They cannot remove the random increments by subtracting a known average. A known mean drift can in principle be accounted for by a decoder, but any actual implementation must know that drift and respect the domain and boundary conditions.
[Paper] In the Discussion, PDF p. 5, the authors suggest that an information–diffusion bound may extend beyond independent Poisson spikes, including systems with correlated noise. Their established basic-model bound is \(D\ge 1/(2\tau^2J)\), with \(J\) the internal information rate and \(\tau\) the synaptic time constant. They do not derive a universal correlated-noise formula there: extending the principle and identifying the appropriate information and time scales are conjectures to be tested.
[Guide derivation] The independence assumption also has a precise scope. Newly generated spike-count fluctuations are conditionally independent given the present state. Shared recurrent fluctuations can still correlate the observed spike trains over time. An extra source of correlated fluctuations would change the projection formula to \(2D=\mathbf v^TQ\mathbf v\), where \(Q\,dt\) is their increment covariance. A matching calculation of information would need the probabilities of joint spike patterns. The paper discusses such correlated models as future extensions (Discussion, p. 5, paragraph beginning “Our spiking model”). It does not prove that every correlated spiking model obeys its Poisson formulas.7
[Interpretation] The diffusion calculation gives \(D\) from spike variability and the network’s return flow. The paper next asks how much information the same neural activity provides about the represented value, and how that information limits \(D\).

title: 5  Spike information limits memory stability
text:
5.1 Internal Fisher Information: rate slopes and spike variability
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated images may contain incorrect or missing labels, arrows, formulas and numbers. Use the chapter text and paper links as the source for the explanation.
[Paper] Burak and Fiete ask how well the network’s own spikes distinguish nearby values of the memory it currently holds. They calculate this internal Fisher information rate \(J\) and show that it limits how slowly the memory can diffuse: \(D\ge1/(2\tau^2J)\). Here \(D\) is the local diffusion coefficient of the represented value and \(\tau\) is the synaptic time constant. The result assumes a stable continuous family of states, weak fluctuations, Poisson spike generation that is independent across neurons conditional on the current rates, and a common synaptic time constant. It holds for arbitrary connection weights and transfer functions under those assumptions. These are the second and third steps of the argument, after Chapter 3’s diffusion calculation. See main Eqs. 3–4, PDF pp. 2–3.1
[Guide derivation: the bound] For neuron \(i\), let \(\bar r_i(\theta)>0\) be its noise-free steady rate and \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\) its change per unit memory coordinate. Let \(v_i\) be the lasting change in the represented value caused by a unit perturbation of that neuron’s outgoing activation, after the other disturbances relax. Chapter 3 gives \(2D=\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i\) and the normalization \(\tau\sum_i v_i r_i'=1\). The paper’s information rate is \(J=\sum_i(r_i')^2/\bar r_i\). Applying Cauchy–Schwarz to \(v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}\) and \(r_i'/\sqrt{\bar r_i}\) gives
\[ \frac{1}{\tau^2}=\left(\sum_i v_i r_i'\right)^2 \le\left(\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i\right) \left(\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}\right)=2DJ. \]
For positive \(J\), dividing by \(2J\) gives \(D\ge1/(2\tau^2J)\). The next section derives why this expression for \(J\) measures information in the spikes; the inequality section develops the bound and its interpretation in more detail.
[Interpretation: information and memory] Imagine a receiving neuron trying to estimate the angle from those spikes. A larger sample can help it distinguish nearby activity patterns, but the represented angle may move while it collects them. The paper relates the information in the spikes to motion within the memory network; the later readout calculation asks what an observer can recover after a delay.
The bound describes each network under the paper’s stated assumptions. When comparing two networks, we must also say what changes and what stays fixed. More information permits a lower minimum diffusion rate; it does not guarantee that a particular network achieves that minimum.
[Background] We retain the memory coordinate \(\theta\), initial value \(\Theta\), firing rate \(\bar r_i(\theta)\), synaptic time constant \(\tau\), and diffusion convention \(\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)=2D\Delta t\). The network projection determines which activity changes remain as changes in the stored value.
[Paper] In “Internal Fisher Information,” main Eq. 3, PDF pp. 2–3, the information per unit time in the network’s spikes about its current attractor coordinate \(\theta\) is
\[ J(\theta)=\sum_i\frac{1}{\bar r_i(\theta)}\left(\frac{d\bar r_i(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2. \]
Here \(i\) indexes neurons, \(\bar r_i(\theta)\) is neuron \(i\)’s steady firing rate at \(\theta\), and \(d\bar r_i/d\theta\) is how fast that rate changes as the represented value changes. This expression assumes positive rates and conditionally independent Poisson spike counts during an observation short enough that the state is effectively fixed. If that observation lasts \(h\) seconds, its information is approximately \(I_h(\theta)=hJ(\theta)\). Supporting text section IV, Eqs. S42–S44, PDF pp. 9–10, develops this expression. The steps below derive it here.
[Background] Let \(h\) be the observation duration in seconds and \(n_i\) neuron \(i\)’s spike count. For this calculation, hold \(\theta\) effectively fixed during observation and assume positive rates. Once that state is fixed, the model treats the counts from different cells as independent Poisson variables. Their mean and variance are both \(\bar r_i(\theta)h\). This is a short observation approximation to the recurrent circuit, whose state can otherwise move while spikes are collected.
[Guide derivation] For neuron \(i\), write \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\) for the change in its steady firing rate per unit change in the represented value \(\theta\). During an observation lasting \(h\), the expected spike count is \(h\bar r_i\). The count sensitivity is the change in that expected count per unit change in \(\theta\): its value is \(h r_i'\). For a small change \(\delta\theta\), the expected count therefore changes by approximately \(h r_i'\,\delta\theta\). The Poisson count variance, our measure of count noise here, is \(h\bar r_i\). Write \(I_{h,i}(\theta)\) for the information in neuron \(i\)’s spike count during the window \(h\). Dividing the squared count sensitivity \((h r_i')^2\) by that variance gives
\[ I_{h,i}(\theta)=\frac{(h r_i')^2}{\bar r_i h} =h\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}. \]
[Paper] For this Poisson model, the squared count sensitivity \((h r_i')^2\) divided by the count variance \(h\bar r_i\) is exactly the single-cell Fisher information \(I_{h,i}\) over duration \(h\). Here \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\) is the rate slope, and \(\bar r_i\) is that cell’s steady firing rate at the represented value \(\theta\). For counts independent across neurons, the single-cell contributions add to give \(I_h\), the information in the population’s counts; dividing by \(h\) gives the information rate \(J\). This is the authors’ Eq. 3, PDF p. 2:
\[ I_h(\theta)=h\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}=hJ(\theta), \qquad \boxed{J(\theta)=\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}.} \]
[Background] To compare possible angles, hold the observed spike counts fixed and vary the proposed \(\theta\). A likelihood compares proposed parameter values by the probability each assigns to those observations. It is not, by itself, a probability distribution over the proposed angles.
[Guide derivation: likelihood and Fisher information] Suppose four spikes were recorded during the short observation. A candidate angle predicting four spikes on average and one predicting sixteen assign different probabilities to that same count. Evaluating those probabilities as the proposed angle changes gives the likelihood. The following calculation makes the link to the paper’s information rate explicit.
For the full vector \(\mathbf n\) of observed counts, independence gives
\[ p(\mathbf n\mid\theta)=\prod_i \frac{[\bar r_i(\theta)h]^{n_i}e^{-\bar r_i(\theta)h}}{n_i!}. \]
Taking the logarithm turns the product into a sum. With \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\),
\[ \ell(\theta)=\log p(\mathbf n\mid\theta) =\sum_i\{n_i\log[\bar r_i(\theta)h]-\bar r_i(\theta)h-\log(n_i!)\}, \]
\[ S(\theta)=\frac{d\ell}{d\theta} =\sum_i\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i}(n_i-\bar r_i h). \]
The score \(S\) is the slope of the log likelihood with respect to the proposed value. A positive score means that a small increase in the proposed angle makes the observed count pattern more likely. A negative score favors a small decrease. At the true value, these signed slopes average to zero over repeated spike samples because \(E[n_i]=\bar r_i h\). Squaring before averaging prevents the positive and negative slopes from canceling:
\[ E[S^2] =\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i^2}\operatorname{Var}(n_i) =h\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}. \]
Products of centered counts from different cells average to zero by conditional independence. The remaining terms use \(\operatorname{Var}(n_i)=\bar r_i h\). The general definition used here is \(I_h(\theta)=E_\theta[S(\theta)^2]\): the mean squared score over data generated at \(\theta\). The supplement instead writes the equivalent expected curvature of the log likelihood. When the positive rates are twice differentiable and differentiation can pass through the sum over counts,
\[ I_h(\theta)=E_\theta[S(\theta)^2] =-E_\theta\!\left[\frac{d^2\ell}{d\theta^2}\right] =h\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}. \]
The equality follows by differentiating the identity \(\sum_{\mathbf n}p(\mathbf n\mid\theta)=1\) twice: \(\partial_\theta^2p=p[(\partial_\theta\ell)^2+\partial_\theta^2\ell]\), so the probability-weighted average of the sum in brackets is zero. This is the connection to SI Eqs. S42–S44, PDF pp. 9–10. It gives \(I_h=hJ\) in the Poisson model. Other spike distributions can give a different expression.
[Interpretation: Fisher information] A receiving neuron gets spikes, not a label saying which angle the memory circuit represents. Fisher information is large when a small change in the stored value changes the expected counts strongly compared with their random spread. It measures how readily the probabilities of possible observations distinguish nearby values. The ratio of squared count sensitivity to count variance is exact here because the counts have the assumed Poisson distribution; it is not the general definition for arbitrary spike statistics.
The comparison is local: a cell can distinguish small changes near one angle yet respond identically at two distant angles. A large \(J\) alone cannot resolve that distant ambiguity. \(J\) is the information rate about the circuit’s current represented value, before choosing a decoder. “Internal” means the value is maintained by the circuit rather than supplied by a present stimulus. With angles in radians, \(I_h\) has units \(\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\) and \(J\) has units \(\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}\); neither is a number of stored bits.2
[Interpretation: implications] The expression explains three ways a code can change:
A rate peak has zero slope, so that cell contributes no information about infinitesimal angle changes at that point under this positive-rate Poisson formula. Other cells with nonzero slopes can still inform the population’s estimate. The following curves show where each cell’s contribution comes from.
Both curves change by the same amount with angle. The higher curve has more Poisson count noise, which explains its lower information away from the peak. The likelihood calculation above shows why the squared count sensitivity divided by count variance is Fisher information for this Poisson model.
[Interpretation] Information limits how accurately the value can be read. An estimator is a rule that turns observed data into an estimated value, here \(\hat\theta(\mathbf n)\). It is unbiased if repeating the observation at a fixed true value gives estimates whose average equals that value. Individual estimates can still be wrong. Their variance measures their trial-to-trial spread around that average.
[Background] The Cramér Rao bound puts a lower limit on that variance for estimators unbiased across the nearby values, under the smoothness conditions used in the proof:
\[ \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\ge\frac{1}{I_h(\theta)}=\frac{1}{hJ(\theta)}.} \]
[Interpretation] Four times the information halves this lower bound on the standard deviation. It does not promise that a particular decoder reaches the bound. The paper uses an approximation in which the spike sample is informative enough for a suitable estimator to approach it.3
[Background] A prior distribution describes which parameter values were more plausible before observing these spikes. A decoder that uses this additional knowledge, or accepts a systematic error, has a different error problem. The bound above also needs care near boundaries or zero firing rates. For sensory estimation the same Poisson formula applies when the rates depend on a present stimulus, whereas here they depend on a maintained internal value.
[Interpretation] Finally, \(I_h=hJ\) assumes that the represented value stays effectively fixed during observation. Longer collection in a freely evolving memory circuit also allows that value to wander. The next section links \(J\) to this physical wandering, and the readout chapter treats what changes when the observer tries to recover the initial value. See main Eq. 3, p. 2 and SI Section IV, pp. 9–10.

5  Spike information limits memory stability

title: 5  Spike information limits memory stability
text:
Example: extra background spikes can make an angle harder to read.

[Example] Consider an illustrative neuron with rate 40 spikes per second at the angle of interest. Near that angle, each degree of change increases its rate by 20 spikes per second. In a 0.1-second observation, its mean count is 4 and its standard deviation is \(\sqrt{4}=2\) spikes. The mean count changes by 2 spikes per degree. Thus the change per degree is as large as one standard deviation of the count noise. 

Now add 120 spikes per second of background firing that does not depend on angle. The mean count becomes 16 and its standard deviation becomes 4 spikes. The change per degree remains 2 spikes. The same angle change is now half as large relative to the noise. Squaring that comparison gives one quarter of the original information. More spikes have made this particular comparison worse because they added variability without increasing the response to angle. 
These numbers describe a chosen local tuning curve and a Poisson count model, not measured neurons. Multiplying the entire tuning curve would be a different change: it would increase the slope as well as the mean rate.



Doubling a cell’s tuning slope while keeping its rate fixed gives four times the local information.
Adding constant background firing while keeping the slope fixed lowers its contribution, as in the example.
Adding another independently fluctuating, tuned cell adds information. Shared fluctuations require a different calculation.









Figure 5.2: Analytic teaching curves \(r_A(\theta)=5+35e^{-\theta^2/(2w^2)}\) and \(r_B(\theta)=r_A(\theta)+20\), in spikes per second, with chosen width \(w=0.6\) rad. The rates have the same derivative. Their individual Poisson information contributions \((r_i^{\prime})^2/r_i\) vanish at the rate peak, where the slope is zero, and are positive on the flanks. Adding baseline firing raises the count noise without changing the slope, reducing local information. These are illustrative tuning curves, not recorded neurons or a demonstrated attractor network.












Derivation: why inverse information bounds estimation variance
[Guide derivation] Assume the same estimator is unbiased throughout a neighborhood of \(\theta\), the probabilities vary smoothly with \(\theta\), and differentiation can be exchanged with summation over the counts. Differentiate \(E_\theta[\hat\theta]=\theta\):
\[ 1=\sum_{\mathbf n}\hat\theta(\mathbf n)\partial_\theta p(\mathbf n\mid\theta) =E[\hat\theta S] =E[(\hat\theta-\theta)S]. \]
The last equality uses \(E[S]=0\). The Cauchy Schwarz inequality says that the squared average product of two variables is no greater than the product of their mean squares. Applying it to estimation error \(\hat\theta-\theta\) and score \(S\) gives
\[ 1\le E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]E[S^2], \qquad \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\ge\frac{1}{Jh}.} \]
Unbiasedness makes the mean squared error equal to the variance. Dividing by \(E[S^2]=I_h=hJ\) gives the bound when that information is positive and finite.

title: 5  Spike information limits memory stability
section: 5.2 Information-Diffusion Inequality: a lower bound on memory diffusion
text:
5.2 Information-Diffusion Inequality: a lower bound on memory diffusion
[Paper] In “Information-Diffusion Inequality,” main Eq. 4, PDF p. 3, the authors bound the diffusion coefficient \(D\) using the information rate \(J\):
\[ D(\theta)\geq\frac{1}{2\tau^2J(\theta)},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad 2D(\theta)J(\theta)\tau^2\geq1. \]
\(D\) measures the local rate at which the represented value \(\theta\) spreads across trials: its short-time displacement variance is \(2D\,dt\). \(J\) is the internal Fisher information rate carried by spikes about the current \(\theta\), and \(\tau\) is the common synaptic time constant. This is the paper’s bound for its weak-noise model, not a claim about all memory circuits. The supporting text, section V, PDF pp. 10–12, Eqs. S45–S56, gives the proof. The shorter derivation below spells out the scalar case.
[Paper] The network has no access to its exact firing rates as noiseless numbers. Its recurrent input is built from the same random spikes that an external observer sees. Burak and Fiete suggest thinking of maintenance as estimating the state again from roughly one synaptic time constant \(\tau\) of the network’s own spikes. For a state held fixed, that sample would supply information \(J\tau\), so even an ideal locally unbiased estimate would have variance at least \(1/(J\tau)\). Comparing this with the variance \(2D\tau\) accumulated over the same time suggests \(2D\tau\ge1/(J\tau)\). One factor of \(\tau\) comes from collecting information; the other comes from accumulating displacement variance. This is the authors’ heuristic; the calculation below establishes the inequality from the projection assumptions. Paper, p. 3.
[Guide derivation] Cauchy Schwarz bounds a dot product by the product of the two vector lengths. Here \(u_i=d\bar s_i/d\theta\) is the change in neuron \(i\)’s steady activation per unit change of the memory value; \(v_i\) gives the lasting change in that value per unit perturbation of \(s_i\). Their normalization \(\sum_i v_i u_i=1\) fixes the dot product, while the two lengths measure diffusion and information. The rate slope is \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\), and \(\tau\) is the common synaptic decay time. From the projection and diffusion calculation,
\[ 2D=\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i, \qquad u_i=\tau r_i', \qquad \sum_i v_i u_i=1. \]
Define two vectors \(x_i=v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}\) and \(y_i=r_i'/\sqrt{\bar r_i}\). Their dot product is
\[ \sum_i x_i y_i=\sum_i v_i r_i'=\frac{1}{\tau}. \]

Their squared lengths are \(\sum_i x_i^2=2D\) and \(\sum_i y_i^2=J\). Cauchy Schwarz therefore gives 
\[ \left(\frac1\tau\right)^2 \le\left(\sum_i x_i^2\right)\left(\sum_i y_i^2\right)=2DJ, \]
or
\[ \boxed{D\ge\frac{1}{2\tau^2J}.} \]

[Interpretation: the bound] This proof uses the general left vector formula, so symmetric weights are unnecessary. It is a shorter teaching reconstruction of the scalar proof in SI Section V. Its assumptions are those used to derive \(D\) and \(J\). It is not a general statement about all possible noisy memory systems.4 
The units agree: \(\tau^2J\) has units of time per coordinate squared, so its reciprocal has the units of diffusion. Small internal information forces a large minimum diffusion coefficient. Large information allows small diffusion, but does not guarantee it.

title: 5  Spike information limits memory stability
section: 5.3 Generalizations: multiple coordinates, time scales, and noise laws
text:
5.3 Generalizations: multiple coordinates, time scales, and noise laws

[Paper] The authors extend the information–diffusion inequality to several coordinates (supporting text section V, PDF pp. 11–12). If the information matrix \(J\) is invertible, the matrix form is
\[ 2D\succeq \tau^{-2}J^{-1}. \]
Here \(D\) is the diffusion matrix: \(2D_{\alpha\beta}dt\) gives the local covariance of coordinate displacements over \(dt\). The matrix \(J\) measures how coordinate changes affect the spike probabilities. The symbol \(\succeq\) means that the difference between the two matrices is positive semidefinite: the bound applies to the variance of every linear combination of coordinates. The calculation below specifies the matrix entries and assumptions.
[Interpretation] A spike can shift more than one coordinate, so the information and diffusion must describe combinations of shifts. For coordinate \(\alpha\), \(\mathbf u^\alpha=\partial\bar{\mathbf s}/\partial\theta_\alpha\) is the change in steady activations per unit coordinate change, and \(\mathbf v^\alpha\) extracts the lasting change in that coordinate from a small activation disturbance. The multi-coordinate projection derives these vectors. 
[Guide derivation] For \(m\) memory coordinates \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m\), let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) identify coordinates and \(i\) identify neurons. The steady rate \(\bar r_i\) depends on all the coordinates; \(\partial_{\theta_\alpha}\bar r_i\) is its slope with respect to coordinate \(\alpha\), holding the others fixed. The information is a matrix,
\[ J_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i \frac{\partial_{\theta_\alpha}\bar r_i\, \partial_{\theta_\beta}\bar r_i}{\bar r_i}. \]
[Interpretation] The matrix calculation assumes that every independent small coordinate change can be distinguished through a change in rates, so \(J\) is invertible. If a nonzero change in coordinates leaves every rate unchanged to first order, that direction has zero local information and \(J\) is singular. For example, if all cells depend locally on \(\theta_1+\theta_2\) only, increasing \(\theta_1\) while decreasing \(\theta_2\) by the same amount is invisible to this local readout. Larger changes or other observations could still distinguish those values.
[Guide derivation] Here \(D\) is the diffusion matrix: \(2D_{\alpha\beta}dt\) is the local covariance of coordinate displacements over \(dt\). The matrix bound \(2D\succeq\tau^{-2}J^{-1}\) means that every linear combination of coordinate displacements obeys the corresponding variance lower bound. Here \(A\succeq B\) means \(\mathbf z^T(A-B)\mathbf z\ge0\) for every real vector \(\mathbf z\). To derive it, recall \(u_i^\alpha=\tau\,\partial_{\theta_\alpha}\bar r_i\) and form \(N\times m\) matrices \(U_{i\alpha}=u_i^\alpha/\sqrt{\bar r_i}\) and \(V_{i\alpha}=v_i^\alpha\sqrt{\bar r_i}\), where \(N\) is the number of neurons and \(m\) the number of memory coordinates. Let \(I\) be the \(m\times m\) identity matrix. Then
\[ U^TV=I,\qquad U^TU=\tau^2J,\qquad V^TV=2D. \]
To establish the bound, set \(Q=V-U(U^TU)^{-1}\). Expanding \(Q^TQ\) and using \(U^TV=I\) gives
\[ Q^TQ=V^TV-(U^TU)^{-1} =2D-\tau^{-2}J^{-1}\succeq0. \]
For any coordinate direction \(\mathbf z\),
\[ \mathbf z^TQ^TQ\mathbf z=\|Q\mathbf z\|^2\ge0. \]
The squared length cannot be negative. This is what the matrix inequality says: after subtracting the lower-bound matrix, the remaining variance is nonnegative in every coordinate combination.
[Interpretation] The bound controls every combination of stored coordinates, including coupled directions that separate scalar bounds would miss. If \(J\) is singular, this ordinary inverse formula cannot be used.5
[Paper] The main article’s “Generalizations” and “Saturation” discussion, PDF pp. 3–4, gives a further case. In the studied model with a synaptic time constant \(\tau\) and a membrane time constant \(\tau_m\), the scalar lower bound becomes \(D\ge 1/[2(\tau+\tau_m)^2J]\). The larger time constant contributes most when the two are very different. The supplement develops this case in section VII, Eqs. S84–S92, PDF pp. 17–19, after its readout analysis. The calculation below specifies the model and separately identifies apparent printed-equation discrepancies.

[Interpretation] The time constant in the inequality comes from the dynamics that carry an activation fluctuation into a lasting memory change. If both synaptic activation and firing rate adjust gradually, which time constant matters? 
[Background] In the basic model, the firing rate changes immediately when the summed input changes. Assume symmetric weights. The extension instead lets neuron \(i\)’s firing rate \(r_i\) approach \(\phi(g_i)\) gradually, with time constant \(\tau_m\), while synaptic activation \(s_i\) still decays with time constant \(\tau\). Here \(g_i\) is its total input and \(\phi\) maps input to a firing rate.
[Background] The filtering introduction explains the continuous-time white-noise convention. The symbol \(\xi_i\) writes the spike fluctuation as a drive in a rate-of-change equation. White noise is an ideal zero-mean input whose fluctuations at different times are uncorrelated. Its continuous-time strength is defined through a delta-function covariance, rather than a finite variance at an individual time. In the Gaussian approximation used here, \(\xi_i\,dt=\sqrt{r_i}\,dB_i\), with independent Brownian increments \(dB_i\). Conditional on the current rates, its contribution over \(dt\) has variance \(r_i\,dt\), the same spike-count variance as in the basic model. The two dynamical equations are
\[ \dot s_i=-s_i/\tau+r_i+\xi_i, \qquad \tau_m\dot r_i=-r_i+\phi(g_i). \]
[Guide derivation] In this symmetric weight extension, the linear state is \((\delta\mathbf s,\delta\mathbf r)\): changes of synaptic activations and firing rates from their steady values. In the matrix below, \(W\) contains the connection weights, \(I\) is the identity matrix, and \(\operatorname{diag}(\phi')\) has the transfer slopes \(\phi'(\bar g_i)\) on its diagonal. The deterministic matrix is
\[ A=\begin{pmatrix} -I/\tau&I\\ \operatorname{diag}(\phi')W/\tau_m&-I/\tau_m \end{pmatrix}. \]

The right tangent is \((\tau\mathbf r',\mathbf r')\). Write the left zero vector as \((\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\). The second block of \((\mathbf a^T,\mathbf b^T)A=0\) gives \(\mathbf b=\tau_m\mathbf a\). The first then gives \(W^T\operatorname{diag}(\phi')\mathbf a=\mathbf a/\tau\), so symmetry again permits \(\mathbf a\propto\mathbf g'\). Normalizing its dot product with the right tangent yields 
\[ a_i=\frac{g_i'}{(\tau+\tau_m)\sum_jg_j'r_j'}. \]

Only the \(s\) block receives the modeled spike noise, so \(2D=\sum_i a_i^2\bar r_i\). The symmetric formula consequently becomes 
\[ 2D=\frac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2} {(\tau+\tau_m)^2[\sum_i g_i'r_i']^2}, \qquad 2D\ge\frac{J^{-1}}{(\tau+\tau_m)^2}. \]

[Interpretation] The sum of the two time constants replaces \(\tau\). When one time constant is much larger, it supplies most of that sum. This result belongs to the two stage model and noise placement just described. The paper does not prove that arbitrary collections of biological time constants can always be added.6 
[Paper] For the alternative in supporting text section VII, PDF p. 19, the authors report that the same information–diffusion inequality holds with additive white Gaussian noise of constant variance. For symmetric weights, a linear transfer function is sufficient to attain equality; for Poisson noise, an exponential transfer function is sufficient. The comparison depends on the noise model and how information is defined for its observations.
[Guide derivation] To explain the comparison, the guide replaces Poisson spike-count fluctuations with independent Gaussian noise of constant strength \(q>0\):
\[ ds_i=F_i(\mathbf s)dt+\sqrt q\,dB_i. \]
[Guide derivation] For an observation interval of length \(h\), the observed mean rate is now Gaussian with variance \(q/h\). Here \(q\) is the constant noise strength specified above. Repeating the score calculation gives \(J=\sum_i(r_i')^2/q\), while projection gives \(2D=q\sum_i v_i^2\). The same Cauchy Schwarz proof yields \(2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}\). Equality requires \(v_i\propto r_i'\) because all cells have the same noise strength. In a symmetric network \(v_i\propto g_i'\), so a linear transfer rule supplies the condition by keeping \(\phi'(g)\) constant across participating inputs.
[Interpretation] In the Poisson case, variance grows with rate and an exponential rule is a sufficient way to attain equality. The pointwise projection condition remains the general criterion. A linear-family example below shows that an exponential transfer rule is not necessary for every family. The difference between these sufficient classes follows from the noise weighting, not from linearity being universally preferable.7


[Guide derivation] This explicit \(q\) formulation is a teaching reconstruction that keeps dimensions and the noise normalization visible. The supplement’s Gaussian subsection establishes the change in equality condition. Here the matched noise and likelihood derivation supplies all factors of \(q\) and \(\tau\) without requiring the reader to infer a normalization from SI Eqs. S94–S95.

title: 5  Spike information limits memory stability
section: 5.4 Saturation of the information-diffusion inequality: when is the bound attained?
text:
5.4 Saturation of the information-diffusion inequality: when is the bound attained?
[Interpretation] Reaching the bound requires the network’s retained response to each cell’s spike noise to match that cell’s information about memory. Specifically, the cell’s lasting effect \(v_i\) must be proportional to its rate slope divided by its rate, \(r_i'/\bar r_i\). A cell that adds retained noise without helping distinguish nearby values prevents equality. In a symmetric network, the transfer function determines whether those effects have the required proportions.
[Guide derivation] Equality requires the two vectors in the proof to be proportional:
\[ v_i=c\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i} \quad\text{for every contributing cell}, \qquad c=\frac{1}{\tau J}. \]

Cells with zero tuning slope cannot contribute extra projected noise if equality is to hold. In a symmetric network, \(v_i\) is proportional to \(g_i'\), and \(r_i'=\phi'(\bar g_i)g_i'\). At each state, the participating cells therefore need a common value of \(\phi'(\bar g_i)/\phi(\bar g_i)\). A sufficient way to satisfy this at all states is to choose that ratio equal to the same constant \(k\) throughout the relevant input range. Solving 
\[ \frac{d}{dg}\log\phi(g)=k \]
gives \(\phi(g)=A e^{kg}\).
[Paper] The authors show that \(\phi(g)=A e^{kg}\), with positive constants \(A\) and \(k\), attains \(D=1/(2\tau^2J)\) for symmetric weights and Poisson noise under the other model assumptions. They also state the converse: that saturation requires an exponential transfer function. The guide’s example below tests that converse separately; the claimed inequality itself is not in question.8
[Interpretation] The guide’s check below finds that further restrictions are needed for that converse: the common ratio may depend on the current memory state. This check is separate from the authors’ published correction to Eq. 2.

Check: equality can also hold with a linear transfer rule

[Guide derivation] The mutual-excitation example shows why equality does not require an exponential transfer rule under the stated general assumptions. This check is the guide’s calculation, not an author-issued correction. Set its bias \(b_0=0\) and use the linear rule \(\phi(g)=g/\tau\) on positive inputs. Its fixed states are \(s_1=s_2=\theta>0\), with \(\mathbf u=(1,1)^T\) and \(\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T\). Both rates are \(\theta/\tau\), and both rate derivatives are \(1/\tau\). Therefore 
\[ 2D=\frac{\theta}{2\tau},\qquad J=\frac{2}{\tau\theta},\qquad 2DJ=\frac{1}{\tau^2}. \]


Equality holds throughout this family even though its transfer rule is linear. At each state both cells receive the same input, and the ratio \(\phi'/\phi=1/\theta\) changes between states. To conclude that equality forces an exponential rule, we need additional restrictions linking the participating input values across cells and states. Continuous variation of the represented value alone does not supply them. This qualification concerns the source’s claim that equality requires an exponential rule. The information–diffusion inequality remains unchanged.  


Example: the same diffusion with a looser information bound.


[Example] Return to the two cell mutual inhibition model, now using \(b=200\) activation units and \(\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}\). This changes the illustrative bias from the Chapter 3 plot, while retaining the same network equations. The model units can also represent groups of neurons, whose rates are sums over their cells. The memory coordinate is an activation difference, not an angle. Here \(\bar r_1=(b+\theta)/(2\tau)\) and \(\bar r_2=(b-\theta)/(2\tau)\). At \(\theta=0\) both rates are \(1000\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Their slopes are \(\pm1/(2\tau)=\pm5\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) per activation unit. Thus  
\[ J=\frac{25}{1000}+\frac{25}{1000}=0.05, \qquad D=\frac{b}{2\tau}=1000. \]
Here \(J\) has units of inverse activation unit squared per second, and \(D\) has activation unit squared per second. The bound is \(1/(2\tau^2J)=1000\), so equality holds at this balanced state. At \(\theta=100\), the rates become \(1500\) and \(500\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\), while their slopes stay \(\pm5\). Now
\[ J=\frac{25}{1500}+\frac{25}{500}=\frac1{15}\simeq0.06667, \qquad \frac1{2\tau^2J}=750. \]
The actual diffusion remains \(1000\). The inequality is strict because the projection coefficients \(v_i\) no longer satisfy the equality condition \(v_i\propto r_i'/\bar r_i\) for the two unequal rates. These coefficients describe how spike fluctuations shift the stored value; they are distinct from the synaptic connection weights \(W_{ij}\). This also shows why equality at a special state does not force the transfer function to be exponential on its whole domain. A constant lower bound attained everywhere and an accidental equality at one state are different claims.







Figure 5.3: Analytic teaching calculation for the chapter’s mutual inhibition example, with \(b=200\) activation units and \(\tau=0.1\) s. The coordinate \(\theta\) is an activation difference. For positive rates \(r_{1,2}=(b\pm\theta)/(2\tau)\), \(J=2000/(40000-\theta^2)\) while \(D=1000\) activation units squared per second. The lower bound \(1/(2\tau^2J)\) equals \(D\) at \(\theta=0\) and falls to 750 at \(\theta=100\). Higher local information permits a lower diffusion bound but leaves the actual diffusion unchanged in this model. The plotted range stays inside the positive-rate domain \(|\theta|<200\).




The gap at \(\theta=100\) shows why a lower minimum allowed by the inequality is not a reduction in the network’s actual diffusion. See Diffusion bound, Eq. 4, p. 3.

section: 5.5 Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed
text:
5.5 Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed



[Paper] The authors report that increasing the population size \(N\), the tuning-curve firing rates, or the synaptic time constant \(\tau\) reduces diffusion in the comparisons made after Eq. 2, PDF p. 2. For the population-size comparison they scale connection weights as \(1/N\), holding each cell’s total input and tuning curve fixed; in the symmetric formula this gives \(D\propto 1/N\). The paper also relates tuning width to information in its discussion, PDF p. 4. The calculations below spell out the controlled comparisons and alternatives.


[Interpretation] The inequality compares diffusion and information for the same network. To compare different networks, we must say what stays fixed. Otherwise an apparent benefit of a parameter change may come from changing another property at the same time. Each comparison below states which tuning curves and inputs stay fixed as neuron number, firing rate, or synaptic decay time changes.  


[Guide derivation] Increasing \(N\) while retaining the same distribution of tuning curves and scaling weights as \(1/N\) keeps individual inputs and rates fixed. The sums in the symmetric formula scale as \(N\) in the numerator and \(N^2\) in the denominator. Consequently \(D\propto1/N\), while \(J\propto N\). This expands the paper’s network-size comparison; it is not a promise about adding arbitrary neurons.  
[Guide derivation] If all tuning rates are multiplied by a factor \(a\), their slopes are also multiplied by \(a\), so \(J\mapsto aJ\). For equality achieving exponential networks, \(D\mapsto D/a\) immediately follows. The same scaling follows from the symmetric diffusion formula when the change preserves \(g_i'\) up to a common scale and preserves the tuning geometry. For a general fixed nonlinear transfer rule, multiplying rates need not preserve those quantities or even the attractor. The paper’s rate comparison is made with the tuning shapes and appropriate network scaling held under control.9
[Guide derivation] Changing \(\tau\) while holding the rate tuning curves and their input relation fixed gives \(D\propto\tau^{-2}\) in the symmetric formula. Maintaining those curves requires retuning the network, because \(\bar s=\tau\bar r\).


[Interpretation] At fixed rates, longer-lasting spike effects give larger mean activations. The activation difference between two nearby stored values also grows in proportion to \(\tau\). In this symmetric comparison, one spike’s unit activation change therefore produces a smaller displacement of the stored value: the projection coefficients scale as \(1/\tau\). The spike variance per unit time stays fixed, so the retained variance scales as \(1/\tau^2\).  

[Example] In contrast, holding activation curves and dimensionless weights fixed in the linear two cell example makes rates scale as \(1/\tau\), so \(D=b/(2\tau)\propto\tau^{-1}\). 
[Interpretation] These two statements concern different controlled model comparisons. A longer synaptic time constant lowers the diffusion coefficient in both; the power of \(\tau\) depends on what the comparison holds fixed.


[Paper] The paper links tuning width to memory persistence: under the sensory-coding comparison it cites, narrower tuning improves persistence for a one-dimensional attractor, whereas broader tuning improves it in three dimensions (main article, PDF p. 4).10
[Guide derivation] The guide reconstruction below makes one such comparison explicit: for tuning width \(w\) in dimension \(d\), \(J\propto w^{d-2}\), so a network saturating the information bound has \(D\propto w^{2-d}\) when peak rates, population density and tuning shape are fixed. These exponents belong to that reconstruction, not to every possible tuning family.  
[Guide derivation] Assume preferred positions \(\mathbf c\) have uniform density \(\rho\) in a \(d\) dimensional stimulus or memory space. Away from boundaries, let identical tuning curves have fixed peak rate \(a\) and a common shape \(f\):
\[ \bar r_{\mathbf c}(\boldsymbol\theta) =a f[(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w]. \]
The width \(w\) is varied while \(a\), \(\rho\), and the shape \(f\) are fixed.
[Guide derivation] For one coordinate direction \(\alpha\), replace the population sum by an integral and substitute \(\mathbf z=(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w\):
\[ J_{\alpha\alpha} \simeq\rho\int d^d c\, \frac{a^2w^{-2}(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{af} =\rho a w^{d-2} \int d^d z\,\frac{(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{f}. \]

[Interpretation] Two factors determine how information changes with tuning width: 

The volume element contributes \(w^d\) because broader fields recruit more neurons.
The squared slope contributes \(w^{-2}\) because broader curves change more slowly.


[Guide derivation] Each diagonal entry therefore scales as \(J_{\alpha\alpha}\propto w^{d-2}\). Now restrict the tuning shape \(f\) to depend only on distance from its center. Uniformly distributing those centers makes every coordinate direction equivalent: off-diagonal information terms vanish, and all diagonal entries are equal. For an exponential network that attains the matrix bound, \(D_{\alpha\alpha}=1/(2\tau^2J_{\alpha\alpha})\propto w^{2-d}\). 
[Interpretation] The resulting comparisons are:

Narrower curves help in \(d=1\).
Width has no leading effect in \(d=2\).
Broader curves help in \(d=3\).


[Interpretation] These conclusions change under another resource constraint. Fixing the total population spike rate instead of peak rate makes \(a\propto w^{-d}\), giving \(J\propto w^{-2}\) in every dimension. Sparse coverage, a large baseline rate, finite boundaries, correlated noise, or a width too small for the population integral can also change the comparison. Attaining equality means the network reaches the diffusion lower bound for its information rate and synaptic time constant. Minimizing diffusion still requires deciding how much information the allowed architecture and firing budget can supply. 




[Interpretation] If an external stimulus produces the same tuning curves as the network’s input free memory states, the sensory and internal Fisher information are equal. In a symmetric exponential network, maximizing this information then improves sensory estimation and minimizes memory diffusion together. This is why the paper suggests that one circuit could support both sensory estimation and memory storage. The mathematical compatibility does not establish where a particular animal stores a memory, and the equality of tuning curves must be checked rather than inferred from the shared formula.11
