title: 6  Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed
text:
6.1 Optimal Observation Time for Memory Readout: separating storage and readout error
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated images may contain incorrect or missing labels, arrows, formulas and numbers. Use the chapter text and paper links as the source for the explanation.
[Paper] Burak and Fiete ask how long an observer should collect spikes when reading a memory that keeps diffusing. For their ideal observer, the characteristic observation time is \(L^*=1/\sqrt{2DJ}\le\tau\): \(D\) is the memory diffusion coefficient, \(J\) is the spike information rate and \(\tau\) is the synaptic time constant. Readout variance continues to fall with observation time but approaches the limit \(\sqrt{2D/J}\). The inequality for \(L^*\) follows from the information–diffusion bound and assumes full access to the spikes. The authors state the result in “Optimal Observation Time for Memory Readout,” PDF p. 4, and develop it in supporting text section VI.
[Guide derivation: useful observation time] Let \(L\) be time spent observing after the recall cue, and let \(P(L)\) be the precision, the reciprocal of the variance, of the ideal estimate of the state at that cue. In the local Gaussian approximation, take \(D\) and \(J\) as constant and assume that the future state increments and observation errors are independent. With no informative prior, \(P(0)=0\). Over a short bin \(h\), state diffusion adds variance \(2Dh\) when the later information is carried back to the earlier state, while the bin’s spikes add precision \(Jh\). Thus
\[ P(L+h)=Jh+\frac{P(L)}{1+2DhP(L)},\qquad \frac{dP}{dL}=J-2DP^2. \]
Separating variables and using \(P(0)=0\) gives \(P(L)=\sqrt{J/(2D)}\,\tanh(\sqrt{2DJ}L)\). Its reciprocal is the readout variance, \(\sqrt{2D/J}\,\coth(\sqrt{2DJ}L)\), with \(\tanh z=(e^z-e^{-z})/(e^z+e^{-z})\) and \(\coth z=1/\tanh z\). The argument of \(\tanh\) becomes one at \(L^*=1/\sqrt{2DJ}\); the information–diffusion bound \(2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}\) then gives \(L^*\le\tau\). The sections below derive the recursion and its assumptions step by step.
[Interpretation] When a recall cue arrives, the stored value has already moved. Later spikes can help estimate the value present at that cue, but they cannot reveal the particular random displacements that occurred before it. Waiting for more spikes also allows the network to move further. The question is how much observation helps when the value being read keeps changing.
[Background: the readout problem] Separate the error accumulated during storage from the error of reading the cue state. We first derive the ideal observer’s limit, then examine the equal-weight observer and partial spike access. Finally, we compare the results with the paper’s printed error claim.
As before, the memory coordinate is \(\theta\), its initial value is \(\Theta\), and its displacement variance is \(2Dt\) for constant diffusion coefficient \(D\) without boundaries or systematic drift. The storage delay \(T\) ends at the recall cue. The observation interval \(L\) begins there. The spike information rate \(J\) measures how clearly nearby present states can be distinguished, and \(\tau\) is the basic model’s common synaptic time constant.
[Paper] The readout section, main PDF p. 4, starts with an initial value \(\Theta\), a storage delay \(T\), and an observer who samples spikes for duration \(L\) after the recall cue. For the locally translation-invariant model with constant \(D\) and independent future fluctuations, the total estimation variance separates as \(V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L)=2DT+V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)\). The first term is the variance of displacement accumulated before the cue; the second is the error in estimating the state present at the cue from the later spikes. The supporting text, section VI, PDF pp. 12–13, derives this decomposition; the guide spells out the conditions below.
[Interpretation] At time \(T\), a recall cue arrives. The observer must estimate the original value \(\Theta\), but only has access to future spikes. The network has already diffused during storage.
[Paper] To solve the readout problem, the supplement approximates the likelihood for the state in each short bin of duration \(h\) by a Gaussian with variance \(1/(Jh)\) (supporting text, PDF p. 13). Here \(J\) is the information rate of the observed spike population. The approximation requires an informative spike sample, not literally infinitely many independent observations in an arbitrarily short physical bin.
[Guide derivation] Let \(x=\theta(T)\) and index subsequent bins by \(k\), starting with \(\theta_0=x\). The increment \(\eta_k\) is the change in the stored value between bins. The observation \(y_k\) summarizes the bin’s population spikes as an estimate of \(\theta_k\), and \(\epsilon_k\) is its estimation error. In this approximation, these increments and errors are independent, zero-mean Gaussian variables. This treats the noise moving the state as separate from the noise in the observed counts, excluding the dependence that can arise when the same spikes both change recurrent activation and supply the observation. The equivalent observation model is
\[ \theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\eta_k, \qquad y_k=\theta_k+\epsilon_k, \]
\[ \operatorname{Var}(\eta_k)=2Dh, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_k)=\frac1{Jh}. \]
[Interpretation] The value \(y_k\) is inferred from spikes, not an additional directly measured physical coordinate. The continuous limit is a convenient mathematical description of the many spike, weak fluctuation regime. It does not assert that an arbitrarily short physical bin already contains enough spikes for a Gaussian fit. The derivations below are exact within this local Gaussian readout model.1
[Guide derivation] For an unbounded coordinate with constant \(D\) and no drift, let \(x=\theta(T)\) and let \(\widehat x\) estimate that state from later spikes. Write the storage displacement as \(s=x-\Theta\) and the readout error as \(e=\widehat x-x\). In this section \(s\) denotes a scalar displacement, not the synaptic activation \(s_i\). The total recall error is their sum:
\[ \widehat x-\Theta=s+e,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(s+e)=\operatorname{Var}(s)+\operatorname{Var}(e) +2\operatorname{Cov}(s,e). \]
Assume the readout is locally unbiased at every possible \(x\) and the future noise is independent of the storage history. Conditional on that history, the readout error then has mean zero. Since \(s\) is fixed by the history, \(\mathbb E[se]=\mathbb E[s\,\mathbb E(e\mid\text{storage history})]=0\). Both errors have zero mean, so their covariance vanishes. In this readout model, translation invariance means that shifting the represented value does not change the statistics of the readout error. Its variance is therefore the same at every \(x\). Denote it by \(V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)\). Using \(\operatorname{Var}(s)=2DT\) gives
\[ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L)=2DT+V_{\mathrm{read}}(L). \]
[Interpretation] The two terms describe different sources of error:
[Paper] The supplement’s decomposition is \(V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L)=2DT+V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)\) in the locally translation-invariant diffusion and readout model. It separates the mean squared displacement before the cue from the subsequent estimator variance; the calculation above states the assumptions that make the cross term vanish.2
[Interpretation: assumptions] State dependence, boundaries, informative priors, or uncertain initial encoding require corresponding changes.
A timeline separates the displacement accumulated before the cue from the error in estimating the cue state afterward.

section: 6.2 Accounting for diffusion makes readout improve toward a limit
text:
6.2 Accounting for diffusion makes readout improve toward a limit
[Paper] Main Eq. 5 and Fig. 3, PDF p. 4, describe the ideal observer’s characteristic observation time and diminishing gains from further spikes. For the local Gaussian readout model, the finite-interval readout variance and its characteristic time are
\[ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)=\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\,\coth\!\left(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L\right), \qquad L^*=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2DJ}}\leq\tau. \]
Here \(L\) is the observation duration after the cue, \(D\) is the memory diffusion coefficient, \(J\) is the spike information rate and \(\tau\) is the synaptic time constant. \(V_{\mathrm{ideal}}\) is the variance of estimating the state at the cue, excluding earlier storage error. As \(L\) grows, it approaches \(\sqrt{2D/J}\); \(L^*\) is a scale of approach, not a sharp stopping time. The bound on \(L^*\) uses the information–diffusion inequality and full spike access. The supporting calculation, Eqs. S58–S75, PDF pp. 13–15, uses a Gaussian readout model; the backward-precision calculation below is a guide reconstruction.

[Interpretation] An observer that accounts for diffusion can use later observations without treating them as direct measurements of \(x\). Their value is limited by the motion separating them from \(x\). This is an ideal inference rule for an observer. The readout calculation does not demonstrate a neural circuit implementing it. Its error can be derived by combining information backward from the end of the observation interval. 
[Guide derivation] The precision of a scalar Gaussian estimate is the reciprocal of its variance. Independent Gaussian measurements of one value add precisions. To verify this, multiply likelihoods proportional to \(\exp[-(x-a)^2/(2V_a)]\) and \(\exp[-(x-b)^2/(2V_b)]\): the coefficient of \(x^2/2\) becomes \(1/V_a+1/V_b\).

Let \(P(L)\) be the precision about the state at the beginning of an interval of length \(L\), using all observations in that interval and no informative prior. Suppose we have already compressed the later part into a likelihood about the next bin’s state with variance \(1/P\). Bringing that likelihood one step backward adds transition variance \(2Dh\), since the next state equals the earlier state plus an independent Gaussian increment. Its precision about the earlier state is therefore 
\[ \frac{1}{1/P+2Dh}=\frac{P}{1+2DhP}. \]

The new earliest observation adds precision \(Jh\). Thus, up to bin endpoint conventions that disappear as \(h\to0\), 
\[ P(L+h)=Jh+\frac{P(L)}{1+2DhP(L)}. \]
Expand the denominator for small \(h\):
\[ P(L+h)=P(L)+[J-2DP(L)^2]h+O(h^2). \]
The continuous equation and starting condition are
\[ \frac{dP}{dL}=J-2DP^2, \qquad P(0)=0. \]
[Interpretation] With no observations, precision starts at zero. The term \(J\) adds information from new observations. The term \(2DP^2\) reduces that gain because later observations are separated from the cue state by diffusion.
[Background] The hyperbolic cotangent is \(\coth z=(e^{2z}+1)/(e^{2z}-1)\). For positive \(z\), it falls from large values toward one. This function describes how the readout variance decreases toward its limit as observation continues.
[Guide derivation: solving the precision equation] The hyperbolic tangent is \(\tanh z=(e^z-e^{-z})/(e^z+e^{-z})\). Its inverse hyperbolic tangent on \((-1,1)\) is \(\operatorname{artanh}z=\tfrac12\log[(1+z)/(1-z)]\), whose derivative is \(1/(1-z^2)\). Set \(a=\sqrt{J/(2D)}\) and \(k=\sqrt{2DJ}\). Separating variables gives
\[ \int_0^{P/a}\frac{dz}{1-z^2}=kL, \qquad \operatorname{artanh}(P/a)=kL. \]
Applying \(\tanh\) to both sides and multiplying by \(a\) gives the precision
\[ P(L)=\sqrt{\frac{J}{2D}}\tanh(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L), \]
Taking the reciprocal of \(P(L)\) gives the finite-time readout variance in the next display.


The identity \(\coth z=1/\tanh z\) connects this result to the finite-time variance. This backward precision derivation is a teaching reconstruction equivalent to the Gaussian covariance calculation in SI Eqs. S58–S75. It makes explicit how diffusion limits the value of later observations.3  
For \(D>0\) and \(J>0\), the solution gives the readout variance at any observation duration \(L>0\):
\[ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L) =\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\coth(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L).} \]

Check: the short-time ideal readout variance
For short intervals, \(\coth z=1/z+z/3+O(z^3)\), so
\[ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)=\frac1{JL}+\frac{2DL}{3}+O(L^3). \]

The equal-weight estimator derived next will agree with these displayed terms. 

[Guide derivation] For long intervals,
\[ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)\longrightarrow\sqrt{2D/J}, \qquad L^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2DJ}}. \]
[Interpretation: approach to the limit] The ideal observer keeps improving, but the improvement becomes small. Its variance relative to the limiting variance is:

\(1.313\) at \(L=L^*\).
\(1.037\) at \(2L^*\).
\(1.005\) at \(3L^*\).

These are variances, so their ratios are not ratios of standard deviations.
[Guide derivation] Using \(2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}\) gives
\[ L^*\le\tau. \]

[Interpretation] Thus the paper’s statement about readout within a cellular time constant concerns a characteristic saturation time under full spike access. It does not mean all benefit ends abruptly at \(\tau\).4

section: 6.3 Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long
text:
6.3 Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long
[Paper] The authors’ naive estimator assumes that the state is fixed during observation and gives all times equal weight. In the local model, its readout variance and best observation duration are
\[ V_{\mathrm{naive}}(L)=\frac{1}{JL}+\frac{2DL}{3}, \qquad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2DJ}}. \]
The first term is uncertainty from the spike sample; the second is error from averaging a state that moves during the interval. Here \(L\) is the observation duration after the recall cue, \(D\) is the diffusion coefficient of the remembered state, and \(J\) is the information rate in the observed spikes about the state. The variance \(V_{\mathrm{naive}}\) concerns estimation of the state at the cue; it excludes the earlier storage error. These formulas appear in supporting text section VI, Eqs. S76–S81, PDF pp. 15–16, and are summarized in the main article, PDF p. 4. We derive them after the ideal observer, following the article.
[Interpretation] A decoder designed for a stationary state averages its observations with equal weight. That reduces independent observation noise, but late observations reflect a state that has moved further from \(x\).
[Guide derivation] Let \(T\) be the storage delay before the cue and \(x=\theta(T)\) the state at that cue. For elapsed time \(t\) after it, write \(\theta(T+t)=x+B_D(t)\), where \(B_D(t)\) is the subsequent zero-mean Brownian displacement, with diffusion coefficient \(D\) and covariance
\[ E[B_D(t)B_D(s)]=2D\min(t,s). \]
The covariance arises because the two values share increments up to the earlier time. Their later increments are independent. Let \(y(t)\) denote the noisy observation of the state at time \(t\) after the cue, in the continuous approximation used here. The continuous equal-weight average is
\[ \hat x_{\mathrm{naive}}=\frac1L\int_0^L y(t)dt. \]
Count noise contributes \(1/(JL)\): \(n=L/h\) bins, each of variance \(1/(Jh)\), give average variance \([n/(Jh)]/n^2=1/(JL)\). The motion contribution is
\[ \frac{2D}{L^2}\int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds. \]

Split the square into its two equal triangles. On the triangle \(0\le s\le t\le L\), the minimum is \(s\). Therefore 
\[ \int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds =2\int_0^L\!dt\int_0^t\!s\,ds =\int_0^L t^2dt=\frac{L^3}{3}. \]
Combining the terms gives
\[ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{naive}}(L)=\frac{2DL}{3}+\frac1{JL}.} \]

The two contributions have opposite dependence on \(L\). Differentiating, 
\[ \frac{dV_{\mathrm{naive}}}{dL}=\frac{2D}{3}-\frac1{JL^2}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt{\frac3{2DJ}}. \]
At that duration the two error terms are equal, and
\[ V_{\mathrm{naive}}^{\min} =\frac2{\sqrt3}\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}. \]
[Interpretation: equal weighting] The optimum satisfies \(L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt3 L^*\le\sqrt3\tau\). Its best variance is \(2/\sqrt3\simeq1.155\) times the ideal observer’s asymptotic variance, and its best standard deviation is about \(1.075\) times as large.
Waiting longer eventually increases error, even with more spikes available. The problem is their equal weighting for a moving state.5
[Example] For the recurring mutual-inhibition example, opposite changes in the two rates signal a change in the activation difference. Its \(D\) describes how that difference wanders; its \(J\) describes how well the spikes distinguish nearby values. The readout calculation combines those same quantities: longer collection reduces count uncertainty while allowing more motion. Here we apply the local model with \(D\) and \(J\) held fixed near the chosen state. The two-cell network has state-dependent \(J\), so these constant-coefficient formulas do not describe excursions across its whole range.

section: 6.4 Limited access can make observation slower
text:
6.4 Limited access can make observation slower
[Paper] The authors consider incomplete spike access in supporting text section VI, PDF p. 16, Eqs. S82–S83 and Fig. S2. If the accessible spikes carry a fraction \(0<\alpha\le1\) of the full information rate \(J\), the accessible information rate is \(J_{\mathrm{obs}}=\alpha J\). Here \(D\) is still the diffusion coefficient of the full memory network. The ideal characteristic observation time becomes \(L^*_{\mathrm{obs}}=1/\sqrt{2D\alpha J}=L^*/\sqrt\alpha\), and its limiting readout variance becomes \(\sqrt{2D/(\alpha J)}\). Thus, reducing the information fraction increases both quantities by \(1/\sqrt\alpha\), while \(D\) describes the original network’s diffusion. The guide derives an independent random-spike-thinning case below and separately checks the printed bound.
[Interpretation] A downstream area may receive only some of the memory network’s spikes. That reduces its information without reducing the fluctuations that already move the full memory network.
[Guide derivation] If every spike is independently retained with probability \(\alpha\), the observed rates and their slopes both scale by \(\alpha\). Substitution in the Poisson information formula gives
\[ J_{\mathrm{obs}}=\sum_i\frac{(\alpha r_i')^2}{\alpha\bar r_i}=\alpha J. \]

The network diffusion coefficient stays \(D\). Hence 
\[ L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2D\alpha J}} =\frac{L^*}{\sqrt\alpha}, \qquad V_{\mathrm{ideal,obs}}(\infty)=\sqrt{\frac{2D}{\alpha J}}. \]
[Interpretation] The same factor \(1/\sqrt\alpha\) multiplies the naive optimal interval and its minimum variance. The information bound implies \(L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*\le\tau/\sqrt\alpha\), which can exceed \(\tau\). A selected subset of neurons has exactly \(\alpha J\) only when it carries that fraction of the information. A fraction of neurons or spikes chosen by a biased rule need not do so.6

Example: limited spike access changes the useful interval.
[Example] Take \(\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}\), \(J=10{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}\), and \(D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}\). These values attain the information bound. Full access gives \(L^*=0.1\,\mathrm{s}\) and limiting readout variance \(0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2\). The naive optimum is \(0.1732\,\mathrm{s}\) with variance \(0.001155\,\mathrm{rad}^2\).
If \(\alpha=0.1\), then \(J_{\mathrm{obs}}=1000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). The ideal characteristic interval becomes \(0.3162\,\mathrm{s}\) and its limiting variance becomes \(0.003162\,\mathrm{rad}^2\). The naive optimum becomes \(0.5477\,\mathrm{s}\). A two second storage delay contributes \(2DT=0.020\,\mathrm{rad}^2\) in both cases, giving total ideal asymptotic variances \(0.021\) and \(0.023162\,\mathrm{rad}^2\). Limited access leaves the storage error unchanged but increases the time and uncertainty involved in reading the cue state.

6.5 Readout saturates, and one printed error bound needs qualification
[Paper] Main Fig. 3, PDF p. 4, compares ideal and equal-weight readout. With \(z=L/L^*\) and variance divided by \(\sqrt{2D/J}\), their curves are \(\coth z\) and \(z/3+1/z\), respectively. The ideal curve decreases toward one; the equal-weight curve reaches \(2/\sqrt3\) at \(z=\sqrt3\) and then rises. Supporting Fig. S2, PDF p. 16, shows the corresponding partial-access comparison.
[Interpretation: Figure 3] Figure 3 isolates readout uncertainty, rescaling variance by \(\sqrt{2D/J}\) and duration by \(L^*\). Write \(z=L/L^*=\sqrt{2DJ}\,L\) for this dimensionless observation duration. In these axes the ideal curve is \(\coth z\) and the naive curve is \(z/3+1/z\). Both diverge like \(1/z\) at short durations because too few spikes are available. The plotted features are:

The ideal solid curve approaches one.
The naive dashed curve reaches \(2/\sqrt3\) at \(z=\sqrt3\), then rises because its equal weighting gives increasing importance to displaced states.
The dotted vertical line marks that naive optimum.

The storage delay contribution \(2DT\) is not part of these rescaled curves. Figure S2 repeats the comparison for partial access, showing the rightward and upward shifts when \(\alpha=0.1\).7


Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure 3








Figure 6.3: The ideal readout error approaches a limit, while the error of equal weighting rises after its minimum. Original Figure 3 from Burak and Fiete (2012), reproduced as an exact artwork excerpt. PDF page 4. Open image at full size.







Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S2








Figure 6.4: Access to a tenth of the spikes shifts the useful observation time and the readout error upward. Original Figure S2 from Burak and Fiete (2012), reproduced as an exact artwork excerpt. PDF page 16. Open image at full size.












Figure 6.5: Original guide construction from the analytic readout formulas in Burak and Fiete (2012), Fig. 3 and Supporting Text, Eqs. S75 and S79–S81, rather than digitized data. Ideal readout approaches a normalized variance of one. Simple averaging reaches \(2/\sqrt3\) at \(z=\sqrt3\) and then worsens. These curves contain no storage variance \(2DT\).




[Interpretation] More observation keeps helping the ideal reader, with diminishing benefit, while equal weighting eventually gives too much influence to a state that has moved.

section: 6.6 Minimum Variance of Stimulus Estimation: checking the printed bound
text:
6.6 Minimum Variance of Stimulus Estimation: checking the printed bound
[Paper, with qualification] The article prints the following lower bound on total variance for estimating the original stimulus after storage delay \(T\) (main Eq. 6, p. 4):
\[ V_{\mathrm{total}}\geq 2D(T+\tau)\qquad\text{(printed claim; see the check below).} \]
Here \(D\) is diffusion, \(T\) is the storage delay, and \(\tau\) is the synaptic time constant. SI Eq. S83 uses a readout term \(2D\tau/\sqrt\alpha\) for fraction \(\alpha\) of the information. The guide’s independent check below finds that this lower-bound claim does not follow in general from the other displayed results; this is not an author-issued correction.
[Guide derivation] The paper’s other derived results imply
\[ 2DJ\ge\tau^{-2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J\ge\frac1{2D\tau^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\le2D\tau. \]

[Interpretation] Thus the ideal asymptotic readout term is at most \(2D\tau\), with equality when the information diffusion inequality is saturated. Substituting an upper bound for this term cannot establish the printed universal lower bound on total error. Within the local Gaussian model, the defensible statement is 
\[ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L) \ge2DT+\sqrt{2D/J}, \]
[Interpretation] Equality is approached as \(L\to\infty\) for the ideal observer. At saturation this asymptotic expression becomes \(2D(T+\tau)\). For partial access the same issue occurs with the factor \(1/\sqrt\alpha\). This is an apparent inconsistency between printed formulas, identified by algebra using the supplied sources. It is not a claim that the authors issued a correction.8
[Example] For a concrete strict inequality case, keep \(\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}\) and \(D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}\) but set \(J=40{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Then \(2DJ=400\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\) exceeds \(\tau^{-2}=100\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\). The limiting readout variance is \(0.0005\,\mathrm{rad}^2\), whereas \(2D\tau=0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2\). At \(T=2\,\mathrm{s}\), the Gaussian ideal total limit is \(0.0205\,\mathrm{rad}^2\), below \(2D(T+\tau)=0.021\,\mathrm{rad}^2\). These values expose the algebraic problem without assuming the bound is saturated.


[Interpretation] When a continuous attractor circuit is used to accumulate an incoming signal over time, its stored value represents the integral of that signal. The short useful readout interval does not imply a short lifetime for this accumulated value. A tuned circuit can continue to represent the mean of accumulated inputs while its variance grows. A leak would instead pull its mean toward a particular value. Diffusion limits the accuracy of the integral and the usefulness of long observation. It does not by itself introduce that restoring pull. Applying these predictions to an animal also requires checking its spike statistics, tuning, drift, access to spikes, and other sources of movement noise.9

title: Part II: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code
text:
Eye drift points to a shared neural drive: Even when a monkey looks at a stationary spot, its eyes drift slightly. This chapter explains how paired measurements of eye angle and the firing of neurons that command eye muscles support a shared neural source of that drift, before considering a particular circuit mechanism.
Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise: Eye movements recorded during steady gaze in monkeys look different over short and long time intervals. This chapter uses their timing to distinguish fluctuations around a fixed command from accumulated changes in the command, while accounting for eye-position measurement error.
A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift: A circuit that stores the intended eye angle is one possible source of fixational drift. This chapter follows the proposed model from interacting neurons through motor neurons and muscles to eye motion, and explains how delayed visual feedback can limit that motion.
Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale: Hippocampal place cells fire more at particular locations as an animal moves. This chapter introduces the rodent and bat recordings, then shows how a smooth random input that exceeds a firing threshold can produce several separate active regions for one cell.
High peaks explain size laws across dimensions: A place cell’s active regions can have different sizes on a route, across a floor, or in a flight volume. This chapter derives why the spatial model predicts different field-size distributions in one, two, and three dimensions, and identifies the high-threshold approximation used in that derivation.
Holes and measurements test the spatial explanation: Recordings show where a hippocampal cell is active as an animal moves through an environment. This chapter tests the spatial model against the shapes and arrangement of those regions, then asks what agreement can reveal about the inputs and connections that produce them.
Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests: The three papers address different links between nerve-cell activity and behavior: retaining a value, producing eye movement, and representing location. This chapter compares what the models and recordings establish, and separates supported connections from further questions about how a complete neural circuit would work.

title: 7  Eye drift points to a shared neural drive
text:
7.1 From stored eye position to muscle action
Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. Between brief, rapid movements called microsaccades, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift. Here drift names the slow eye movement, which can be largely random. Systematic drift in the memory equations instead means a nonzero mean velocity. Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them? Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.1
The paper’s estimate of the common contribution can be read directly as
\[ \chi\simeq\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\Delta\widehat E,\Delta E)}{\operatorname{Var}(\Delta E)}, \qquad \langle\chi\rangle_w=0.82\pm0.07. \]
Here \(\Delta E\) is measured horizontal eye displacement during 350 ms, \(\Delta\widehat E\) is the displacement reconstructed from one motor neuron’s spikes, and \(\chi\) estimates the fraction of displacement variance due to the shared drive. The reported value is a weighted average over cells and its weighted error. This interpretation assumes that the shared signal has the same calibrated gain in both quantities and that the remaining fluctuations are approximately uncorrelated. The covariance section derives the formula and examines these assumptions; see paper, PDF p. 5.
[Guide derivation: the shared variance estimate] Write \(X=\Delta\widehat E=C+\varepsilon\) and \(Y=\Delta E=C+\eta\), where \(C\) is the shared contribution to displacement after calibration, \(\varepsilon\) is the remaining prediction fluctuation, and \(\eta\) is the remaining eye-displacement fluctuation. Expanding the covariance gives
\[ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Var}(C) +\operatorname{Cov}(C,\eta)+\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon,C) +\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon,\eta). \]
If the shared component has equal calibrated gains and the other covariance terms are small, the numerator estimates \(\operatorname{Var}(C)\). Dividing by \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) estimates the fraction of eye-displacement variance shared with the neural prediction. The later calculation considers the residual private contribution from the recorded cell and the consequences of unequal gains.
This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory.
A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye’s movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions.
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated overviews may contain incorrect labels, arrows, formulas, or numbers. Use the chapter text and cited papers for the scientific claims.
The eye anatomy and motor action explain why a position must be maintained by an ongoing command. The oculomotor integrator supplies the lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the foundations and network model stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.2
The signal reaches ocular motoneurons (OMNs), whose spikes activate the eye muscles. The recordings came from the abducens nucleus, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward. Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types by how their firing changed with eye position and movement. Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the ocular plant, turn neural activity into movement.3
There are three possible contributions to an observed fixational drift:
Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging. This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement. The shared drive and common command below mean the signal sent to many OMNs. The variable \(C\) later measures its contribution to eye displacement after motor and muscle filtering.

title: 7  Eye drift points to a shared neural drive
section: 7.2 The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time
text:
7.2 The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time

The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye’s angle while an electrode recorded one neuron’s spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement. There were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.45 


The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals. They do not create 57 independent animal samples.6  


Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 7








Figure 7.3: Fixation segment durations and counts vary across cells and animals. Original Extended Data Figure 7 from Ben-Shushan et al. (2022); exact artwork excerpt. PDF page 12. Open image at full size.





The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell’s activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect gain during drift would change the inferred common variance. Gain is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other.







Figure 7.4: The recordings pair one motor neuron with eye movement. Private spike variability acts at individual cells, downstream physical variability acts on movement, and measurement noise enters the eye-position record. The attractor storage source is proposed; the dashed analysis path is a calculation from one cell through its calibrated filter. title: 7  Eye drift points to a shared neural drive
section: 7.3 A fitted model links movement to firing rate
text:
7.3 A fitted model links movement to firing rate

Position alone does not predict a motor neuron’s activity during a movement. At the same position, firing can differ when the eye is moving or accelerating. The paper therefore fits 
\[ \widehat f(t)=k[E(t+\Delta t)-E_T] +r\dot E(t+\Delta t)+m\ddot E(t+\Delta t). \]
Here \(E\) is horizontal eye position in degrees and \(\widehat f\) is predicted firing rate in spikes/s. The position threshold \(E_T\) sets where the position term reaches zero. The coefficients have units
\[ [k]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{s}\,\text{deg}},\qquad [r]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{deg}},\qquad [m]=\frac{\text{spikes}\,\text{s}}{\text{deg}}. \]
Multiplying by position, velocity, and acceleration gives spikes/s in all three terms.

The position sensitivity \(k\) is the fitted change in firing rate per degree of eye position when velocity and acceleration are fixed. Similarly, \(r\) is the fitted rate change per unit eye velocity, and \(m\) is the fitted rate change per unit eye acceleration. The position term describes ongoing firing associated with holding the eye at an angle. The velocity term allows a different rate while the eye passes through that same angle. The acceleration term allows another change while its velocity changes. Thus \(k\), \(r\), and \(m\) describe different demands on the motor signal. They are fitted coefficients of the combined neural and mechanical relationship. In particular, \(m\) is not a direct measurement of the eye’s mass. The delay \(\Delta t\) is in seconds: firing at time \(t\) predicts movement at the later time \(t+\Delta t\) for a positive neural lead. This is the paper’s Eq. 2, including its threshold and time shift.7 
The observed rate \(f(t)\) was estimated as the inverse of the interval between successive spikes, constant between those spikes. For each cell, the authors minimized the sum of squared rate errors,
\[ L=\sum_{a=1}^{n_{\rm trials}}\sum_{t_j\in[0,T_a]} \left[f_a(t_j)-\widehat f_a(t_j;k,r,m,\Delta t,E_T)\right]^2. \]
\(a\) labels trials, \(T_a\) is trial duration, and \(t_j\) is a sampled time within that trial. This is Eq. 3 with the trial count renamed so that it cannot be confused with a neuron count. Fits used full trials, including fixation and pursuit. To predict a trial’s rate, that trial was left out of the parameter fit. Acceleration was estimated from velocity after local polynomial smoothing over 21 ms. Trials in which the rate fell below 20 Hz were discarded: the linear formula is intended for active cells above firing threshold, whereas firing cannot become negative.8



During fixation, the authors subtracted each segment’s mean firing rate, joined the segments, and compared observed and predicted rate fluctuations. Figure 1c illustrates a weak relationship for one cell. Fig. 1d shows a positive population effect. The authors used a one sided t test: it compares the mean correlation across 57 cells with zero, after dividing that mean by its estimated sampling uncertainty. The positive direction was the one being tested.
The p value is the probability that this test would give a value at least as large as observed if the population mean correlation were zero and the test’s sampling assumptions held. The reported \(p=3\times10^{-9}\) measures how unusual the result is under that reference. It is not the probability that the zero-mean hypothesis, or a proposed neural mechanism, is true. A weak single cell relationship is expected here because the tiny movement produces small rate changes against much larger spike variability. This is evidence of a relationship, before any estimate of the fraction of common motion.9

Calculation: what the correlation test compares
Let \(R_i\) be the correlation for cell \(i\), \(\bar R\) the mean across \(n=57\) cells, and \(s_R\) their sample standard deviation. The number compared with the reference distribution, called the test statistic, is \(t=\bar R/(s_R/\sqrt{n})\). The denominator estimates the uncertainty in the mean. The reference is the Student t distribution with \(n-1=56\) degrees of freedom: the distribution of this ratio for independent, identically distributed normal observations with true mean zero. Applying it to the cell correlations uses that sampling approximation. The one sided p value is the reference probability above the observed \(t\). The observations in this calculation are cells recorded from two monkeys, not 57 independent animals.

title: 7  Eye drift points to a shared neural drive
section: 7.4 A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell’s spikes
text:
7.4 A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell’s spikes
The mathematical-tools chapter introduces impulse responses and convolution. Here they reconstruct eye position from a recorded spike train.


To ask how much eye movement is shared with a neuron, it helps to express both signals in degrees. The paper reverses the fitted relationship: a cell’s spike train becomes the input, and its prediction of eye position becomes the output. This operation is an inverse of the movement-to-rate fit, rather than a new fit to small drift residuals.  
Let \(x(t)=E(t)-E_T\). Ignoring the time shift for a moment, the deterministic relation is
\[ m\ddot x+r\dot x+kx=f. \]
A causal filter computes its present output from present and past input. For the equation above, its impulse response \(h_0(u)\) is the position response to one instantaneous spike at time zero. To factor the equation, consider a time component \(e^{pt}\): \(p\) is its exponential growth or decay rate in inverse seconds, and differentiation multiplies it by \(p\). The algebraic ratio of output to input for that component is
\[ H_0(p)=\frac{1}{mp^2+rp+k} =\frac{1}{m(p+1/\tau_+)(p+1/\tau_-)}. \]
Factoring the quadratic gives the slow and fast decay times
\[ \tau_+=\frac{2}{r/m-\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}},\qquad \tau_-=\frac{2}{r/m+\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}}. \]
These are the paired signs in the paper’s Eq. 7, with \(\tau_+>\tau_-\) when \(k,r,m>0\) and \(r^2>4km\). Under these conditions both components decay without oscillation.
At rest, the inverse equation gives \(x=f/k\): with the threshold fixed, doubling \(k\) halves the position offset predicted from the same steady firing rate. During a change, \(r\) and \(m\) also affect the response through the two timescales. This is a consequence of the fitted relationship, not evidence that changing one recorded neuron’s rate alone sets eye position. The same factorization gives two useful identities:
\[ \tau_+\tau_-=\frac{m}{k},\qquad \tau_++\tau_-=\frac{r}{k}. \]
[Guide derivation: weights of the two decaying responses]
We can obtain the response to a spike directly from the differential equation. After the spike, the input is zero, and each of the two exponentials solves the remaining homogeneous equation. Write their combination as
\[ h_0(u)=A e^{-u/\tau_+}+B e^{-u/\tau_-},\qquad u>0. \]


To find \(A\) and \(B\), treat the spike as a short pulse of unit area and shrink its duration to zero. The position change during that pulse tends to zero, so \(h_0(0^+)=0\). Integrating \(m h_0''+r h_0'+k h_0\) across the pulse gives \(m h_0'(0^+)=1\): the velocity changes by \(1/m\), while position and velocity before the causal response are zero. Therefore  
\[ A+B=0,\qquad -\frac{A}{\tau_+}-\frac{B}{\tau_-}=\frac1m. \]

Substituting \(B=-A\) gives \(A(1/\tau_- -1/\tau_+)=1/m\), hence \(A=\tau_+\tau_-/[m(\tau_+-\tau_-)]\). Making the response zero before the spike gives the impulse response \(h_0(u)\). 
The corresponding impulse response is
\[ h_0(u)=\frac{\Theta(u)}{m}\, \frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{\tau_+-\tau_-} \left(e^{-u/\tau_+}-e^{-u/\tau_-}\right). \]
\(\Theta(u)\) is zero for \(u<0\) and one for \(u>0\), which makes the response zero before the input. Restoring the fitted neural lead delays this response: \(h(u)=h_0(u-\Delta t)\). Write the spike train as \(\xi(t)=\sum_j\delta(t-t_j)\), where \(\delta\) is an ideal instantaneous impulse of unit area, so integration over one spike counts one event. The prediction is
\[ \widehat E(t)=E_T+\int_{-\infty}^{t}h(t-v)\xi(v)\,dv =E_T+\sum_j h(t-t_j). \]
These expressions reproduce Eqs. 4–6, including the factor \(\tau_+\tau_-/m\) and the delay. The convolution integral adds the responses to all past spikes. With spike count treated as a count, \(\xi\) has units spikes/s and \(h\) has units degrees/spike. Each spike contributes a decaying position response. Adding those responses produces degrees.10
For a constructed example, take \(k=4\) spikes/(s deg), \(\tau_+=0.120\) s, and \(\tau_-=0.005\) s. The identities above require \(r=0.500\) spikes/deg and \(m=0.00240\) spikes s/deg. Then
\[ h_0(u)=2.174\left(e^{-u/0.120}-e^{-u/0.005}\right) \ \text{deg/spike},\quad u>0, \]
and its area is \(2.174(0.120-0.005)=0.250\) deg s/spike, equal to \(1/k\). A steady rate of 80 spikes/s predicts an offset of 20 degrees above \(E_T\). This checks the gain and the time constants.

Check: static gain and equal decay times
The kernel’s area checks its normalization:
\[ \int_0^\infty h_0(u)\,du =\frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{m(\tau_+-\tau_-)}(\tau_+-\tau_-) =\frac1k. \]

Thus a constant input rate \(f_0\) predicts \(E_T+f_0/k\), exactly the static forward relation. A kernel with unit area would give the wrong conversion unless \(k\) had already been absorbed into the input. When the two decay times coincide, \(r^2=4km\), the limit is \(h_0(u)=\Theta(u)u e^{-u/\tau}/m\). The distinct exponential formula is used for the fitted responses in the paper. 




Figure 2a–b shows typical fitted times of about 5 ms and 120 ms. Figure 2c shows that a single cell’s reconstructed drift is much noisier than the measured movement. Pearson correlation is the ordinary linear correlation defined as \(\rho\) in the foundations; this paper writes it as \(R\). Across 350 ms displacement pairs, the mean Pearson correlation was \(\langle R\rangle=0.17\pm0.02\), where the error is the standard error of the mean (SEM). SEM estimates uncertainty in the across-cell mean, rather than the spread of individual cells or uncertainty across animals. The one sided test gave \(p=3.8\times10^{-12}\). Shuffling which measured segment was paired with which spike prediction centered the comparison near zero. Here and below \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) over cells means a population average.11   


Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 2








Figure 7.6: Single motor neuron predictions are noisy, while the population supports a shared component. Original Figure 2 from Ben-Shushan et al. (2022); exact artwork excerpt. PDF page 4. Open image at full size.

title: 7  Eye drift points to a shared neural drive
section: 7.5 The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise alone
text:
7.5 The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise alone
A correlation of 0.17 does not immediately tell us how much motion comes from the common command. First we can ask a more limited question: could all the motion come from independent motor neuron fluctuations?
For a centered displacement \(Y\) and one centered prediction \(X\), the best linear prediction \(bX\) minimizes \(\operatorname{Var}(Y-bX)\). Differentiating with respect to \(b\) gives \(b=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)\). Its explained fraction of variance is
\[ \frac{b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =R^2. \]
This is the coefficient of determination for a linear prediction with a fitted gain. It does not assert that the raw, unscaled position predictor itself has a small squared error.
Suppose there are \(N_m\) independent single neuron predictors \(X_i\). Standardize each to variance one and also standardize \(Y\). Independence makes the \(X_i\) uncorrelated, so the residual after using them all has variance
\[ \operatorname{Var}\left(Y-\sum_i R_iX_i\right) =1-2\sum_iR_i^2+\sum_iR_i^2 =1-\sum_iR_i^2\ge0. \]

Consequently \(\sum_iR_i^2\le1\), and an average neuron explains at most \(1/N_m\). This proves the bound used in Supplementary Eq. S1. It does not require equal muscle effects from all neurons. Applying it to the sampled cells does require their average explanatory power to represent the relevant motor population.12 
The authors avoid directly averaging noisy squared correlations. Instead,
\[ \langle R^2\rangle-\langle R\rangle^2=\operatorname{Var}(R)\ge0, \qquad \langle R^2\rangle\ge(0.17)^2=0.0289. \]


Thus the estimated mean correlation implies an average explained fraction of at least about 2.9%. For 1,000 independently contributing motor neurons, the bound would be 0.1%. For several thousand it is smaller. The mismatch argues against independent OMN noise as the sole source. Shared fluctuations can allow many cells to explain the same part of the movement, so their explained fractions can overlap.13  
This step finds shared variation. Locating its source upstream also uses a biological premise: the private variability generated within OMNs is taken to be independent across cells. The paper supports that premise using anatomical and stimulation studies indicating little local recurrent coupling in the relevant motor nuclei. It was not tested by simultaneous recordings in this data set. Common inputs can correlate the total activity of OMNs even when their privately generated spike noise is independent.14

title: 7  Eye drift points to a shared neural drive
section: 7.6 Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance
text:
7.6 Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance

The variance bound establishes that a shared signal exists, but leaves its size open. The next calculation uses the inverse filter’s calibrated gain in degrees. For one 350 ms interval, write the measured displacement and the single cell prediction as 
\[ Y=\delta E=C+\eta,\qquad X=\delta\widehat E=C+\epsilon, \]
where \(C=\delta E_C\) is the common upstream contribution, \(\eta\) combines motor neuron, muscle, and measurement contributions to measured displacement, and \(\epsilon\) is the prediction error from the individual cell. All are displacement variables in degrees. The calculation assumes:


The common contribution enters both signals with unit gain, meaning the same one-for-one displacement scale.



\(C,\eta,\epsilon\) are pairwise uncorrelated to the required accuracy.

Expanding the covariance shows why those assumptions matter:
\[ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Var}(C) +\operatorname{Cov}(C,\eta)+\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,C) +\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,\eta) \simeq\operatorname{Var}(C). \]

The common fraction is therefore estimated by 
\[ \chi=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(C)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} \simeq\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}. \]
These are Eqs. 11–15 in displacement form. The gain assumption requires that the relation calibrated during larger movements still applies during drift. There is also a small covariance between \(\epsilon\) and \(\eta\), because the recorded neuron’s private spikes contribute both to its predictor and to actual eye motion. The paper neglects this contribution as order \(1/N_m\) under its many neuron model.15
Correlation divides the same covariance by a different denominator:
\[ R=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}, \qquad \chi\simeq R\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. \]
Large private noise in a cell inflates \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) and makes \(R\) small. It need not make the common contribution to the real movement small, because many independent private contributions average down there.

Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82.
These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. Take independent centered variables with
\[ \operatorname{Var}(C)=0.00820\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\eta)=0.00180\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=0.22446\ \text{deg}^2. \]
Then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.01000\), \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.23266\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.00820\), all in deg\(^2\). It follows that
\[ R=\frac{0.00820}{\sqrt{0.01000\times0.23266}}\simeq0.170, \qquad \chi=\frac{0.00820}{0.01000}=0.820. \]

One cell explains \(R^2\simeq2.89\%\) of displacement variance after linear rescaling, while the common signal supplies 82% of actual displacement variance. The larger, poorly predicted part of the single cell signal is private prediction noise. 







Figure 7.7: The same common variance enters movement and the single cell predictor, but the predictor has much more private noise. Increasing only private predictor variance lowers correlation R while the common movement fraction χ stays at 0.82. The marked point uses the chapter’s constructed example. Calculations assume unit common gain and mutually uncorrelated contributions; they are not recorded cell data. Based on Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main p. 10, Eqs. 11–15.





The bars use the same physical scale, so the equal common pieces have equal lengths. See Shared and private variability, Eqs. 11–15, p. 10. 

In the experiment, each cell gives a noisy estimate \(\chi_i\), and those estimates can lie outside \([0,1]\). The underlying variance fraction remains in that interval under the model, but the sample covariance need not. The paper estimates each standard error \(\Delta\chi_i\) mainly from covariance uncertainty, treating the measured displacement variance in the denominator as comparatively well determined. It then uses inverse variance weighting:
\[ w_i=\frac{1}{(\Delta\chi_i)^2},\qquad \widehat\chi=\frac{\sum_iw_i\chi_i}{\sum_iw_i},\qquad \sigma_{\widehat\chi}=\left(\sum_iw_i\right)^{-1/2}. \]

To see the weighting, let normalized weights \(a_i\) sum to one. Independent errors give variance \(\sum_i a_i^2(\Delta\chi_i)^2\) for \(\sum_i a_i\chi_i\). Minimizing this subject to \(\sum_i a_i=1\) gives \(a_i\propto1/(\Delta\chi_i)^2\) and the error above. The paper additionally assumes approximately normal errors around a common value. The last expression is a propagated estimation error under those assumptions. It does not measure variation across animals or uncertainty in the gain and independence assumptions. The reported result was \(0.82\pm0.07\), a weighted mean and weighted error for horizontal displacement over 350 ms. It is neither a fraction of distance traveled nor the fraction that one neuron’s spikes accurately predict.16

7  Eye drift points to a shared neural drive

title: 8  Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise
text:
8.1 Independent measurement error adds a constant offset to the MSD
The shared movement estimate concerns a single interval length. It leaves open whether the command merely fluctuates around a stable value or keeps accumulating changes. Comparing displacements over different time separations can distinguish these possibilities, but the smallest measured displacements may include a large contribution from recording error.
The mean squared displacement measures the average squared position change over a chosen interval. Separating the recording error from that quantity is necessary before interpreting its growth. To test whether the command accumulates changes, we compare two possible inputs after a decaying muscle response: fluctuations that do not accumulate and a position that wanders by diffusion. Their different long interval behavior explains how a smooth eye movement can still reflect a wandering stored value.
For lag \(\ell\), the quantity being compared is the mean squared displacement \(M(\ell)=\mathbb E[(E(t+\ell)-E(t))^2]\), where \(E\) is eye position. If position measurement errors have variance \(\sigma_m^2\), are independent between sampled times, and are uncorrelated with true eye movement, the paper’s positive-lag correction is
\[ M_{\rm obs}(\ell)=M(\ell)+2\sigma_m^2,\qquad \ell>0. \]
Here \(M_{\rm obs}\) is the MSD calculated from measured positions, including measurement noise, while \(M\) is the MSD of the true eye position. The corrected \(M\) keeps growing over the measured range. In the paper’s circuit model, an internally diffusing position has \(M_{\rm internal}(\ell)\simeq2D\ell\) over the relevant time range, where \(D\) is the internal position diffusion coefficient; the muscles filter it before it becomes eye motion. The derivations and their assumptions follow below. See paper, Eqs. 18–19, p. 10 and integrator diffusion, PDF p. 6.
[Guide derivation: measurement error and diffusion] Let \(E_{\rm obs}(t)=E(t)+\nu(t)\), where \(\nu\) is position measurement error. For a positive lag, the measured displacement is \(\Delta E_{\rm obs}=\Delta E+\nu(t+\ell)-\nu(t)\). On squaring and averaging, the cross term vanishes under the assumptions above. The two independent errors each contribute variance \(\sigma_m^2\), so \(M_{\rm obs}(\ell)=M(\ell)+2\sigma_m^2\). At zero lag the same error is subtracted from itself, so this positive-lag correction does not apply.
For the internal position, model a displacement as \(\Delta B=\sqrt{2D}\,\Delta W\), where the Brownian increment \(\Delta W\) has mean zero and variance \(\ell\). Thus \(\mathbb E[(\Delta B)^2]=2D\ell\). This is the internal signal before the muscle filter; the observed eye MSD need not be linear at short lags.
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated overviews may contain incorrect labels, arrows, formulas, or numbers. Use the chapter text and cited papers for the scientific claims.
Using the earlier definition of mean squared displacement,
\[ M(\ell)=\mathbb E\{[E(t+\ell)-E(t)]^2\} \]
is the mean squared displacement, or MSD, at lag \(\ell\). The data estimate it within each microsaccade free segment, then average the available segment estimates at each lag. Larger lags have fewer eligible segments. The 1 ms sampling sets the available lag spacing.1
At short lags, the displacement can be smaller than the search coil’s measurement error. Suppose its reading is \(E_{\rm obs}(t)=E(t)+\nu(t)\). The measurement error is assumed to have:
For a positive lag, let \(\delta E=E(t+\ell)-E(t)\) be true eye displacement and \(\delta\nu=\nu(t+\ell)-\nu(t)\) the change in measurement error. Then
\[ \begin{aligned} M_{\rm obs}(\ell) &=\mathbb E[(\delta E+\delta\nu)^2]\\ &=M(\ell)+\mathbb E[\nu(t+\ell)^2]+\mathbb E[\nu(t)^2] -2\mathbb E[\nu(t+\ell)\nu(t)]\\ &=M(\ell)+2\sigma_m^2. \end{aligned} \]
The mixed movement-error term vanishes by independence. This is Eqs. 18–19. The correction is the variance of a difference of two errors, \(2\sigma_m^2\), rather than the variance of a single position error. At exactly zero lag the same error is subtracted from itself, so the MSD is zero. A positive lag plateau near zero lag can still occur when successive measurement errors are independent.2
The authors estimated the plateau contribution at order \(10^{-3}\) deg\(^2\), checked its scale with a coil fixed in space, and subtracted that contribution from the observed MSD. This is a correction of an average statistic, not knowledge of each trial’s unknown noise. Smoothing the eye trajectories instead would also change the movement statistics the analysis seeks to measure. If the plateau estimate has uncertainty \(10^{-4}\) deg\(^2\), a corrected MSD of that size is unreliable even when the plateau itself is much larger. The peer review response uses this example to explain the shortest lag limitation.3
For instance, a constructed measured MSD of \(0.0014\) deg\(^2\) with an estimated noise contribution \(0.0010\) deg\(^2\) leaves \(0.0004\) deg\(^2\). A \(0.0001\) deg\(^2\) uncertainty in the subtraction is already 25% of that result. This is why a corrected short lag point needs an uncertainty assessment as well as a positive value. If measurement errors were temporally correlated, the correction would instead be \(2[\sigma_m^2-C_\nu(\ell)]\), where \(C_\nu\) is their covariance at lag \(\ell\). A constant subtraction would then need revision.
For a constructed Brownian movement with \(D=0.010\) deg\(^2\)/s, adding independent position measurement errors with \(2\sigma_m^2=0.0010\) deg\(^2\) shifts every positive-lag MSD upward by the same amount.
The Brownian movement is chosen only to make the constant offset visible. See Measurement noise correction, Eqs. 18–19, p. 10.

title: 8  Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise
section: 8.2 The MSD plateaus for filtered white noise but grows for filtered diffusion
text:
8.2 The MSD plateaus for filtered white noise but grows for filtered diffusion
The filtering introduction separates stationary filtered noise from a filtered position command that keeps accumulating changes. Here the lag dependence is compared with the eye recordings.
The corrected MSD keeps increasing over the observed range, toward a second, while its logarithmic slope decreases and remains between one and two. Define that local slope by the derivative below, where \(M'(\ell)=dM/d\ell\) is the change of MSD per unit lag:
\[ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{d\log M(\ell)}{d\log\ell} =\frac{\ell M'(\ell)}{M(\ell)}. \]

Ordinary diffusion has \(M=2D\ell\) and \(\alpha=1\). A roughly constant velocity over a short interval gives displacement \(v\ell\) and \(M=\mathbb E[v^2]\ell^2\), so \(\alpha=2\). Growth faster than linear is called superdiffusion. Here it describes a finite range of lags. It does not assert a single power law for arbitrarily long times.4 


Could temporally uncorrelated motor noise acquire the observed MSD just by passing through muscles? A low pass filter suppresses rapid input changes relative to slow ones. The input is idealized as white noise, so fluctuations at unequal times are uncorrelated. A stable, decaying response to this noise produces a stationary process in the sense needed here: its mean is constant and its covariance depends only on time separation. Its position variance consequently does not grow with absolute time. Let \(\xi(t)\) be the random input and \(h(u)\) the eye’s response at elapsed time \(u\) after an impulse. The convolution \(E=h*\xi\) adds the effects of all past input values, \(E(t)=\int_0^\infty h(u)\xi(t-u)\,du\). The input has  
\[ \mathbb E[\xi(t)\xi(t')]=A\delta(t-t'). \]
The noise intensity \(A\) has units input\(^2\) times seconds. Expanding the convolution and using the delta function yields, for \(\ell\ge0\),
\[ C_E(\ell)=\mathbb E[E(t)E(t+\ell)] =A\int_0^\infty h(u)h(u+\ell)\,du. \]
For a stationary centered position, expanding the squared difference then gives
\[ M(\ell)=2[C_E(0)-C_E(\ell)]. \]



If the kernel decays sufficiently rapidly, its overlap with a shifted copy tends to zero. The MSD consequently approaches \(2C_E(0)\), a finite plateau. This reconstructs the reasoning of Eqs. 20–22.5   
For the one exponential filter \(h(u)=\Theta(u)e^{-u/\tau}/\tau\), \(\tau\) is its response time, and \(\Theta(u)\) is zero before the impulse (\(u<0\)) and one afterwards (\(u>0\)). The output covariance and MSD are
\[ C_E(\ell)=\frac{A}{2\tau}e^{-\ell/\tau},\qquad M_{\rm white}(\ell)=\frac A\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau}). \]
Substituting the exponential into the covariance integral makes the result explicit:
\[ C_E(\ell)=\frac{A e^{-\ell/\tau}}{\tau^2} \int_0^\infty e^{-2u/\tau}\,du =\frac{A}{2\tau}e^{-\ell/\tau}. \]
Using \(M(\ell)=2[C_E(0)-C_E(\ell)]\) then gives the MSD above.
This simple filter has a short lag MSD proportional to \(\ell\) and a long lag plateau. A double exponential filter is smoother at short lags, but still gives a plateau because its kernel also decays. Increasing \(A\) raises the curve without removing its flattening. The paper’s simulated private OMN noise, passed through muscle dynamics, is both too small and too flat at long lags. In Fig. 3b, using 2,000 heterogeneous OMNs, its contribution is about 1% of the observed variance near 900 ms.6


Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 3








Figure 8.5: Private motor neuron noise cannot explain the measured displacement over longer lags. Original Figure 3 from Ben-Shushan et al. (2022); exact artwork excerpt. PDF page 6. Open image at full size.






Filtered white noise cannot explain continued long-lag growth. Suppose instead the input is a stored position \(B(t)\) undergoing Brownian motion with \(\mathbb E[(B(t+\ell)-B(t))^2]=2D\ell\). Its position variance accumulates. A low pass filter with nonzero static gain smooths the path while retaining that accumulating long time displacement variance. The following one exponential example is a teaching reconstruction, not the paper’s full muscle model. It derives how smooth movement can have a slope between one and two even though the stored position undergoes ordinary diffusion. 
Let
\[ \tau\dot E+E=B,\qquad dB=\sqrt{2D}\,dW. \]
Here \(B\) is the changing position command and \(E\) is the eye angle that follows it, both in degrees. The mismatch \(B-E\) drives velocity: a command to the right of the current position makes the eye move right. For the same mismatch, a larger response time \(\tau\) gives a smaller velocity, so the eye takes longer to catch up and smooths rapid command changes more strongly. This response time belongs to the simplified eye filter. It is not automatically the synaptic decay time used in the memory model.
\(W\) is a Brownian process with unit increment variance per unit time, so \(D\) has units deg\(^2\)/s. Define velocity \(v=\dot E=(B-E)/\tau\). Taking its increment gives
\[ \tau\,dv=-v\,dt+\sqrt{2D}\,dW. \]
Velocity loses its past value over time \(\tau\) and receives new random input. To add the surviving effect of those inputs, divide the past into short intervals of width \(h\). The Brownian change \(\Delta W_j=W(u_j+h)-W(u_j)\) has mean zero and variance \(h\). Changes in disjoint intervals are independent. Its contribution to the velocity at time \(t\) is approximately \((\sqrt{2D}/\tau)e^{-(t-u_j)/\tau}\Delta W_j\): the initial change has decayed between \(u_j\) and \(t\).

The integral against \(dW(u)\) denotes the limit of these weighted sums as \(h\) tends to zero. It does not require an ordinary derivative of the Brownian path. After the initial velocity has decayed, extending the input history into the distant past gives 
\[ v(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2D}}{\tau}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-(t-u)/\tau}\,dW(u). \]
For a lag \(s\geq0\), let \(C_v(s)=\operatorname{Cov}[v(t),v(t+s)]\) be the velocity covariance. Multiply the sums for \(v(t)\) and \(v(t+s)\) and average. Products of distinct increments have zero mean. The same increment contributes its variance \(h\), so the sum becomes an ordinary overlap integral over their shared past:
\[ \begin{aligned} C_v(s) &=\frac{2D}{\tau^2}\int_{-\infty}^{t} e^{-(t-u)/\tau}e^{-(t+s-u)/\tau}\,du\\ &=\frac{2D}{\tau^2}e^{-s/\tau}\int_0^\infty e^{-2r/\tau}\,dr =\frac D\tau e^{-s/\tau}. \end{aligned} \]
Here \(r=t-u\) is the age of an input increment. Covariance is even in the lag, so \(C_v(s)=(D/\tau)e^{-|s|/\tau}\) for either sign of \(s\). Integrating velocity over an interval gives position change. The double integral over its covariance reduces to
\[ \begin{aligned} M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell) &=\int_0^\ell\int_0^\ell C_v(u-v)\,du\,dv\\ &=2\int_0^\ell(\ell-s)C_v(s)\,ds\\ &=2D[\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})]. \end{aligned} \]
At short lags, \(1-e^{-\ell/\tau}=\ell/\tau-\ell^2/(2\tau^2)+\cdots\), so
\[ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq(D/\tau)\ell^2. \]
The eye keeps approximately the same velocity over that interval. At long lags,
\[ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq2D(\ell-\tau), \]
which grows linearly rather than approaching a plateau.
Holding the internal diffusion coefficient \(D\) fixed, increasing \(\tau\) reduces short-lag displacement and moves the transition to linear growth to longer lags. It does not stop accumulating error: the long-lag MSD growth rate still approaches \(2D\). Increasing \(D\) instead raises the entire MSD curve in proportion, at fixed \(\tau\). The local logarithmic slope of this MSD is
\[ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{\ell(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})} {\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})}, \]

approaching two at short lags and one at long lags. At \(\ell=\tau\) it is \(e-1\simeq1.718\). At \(\ell=5\tau\) it is about \(1.239\). Thus an intermediate slope can arise from filtering ordinary diffusion, without faster than Brownian accumulation inside the memory circuit. 
The curves compare the two inputs after the same filter with one exponential response, also called a one pole filter.







Figure 8.6: Filtering stationary white input produces an MSD plateau; filtering Brownian stored position preserves long-lag growth. Each panel uses its own normalization, \(M_{\mathrm{white}}/(A/\tau)\) and \(M_{\mathrm{Brownian}}/(2D\tau)\), so the figure compares shapes without matching physical noise amplitudes. Original guide calculation for the one-pole teaching model, connected to Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Fig. 3 and main Eqs. 20–22; these are not measured data or the fitted full-model curves.




The white-input short-lag slope of one belongs to this one-pole example.

The actual muscle response contains fast and slow exponential components, and the full model also contains motor neuron filtering and feedback. Those ingredients change the detailed curve. The one exponential derivation teaches the distinction relevant to Fig. 3: a decaying low pass filter of stationary white noise saturates, whereas the same filter, with nonzero static gain, retains accumulating displacement from a wandering position. A slow correlated peripheral source is a different hypothesis from the temporally uncorrelated noise rejected by this comparison.

title: 9  A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift
text:
9.1 A noisy integrator can reproduce drift after muscle filtering
The recordings support a shared source before the motor neurons, and the movement’s timing is compatible with a stored position that wanders. Neither result identifies the circuit that supplies that command. A noisy memory circuit is a proposed explanation whose output must pass through the motor neurons and muscles before it can be compared with eye movement.
Following that complete path lets the model test whether neural noise can produce both the amount and timing of the observed drift. Its spike variability, neuron count and time constants determine how much freedom this match allows. Comparing the model with the separate recording and timing results then shows what the study supports, and why it still leaves other upstream sources possible.
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated overviews may contain incorrect labels, arrows, formulas, or numbers. Use the chapter text and cited papers for the scientific claims.
The recording analysis places much of the drive upstream of OMNs. To test whether integrator noise could supply it, the authors build a model from a noisy memory circuit through to the eye. The model adapts an earlier goldfish integrator architecture to primate tuning and variability. The model has two groups of integrator neurons. One group fires more when the eye points farther right. The other fires more when it points farther left. Neurons excite cells in their own group and inhibit cells in the other group. The connection strengths are tuned so that the circuit can approximately maintain a range of represented eye positions.1
For the right population, the model’s rate is
\[ \lambda_i^R(t)=\left[\zeta_i^R E_{OI}(t)+\lambda_i^0+\zeta_i^R F(t)\right]_+, \qquad [a]_+=\max(a,0). \]
\(E_{OI}\) is the internally represented position in degrees, \(\zeta_i^R\) is a tuning slope in spikes/(s deg), and \(\lambda_i^0\) is a rate offset in spikes/s. Taking the maximum with zero prevents negative firing. \(F\) is a feedback input in degrees, defined below. The matching left neuron has the opposite slope, \(\zeta_i^L=-\zeta_i^R\). In an active neuron, a change of one degree changes its rate by \(\zeta_i\).
The model scales each spike train into an input \(X_i\) with a saturating mean response. This input changes the neuron’s synaptic output \(S_i\), the lingering effect of its spikes on neurons receiving them. A weighted difference between the two groups’ synaptic outputs gives the represented eye angle \(E_{OI}\). This value sets the firing rates again, closing the feedback loop:
\[ \tau_s\dot S_i^R=-S_i^R+X_i^R,\qquad X_i^R(t)=\frac{\xi_i^R(t)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(t)},\qquad E_{OI}(t)=\sum_i\eta_i[S_i^R(t)-S_i^L(t)]. \]
Here \(\xi_i^R\) is a spike train generated at rate \(\lambda_i^R\), \(\tau_s\) is the synaptic decay time, and \(\lambda_t=60\) Hz sets the rate scale in the nonlinear synaptic response. Treating spikes as counts, \(X_i\) and \(S_i\) are dimensionless, and the weights \(\eta_i\) are in degrees. Between spikes, \(S_i\) decays exponentially. One spike adds a jump of \(1/[\tau_s(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)]\). Replacing spikes by their mean rate gives a drive \(\lambda_i^R/(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)\) that approaches one as the rate increases. This is the model’s saturating synaptic effect, rather than the purely linear synapses of the basic 2012 example.2
Persistence requires a further condition on that feedback. Set \(F=0\) and replace spikes by their mean rates. Define the mean saturated drives at a proposed stored value \(z\) by
\[ q_i^R(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^R(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(z)}, \qquad q_i^L(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^L(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^L(z)}. \]
Multiply each synaptic equation by its readout weight, subtract the left contribution, and sum. Since the same \(\tau_s\) applies to every unit, the readout obeys
\[ \tau_s\dot E_{OI}=-E_{OI}+G(E_{OI}), \qquad G(z)=\sum_i\eta_i[q_i^R(z)-q_i^L(z)]. \]
An exact continuum of persistent readout values would require \(G(z)=z\) over the represented range. For a small displacement from a fixed value, Taylor expansion gives
\[ \tau_s\,\frac{d\,\delta E_{OI}}{dt} =[G'(z)-1]\delta E_{OI}. \]
Here \(\delta E_{OI}\) is the small change in the represented eye angle, and \(G'(z)=dG/dz\) measures how much the feedback readout changes per degree of that angle. Thus \(G'(z)=1\) is the local neutral condition for the stored coordinate. Stable directions of the remaining synaptic state are also needed for an attractor. The weights were optimized to approximate the fixed-point relation across \(-50\) to \(50\) degrees. Residual mismatch can produce deterministic drift, so this finite optimized circuit provides approximate persistence rather than an exactly neutral continuum. The tuning slopes and thresholds were sampled to match reported macaque relationships and variation. With spikes, perturbations along the nearly neutral direction also accumulate. This reduction is a teaching derivation from the paper’s equations. Figure 4 separates the resulting internal diffusion from later muscle smoothing.3
The motor neurons receive this position signal:
\[ \lambda_i^M(t)=[k_i(E_{OI}(t)-E_{T_i})]_+, \qquad \tau_{MN}\dot s_i^M=-s_i^M+\xi_i^M. \]
\(\lambda_i^M\) is a motor rate in spikes/s and \(E_{T_i}\) is that neuron’s position threshold in degrees. Its position sensitivity \(k_i\) is the change in firing rate per degree of represented position while the unit is active. \(\xi_i^M\) is its generated spike train. The filtered output \(s_i^M\) also has units spikes/s, with decay time \(\tau_{MN}\). One spike makes a jump of \(1/\tau_{MN}\). At constant mean rate, the mean output is that rate.
Each motor unit’s muscle and plant response is represented by a position contribution \(E_i\) satisfying
\[ s_i^M=k_i(E_i-E_{T_i})+r_i\dot E_i+m_i\ddot E_i, \qquad E=\frac1{N_m}\sum_{i=1}^{N_m}E_i. \]
These are Eqs. 28–31. Here \(E_i\) is motor unit \(i\)’s position contribution, \(N_m\) is the number of motor neurons being averaged, and \(E\) is their model eye position. The coefficient \(r_i\) sets the rate response to velocity and \(m_i\) the response to acceleration; dots denote time derivatives. The second order equation uses the same roles and units as the forward fit. At constant \(E_{OI}\), an active unit has mean \(s_i^M=k_i(E_{OI}-E_{T_i})\), giving mean \(E_i=E_{OI}\) when derivatives vanish. Averaging therefore transmits the common position while reducing independent private fluctuations. This is an effective model of combined motor output, not a claim that one motor unit moves an isolated eye of its own.4
The model used diverse thresholds and response coefficients, with motor thresholds sampled between \(-45\) and \(-5\) degrees, and imposed \(m_i<r_i^2/(4k_i)\) to give nonoscillatory individual response kernels. Main Methods report \(N=30{,}000\) integrator neurons, \(N_m=1{,}000\) OMNs, and \(\tau_s=20\) ms for the main full simulation. The separate private OMN comparison in Fig. 3 used 2,000 OMNs. These neuron counts belong to different simulation comparisons.5
As the eye moves while viewing a stationary target, the target’s image moves across the retina. The authors assume that visual feedback responds to this recent image motion rather than to an absolute target-position error. Their delayed feedback model is:
\[ F(t)=A[E(t-\tau_d)-E_{OI}(t)], \qquad \tau_d\simeq70\ \text{ms}. \]
Both positions are in degrees, so \(A\) is dimensionless in this formulation. The main value is \(A=0.015\). If gaze and its internal representation have recently moved rightward, the delayed position is to their left, making \(F\) negative. Its contribution to the integrator rates then opposes continued rightward movement. For a slowly varying position that the eye tracks, \(E(t-\tau_d)-E_{OI}(t)\simeq-\tau_d\dot E(t)\), showing the velocity-like action and sign. The approximation requires tracking and slow change over the delay.6
The effect on the ongoing MSD must be checked from the coupled model, rather than inferred from the delay alone. A short MSD lag is a separation between two samples in a running process, not the time since a new perturbation. Past measurements can already affect both samples, and \(F\) also contains the immediate term \(-A E_{OI}(t)\). Extended Data Fig. 3 compares the model with and without feedback: feedback changes amplitude across lags, while its larger effect on logarithmic slope occurs at longer lags. Figure 5 shows the full model. Muscle filtering supplies the short-lag smoothness, and feedback improves the detailed longer-lag fit. These are results of this model comparison, not a hard delay-based cutoff or a claim excluding visual control under other tasks.7
