section: 9.2 Spike regularity and circuit parameters set the model’s drift scale
text:
9.2 Spike regularity and circuit parameters set the model’s drift scale
The paper states its network-scale comparison as
\[ D\propto\frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{N\lambda_0 k_0^2\tau_s^2}. \]
Here \(D\) is the internal eye-position diffusion coefficient, \(N\) the number of integrator neurons, \(\mathrm{CV}\) their interspike-interval coefficient of variation, \(\lambda_0\) a typical firing rate, \(k_0\) a typical position sensitivity, meaning how much the firing response changes for a change in represented position, and \(\tau_s\) the synaptic time constant. This is a scaling relation, not an exact prediction for every network. The paper does not specify a fractional normalization for \(k_0\); the calculation below explains why that detail matters when comparing changes in firing rate. See paper, Eq. 1, PDF p. 6.
[Guide derivation: the scaling and sensitivity] The following simplified calculation makes the rate and sensitivity dependence explicit. For \(N\) similar independent neurons with rate \(\lambda_0\) and absolute position slope \(a=d\lambda/dE\), the Poisson information rate is \(J\simeq Na^2/\lambda_0\). For a stationary renewal spike train observed for a long window \(L\), the count variance is approximately \(\lambda_0L\,\mathrm{CV}^2\). Using the information–diffusion relation as a scale for comparable network geometry gives
\[ D\ \propto\ \frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{\tau_s^2J} \simeq\frac{\mathrm{CV}^2\lambda_0}{N a^2\tau_s^2}. \]
With the fractional slope \(b=a/\lambda_0\), this becomes \(D\propto\mathrm{CV}^2/(N\lambda_0 b^2\tau_s^2)\). It has the paper’s printed dependence if \(k_0\) means this fractional slope, but the paper does not state that normalization. This is a guide scale calculation, not an exact derivation of the full model with saturating synapses and sub-Poisson spikes. The next steps show the count-variance and information calculations.
An agreement in amplitude is informative only if we know how much freedom the model has. The paper uses regular spike trains. The spike variability section defined the interspike interval coefficient of variation (CV) as the interval standard deviation divided by its mean. A Poisson process at constant rate has CV one. The model uses about 0.22 for integrator neurons and about 0.07 for OMNs. Such firing is called sub-Poisson spiking here because its long window count variability is lower than a Poisson process at the same rate, under the interval construction used in the model.8

The construction starts with a Poisson process at \(M\) times the desired rate and retains every \(M\)th spike. At constant rate, a retained interval is the sum of \(M\) independent exponential intervals. Each initial interval has mean \(1/(M\lambda)\) and variance \(1/(M\lambda)^2\). The retained interval therefore has mean \(1/\lambda\), variance \(1/(M\lambda^2)\), and CV \(1/\sqrt M\). This preserves the mean rate while reducing variability. Its use at changing rates is part of the model. The simple interval derivation assumes a constant rate. 

At constant rate, the retained intervals are independent. This is a renewal process, a spike process whose successive intervals are independent and identically distributed. Let their mean be \(\mu=1/\lambda\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_I\). The time to \(n\) spikes has variance \(n\sigma_I^2\). For a long fixed window \(L\simeq n\mu\), a fluctuation in total interval time produces the opposite fluctuation in count divided by \(\mu\). Thus 
\[ \operatorname{Var}(n)\simeq\frac{n\sigma_I^2}{\mu^2} \simeq\lambda L\left(\frac{\sigma_I}{\mu}\right)^2 =\lambda L\,\mathrm{CV}^2. \]
This explains why the diffusion scale contains CV squared: it is the strength of the accumulated spike fluctuations relative to the Poisson case. The diffusion calculation and information bound show how projecting those fluctuations onto a neutral memory direction adds a factor proportional to \(1/\tau_s^2\) and, for a comparable independent population, \(1/N\).
Rate and sensitivity need more care. Write the absolute local rate slope as \(a=d\lambda/dE\), in spikes/(s deg). For a scale estimate, first use the simpler Poisson model with linear synapses. If \(N\) similar cells fire near rate \(\lambda_0\), their Poisson information per unit time about position is
\[ J\simeq\frac{Na^2}{\lambda_0}. \]
Using the information-diffusion relation as a scale, including the \(\mathrm{CV}^2\) factor just derived and holding the network geometry fixed,
\[ D\ \propto\ \frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{\tau_s^2J} =\frac{\mathrm{CV}^2\lambda_0}{N a^2\tau_s^2}. \]
If instead sensitivity is expressed as the fractional slope \(b=a/\lambda_0\), in inverse degrees, the same expression becomes
\[ D\ \propto\ \frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{N\lambda_0 b^2\tau_s^2}. \]
This second form has the dependence printed in the paper’s Eq. 1, \(D\propto\mathrm{CV}^2N^{-1}\lambda_0^{-1}k_0^{-2}\tau_s^{-2}\).  However, its surrounding text calls \(k_0\) position sensitivity without specifying fractional normalization. If it means the absolute slope in Hz/degree, the Poisson estimate above instead puts \(\lambda_0\) in the numerator at fixed slope. The printed inverse-rate dependence matches a fractional slope. The printed expression is a proportionality, so an omitted factor can carry units; units alone do not establish a printing error. This calculation is a scale estimate under fixed network geometry. The full 2022 model has saturating synapses and sub-Poisson spike trains, so inserting CV squared into the simpler Poisson relation does not give an exact formula for that network.9 
Within this scale estimate, at fixed network geometry and under the noise assumptions above:

Doubling \(N\) halves it.
Doubling CV multiplies it by four.
Doubling \(\tau_s\) divides it by four.
Doubling the absolute slope at fixed rate also divides it by four.

Increasing rate reduces diffusion when the fractional slope is fixed, because more spikes then also supply a proportionally steeper absolute slope. Increasing rate at fixed absolute slope is a different comparison and increases the scale in the first formula. A rate change alone does not specify which comparison is intended.
Could the measured CV itself mostly reflect drift rather than private spike variability? Supplementary Notes test this. Let \(\lambda(t)=\bar\lambda+aB(t)\) during a fixation of length \(T\), with the rate changes small relative to \(\bar\lambda\). Here \(\bar\lambda\) is the baseline rate, \(a\) its change per unit eye position, and \(B(t)\) the Brownian position displacement, with \(\mathbb E[B(t)^2]=2Dt\). Write \(\bar B=T^{-1}\int_0^T B(t)\,dt\) for its mean within that fixation. For a Brownian path starting at zero, the expected time averaged squared position is \(DT\), and the expected squared time mean is \(2DT/3\). Subtracting gives the expected within-segment position variance \(DT/3=2DT/6\):
\[ \mathbb E\!\left[\frac1T\int_0^T(B(t)-\bar B)^2dt\right] =\frac{DT}{3}. \]
The second term follows from \(\mathbb E[B(t)B(s)]=2D\min(t,s)\) and \(T^{-2}\int_0^T\int_0^T2D\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds=2DT/3\). Expanding \(1/(\bar\lambda+aB)\) to first order gives \(1/\bar\lambda-aB/\bar\lambda^2\). Dividing its standard deviation by its mean then gives
\[ \mathrm{CV}_{\rm drift}\simeq \frac{|a|}{\bar\lambda}\sqrt{\frac{2DT}{6}}. \]

With the supplement’s values \(a=1/15\) spikes/(s arcmin), \(2D=100\) arcmin\(^2\)/s, \(T=0.5\) s, and \(\bar\lambda=80\) Hz, this is about \(0.0024\), well below the OMN CV near 0.07. These are an order of magnitude check, not a fitted diffusion constant for the whole model. Since one degree is 60 arcmin, that \(2D\) equals \(0.0278\) deg\(^2\)/s, or \(D=0.0139\) deg\(^2\)/s.10

title: 9  A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift
section: 9.4 The evidence places shared drive upstream without identifying one circuit
text:
9.4 The evidence places shared drive upstream without identifying one circuit
The data and model answer different questions about where the drive originates:

The common variance estimate supports a drive upstream of OMNs, given the calibration and noise assumptions.
The MSD comparison supports a command that accumulates variation over the measured interval, rather than stationary white noise passed through a decaying muscle filter.
The circuit model shows that integrator noise with plausible parameters can generate such a command and explain its filtered amplitude and timing.


Those results do not uniquely locate the noise inside integrator neurons. Two missing tests limit that conclusion: 


No integrator neurons were recorded in this study.



No selective change of that circuit tested whether it was necessary for drift.

Noisy inputs to the integrator, or an already diffusive upstream signal, remain possible. The authors make this distinction in the Discussion and explicitly in their peer review response. Several combinations of neuron count, variability, and synaptic time constant can also fit an amplitude, so matching one curve does not uniquely recover those parameters.12

The study’s empirical scope is horizontal motion during these fixation segments in two animals. Visual tasks, feedback, and other sources of input can alter the statistics. Its contribution to the connection with the 2012 theory is more precise: a continuous memory can diffuse internally, while a mechanical output of that memory looks smooth and superdiffusive at shorter lags. To compare a memory theory with behavior, the mapping from stored value to measured movement is part of the calculation.

title: 10  Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale
text:
10.1 Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields
The study compares recordings of hippocampal place cells from bats flying through tunnels, rats moving over an arena floor, and bats flying through a room. For tunnel flights, the analysis uses distance along an approximately one-dimensional route, although the tunnel itself has width and height. The floor map uses two position coordinates, and the room map uses three.
A cell recorded on a short track may have one smooth firing hill. On a long track, the same kind of cell may have several separated fields, each with a different width and height. In a room, its active regions can bend, split, and surround inactive holes. How could one model produce this variety and still make useful predictions?
Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak propose that a cell’s spatial input is a smooth random function. This function can be interpreted as the average combined input arriving through the cell’s synapses at each animal position. The model cell has positive firing rate where this input exceeds a threshold. The recordings estimate firing rates rather than measuring this input directly.1 The model predicts distributions of field lengths, areas, and volumes, rather than the location of a particular cell’s next field. Its strongest tests check whether fitting field sizes and counts also explains field shapes and holes.2
The paper writes this threshold rule as a rectified input (STAR Methods, Eq. 3). In the notation used here it is
\[ F(x)=a\,[z(x)-q]_+,\qquad [u]_+=\max(u,0). \]
Here \(x\) is the animal’s position, \(z(x)\) is the mean-centered input divided by its standard deviation, \(q\) is the threshold in those standard-deviation units, \(F(x)\) is the predicted firing rate, and \(a>0\) sets its scale. Thus the cell is active where \(z(x)>q\).
[Guide development: the threshold rule] Let the input before centering be \(H(x)\), with constant mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_h>0\). If the cell’s response is modeled as \(F(x)=G[H(x)-H_{\rm th}]_+\) for a positive gain \(G\) and input threshold \(H_{\rm th}\), define
\[ z(x)=\frac{H(x)-\mu}{\sigma_h},\qquad q=\frac{H_{\rm th}-\mu}{\sigma_h},\qquad a=G\sigma_h. \]
Since \(H(x)-H_{\rm th}=\sigma_h[z(x)-q]\) and \(\sigma_h>0\), substituting gives \(F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+\). This is a change of units within the paper’s model: it does not derive thresholded firing from the animal recordings. The following section states the Gaussian-map and smoothness assumptions.
We begin on a track, where a field starts at an upcrossing, a point where the input crosses upward through the threshold. Counting these crossings gives the average number of fields. Combining that count with the lengths of active fields and inactive gaps then separates the effect of the threshold from the distance over which the map changes. These calculations establish the parameters needed for the later predictions of sizes and shapes.
Spatial randomness here describes different possible rate maps. Once a map is drawn, it is fixed while the animal moves through it. The spatial coordinate is not time, and the model does not by itself describe memory drift, spike timing, or learning.
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated overviews may contain incorrect labels, arrows, formulas, or numbers. Use the chapter text and cited papers for the scientific claims.
The random-field introduction establishes the fixed-map meaning and covariance assumptions. Its input standard deviation \(\sigma_0\) is written \(\sigma_h\) here, and its local distance scale \(\ell_c\) is written \(\sigma\).
To predict a field’s width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. A histogram of firing rates alone loses that information: rearranging its values could turn one broad field into many tiny fields without changing the histogram.
The model assigns an input \(h(x)\) to each position \(x\), with nearby values linked so that a cell can have a continuous active region. A Gaussian process specifies a distribution of maps such that the values at any finite set of positions form a jointly Gaussian random vector. A jointly Gaussian vector is one for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian. This joint rule constrains how inputs at different positions can vary together, beyond requiring a Gaussian histogram at each position.
The mean sets the average input, and the spatial covariance describes how inputs at two positions vary together across possible maps. These functions determine the joint Gaussian laws. The chosen covariance must also make the maps smooth enough for the derivatives used below. After a map is drawn, moving the animal changes which position is evaluated, not the map itself.
Three assumptions have different jobs:
A Gaussian distribution of values does not guarantee this smoothness. For example, a covariance proportional to \(e^{-|x-y|/b}\) has a sharp corner at zero separation and does not supply the differentiable paths assumed below.
Set the mean to zero and write \(\sigma_h^2=C(0)\) for input variance. A constant input mean can be absorbed into the threshold. It is useful to normalize the input,
\[ z(x)=\frac{h(x)}{\sigma_h},\qquad F(x)=a\,[z(x)-q]_+, \quad [u]_+=\max(u,0). \]
Here \(z\) has variance one, \(q\) is a dimensionless threshold, and \(a>0\) converts normalized input to firing rate, in Hz. The paper writes \(\theta\) for \(q\), \(r\) for covariance, and \(D\) for spatial dimension. This guide uses \(q,C,d\) to avoid conflicts with earlier chapters. The original input threshold is \(q\sigma_h\). In the paper’s Equation 3 the firing rate is proportional to \([h-q\sigma_h]_+\), which is equivalent to this form after choosing the gain.4
The input threshold summarizes how much combined input is needed before the model cell fires. It can reflect the cell’s own response properties and inhibitory input. Raising \(q\) at a fixed input map leaves fewer positions active. If the absolute threshold above the input mean is positive and held fixed, increasing the input standard deviation \(\sigma_h\) lowers \(q\), making activity more widespread. Changing \(a\) instead changes rates within active regions while preserving their zero-rate boundaries. A fixed positive detection cutoff in Hz would change this last conclusion. A fitted threshold describes the balance of input and response. It does not identify which biological quantity changed.
The excursion set above \(q\) is
\[ A_q=\{x:z(x)>q\}. \]
Each connected piece of \(A_q\) is a model place field. In one dimension its size is length. In two and three dimensions it is area and volume. Two nearby peaks belong to one field if an above-threshold path joins them. Counting peaks and counting fields therefore answer different questions.
For a one dimensional stationary process, differentiation of covariance gives
\[ \operatorname{Var}(h')= \left.\partial_x\partial_y C(y-x)\right|_{y=x}=-C''(0). \]
The minus sign comes from differentiating \(y-x\) once with respect to each variable. The paper defines the spatial scale
\[ \sigma=\sqrt{-\frac{C(0)}{C''(0)}}; \qquad \operatorname{Var}(z')=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}. \]
Thus \(\sigma\) compares typical height with typical slope and has units of distance. In an isotropic field, the same definition applies along any unit direction. For the smooth Gaussian covariance \(C(\Delta x)=\sigma_h^2\exp[-\|\Delta x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)]\), it is exactly the parameter in that exponent. The paper uses a Gaussian covariance for its simulations. Other smooth covariances can share this local scale while having different longer distance structure.5
A simulated Gaussian input map with covariance \(C(\Delta x)=\exp[-(\Delta x/\sigma)^2/2]\) gives the firing map below when \(q=0.8\) and \(a=6\) Hz. Position is shown in units of \(\sigma\).
Thresholding changes the distribution of values and can separate one smooth input curve into several fields. Both panels describe the same fixed map over space, so neither curve is a trajectory over time. See Gaussian input and firing rate, STAR Methods Eqs. 2–3, p. e1.

title: 10  Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale
text:
Mathematical definitions: Gaussian processes and spatial covariance

For chosen positions \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), the input vector is \((h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_n))\). Its mean vector and covariance matrix are obtained by evaluating two functions, 
\[ m(x)=\mathbb E[h(x)],\qquad C(x,y)=\mathbb E[(h(x)-m(x))(h(y)-m(y))]. \]

The expectation runs over possible maps, or over cells assumed to share these statistics. For jointly Gaussian vectors, zero covariance between two subvectors implies their independence. That extra property, which does not hold for general distributions, will simplify the crossing calculation. The values after thresholding will generally not have a Gaussian distribution.3 





Stationarity means that moving the observation window does not change the map’s probability law. Here it gives a constant mean and a covariance \(C(x,y)=C(y-x)\) that depends on separation. It does not say that a particular map is flat.




Isotropy means that rotating the separation does not change the covariance: in several dimensions, \(C(\Delta x)\) depends only on \(\|\Delta x\|\). It rules out a preferred direction in the model’s statistics. Stationarity alone does not imply isotropy.



Smoothness controls whether the map has well defined spatial derivatives. Crossing calculations require differentiable sample functions and nondegenerate joint distributions: the relevant vector of heights and derivatives must have an invertible covariance matrix, rather than obey an exact linear constraint. Peak calculations require second derivatives and enough regularity to control their local approximation.

Values above \(q\) are reduced by \(q\) and multiplied by \(a\). The shaded connected intervals are the model fields. This is a simulated teaching map with chosen parameters, not a recorded cell. text:
10.2 Upcrossings count fields, with an endpoint correction
A field starts at an upcrossing, so its expected count can be found by counting upward passages through the threshold. A small interval around each crossing has a width determined by its slope. This lets us count crossings without locating every root.
For the paper’s smooth stationary Gaussian model, the predicted mean number of upcrossings per unit distance is
\[ \nu_+(q)=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\sigma}. \]
Here \(q\) is the normalized threshold and \(\sigma\) is the spatial scale defined above. On a long track, this is also the mean field count per unit length. A finite track needs the endpoint correction derived below. This is the Kac–Rice result used in Supplemental Methods S3; it does not require the high-threshold approximation.
Consider a differentiable fixed curve and a simple upward crossing \(x_0\) of \(q\), with slope \(v=z'(x_0)>0\). Close to the crossing,
\[ z(x)-q\simeq v(x-x_0). \]

The curve lies in the vertical band \(|z-q|<\varepsilon\) for a spatial distance approximately \(2\varepsilon/v\). Integrating \(z'(x)/(2\varepsilon)\) over that interval contributes one. Restricting to positive slopes counts only upward crossings. Under the usual regularity conditions, averaging this counting identity gives the Kac–Rice formula for the mean upcrossing density, 
\[ \nu_+(q)=\int_0^\infty v\,p_{z,z'}(q,v)\,dv. \]
The density \(p_{z,z'}(q,v)\) describes how often height is near \(q\) and slope near \(v\). Multiplication by \(v\) compensates for the shorter spatial window of a steep crossing. Multiplying the probability of being above threshold by a typical slope would miss this weighting.6
We can evaluate the integral because height and slope are independent here. Stationarity gives
\[ \mathbb E[zz']=\frac12\frac{d}{dx}\mathbb E[z(x)^2]=0. \]

Height and slope are jointly Gaussian. Zero covariance therefore makes them independent. Their distributions are \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(z'\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^{-2})\). Consequently, 
\[ \begin{aligned} \nu_+(q) &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^\infty v\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\sigma^2v^2/2}\,dv\\ &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} =\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\sigma}. \end{aligned} \]

In the integral, use \(u=\sigma^2v^2/2\), so \(v\,dv=du/\sigma^2\). This result is exact for the stated smooth stationary Gaussian model. A high threshold is not needed. Its units are inverse distance: increasing \(\sigma\) stretches the map and reduces crossings per metre. 
A fixed smooth curve shows how to count a field already active at the left edge and why the crossing integral weights each slope.







Figure 10.4: Two upcrossings start two new fields, and one field is already active at the left edge. The local tangent panels show that a steeper crossing occupies a narrower threshold band, while slope weighting makes each crossing contribute one. This is a guide construction, not a sampled cell or a new fit. It illustrates Mainali et al. (2025), Figure 1A–B and Supplemental Methods S3, Equations S11–S15.




The count includes every connected active interval intersecting the track. Discarding clipped boundary fields would change this convention.
On a finite track \([0,L]\), each upcrossing starts a field, but a field may already be active at the left endpoint. If \(N_L\) counts all components intersecting the track, then, under regularity conditions that exclude tangencies and give nonzero slopes at crossings,
\[ N_L=N_+(q;[0,L])+\mathbf1\{z(0)>q\}, \qquad \mathbb E[N_L]=L\nu_+(q)+Q(q), \]
Here \(N_+(q;[0,L])\) counts upward crossings within the track, and \(\mathbf1\{z(0)>q\}\) equals one if the left endpoint is active and zero otherwise. The probability \(Q(q)=1-\Phi(q)\) uses the standard normal cumulative distribution function \(\Phi\). The last term is the endpoint correction. Removing incomplete boundary fields changes the counting convention, so the same correction cannot then be used unchanged. This identity also gives the paper’s exact one dimensional mean Euler characteristic, Equation 8. In one dimension, the Euler characteristic is the number of connected active intervals, so it is the field count used here. The later topology chapter extends this count to maps with holes.7

section: 10.3 Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scale
text:
10.3 Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scale
A low field count can result from a high threshold or a slowly varying map. Field lengths help separate those possibilities.

At a uniformly chosen position, the probability of activity is \(Q(q)\). Here \(q\) is the normalized threshold and \(Q(q)=1-\Phi(q)\) is the chance that a standard normal value exceeds it. Hence a track of length \(L\) has expected occupied length \(LQ(q)\). On a long stationary track, the average occupied length per field is the occupied length per unit distance divided by the number of fields per unit distance. Write \(\mu_s\) for mean active-field length, \(\mu_g\) for mean inactive-gap length, and \(\nu_+(q)\) for the mean number of upcrossings per unit distance. The corresponding gap calculation uses the inactive fraction \(\Phi(q)\): 
\[ \begin{aligned} \mu_s&=\frac{Q(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma Q(q)e^{q^2/2},\\ \mu_g&=\frac{\Phi(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma\Phi(q)e^{q^2/2}. \end{aligned} \]
These are stationary per-field and per-gap means, ignoring clipping at track boundaries. They are not an assertion that the expectation of a finite sample’s ratio equals the ratio of its expectations. Subject to suitable averaging over a long track or many maps, they give the inference rule in Methods S3, Equations S14–S15.8
Adding and dividing removes one unknown at a time:
\[ \mu_s+\mu_g=2\pi\sigma e^{q^2/2},\qquad \frac{\mu_s}{\mu_s+\mu_g}=Q(q). \]

Thus 
\[ q=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\mu_g}{\mu_s+\mu_g}\right), \qquad \sigma=\frac{\mu_s+\mu_g}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2}. \]


For example, \(q=1.1\) and \(\sigma=2.4\) m, the fitted parameters reported for the 200 m bat tunnel, give \(Q(q)=0.1357\), \(\nu_+=0.03621\) per metre, \(\mu_s=3.746\) m, and \(\mu_g=23.868\) m in the continuous model. Putting these two means into the inversion recovers \(q=1.1\) and \(\sigma=2.4\) m. The expected number of intersecting fields on a 200 m track is \(7.2425+0.1357=7.3782\), including the left endpoint term. These are calculations from the fitted model, not fresh estimates from raw recordings.  



The means do not imply a full gap or count distribution. At high thresholds, distant rare excursions can approach independent events if correlations decay sufficiently with distance. In that regime, field locations approach a Poisson process, counts in a long interval are approximately Poisson, and gaps are approximately exponential. Smoothness and stationarity alone do not ensure this independence. A periodic Gaussian process, for example, retains long distance dependence. Upward and downward crossings that enclose the same small field remain strongly related even when fields far apart are almost independent.   
Experimental selection also matters. If cells with no fields are excluded, let \(N\) be a cell’s number of fields, \(n\) a possible count, and \(\lambda\) the unconditioned mean count. A Poisson model then gives
\[ \Pr(N=n\mid N\ge1)= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n}{n!(1-e^{-\lambda})},\quad n\ge1, \qquad \mathbb E[N\mid N\ge1]=\frac{\lambda}{1-e^{-\lambda}}. \]
The mean follows because the omitted \(n=0\) term contributes zero to \(\sum n\Pr(N=n)=\lambda\), while conditioning divides all remaining probabilities by \(1-e^{-\lambda}\). For \(\lambda=1\), \(36.8\%\) of cells are excluded and the observed mean is \(1.582\), not one. Using \(1.582\) as the unconditioned mean would infer too many fields. The paper applies this correction to its two dimensional count fit, Equation 5.9

title: 11  High peaks explain size laws across dimensions
text:
11.1 Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic
Knowing the average field length does not tell us how often fields fall within a given size range. Why should the same spatial model give one size distribution on a track, another in an arena, and a third in a room? The next step is to find the shape of a typical field when only unusually high input peaks rise above the threshold.
Near such a peak, the smooth input is approximately a downward parabola. Its height above the threshold sets a radius, and converting that radius into length, area or volume gives the different size laws. Cuts through a map test its spatial structure, and slopes at field edges provide a separate check on the predicted field widths. The size laws use a high threshold approximation. The boundary-slope law has a separate exact derivation under the smooth stationary Gaussian assumptions.
We keep the earlier notation: \(z(x)\) is the spatial input normalized to variance one, \(q\) is its threshold, \(\sigma\) is its local distance scale, and \(a\) converts positive excess input into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is \(d\). The firing rule remains \(F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+\), where \([u]_+=\max(u,0)\).
The central prediction is the paper’s Equation 1: in the high-threshold limit, the probability density of a field of size \(s>0\) is
\[ p_d(s)=\frac{2\beta}{d}s^{2/d-1}\exp\!\left(-\beta s^{2/d}\right). \]
Here \(d\) is the number of spatial dimensions; \(s\) means length in 1D, area in 2D, and volume in 3D. The positive scale is \(\beta=q^2/(2\sigma^2v_d^{2/d})\) in the high-threshold geometry, where \(v_d\) is the volume of the unit ball: \(v_1=2\), \(v_2=\pi\), and \(v_3=4\pi/3\). It depends on the threshold and local spatial scale. For instance, \(d=1\) gives a Rayleigh-shaped length density, while \(d=2\) gives an exponential area density. This is an asymptotic prediction for high thresholds, not an exact law for every finite threshold.
[Guide development: from high peaks to the size density] Select a typical field away from an environment boundary and let \(\epsilon\) be its peak’s excess above the high threshold \(q\). The paper’s high-excursion argument gives \(U=q\epsilon\) an approximately exponential distribution of mean one as \(q\to\infty\). In one dimension this follows from the ratio of high upcrossing densities: the chance that a selected peak above \(q\) also exceeds \(q+u/q\) approaches \(e^{-u}\). In higher dimensions the ratio of the additional leading peak-count factors tends to one in the same limit. This step assumes the smooth, stationary, isotropic Gaussian model and well-separated high fields; it is an approximation, not a proof for every covariance or a finite-threshold identity.
Near such a high peak, put the peak at \(x=0\). Its average curvature is approximately \(-q/\sigma^2\) in each spatial direction, so \(z(x)-q\simeq\epsilon-q\|x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)\). The threshold crossing occurs at radius \(r_*\simeq\sigma\sqrt{2\epsilon/q}\). An approximately round field therefore has size
\[ s\simeq v_dr_*^d=v_d\left(\frac{\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\right)^d U^{d/2}, \qquad U=\beta s^{2/d},\qquad \beta=\frac{q^2}{2\sigma^2v_d^{2/d}}. \]
For a possible size \(S>0\), the high-threshold approximation makes the events \(s\le S\) and \(U\le\beta S^{2/d}\) approximately equivalent. With \(\Pr(U>u)\to e^{-u}\), the high-threshold approximation gives \(\Pr(s\le S)\simeq1-e^{-\beta S^{2/d}}\). Differentiating it gives \(p_d(S)=(2\beta/d)S^{2/d-1}e^{-\beta S^{2/d}}\), the formula above. The derivative supplies the change-of-variable factor; it is why simply relabeling the exponential density would give the wrong result. The following sections expand the peak and geometry arguments, their conditions, and finite-threshold checks.
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated overviews may contain incorrect labels, arrows, formulas, or numbers. Use the chapter text and cited papers for the scientific claims.
The peak-geometry introduction explains why radius depends on peak excess and why dimension changes the size law. Here its distance scale \(\ell_c\) is written \(\sigma\), and the curvature approximation is derived explicitly.
The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. To obtain that distribution, we examine the small region around a peak that barely exceeds a high threshold.
The following is a teaching reconstruction of the high excursion argument in Methods S4, with algebraic corrections made explicit below. It assumes:
It is not a proof of the full excursion convergence theorem for every allowed covariance.1
The Hessian is the matrix \(H\) of second spatial derivatives. Its eigenvalues describe curvature along the principal directions. At a point \(x_0\) where the gradient is zero, a small displacement \(\delta x\) changes the normalized input approximately by
\[ z(x_0+\delta x)-z(x_0)\simeq\tfrac12\delta x^T H\delta x, \qquad H_{ij}=\left.\frac{\partial^2z}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}\right|_{x_0}. \]
For this smooth scalar field, \(H\) is symmetric and has perpendicular principal directions. Along a unit eigenvector, the corresponding eigenvalue is the second derivative in that direction: negative curvature bends the map downward, positive curvature upward. The entries of \(H\) have inverse distance squared units because \(z\) is dimensionless.
Isotropy and the definition of \(\sigma\) imply
\[ \operatorname{Cov}(\partial_i\partial_j z,z) =-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\sigma^2}. \]
Here \(\delta_{ij}\) is one for equal indices and zero otherwise. For jointly Gaussian variables, conditioning \(Y\) on a scalar \(Z\) of variance one gives \(\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=b]=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)b\) when both means vanish. One way to see this is to write \(Y=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)Z+\epsilon\). The remainder has zero covariance with \(Z\) and is therefore independent of it. Applying this to each Hessian entry gives
\[ \mathbb E[H\mid z=b]=-\frac{b}{\sigma^2}I. \]
Here \(b\) is the selected height of the normalized input and \(I\) is the identity matrix. The conditional fluctuations around this mean have a variance that does not grow with \(b\). For a high peak, the negative mean curvature is of order \(q\), so its relative fluctuations become small. Conditioning the gradient to zero does not change this Gaussian conditional mean, because the gradient has zero covariance with both height and Hessian in a stationary isotropic field. Selecting an actual maximum also weights curvatures, but its leading high peak shape is the same.
Let the peak height be \(q+\epsilon\), with \(\epsilon>0\), and put the peak at the origin. The gradient there is zero. The Taylor expansion becomes, to leading order,
\[ z(x)-q\simeq\epsilon-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}\|x\|^2. \]
It is positive inside an approximately round region of radius
\[ r_*\simeq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon}{q}}. \]
The remaining question is how \(\epsilon\) is distributed when we select one high field at a time. In one dimension, the number of high maxima is asymptotically the number of upcrossings, proportional to \(e^{-q^2/2}\). Therefore the fraction of peaks above \(q\) that also exceed \(q+\epsilon\) is approximately
\[ \frac{e^{-(q+\epsilon)^2/2}}{e^{-q^2/2}} =e^{-q\epsilon-\epsilon^2/2}. \]
Define \(U=q\epsilon\). At fixed \(u\ge0\) and as \(q\) increases,
\[ \Pr(U>u)\simeq e^{-u-u^2/(2q^2)}\longrightarrow e^{-u}. \]
Thus the scaled excess height approaches an exponential variable of mean one. In several dimensions, high peak counts have the additional leading factor \(q^{d-1}\). Its ratio at \(q+u/q\) and \(q\) tends to one, so the same excess-height limit remains. The higher dimensional count factor will also follow from the Euler characteristic calculation. A rigorous conclusion requires control of the remainder and of components containing multiple peaks, beyond this local argument.
In one dimension, the full field length is \(s=2r_*\). Eliminating \(\epsilon\) gives
\[ s\simeq\frac{2\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\sqrt U, \qquad \epsilon\simeq\frac{q s^2}{8\sigma^2}. \]
This supplies two distinct predictions:
The exponent two concerns rate versus linear size. In three dimensions a suitable linear size is \(s^{1/3}\) when \(s\) denotes volume.
At moderate thresholds the omitted shape fluctuations matter. Figure 3C reports a rate versus length exponent of \(1.42\) in the 200 m bat data and \(1.46\) in finite threshold model simulations. Figure 3D reports \(1.75\) versus \(1.71\) using cube root of volume in 3D. These are compatible with a model that approaches exponent two only as the threshold becomes large. They are not measurements of the limiting exponent. Figure 5A–C illustrates the progression toward simpler, usually single peak fields as \(q\) increases. Figure 4C tests this trend in the shorter bat tunnel.2

Example: curvature distinguishes a peak from a saddle


Take two displacement coordinates in metres and put the critical point at the origin. For \(H=\operatorname{diag}(-2,-8)\) m\(^{-2}\), the local quadratic is \(z-z(0)=-(x_1/\mathrm{m})^2-4(x_2/\mathrm{m})^2\). The surface falls in both directions, more steeply along \(x_2\), so the origin is a peak. With \(H=\operatorname{diag}(-2,8)\) m\(^{-2}\) it falls along \(x_1\) but rises along \(x_2\): the origin is a saddle. These two local examples illustrate the geometry; the high peaks in the isotropic model become approximately round only in the stated limit.

























The length is a scaled square root of an exponential variable, giving a Rayleigh distribution.



The peak firing rate is \(a\epsilon\), so at fixed high \(q\) it is proportional to \(s^2\).

title: 11  High peaks explain size laws across dimensions
section: 11.2 Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension
text:
11.2 Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension
A round region’s radius and its volume have different units and different distributions. This geometric conversion explains why the model predicts different histograms in a track, an arena, and a room.
Let \(v_d=\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(1+d/2)\) be the volume of a unit ball in \(d\) dimensions. For \(d=1,2,3\), it is \(2,\pi,4\pi/3\). The symbol \(\Gamma\) is the gamma function, defined for \(t>0\) by \(\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du\). It extends factorials: \(\Gamma(n+1)=n!\).
Using the radius from the preceding section, the field size is
\[ s\simeq v_d\left(\frac{\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\right)^d U^{d/2}, \qquad U=\beta s^{2/d},\qquad \beta=\frac{q^2}{2\sigma^2v_d^{2/d}}. \]
The same local radius gives a length, an area, or a volume depending on the dimension of the region.







Figure 11.4: In the high-threshold approximation, excess peak height fixes a radius, and converting that radius into length, area, or volume gives powers 2, 1, and 2/3 in \(U=\beta s^{2/d}\). The round regions are a guide reconstruction of the limiting geometry, not observed field shapes. See Mainali et al. (2025), Equation 1 and Supplemental Methods S4, with the parabola constants checked in this chapter.




The round shape and exponential excess belong to the high-threshold limit, so they do not make every measured place field spherical.
Within the high threshold limit, \(U\) has density \(p_U(u)=e^{-u}\) for \(u>0\). As in the mathematical-tools chapter, let \(s\) be the random field size and \(S>0\) a possible cutoff. The map \(u(S)=\beta S^{2/d}\) is increasing, so \(s\le S\) and \(U\le u(S)\) describe the same event. Its probability is therefore
\[ \Pr(s\le S)=\Pr(U\le\beta S^{2/d}) =1-e^{-\beta S^{2/d}}. \]
Differentiating with respect to the cutoff \(S\) gives the density of field size. The derivative \(du/dS\) is the change-of-variable factor: for a short size interval, \(p_d(S)\,dS\simeq p_U(u)\,du\). A stretched interval in \(u\) has more probability, so its density per unit size includes the stretch. Since \(u(S)\) increases, this factor is positive:
\[ \begin{aligned} p_d(S)&=e^{-\beta S^{2/d}}\frac{d}{dS}(\beta S^{2/d})\\ &=\frac{2\beta}{d}S^{2/d-1}e^{-\beta S^{2/d}},\qquad S>0. \end{aligned} \]
This is the paper’s Equation 1. It is also written \(p_d(s)\) when \(s\) denotes the size at which the density is evaluated. The expression for \(\beta\) above is its leading high threshold geometric scale, not an exact finite threshold identity. A finite threshold simulation can share the approximate shape while having a different fitted scale.3
The mean field size \(\mu_s=\mathbb E[s]\) and its corresponding scale are
\[ \mu_s=\Gamma(1+d/2)\beta^{-d/2},\qquad \beta=\left[\frac{\Gamma(1+d/2)}{\mu_s}\right]^{2/d}. \]
[Guide derivation: normalization and higher size moments] The same substitution verifies normalization: \(\int_0^\infty p_d(s)\,ds=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du=1\). It also supplies every positive moment,
\[ \mathbb E[s^k] =\beta^{-kd/2}\int_0^\infty u^{kd/2}e^{-u}\,du =\beta^{-kd/2}\Gamma(1+kd/2). \]
Setting \(k=1\) gives the mean and rearranging gives the scale formula immediately above.
Size has units of distance to the power \(d\), while \(\beta\) has units of inverse distance squared in every dimension. This makes \(\beta s^{2/d}\) dimensionless, and makes \(p_d(s)\) a density per unit size. These checks catch mistakes in changing variables.
Writing dimensionless size as \(w=\beta^{d/2}s\) removes the size scale. The dimensional size laws then differ in shape, while the transformed variable \(U=\beta s^{2/d}=w^{2/d}\) has the same exponential law.







Figure 11.5: The limiting size densities differ with spatial dimension: one dimensional length is Rayleigh, two dimensional area is exponential, and three dimensional volume has a density that rises without bound as size approaches zero, while its integral remains one. Their survival probabilities, the probabilities of exceeding a threshold, coincide after transformation to \(U=\beta s^{2/d}\), where \(\Pr(U>u)=e^{-u}\). These are exact calculations from the high-threshold limiting law, not finite-threshold simulations or measured histograms. Based on Mainali et al. (2025), main Eq. 1, p. 1111, and Methods S3.




Removing units does not erase the difference between length, area, and volume distributions. The nonlinear transformation to U removes that shape difference. Its shared exponential law is the assumption used in the change of variables. See Field-size laws, Eq. 1, p. 1111.




Table 11.1: Field-size laws in one, two, and three dimensions.











Space
Meaning of \(s\)
Density
Consequence




\(d=1\)
length
\(2\beta s e^{-\beta s^2}\)
Rayleigh. Density vanishes at zero.


\(d=2\)
area
\(\beta e^{-\beta s}\)
Exponential. Mean area is \(1/\beta\).


\(d=3\)

\((2\beta/3)s^{-1/3}e^{-\beta s^{2/3}}\)
Weibull with shape \(2/3\). Density rises without bound near zero but is integrable.








A Weibull distribution has survival probability \(\Pr(\text{size}>s)=\exp[-(s/b)^k]\) for size \(s>0\), scale \(b>0\), and shape \(k>0\). This is the chance that a field is larger than \(s\). Here \(k=2/d\) and \(b=\beta^{-d/2}\). In 3D the diverging density does not mean a positive probability of exactly zero volume. The probability of \(0<s<\delta\) still tends to zero as \(\delta\to0\). 
For a concrete comparison, set \(\sigma=1\) m and \(q=5\) in this limiting calculation. The mean size is \(0.5013\) m in 1D, \(0.2513\) m\(^2\) in 2D, and \(0.1260\) m\(^3\) in 3D. These values describe the same local distance scale and threshold, rather than fields with the same numerical size in different units. More generally, the geometry and moment formula simplify to \(\mu_s\simeq(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma/q)^d\).


This approximation has a measurable error even for a smooth Gaussian process. At \(q=1.1,\sigma=2.4\) m, its 1D mean is \(5.469\) m, compared with the exact stationary crossing result \(3.746\) m, an overestimate of \(46.0\%\). At \(q=5\) the error is \(3.73\%\). This is why the paper compares data to finite threshold simulations as well as to limiting curves.  

Source check: three printed steps in the supplement
The printed supplement appears to contain three algebraic errors in this calculation:

Equation S18 prints multiplication by mean size where the preceding moment formula requires division.
Equation S23 omits a factor \(\sqrt2\) when solving the parabola in S22 for full width.
In S25 the finite-height quadratic exponent should be negative.

The derivation above retains the main paper’s distributional form and obtains the constants from the displayed parabola, the moment integral, and the independent crossing calculation. These corrections concern the printed derivation. They do not establish that the simulation code or empirical fits used the same mistakes.4

section: 11.3 Slices test spatial structure beyond field volume
text:
11.3 Slices test spatial structure beyond field volume
A model can fit field volumes and still place activity incorrectly within those volumes. Slicing the map tests that internal spatial structure.

Restrict a Gaussian field to a straight line \(x=x_0+tv\), where \(x_0\) is a chosen starting position, \(v\) is the line’s unit direction, and \(t\) is distance along the line, not time. At any chosen values \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\), its values are a subset of the original jointly Gaussian values. They therefore remain jointly Gaussian. Along the line the covariance is \(C((t-t')v)\). For a unit direction in an isotropic field it has the same local length scale \(\sigma\). The same argument applies to a flat plane. First slicing and then thresholding gives the same active portions as thresholding and then slicing.5 


Thus a line through a 2D or 3D map has the one dimensional excursion prediction, and a plane through a 3D map has the two dimensional prediction. The field being counted is now a connected active interval or patch in that slice. One 3D component can be missed, cut into multiple pieces, or intersect several slices.  
Choosing one original field uniformly and cutting through its centre is different from choosing lines uniformly through space. Large fields are more likely to be hit by a spatially sampled line, and most hits pass away from their centres. The Gaussian restriction argument describes excursions along the sampled line. The radius distribution for fields counted once each cannot be used directly as the distribution of lengths observed along a line. In the high peak picture, an isotropic \(d\) dimensional field has a radius of order \(\sigma/q\). Converting this same radius into \(d\) dimensional size and then cutting it requires both hit probability and cut position.
Figure 2 separates the measurements by spatial dimension:


Panels A–B illustrate 2D thresholding. C measures lengths along slices, D measures original field areas, and E counts fields per observed cell.




F–G show 3D examples. H, I, and J compare line lengths, planar areas, and full volumes.

Figure 11.6: Sections through two and three dimensional maps follow the size law for the dimension of the section. Original Figure 2 from Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025). Exact artwork excerpt. PDF page 5. Open image at full size.






The dashed analytical curves change with the dimension of the measurement, even within one recorded map. The alternative spherical-field model in Figure S2 matches empirical volumes and peak rates by construction but fails these slice distributions and the topology test. Matching volumes alone is therefore insufficient.6

section: 11.4 Why slopes at field boundaries are Rayleigh
text:
11.4 Why slopes at field boundaries are Rayleigh
The derivative at an arbitrary position is Gaussian. A field boundary is a selected position, however, and selecting it changes the derivative distribution.
Return to the crossing integral, using \(v=z'(x)\) for the local derivative of normalized input per unit distance. Retain only slopes between \(v\) and \(v+dv\). Their contribution is proportional to \(v p_{z'}(v)dv\), where \(p_{z'}(v)\) is the probability density of the derivative at an arbitrary position. Dividing by the total contribution of positive slopes gives the slope density at a typical upcrossing:
\[ p_{\uparrow}(v) =\frac{v p_{z'}(v)}{\int_0^\infty w p_{z'}(w)\,dw} =\sigma^2v\exp[-\sigma^2v^2/2],\qquad v>0. \]

The height density cancels because height and slope are independent. This Rayleigh law is therefore independent of \(q\) under the smooth stationary Gaussian model, without a high threshold approximation. Absolute slopes at downward boundaries have the same law. The rate slope is \(av\), so its scale also depends on the firing rate gain. This selection effect explains why a half Gaussian law for a positive derivative sampled uniformly in space would be wrong at crossings.7 

Independent check: recover field width from its boundary slope
There is also an independent check on the high threshold width constant. Starting at an upcrossing with slope \(v\), the local excursion is approximately
\[ z(x)-q\simeq vx-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}x^2. \]
Its second root is \(s=2\sigma^2v/q\). Changing variables in the exact crossing slope law gives \(p(s)=2\beta s e^{-\beta s^2}\) with \(\beta=q^2/(8\sigma^2)\), the same constant as the peak calculation for \(v_1=2\).


Figure 3A identifies which width, peak, and slopes are measured. B compares local peak counts, C–D compare rate and size, and E compares boundary slopes. The paper measures boundary slopes by a finite difference between samples 0.1 m apart. This approximates a derivative and has its own spatial resolution. It is not a direct observation of the underlying synaptic input.

title: 12  Holes and measurements test the spatial explanation
text:
12.1 Holes distinguish maps with the same field count
Two maps can have the same field sizes and counts while arranging their active regions differently. One may contain rings or tunnels that the other lacks. Can the Gaussian spatial model account for these differences, and how much would that agreement tell us about the circuit that produced the maps?
We first count connected regions and holes together, which gives a prediction across activity thresholds. The boundary of the observed environment matters for this calculation, so we keep its contributions. We then examine which measured quantities set the model’s parameters and which provide further tests. Finally, a sum of many randomly weighted inputs shows one way a circuit could produce Gaussian spatial input, while making clear which assumptions and circuit measurements that explanation still needs.
The input map varies with position but remains fixed in time in this model. As before, \(q\) is the threshold applied to normalized input, \(\sigma\) is the local spatial scale, and \(a\) converts normalized input above threshold into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is \(d\). It is separate from the diffusion coefficient \(D\) used in the memory chapters.
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated overviews may contain incorrect labels, arrows, formulas, or numbers. Use the chapter text and cited papers for the scientific claims.
Two maps can have the same field count and total active area but different holes. As the input threshold \(q\) rises, active regions shrink and can split or disappear. The numbers of components and holes can change.
The Euler characteristic, written \(\chi\) and unrelated to the common variance fraction \(\chi\) in the eye chapter, combines these counts differently in each dimension:
These counts are the first three Betti numbers: numbers of independent components, loops, and cavities, respectively.1
For a smooth, stationary, isotropic Gaussian input on a closed interval, square, or cube of side length \(L\), the paper predicts the mean Euler characteristic (Eqs. 8–10). Let \(r=L/\sigma\) and \(Q(q)=\Pr(Z>q)\) for a standard normal variable \(Z\). Then
\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[\chi_1]&=Q(q)+\frac{r}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2},\\ \mathbb E[\chi_2]&=Q(q)+\left[\frac{2r}{2\pi}+\frac{r^2q}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\right]e^{-q^2/2},\\ \mathbb E[\chi_3]&=Q(q)+\left[\frac{3r}{2\pi}+\frac{3r^2q}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}+\frac{r^3(q^2-1)}{(2\pi)^2}\right]e^{-q^2/2}. \end{aligned} \]
The subscript gives the spatial dimension, \(q\) is the normalized input threshold, and \(\sigma\) is the local spatial scale. The terms involving powers of \(r\) include interior and boundary contributions. These formulas predict the mean signed topology, not necessarily the number of fields when holes or tunnels are present. The calculation below explains their terms.
The expected Euler characteristic has an exact Gaussian formula even where identifying it with field count would be wrong. We already derived the 1D case. To understand the higher dimensional factors, we use a mathematical result. A critical point is a location where the gradient is zero. For a smooth function on a compact domain with invertible Hessians at its critical points and suitable boundary conditions, Morse theory expresses the Euler characteristic as a signed count of critical points, including boundary contributions. We do not prove that topological theorem here. The calculation below shows how its Gaussian expectation produces the paper’s polynomials and boundary terms. The general Gaussian result is given by Taylor’s kinematic formula.2
The signs have a geometric meaning. In 2D, lowering the threshold through a maximum creates an active component, adding one to \(\chi\). Passing a saddle joins two components or opens a hole, subtracting one. Passing a minimum fills a hole, adding one. As in the peak and saddle example, the Hessian has two negative eigenvalues at a maximum, opposite signs at a saddle, and two positive eigenvalues at a minimum. The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues; for a two-dimensional Hessian, \(\det(-H)\) is the product of their negatives. It therefore has the required signs \(+,-,+\). These signs require nonzero eigenvalues; a flat critical direction needs a different analysis. The boundary terms account for changes at the edge of the observed region.
First take the interior of a \(j\) dimensional region, with \(j\le3\), and set \(\lambda=\sigma^{-2}\). Here \(z\) is the unit-variance input map, \(H\) is its Hessian of second spatial derivatives, and \(\nabla z\) is its gradient. A critical point has gradient zero. The multidimensional Kac–Rice rule counts these zeros with the absolute Hessian determinant. The Morse signs replace that absolute determinant by \(\det(-H)\). The resulting signed density above level \(q\) is
\[ \eta_j(q)=p_{\nabla z}(0) \int_q^\infty \mathbb E[\det(-H)\mid z=b,\nabla z=0]\,\phi(b)\,db, \]
Here \(\eta_j(q)\) is the expected signed critical-point count per unit \(j\)-dimensional volume above threshold \(q\), \(b\) is a possible input height in the integral, and \(p_{\nabla z}(0)\) is the gradient density at zero. The standard-normal height density is \(\phi(b)=e^{-b^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\). The gradient’s \(j\) components are independent Gaussians of variance \(\lambda\), so \(p_{\nabla z}(0)=(2\pi\lambda)^{-j/2}\). The determinant measures how spatial volume near a gradient zero converts to gradient volume, just as the slope did for a scalar crossing.
The resulting signed densities are
\[ \eta_1=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\sigma},\qquad \eta_2=\frac{q e^{-q^2/2}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\sigma^2},\qquad \eta_3=\frac{(q^2-1)e^{-q^2/2}}{(2\pi)^2\sigma^3}. \]
These are signed densities per length, area, and volume, not three formulas for positive field counts.
[Guide derivation: the Gaussian determinant average] Write the conditional Hessian as \(H=-b\lambda I+G\), where \(G\) has zero mean. Differentiating an isotropic covariance four times gives, for distinct indices \(i,k\),
\[ \mathbb E[G_{ii}G_{kk}]=\kappa-\lambda^2, \qquad \mathbb E[G_{ik}^2]=\kappa. \]
The constant \(\kappa\) describes a fourth derivative of covariance. Conditioning on height subtracts \(\lambda^2\) from the covariance of the two diagonal entries, but not from the off-diagonal variance. Hence each pair contributes
\[ \mathbb E[G_{ii}G_{kk}-G_{ik}^2]=-\lambda^2. \]
For \(j=1\), \(\mathbb E[\det(-H)\mid b]=b\lambda\). For \(j=2\), expand the two by two determinant to obtain \(\lambda^2(b^2-1)\). For \(j=3\), the leading term is \(b^3\lambda^3\). The three index pairs each contribute \(-b\lambda^3\), and all odd centered Gaussian products vanish. The result is \(\lambda^3(b^3-3b)\). The unknown fourth derivative \(\kappa\) has canceled.
Integrating the three polynomials gives
\[ \begin{aligned} \int_q^\infty b\phi(b)\,db&=\phi(q),\\ \int_q^\infty(b^2-1)\phi(b)\,db&=q\phi(q),\\ \int_q^\infty(b^3-3b)\phi(b)\,db&=(q^2-1)\phi(q). \end{aligned} \]
For example, differentiate \(-q\phi(q)\) to get \((q^2-1)\phi(q)\), which verifies the second integral using its vanishing upper endpoint. Combining the determinant, gradient density, and integral gives the signed densities above.
Now include the boundary of an ordinary closed square or cube of side \(L\), whose opposite faces are not joined and with every intersecting component retained. On a \(j\) dimensional face, derivatives along the face give the same calculation as above. Each of its \(d-j\) gradient components perpendicular to the face and directed out of the box must have the appropriate sign to contribute to the boundary Morse count. Symmetry and independence give a factor \(2^{-(d-j)}\). There are \(2^{d-j}\binom dj\) such faces, each of size \(L^j\). Their combined coefficient is therefore \(\binom djL^j\). Corners supply \(Q(q)\) in total, where \(Q(q)=\Pr(Z>q)\) for a standard normal variable \(Z\), as in the one-dimensional crossing calculation. With \(r=L/\sigma\), the formulas become
\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[\chi_1]&=Q(q)+\frac{r}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2},\\ \mathbb E[\chi_2]&=Q(q)+ \left[\frac{2r}{2\pi}+\frac{r^2q}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\right]e^{-q^2/2},\\ \mathbb E[\chi_3]&=Q(q)+ \left[\frac{3r}{2\pi}+\frac{3r^2q}{(2\pi)^{3/2}} +\frac{r^3(q^2-1)}{(2\pi)^2}\right]e^{-q^2/2}. \end{aligned} \]
These reproduce the paper’s Equations 8–10 for interval, square, and cube geometry. They are not the formulas for a periodic box. For a rectangle or rectangular room, replace \(2L\) or \(3L\) by the sum of side lengths, \(3L^2\) by the sum of pairwise side products, and \(L^3\) by volume. A general domain requires its own geometric boundary factors. Applying only the volume term to a small room would discard real boundary contributions.
The formulas have two limiting checks:
At intermediate thresholds the higher dimensional signed densities can be negative because tunnels or holes outnumber components. For example a cube with \(L/\sigma=10\) has expected \(\chi=-20.06\) at \(q=0\). A negative expected Euler characteristic is meaningful. A negative expected field count would not be.
Thresholding one fixed smooth map separates the number of connected fields from the number of holes.
A negative chi means that holes outnumber components in this 2D example. It does not mean a negative number of fields. When holes are absent, chi equals the component count.
At a sufficiently high threshold, almost every component is a small solid blob with one peak and no holes. Then \(\chi\simeq N\). For a large box, retaining the leading volume term and the leading power of \(q\) gives
\[ \mathbb E[N]\simeq \frac{V}{(2\pi)^{(d+1)/2}\sigma^d} q^{d-1}e^{-q^2/2}, \]
where \(V\) is environment length, area, or volume. For a large domain with negligible boundary contributions, the pooled field-weighted mean size \(\mu_s\) is the expected total active volume \(VQ(q)\) divided by the expected component count, counting each field once. This ratio is not generally the expected value of the per-map average field size in a finite domain. Use \(Q(q)\simeq e^{-q^2/2}/(\sqrt{2\pi}q)\) for high positive \(q\). The factors \(V\) and \(e^{-q^2/2}\) cancel, leaving \(\mu_s\simeq(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma/q)^d\). This independently checks the size-law mean. The exact EC formula and this approximate component count have different ranges of validity.3
Read Figure 3F–H as whole curves, rather than single field counts. Increasing the applied firing rate cutoff by \(t\ge0\) changes the normalized level to \(q+t/a\). It can reveal separation between peaks or remove components. The measured maps only test levels at or above their original effective cutoff. The rest of an analytic curve is a prediction. The gain was matched using mean maximum firing rate before the EC comparison, so the horizontal conversion from Hz to normalized level also uses fitted information. Two dimensional holes and three dimensional tunnels help explain the nonmonotonic curves.4

In 1D it equals the number of connected active intervals.



In 2D it is the number of connected components minus the number of independent holes. Three disjoint disks have \(\chi=3\). One connected ring has \(\chi=1-1=0\).



In 3D it is components minus independent tunnels plus enclosed cavities. A solid ball has \(\chi=1\), a solid ring has \(\chi=0\), and a hollow spherical shell has \(\chi=2\).

































As \(q\to-\infty\), the whole box becomes active and all three expectations tend to one.
As \(q\to+\infty\), they tend to zero.

section: 12.2 What was fitted and what was tested
text:
12.2 What was fitted and what was tested

The experiments supply estimated firing rate maps, not the hidden Gaussian input. To assess a prediction, we must therefore track both which summaries set its parameters and which processing decisions change the map’s geometry. 


The paper reanalyzes earlier bat and rodent recordings. It uses different available summaries in different conditions. The inspected article and supplement do not clearly give the final included cell count for every analysis, particularly the long-tunnel and 3D reanalyses. Counts from an original recording study should therefore not be silently substituted for those final samples.5  




Table 12.1: Fitted quantities and additional comparisons.










Condition
Quantities used to choose parameters
Main additional comparisons




Bats, 200 m tunnel
mean field length and mean gap
full distributions, log-length moments, peaks, boundary slopes, rate versus width, EC


Bats, 6 m tunnel
mean field length and occupied fraction
length distribution and simpler field shapes. Figure 5D reports 40 cells.


Bats in a 130 m tunnel and rats in a 48 m maze
mean length and mean field count
length distributions and parameter trends. Rat details are in Figure S1.


Mice, 40 m virtual track

areas, counts, line slices, and EC. Slice and EC analyses of the raw maps use 20 supplied cells.


Bats, 5.8 by 4.6 by 2.7 m room
mean volume and occupied volume fraction
volumes, line/plane slices, rate versus linear size, EC, surface curvature







The STAR Methods call the virtual-track animals rats in one sentence. Figure 1F and the main results identify them as mice. Several STAR figure cross-references also appear displaced. The table follows the main figure captions and the analyses described in full, rather than those isolated labels.

Figure 1C distinguishes a limiting analytical Rayleigh curve from the finite threshold simulation histogram. Its parameters were constrained by both mean length and mean gap, so the full length histogram is an additional check. Figure 1D does the same for gaps. Panel E tests whether the shape of the log-length distribution agrees with the model beyond its mean and variance.

For \(Y=\log s\), write \(m_k=\mathbb E[(Y-\mathbb EY)^k]\). Skew, \(m_3/m_2^{3/2}\), measures signed asymmetry: the cubed deviations retain their signs, so unusually large log lengths contribute positively and unusually small ones negatively. Excess kurtosis, \(m_4/m_2^2-3\), measures the fourth moment relative to a Gaussian with the same variance. The fourth power weights large departures from the mean strongly, on either side. A positive value means a larger fourth moment than that Gaussian reference. A lognormal distribution of lengths makes \(Y\) Gaussian and both quantities zero. Nonzero population values therefore rule out that lognormal description. Zero values alone do not prove it, and finite sample estimates fluctuate, which is why the figure compares simulated sampling distributions.6  
For the long-tunnel data, the authors compared the Gaussian excursion model with a fitted lognormal using likelihoods, the probabilities or densities each model assigns to the observed data, and criteria that penalize fitted parameter count. Those comparisons favored the Gaussian model. These are in-sample model comparisons. They are not reported held-out forecasts. Model histogram error bars come from \(10^4\) simulations matched to the number of recorded cells. They do not quantify every source of animal-level or measurement uncertainty.7
The processing choices affect the quantities being compared:

Bat maps were rectified at about 0.5 Hz for denoising: rates below this cutoff were set to zero, removing weak activity from the measured fields.
The 3D maps, sampled in 10 cm bins, also received a median filter, which replaces each bin’s rate with a middle-ranked rate in its local neighborhood. The paper used a neighborhood two bins wide on each axis. This reduces isolated high or low values but can also change small field features.
Fields larger than three standard deviations above mean 3D volume were removed as possible merges, including from slice analyses.
Peak counting excluded incomplete boundary fields and used a range of smoothing widths.
The 1D rate versus width comparison used an additional 1 Hz cutoff.


These decisions can remove small components, alter peaks, and change tails. They belong to the definition of the analyzed fields.8 
Figure S1 matches the rat maze’s 15 cm minimum length cutoff in simulations and removes unusually large empirical fields. Changing that cutoff changes log-length moments. Figure S5 shows sensitivity of the higher-moment comparison across small denoising thresholds, while the rate versus width slope becomes stable above about 1 Hz. Figure S2 compares the spherical-field alternative and measures boundary curvature. Locally, mean curvature averages bending in two principal directions and Gaussian curvature multiplies them: a spherical patch bends the same way in both directions, while a saddle bends in opposite directions. These are extra shape measurements. They are not needed to derive the field-size law. Surface representations and finite differences affect their estimates.9


Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure S1








Figure 12.4: The rat comparison uses the same minimum field length in recorded and simulated maps. Original Figure S1 from Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025). Exact artwork excerpt. PDF page 2. Open image at full size.







Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure S5








Figure 12.5: Denoising thresholds alter log size moments, while the rate versus width slope stabilizes above about one Hz. Original Figure S5 from Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025). Exact artwork excerpt. PDF page 7. Open image at full size.








Figure 4A–B summarizes fitted parameter changes across a small set of environments. The correlation length increases with environment size while the threshold generally decreases. At fixed \(q\), increasing \(\sigma\) reduces crossings per metre. At fixed \(\sigma\), the crossing density is proportional to \(e^{-q^2/2}\): lowering a positive \(q\) toward zero increases it, while lowering a negative \(q\) decreases it. Both parameters also affect mean length, so these effects must be considered together. Figure S3 reports count scaling exponents below one and hence a weak decline in count per unit environment size. These cross-experiment trends do not establish a biological scaling law. In particular, the 3D table’s reported \(\sigma=4.0\) has an unclear distance-unit conversion relative to the spatial binning, so it should not be read as a verified value in metres.10

Figure 12.6: Fitted map scale grows with environment size, while the threshold and field shape also change. Original Figure 4 from Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025). Exact artwork excerpt. PDF page 8. Open image at full size.

The model also allows differences between cells. Figure S4 draws a positive threshold separately for each cell and keeps that threshold for two otherwise independent maps representing opposite flight directions. Low-threshold cells tend to have more and larger fields in both maps. This shared cell property creates correlations between flight directions even when field locations differ between directions. Two distribution parameters were chosen to match the two empirical correlations, so those correlations are fitted features of this extension. Its continued agreement with length and gap distributions is the additional comparison. This extension should not be described as a two-parameter model shared by all cells.11

title: 12  Holes and measurements test the spatial explanation
section: 12.3 Random input weights can generate Gaussian maps
text:
12.3 Random input weights can generate Gaussian maps
The statistical model becomes biologically useful if it suggests how a circuit could make the maps. A random weighted sum of many inputs is one possible mechanism, and the supplement makes its assumptions explicit.
At position \(x\), each input cell contributes according to its spatial firing profile. Fixed connection weights determine how those contributions combine at the receiving cell. The source treats the sum as effective input relative to a background that can be balanced through inhibition or regulation of excitation and inhibition. The signed random weights below are part of this simplified input model. They do not establish the signs of individual biological synapses.
Let \(u_i(x)\) be the fixed spatial tuning of input neuron \(i\), and let independent weights \(W_i\) have zero mean and variance \(v_W\). The profiles \(u_i\) may have nonzero spatial means. The expectation below is over weights: their zero means make the summed input \(h(x)\) have mean zero. The summed input is
\[ h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n W_i u_i(x). \]

At a finite list of positions this is a sum of independent random vectors, one per input cell. Under a multivariate central limit condition, with a suitable normalization and no single input dominating, the sum approaches a Gaussian vector as the number of contributing inputs grows. Applying this at every finite list supplies the Gaussian-process description. This Gaussian limit requires many contributing inputs at each position. A large anatomical input count alone does not establish how many inputs contribute there.12 
The covariance calculation exposes which assumption supplies spatial structure:
\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[h(x)h(y)] &=\sum_{i,j}\mathbb E[W_iW_j]u_i(x)u_j(y)\\ &=v_W\sum_i u_i(x)u_i(y). \end{aligned} \]

The same fixed weight multiplies an input cell’s activity at both positions. For positive input profiles, cells active at both \(x\) and \(y\) therefore make positive contributions to covariance across possible weight choices. Little overlap gives a smaller contribution. For profiles defined as deviations from background, the products can also be negative. Broad input profiles can produce broad spatial covariance, as the Gaussian example below shows. 
If inputs are translated copies \(u_i(x)=u_0(x-x_i)\) with centres densely and uniformly covering space at density \(\rho\), the sum is approximately
\[ C(y-x)\simeq v_W\rho\int u_0(s)u_0(s+y-x)\,ds. \]
The assumptions supply different parts of the model:

Uniform coverage supplies stationarity away from boundaries.
Smooth input tuning supplies smoothness.
Random weights supply the Gaussian limit under their independence and size conditions.

For input profiles with different shapes, average the last integral over the distribution of those shapes, as in Methods S2, Equation S8.
At fixed profile shape, increasing the weight variance \(v_W\) or input density \(\rho\) increases the covariance amplitude. It does not change the normalized spatial dependence in this construction. Widening each input profile broadens the distances over which positions share input. It can also change the covariance amplitude and hence the normalized threshold \(q\) when the absolute threshold is fixed. To isolate an effect of spatial scale at fixed \(q\), the input amplitude or absolute threshold must be adjusted accordingly.

For example, take \(u_0(s)=R_0e^{-s^2/(2b^2)}\) in one dimension, where \(s\) is distance from an input cell’s centre, \(R_0\) is its peak firing rate, \(b>0\) is the profile width, and \(\Delta=y-x\) is the separation between the two positions whose input covariance is being calculated. To develop the covariance integral, first complete the square: \([s^2+(s+\Delta)^2]/(2b^2)=(s+\Delta/2)^2/b^2+\Delta^2/(4b^2)\). The shifted Gaussian integrates to \(\sqrt\pi b\), giving 
\[ \int u_0(s)u_0(s+\Delta)\,ds =R_0^2\sqrt\pi b\,e^{-\Delta^2/(4b^2)}. \]
The covariance has Gaussian width parameter \(\sqrt2 b\). Its second derivative at zero gives the same correlation length, \(\sigma=\sqrt{-C(0)/C''(0)}=\sqrt2 b\). Thus widening the input profile increases the correlation length in proportion to \(b\) in this ideal construction. The square of the Gaussian width doubles relative to \(b^2\), which is consistent with the supplement’s description of twice the width if that description uses the squared width. This comparison describes the input covariance; field sizes also depend on the threshold and need not change by the same factor.13

Agreement with the Gaussian field predictions supports this random-summation account as a possible explanation. It does not uniquely recover synaptic weights from rate maps. Correlated inputs, a structured component added to many random contributions, plasticity, or recurrent processing could also produce approximately Gaussian spatial input under some conditions. The paper measures rate maps, rather than the relevant weights or subthreshold input directly. Its analyzed environments were familiar and fairly uniform. Stationarity may fail near landmarks, boundaries, rewards, or in changing tasks.14 

Thresholding a smooth spatial Gaussian input predicts field arrangement, shape, and topology from a small set of parameters. Several comparisons with recordings support these predictions. Inferring a circuit mechanism from this agreement requires additional measurements or perturbations.

title: 13  Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests
text:
13.1 The three papers constrain maps, dynamics, and movement
A model can explain the shape of a neural code without explaining how that code is maintained. It can also explain fluctuations inside a circuit without uniquely locating the source of a measured behavior. Comparing the three papers requires keeping each claim with the mathematical or experimental test that supports it.
To connect them, we first separate the spatial map, the changing represented position, and the movement measured downstream. A short calculation then shows how a common position error can make cells with different tuning change together. Comparing that calculation with each paper’s evidence and related studies identifies what a joint experiment would still need to measure.
Unreviewed draft diagrams. These AI-generated overviews may contain incorrect labels, arrows, formulas, or numbers. Use the chapter text and cited papers for the scientific claims.
For a circuit representing position, three questions arise:
The objects differ even when the word position appears in all three. In 2012, \(\theta(t)\) locates a network state on its attractor. In 2022, the internal eye-position command and actual eye angle are separate quantities linked through motor neurons and mechanics. In 2025, \(x\) locates an animal in an environment, and \(h_i(x)\) is a spatial input function assigned to a cell. The Gaussian process does not update a remembered \(x\) through time.
The guide map gives a visual comparison of these three questions.
The 2012 and 2022 connection is direct: neural noise can move a maintained eye-position command, which then drives muscles. The 2022 result provides evidence for a substantial shared source before the final motor neurons and shows that integrator diffusion is sufficient within the constructed model. It does not measure the circuit’s Fisher information or test equality in the 2012 bound. The place-field model describes spatially irregular tuning curves. To connect those curves to memory dynamics, we must also specify how the represented position moves.
