title: 13  Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests
section: 13.2 A shared position error changes rates according to their tuning slopes
text:
13.2 A shared position error changes rates according to their tuning slopes
Suppose a network maintains a one-dimensional estimate \(x(t)\) and cell \(i\) has a fixed expected-rate function \(f_i(x)\). Its time-dependent expected rate is
\[ R_i(t)=f_i(x(t)). \]

Here \(f_i\) describes spatial tuning and \(x(t)\) describes dynamics. A source of time variation has entered even though \(f_i\) is fixed. Actual spike counts add another layer of variability around the expected rate. This construction is a guide calculation connecting the papers’ objects, not a model tested jointly by the three studies. 
Consider a short interval of duration \(t\) starting at \(x_0\). Assume that the estimate’s local displacement \(\delta x=x(t)-x_0\) has mean zero and variance \(2Dt\), where \(D\) is the diffusion coefficient of the represented position. The displacement must be small enough to linearize each rate curve; \(f_i'(x_0)=df_i/dx|_{x_0}\) is cell \(i\)’s rate change per unit position change at the start. Taylor expansion gives
\[ f_i(x_0+\delta x) =f_i(x_0)+f_i'(x_0)\delta x+O((\delta x)^2). \]
The \(O((\delta x)^2)\) term collects smaller corrections of quadratic or higher order for small displacements. To leading order, the change is \(\delta R_i=f_i'(x_0)\delta x\). Multiplying the centered changes for neurons \(i\) and \(j\) and averaging yields
\[ \operatorname{Cov}(\delta R_i,\delta R_j) \simeq f_i'(x_0)f_j'(x_0)\operatorname{Var}(\delta x) =2Dt\,f_i'(x_0)f_j'(x_0). \]
This covariance concerns expected-rate changes caused by the common represented displacement, conditional on the starting position. It is not a formula for every covariance in a spiking recurrent network. It neglects higher-order changes in tuning and additional private or shared fluctuations. Near a threshold or over a large spatial displacement, the linear approximation must be revisited.


13.2.1 Example: opposite rate changes from the same position error


Calculation and figure
Let the local slopes of two rate curves be \(f_1'=2\) Hz/m and \(f_2'=-1\) Hz/m. Suppose \(D=0.01\) m²/s and the interval is 0.5 s. Then the variance of the common position displacement is \(2Dt=0.01\) m². The contributions to rate variance and covariance are
\[ \operatorname{Var}(\delta R_1)=2^2(0.01)=0.04\ \mathrm{Hz}^2, \]
\[ \operatorname{Var}(\delta R_2)=(-1)^2(0.01)=0.01\ \mathrm{Hz}^2, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\delta R_1,\delta R_2)=(2)(-1)(0.01) =-0.02\ \mathrm{Hz}^2. \]
With only this one source, the two rate changes have correlation \(-1\): one rises whenever the other falls. Adding independent private noise lowers the magnitude. The negative covariance here comes from opposite tuning slopes under a common position change. It does not establish an inhibitory connection between the cells.
For the same slopes, set both expected rates to 10 Hz at the starting position. The upper plot shows the fixed rate curves. The lower plot shows their changes under a common position displacement.







Figure 13.2: A common displacement of \(+0.1\) m increases rate 1 by \(0.2\) Hz and decreases rate 2 by \(0.1\) Hz. The changes lie on one line. With displacement variance \(0.01\) m², their covariance is \(-0.02\) Hz² and their correlation is \(-1\). The 10 Hz baseline is chosen only to display positive rates. These are exact lines from the guide’s local example, not recorded data.




Both changes are set by the same position displacement, so they occupy one direction in the two-rate plane. Independent private fluctuations would spread them away from that line.



Irregular single-cell responses can therefore coexist with population changes along just one direction. To test whether a shared position error causes that pattern, one must measure how the rate changes align with the tuning curves. Field shapes alone do not supply that evidence.

title: 13  Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests
section: 13.3 Each model needs a test matched to its claim
text:
13.3 Each model needs a test matched to its claim
The shared-position calculation predicts how rates would change together. Establishing that connection requires measurements of those changes as well as the spatial maps. Each paper tests a different part of the proposed connection:

Place-field statistics: A model that matches one distribution may have enough adjustable parameters to do so for several different reasons. The place-field paper gains support by fitting arrangement parameters and then comparing additional features, including slices and shape statistics. The separate firing-rate multiplier used in some comparisons should remain visible when counting how many quantities were predicted without further fitting. A successful high-threshold formula is also a statement about its limiting assumptions. Finite-threshold simulations and the original recordings provide different kinds of checks.




Eye drift: The eye paper calibrates a movement-to-firing relationship, inverts it, and compares the resulting single-neuron displacement predictions with measured displacement. Shared covariance then carries information that independent private fluctuations cannot supply under the decomposition’s assumptions. The additional MSD comparison tests the time structure: increasing stationary motor-noise amplitude cannot by itself reproduce the accumulating upstream signal. Calibration validity, source correlations, two animals, and horizontal movement remain part of the result’s scope.





Memory stability: The 2012 inequality \(D\ge 1/(2\tau^2J)\) is a mathematical constraint rather than an experimental fit: \(D\) is memory diffusion, \(J\) is the internal spike information rate, and \(\tau\) is the synaptic time constant. Its derivation specifies what noise and dynamics it covers. An experimental comparison would need estimates of diffusion, the relevant time constants, and the appropriate instantaneous information rate, all under compatible conditions. Agreement with \(1/N\) scaling alone would not test the entire inequality, since several mechanisms can share that scaling.

[Guide derivation: the memory bound] At the represented value \(\theta\), let \(\bar r_i\) be neuron \(i\)’s steady firing rate and \(r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta\) its rate slope. Let \(v_i\) be the lasting change in \(\theta\) from a unit activation perturbation in that neuron. For a stable continuous family with one neutral memory direction, in the weak-noise Poisson model with independent spike generation conditional on rates and a common \(\tau\), normalize the projection so a unit coordinate change is read as one unit. Then the projection gives \(2D=\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i\) and \(\tau\sum_i v_i r_i'=1\); the local spike information rate about the current attractor state is \(J=\sum_i(r_i')^2/\bar r_i\) for positive rates. Cauchy–Schwarz then gives \(1/\tau^2=(\sum_i v_i r_i')^2\le(\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i)(\sum_i(r_i')^2/\bar r_i)=2DJ\), hence \(D\ge1/(2\tau^2J)\) when \(J>0\). The full projection and information calculations appear in Part I of this guide.2

title: 13  Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests
section: 13.4 Related studies change assumptions and leave circuit choices open
text:
13.4 Related studies change assumptions and leave circuit choices open
Related studies test the assumptions and ask questions the three papers leave open:

Integrating movement: The eye-position account begins with Seung’s line-attractor model. Aksay and colleagues then used recordings and perturbations in goldfish to constrain integrator circuitry. These establish the dynamical problem and experimental architecture behind the 2022 model. Neither supplies the macaque displacement-variance estimate. Burak and Fiete’s earlier grid-cell study examines path integration, updating a position estimate from movement. In its model, velocity drives recurrent population activity, and errors accumulate in the position estimate. Its accuracy ranges belong to the simulated networks and parameter choices, rather than all biological grid circuits.3
Storage capacity and changing synapses: Noise-driven storage also connects to memory capacity. Koyluoglu and colleagues ask how noise limits recall as the delay and number of stored items increase. Their comparison with human data shows why direct storage of several independent values need not capture observed behavior. Transformations before and after storage alter the performance prediction. Seeholzer and colleagues examine how short-term changes in synaptic strength affect diffusion and systematic drift. These papers change the storage assumptions rather than invalidate the 2012 calculation inside its original model.4
Recordings from larger environments: For place fields, Eliav and colleagues’ long-tunnel recordings and Harland and colleagues’ large-arena recordings supply the multiple-field, multiple-scale observations. Yartsev and Ulanovsky supply the three-dimensional bat recordings. The 2025 paper reanalyzes those existing data, so its agreement across dimensions is not three newly collected experiments under one protocol. The later study by Maimon and colleagues directly compares CA3 and CA1 in large tunnels: predominantly single fields in CA3 contrast with multiple fields in CA1, while field sizes are similar. That distinction supports treating the CA1 statistics and the upstream spatial circuit as related but separately constrained parts of the explanation.5



Connectivity and learning: Gaussian spatial statistics do not identify a unique pattern of connections. Druckmann and colleagues report structured synaptic connectivity between hippocampal regions. Bittner and colleagues show how electrical events in dendrites, the branching input structures of neurons, can induce changes in synaptic strength and form CA1 place fields. Structure and learning can therefore be present even when a random-function model describes many aggregate field statistics. The model’s success leaves open which circuit mechanism produces these maps. Input, connectivity, learning, or perturbation measurements could distinguish the possibilities.6



Benefits for perception: The source and use of eye motion are different questions. Nghiem and colleagues combine human eye tracking with a model of how eye movement affects visual signals to explain why an intermediate amount of fixational motion can help fine visual discrimination. A movement that partly originates from internal noise can still have useful sensory consequences, and feedback can regulate its statistics. Benefit for perception does not uniquely identify the neural generator.7

title: 13  Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests
section: 13.5 A joint test would compare tuning maps with population fluctuations
text:
13.5 A joint test would compare tuning maps with population fluctuations
A joint test needs tuning maps and fluctuations from the same population. A possible sequence is:

Estimate the tuning maps and their uncertainty.
Measure fluctuations when external signals provide little correction of the represented position. Test whether their covariance aligns with the changes implied by the tuning maps.
Fit diffusion only over a range where the local approximation and measurement corrections are justified.
If comparing behavior, include the physical or neural filters between the representation and the measurement.


These measurements would test whether one system satisfies both spatial-statistics and dynamical-stability constraints. A static Gaussian-process fit alone cannot supply the diffusion coefficient. A diffusion fit alone cannot establish the distribution of fields. Agreement with both would constrain the model more than either fit alone. A mismatch would require further tests of spatial input statistics, recurrent maintenance, the observation filter, or their coupling. This is proposed follow-up work, not a replication claimed by this guide.

title: Part III: Neural memory in electronic hardware
text:
Chapters in this part
Unreviewed draft diagram. This AI-generated image may contain incorrect or missing labels, arrows, formulas and numbers. Use the Part text and paper links as the source for the explanation.
John von Neumann, The Computer and the Brain (1958), printed page 66, PDF page 78.
Von Neumann compares mutually stimulating nerve cells with electronic circuits that preserve a state through feedback. In the following pages he also questions whether active elements alone could provide the nervous system’s main large-capacity store. His comparison invites us to distinguish a memory’s physical mechanism from the information it keeps. It does not establish that every brain memory uses persistent activity, or that present hardware follows one historical line from his book.
The setting here is experimental and computational neuroscience joined with electronic engineering. We ask how a silicon circuit can retain a quantity such as an angle, and what physical processes limit its accuracy. A durable connection weight, a lasting activity pattern, and an accurately remembered value are three different achievements.
The path begins by identifying weights, changing states and the value represented by a circuit. We then follow feedback through flip-flops, multilevel circuits, recurrent rings and oscillators. The next chapter asks how a single disturbance and ongoing noise change those states, connecting stability to the neural dynamics in Part I. We compare physical and digital implementations, then end with repeated-trial measurements, readout and the lessons of Part II. The hardware research snapshot is current to October 30, 2026.
For a first pass, read the physical explanations, main results, and interpretations. Worked calculations and deeper derivations are folded. The comparison assumes the calculus, basic probability, and linear algebra used earlier. Electronics terms are introduced as they become necessary.
The contribution labels describe the role of each result here. Central is a main finding of the cited paper. Supporting establishes or qualifies that finding. Background supplies needed concepts. Guide-derived identifies an explanation, comparison, or proposed test developed in this guide.

title: Part III: Neural memory in electronic hardware
text:
A stored weight and a remembered value are different states: A silicon circuit can keep a connection strength unchanged while losing the angle it was asked to remember. It can also keep that angle while its individual electrical signals change. To compare electronic memory with the neural memory in Part I, we first need to identify what information each physical quantity represents. This chapter separates the connection settings, the changing state of each artificial neuron, and the value represented by their joint activity. That separation will let us ask what feedback actually preserves.
Electronic feedback circuits store and transform neural-like states: Compare electronic circuits and neuromorphic networks with neural models of persistent activity, eye control, and spatial representation. Identify what each architecture stores, how its components interact, how noise and readout affect its state, and what each cited result establishes.
Discrete restoration and continuous random wandering produce different memory errors: A circuit can remain active for seconds even when its individual voltages decay in milliseconds. The explanation is feedback: activity supplies new input before old input disappears. But long-lived activity does not by itself identify what is being preserved. This chapter first explains how feedback extends a time scale, then distinguishes a restoring discrete memory from a freely changing continuous one. Measured silicon circuits show why this distinction matters beyond a mathematical model.
Neuromorphic chips choose where physics performs the calculation: Suppose we want to study how a noisy network retains an angle. One machine can calculate every state update as arithmetic. Another can let capacitor voltages perform part of the dynamics. A third can use material conductances to multiply inputs by stored weights. The scientific choice is which physical effects we want to control, measure, or exploit. This chapter compares these implementations and then examines recent demonstrations of memory and learning.
Memory experiments must separate device error from network dynamics: The earlier stability comparison followed the response to one disturbance. A memory experiment instead repeats a cue and observes what happens as disturbances continue over time. After an angle cue, the estimate may be wrong because the state wandered, because unequal connections pull it toward another angle, or because the observer reads it poorly. This chapter separates mean motion from trial-to-trial spread, relates spread to circuit noise and asks what the output reveals about the state. Its tests and reduced models are proposed tools, not results demonstrated on every platform in the preceding chapter.
crumbs: Part III: Neural memory in electronic hardware

title: 14  A stored weight and a remembered value are different states
text:
14.1 A connection setting shapes activity. The activity can represent a cue
A silicon circuit can keep a connection strength unchanged while losing the angle it was asked to remember. It can also keep that angle while its individual electrical signals change. To compare electronic memory with the neural memory in Part I, we first need to identify what information each physical quantity represents. This chapter separates the connection settings, the changing state of each artificial neuron, and the value represented by their joint activity. That separation will let us ask what feedback actually preserves.
Draft diagrams: These unreviewed generated images may contain missing labels, incorrect numbers or misleading relationships. Use the chapter text and sources as the reference.
Imagine giving a circuit a brief cue for an angle of \(30^\circ\). After the cue ends, a connected group of artificial neurons remains active. We estimate the remembered angle from which neurons are active and how strongly. The experiment involves:
Keeping the weights unchanged preserves the circuit’s rule of operation. Keeping the cue available requires the resulting activity to preserve information about that cue. Training can change the first object. Remembering a new angle can change the second and third without any further training.
Neuromorphic computing implements computations inspired by neural circuits using electronic systems organized around neurons, connections, events, or their dynamics. Some systems calculate neural states as digital numbers. Others use voltages and currents that evolve physically. A system can combine both approaches. The word alone does not tell us where its memory is stored or whether it demonstrates a biological memory mechanism.
Working memory, in this Part, means keeping information about a recent input available for a later task. Persistent activity is one candidate mechanism. A slowly decaying state, a sequence of states, or an explicit digital buffer can also store recent information. We must specify the allowed delay and readout error before calling one implementation adequate.

title: 14  A stored weight and a remembered value are different states
text:
Connection weights determine how a signal from one neuron changes another neuron’s state. A weight can be fixed throughout the trial.
Neuron and synapse states change during the trial. Examples include a voltage, a current left by recent inputs, or a number representing either quantity.
The remembered angle is a property of the joint state, recovered by a readout rule. It need not occupy one dedicated storage cell.





Example: the same weights can hold different angles.
Suppose a ring of 32 artificial neurons has fixed local excitation and broader inhibition. A cue near neuron 3 creates a localized group of active neurons there. A later trial cues neuron 11 and creates a group near that location. The same connection weights support both trials. A decoder assigns an angle to the active group’s center. If the group moves after the cue, the decoded angle changes even though every stored weight remains correct. This is an example constructed to illustrate the distinction. It is not a specification of a chip.

title: 14  A stored weight and a remembered value are different states
section: 14.2 Bits, capacitor voltages, and material conductances store different physical states
text:
14.2 Bits, capacitor voltages, and material conductances store different physical states
The neural model still needs a physical implementation. If the model has a variable called membrane voltage, a chip may store it as a binary number or as an actual circuit voltage. Those choices expose the computation to different errors. Current is electric charge flowing per unit time, measured in amperes (coulombs per second). Voltage is an electrical energy difference per unit charge, measured in volts (joules per coulomb).
A capacitor stores separated electric charge. For fixed capacitance \(C\), its stored charge \(Q\) and voltage difference \(V\) satisfy \(Q=CV\). Charge is measured in coulombs and capacitance in farads (coulombs per volt). Supplying current changes \(Q\), so it changes the stored voltage.

Digital storage uses distinguishable physical ranges to represent discrete symbols, usually bits. In static random-access memory (SRAM), powered transistor feedback maintains one of two states representing a bit. Several bits can encode a weight or a changing neuron variable. Reliable bits do not imply unlimited numerical precision: a finite word represents only finitely many values. 
Analog state represents a model quantity through the magnitude of a physical variable, such as capacitor voltage. Input current changes stored charge and so changes voltage. Leakage changes that voltage during a quiet interval. Feedback or new input can oppose the leakage. In BrainScaleS-2, the membrane state evolves this way, while local SRAM stores the synaptic weights.1
Phase-change memory (PCM) stores information in a material’s atomic arrangement, including the proportions of ordered and disordered regions, which affect its electrical resistance. Programming pulses heat the material. Its heating and cooling history changes the arrangement. Conductance measures the current produced per unit applied voltage where current is approximately proportional to voltage. It is the inverse of resistance, the voltage required per unit current. Reading the conductance can recover a stored weight. Such storage is nonvolatile: it can retain its state without continuous power, within its retention limits. Nonvolatile weights can remain after the changing neural state has disappeared.
The following choices locate the stored quantity before we compare complete machines.




Table 14.1: Physical states and the information they can represent.











Implementation
Quantity representing information
Example role
Error relevant to that role

Here device mismatch means persistent differences between nominally identical circuit elements. It differs from fluctuations that vary from moment to moment. A fixed mismatch can create a repeatable bias. Changing noise can create a different trajectory on each trial. We will measure these separately.

title: 14  A stored weight and a remembered value are different states
section: 14.3 The stored state matters through the update it produces
text:
14.3 The stored state matters through the update it produces
To understand a machine’s memory, follow one input through it. On a digital spiking processor, an arriving event identifies connections, their weights contribute to inputs, and a program updates stored neuron variables. Those variables determine whether to send further events. Loihi 2 provides local digital state and weight memory with programmable neuron and learning rules. SpiNNaker2 uses many processor cores whose software updates neural states stored with weights in local SRAM. Their event communication does not make every model variable evolve continuously in physical time.23
In an analog neural circuit, an input can directly supply current to a capacitor. Transistors implement leakage and other responses as the voltage evolves. Digital circuits may still route the events and store the settings. Mixed-signal hardware combines analog circuit variables with digital storage, communication, or calculation. The division of labor, rather than the label, determines which dynamics are physical and which are calculated.
PCM supplies a third use of physics. At a fixed, sufficiently small read voltage, a cell’s current is approximately \(I=GV\), where \(I\) is current, \(V\) is applied voltage, and \(G\) is conductance, measured in siemens (amperes per volt). The stored conductance represents a weight. In Le Gallo and colleagues’ chip, the duration of a read pulse represents the input magnitude. For one positive contribution with fixed \(G\) and \(V\), a pulse lasting \(T\) seconds passes charge \(Q\simeq GVT\). The contribution is proportional to the product of weight and input duration. Currents from several cells add, and the chip converts the combined current over time to digital values. Signed inputs and weights require additional polarity handling beyond this simple example.4
In-memory computing performs some operations where the values are stored, reducing the need to transfer them to a separate arithmetic unit. The 64-core PCM chip demonstrates this approach to neural-network inference, with digital processing also part of the system. Its weighted response results from both the stored material state and the applied input signal.
A circuit’s storage medium tells us how a value is retained between updates. Its update rule tells us how that value affects subsequent computation. Both are needed to explain memory. The next chapter follows the feedback in flip-flops, multilevel circuits, and rings of artificial neurons. Those examples will let us compare what happens when a remembered state is disturbed.

title: 15  Electronic feedback circuits store and transform neural-like states
text:
15.1 Electronic architectures can share neural organization while storing different things
How can a circuit remember a value after the signal that set it has ended? In Part I, interconnected neurons keep an activity pattern going, and the pattern can represent an angle. Electronic circuits can also use feedback to maintain states. Here we follow that shared idea from a two-state flip-flop to a ring of artificial neurons, and ask which properties actually carry over.
Hassabis and colleagues’ review Neuroscience-Inspired Artificial Intelligence proposes a two-way exchange: findings about brains can suggest algorithms for AI, while AI models can give neuroscience ideas and tools to test. The authors discuss shared computational principles, not a claim that every useful electronic circuit reproduces a biological mechanism.1 The comparison in this chapter is likewise a guide-derived explanation of circuit organization, supported by the separate experiments cited below.
For each architecture, ask three questions: what physical state changes, what does feedback do, and what value can be read from the state? We start with circuits familiar from electronics, then connect them to spikes, synaptic activation and network memory. Folded examples give a closer look at particular devices. The earlier comparison of stored weights and activity explains why the three roles must be kept separate. The next chapter follows a disturbance through these circuits before adding ongoing noise; a later chapter asks how well their states can be measured.
Draft diagrams: These unreviewed generated images may contain missing labels, incorrect numbers or misleading relationships. Use the chapter text and sources as the reference.
Feedback occurs when a change in a circuit’s output affects its later input. Whether feedback restores a state, changes it repeatedly, or supports a family of states depends on the connections and component responses.
In the neural model, the connection \(W_{ij}\) specifies how activation from neuron \(j\) affects neuron \(i\). The changing activation \(s_j\) reflects the accumulated, decaying effect of spikes. A population pattern of these changing activations can represent a value \(\theta\). In an electronic circuit the corresponding objects might be a programmed conductance, a capacitor voltage or current, and a value decoded from several signals. Which physical quantity plays which role must be checked for each design.
The list below is a reading map, not a claim that the circuits have identical equations or are biological models. A flip-flop and multilevel memory show how feedback can hold discrete states. An oscillator and a ring attractor illustrate different ways a displacement can persist.
The first two are useful comparisons, not automatically neural networks. The ring is a network when its connected units and their dynamics implement the stated interactions. We now follow the feedback in each case.

title: 15  Electronic feedback circuits store and transform neural-like states
text:
Flip-flop: feedback restores one of two states; the output indicates a bit.
Multilevel memory: feedback restores one of several preferred voltage levels; the output indicates a discrete level.
Recurrent ring: an activity bump can persist at different positions; its position indicates a direction.
Oscillator: feedback sustains a cycle; its phase gives the position within that cycle and normally advances with time.
Pulse-based neuron circuit: graded input can set pulse timing or rate; a circuit state can accumulate and leak input.

title: 15  Electronic feedback circuits store and transform neural-like states
section: 15.2 A flip-flop maintains one of two states through feedback
text:
15.2 A flip-flop maintains one of two states through feedback
Two inverting stages can be cross-coupled so that each stage’s output is the other’s input. An inverting stage responds to a high input with a low output and to a low input with a high output. If the first output is high, it drives the second low; that low output in turn supports the first being high. The reverse arrangement is also possible. A setting signal selects a state; after it is removed, powered feedback can maintain the selected pattern. The stored bit is read from one output.
A small disturbance is corrected if the new state is still within the set of states that return to the original one. This set is its region of attraction. A sufficiently strong disturbance or an input intended to switch the device can move it to the other state. Bistability means the same fixed circuit conditions support two locally stable states. The two coupled stages are an analogy for recurrent neural activity, but a binary latch does not by itself retain an arbitrary angle. The next chapter’s stability comparison develops this distinction.2
Giulioni and colleagues built a recurrent electronic network of spiking artificial neurons that exhibited low and high activity states. It is a closer network analogy than a two-stage latch: many artificial neurons participate in maintaining each state. Their experiment examined persistent activity and noise-related transitions, rather than storage of a continuously variable angle.3

title: 15  Electronic feedback circuits store and transform neural-like states
section: 15.3 Multilevel circuits hold several preferred states
text:
15.3 Multilevel circuits hold several preferred states
The same question extends beyond two levels: could feedback hold one of several voltages? Alhawari and Perrott fabricated a CMOS circuit with ten stable operating points. An input first sets a voltage; when its input switch is opened, nonlinear feedback moves the voltage toward a nearby stable level. The retained voltage identifies a level while the circuit is powered.4

Example: reading a voltage between two levels.
Imagine adjacent preferred levels at 0.40 V and 0.50 V. If a setting input leaves the state in the first level’s region of attraction, the feedback carries it toward 0.40 V; from the second region it moves toward 0.50 V. The boundary between regions depends on the circuit and need not be exactly halfway. These values illustrate the mechanism and are not measurements from the ten-level device.

Ten levels can distinguish more values than two, but each stable point has a region that pulls nearby voltages toward it. Increasing the number of discrete levels does not alone create the ideal continuous family of steady states used in the 2012 model. In principle, a sufficiently large noise disturbance can cause a jump between levels; this general switching mechanism differs from the local wandering of a neutral memory coordinate. The ten-level study is cited here for its stable levels, not as a measurement of those jumps.

title: 15  Electronic feedback circuits store and transform neural-like states
section: 15.4 Ring networks store a value in the position of an activity bump
text:
15.4 Ring networks store a value in the position of an activity bump
Suppose artificial neurons are assigned preferred directions around a circle. Each excites nearby units, while inhibitory interactions suppress more distant activity. A brief cue can activate a localized group. Recurrent input then helps that group maintain its activity after the cue is removed; a suitable movement signal can shift the group. The position of the bump represents direction. The weights describe how units influence one another; they are not the angle itself.
Massoud and Horiuchi demonstrated a physical head-direction system with a 32-neuron ring, testing bumps initialized at 32 indexed locations. Some connections were routed through an external digital processor. Kreiser and colleagues implemented a recurrent head-direction network on the mixed analog and digital ROLLS neuromorphic chip. In the latter experiment, movement signals shifted the activity and a visual landmark corrected accumulated heading error. Device mismatch and movement-estimation error both contributed to the error; the experiment did not isolate the diffusion coefficient of the 2012 model.56
The analogy to Burak and Fiete’s ring model concerns the organization of feedback and the encoded coordinate. A ring layout alone does not guarantee a stable bump or a continuum. Real circuits have finite units, unequal components and noise; they can favor particular positions. A set of measured positions is evidence for a graded representation at that resolution, not proof of an exact continuous attractor.

title: 15  Electronic feedback circuits store and transform neural-like states
section: 15.5 Oscillator phase can wander while oscillation persists
text:
15.5 Oscillator phase can wander while oscillation persists
A multivibrator or a suitable ring of inverting stages can repeatedly switch rather than settle to a fixed state. Its phase describes where it is in one cycle. Even in a perfect oscillator, phase advances: after one period it returns to the same point in the cycle. A timing disturbance can make later cycles arrive early or late relative to a reference.
This resembles the neural memory’s neutral direction, a direction in which a displacement is not driven back to its previous value: the system can return toward its usual cycle after a disturbance while keeping a phase shift. In an ideal continuous attractor, a bump can return toward its usual shape while retaining a shift in position. The comparison concerns the error relative to the expected phase, because oscillator phase also advances without noise. It does not make a ring oscillator a stationary ring-attractor memory.
Electronic oscillator research studies timing fluctuations using phase noise and jitter, the variability in the timing of oscillator events. Hajimiri, Limotyrakis and Lee analyze phase noise in ring oscillators and compare their theory with measurements. The noise sources and conditions must be identified before treating phase variance as a simple diffusion law.7

title: 15  Electronic feedback circuits store and transform neural-like states
section: 15.6 Pulse trains and analog states implement different neural variables
text:
15.6 Pulse trains and analog states implement different neural variables
An individual electronic pulse is a brief event. A pulse rate describes the number of pulses per unit time, averaged over an interval or defined as a conditional expected rate. Many pulses, each contributing charge to a capacitor, can produce a changing voltage. Between pulses, leakage or a designed discharge path reduces that voltage. A transistor can convert voltage into a current or affect the timing of later pulses.
This gives a physical reading of the chain in Chapter 1: spikes are events; \(r_i\) is their conditional firing rate; \(s_i\) is the modeled accumulation of their decaying synaptic effects. These roles can be implemented by different circuit variables. A short observation can have no pulses even at a positive expected rate, and a long-time average can conceal pulse timing and shared fluctuations.
Some transistors can also hold several programmable conductance levels. Those levels often represent synaptic weights \(W\), not the moment-to-moment neuron state \(s\) or the stored angle \(\theta\). Other devices exhibit neuron-like integration and firing. In a 2022 anti-ferroelectric transistor study the device was measured, while the larger digit-recognition network using its properties was evaluated in simulation.8 A multilevel device is therefore a possible component, not proof that a recurrent memory network has been built.
The later chip comparison locates these roles in different machines. Loihi 2 and SpiNNaker 2 update represented neural states digitally; BrainScaleS-2 uses analog circuit dynamics for membrane states and digital storage for weights. In phase-change computing, material conductances can store weights while surrounding circuits or a host perform other operations. These hardware choices do not by themselves establish that a particular network implements a continuous attractor.

title: 15  Electronic feedback circuits store and transform neural-like states
section: 15.7 Drift and Fisher information measure different limits on memory
text:
15.7 Drift and Fisher information measure different limits on memory
Preview. After the next chapter examines how a circuit responds to one disturbance and to ongoing noise, the hardware experiment returns to the following measurements. They connect a circuit’s physical state to what an observer can infer from its signals.

Preview: drift and information measurements
If an electronic bump is meant to preserve an initial direction, repeat the same setting and delay many times. Decode its position after each delay. The mean displacement shows repeatable bias; the spread across trials shows variability. When a local diffusion model with constant coefficient \(D\) applies, the predicted variance of the position change after delay \(t\) is \(2Dt\). Device mismatch can instead create preferred positions or systematic motion. Measurement noise and movement-input errors require separate controls. The hardware experiment develops these distinctions.
Fisher information describes how well the probability distributions of measured signals distinguish nearby values of a parameter. To estimate it for an electronic ring, one could record the available outputs at nearby controlled bump positions and model their variability. The result depends on which signals are observed and for how long. It concerns the current represented position; diffusion concerns how that position changes from its initial value.
For their neural model, Burak and Fiete find \(D\ge 1/(2\tau^2J)\): \(D\) is memory diffusion, \(J\) is the internal spike information rate, and \(\tau\) is the synaptic time constant. See the information-bound derivation and assumptions. The same calculation is not automatically a bound for all transistor circuits: the dynamics, noise statistics, observations and time scales must be matched first. Likewise, Ben-Shushan and colleagues’ eye measurements test an explanation of biological motor variability; a chip analogy cannot establish the eye circuit’s wiring. Mainali and colleagues study spatial firing-field statistics, not whether a ring circuit autonomously retains a position. A population pattern can encode a variable in both settings, but those are different experimental claims.

The architectural question to carry forward is therefore concrete: which physical state represents the value, which feedback acts on it, and which disturbances can the circuit correct?

title: 16  Discrete restoration and continuous random wandering produce different memory errors
text:
16.1 Feedback can extend persistence beyond a component’s decay time
A circuit can remain active for seconds even when its individual voltages decay in milliseconds. The explanation is feedback: activity supplies new input before old input disappears. But long-lived activity does not by itself identify what is being preserved. Starting with the preceding flip-flop and ring examples, this chapter follows one disturbance, then asks what happens when noise keeps perturbing the circuit. It explains how feedback extends a time scale and distinguishes a restoring discrete memory from a freely changing continuous one. Measured silicon circuits show why this distinction matters beyond a mathematical model.
Draft diagrams: These unreviewed generated images may contain missing labels, incorrect numbers or misleading relationships. Use the chapter text and sources as the reference.
Physical mechanism. An isolated capacitor loses a voltage difference when charge leaks through a resistance. In a recurrent circuit, its output can cause an input current that replaces some of that charge. The competition between loss and replacement sets the decay of the collective state. For a neural population, the same competition occurs between decay of synaptic input and input supplied by recurrent spikes.
Let \(u\) be the amplitude of one small activity disturbance around a reference state. A simple linear model is
\[ \tau_s\frac{du}{dt}=-u+g u+I(t). \]
Here \(\tau_s\) is the component decay time, \(g\) is dimensionless recurrent feedback gain, and \(I(t)\) is external drive expressed in the same units as \(u\). The term \(-u\) removes activity, and \(gu\) replaces a fraction of that loss. After the cue ends, \(I=0\). For \(g<1\),
\[ u(t)=u(0)e^{-t/\tau_{\rm eff}},\qquad \tau_{\rm eff}=\frac{\tau_s}{1-g}. \]
Interpretation. Raising \(g\) toward one slows forgetting. At \(g=1\), this ideal linear mode retains every amplitude. For \(g>1\), it grows until effects omitted from the linear model become important. Long persistence requires a balance of physical processes. It is not determined by the storage element’s decay time alone.
The next issue is which disturbances the feedback corrects. Retaining any amplitude requires a different response from restoring one chosen amplitude.
crumbs: Part III: Neural memory in electronic hardware
16  Discrete restoration and continuous random wandering produce different memory errors

title: 16  Discrete restoration and continuous random wandering produce different memory errors
text:
Derivation: feedback reduces the net decay rate

With no external input, divide the differential equation by \(\tau_s\): \(du/dt=-(1-g)u/\tau_s\). Multiplying by \(e^{(1-g)t/\tau_s}\) makes the derivative of \(u e^{(1-g)t/\tau_s}\) zero. Its value is the initial amplitude \(u(0)\). Comparing the resulting exponential with \(e^{-t/\tau_{\rm eff}}\) gives the effective time constant above. This is one linear mode near a chosen state, not a full transistor or spiking-network model. 


Example: a small gain error changes a long memory time.
Choose \(\tau_s=10\) ms. Gain \(g=0.99\) gives \(\tau_{\rm eff}=1\) s. Changing the gain to \(0.98\) reduces that time to \(0.5\) s. Changing it to \(0.995\) increases it to \(2\) s. The component decay time is unchanged in these three cases. The example predicts sensitivity to adjusting the feedback strength, not a measured lifetime on any chip.

16  Discrete restoration and continuous random wandering produce different memory errors

title: 16  Discrete restoration and continuous random wandering produce different memory errors
section: 16.2 A bit corrects small displacements. A continuous memory preserves some of them
text:
16.2 A bit corrects small displacements. A continuous memory preserves some of them

Physical mechanism. In a two-state electronic memory, feedback pushes a slightly disturbed state back toward the same stable state. A sufficiently large disturbance can switch it to the other state. In an ideal continuous attractor, disturbances away from the family of memory states decay, but a displacement along that family represents another valid value. The circuit has no restoring signal telling it which earlier value to recover. Seung used this distinction to compare discrete electronic memory with graded eye-position memory.1
First consider one brief push with no further noise. In the flip-flop, a voltage shifted within its original region of attraction returns toward the voltage associated with the selected bit. In the ideal ring, a disturbance that changes the bump’s shape can decay, while a small shift of its position leads to a nearby remembered angle. This is the physical counterpart of the restoring and neutral directions in the Part I linearization. Now ask what changes when random pushes keep arriving instead of occurring only once.

This is a distinction between dynamics, not a division between all digital and all analog machines. Analog transistors can maintain discrete bits. Digital processors can calculate a continuous-state neural model to finite precision. Stored bits may remain correct while repeated numerical updates produce a wandering decoded angle. 
Mathematical comparison. Let \(e\) measure a local displacement from one stable state. If restoration has strength \(\kappa>0\) and random perturbations have diffusion coefficient \(D\), a reduced model is
\[ de=-\kappa e\,dt+\sqrt{2D}\,dW_t. \]
The Brownian increment \(dW_t\) has variance \(dt\). Here \(\kappa\) has units of inverse time and \(D\) has units of \(e^2\)/time. Starting exactly at the stable state,
\[ \operatorname{Var}(e(t))=\frac{D}{\kappa}\bigl(1-e^{-2\kappa t}\bigr). \]
For a neutral memory direction with \(\kappa=0\), the corresponding result is \(\operatorname{Var}(e(t))=2Dt\). Restoration limits small local fluctuations. A neutral direction accumulates them.

Derivation: restoring feedback limits local spreading

For displacement \(e(t)\) from the chosen stable state, restoration strength \(\kappa\), and diffusion coefficient \(D\), the linear stochastic equation has solution \(e(t)=\sqrt{2D}\int_0^t e^{-\kappa(t-s)}dW_s\) when \(e(0)=0\). Here \(s\) is the integration time and \(dW_s\) is the Brownian increment at that time. Independent Brownian increments make its variance the integral of the squared weighting function: \(2D\int_0^t e^{-2\kappa(t-s)}ds=D(1-e^{-2\kappa t})/\kappa\). As \(\kappa\) tends to zero, expanding the exponential gives \(2Dt\). This is a local model inside one stable state’s region of attraction. It does not describe rare switches between digital states or estimate a hardware bit-error rate. 

Interpretation. Adding restoration to an angle memory can reduce random spread by drawing nearby angles toward preferred positions. That also reduces the set of distinct values retained. Pinning means that imperfections or imposed structure draw a nominally continuous memory toward preferred states. A flat error variance can mean successful retention near one preferred value while other cues have been biased toward it. Both mean error and spread are needed.

For their neural model, Burak and Fiete’s information–diffusion bound is \(D\ge 1/(2\tau^2J)\), where \(D\) is memory diffusion, \(J\) is the internal spike information rate, and \(\tau\) is the synaptic time constant. It is not a lower bound on the error of every electronic memory. A digital device that freezes a number, uses explicit error correction, or changes the noise and readout assumptions poses a different problem. To transfer the bound, match the dynamics, noise, available observations, and time scale first.2

title: 16  Discrete restoration and continuous random wandering produce different memory errors
section: 16.3 Silicon experiments distinguish discrete persistence from graded representation
text:
16.3 Silicon experiments distinguish discrete persistence from graded representation
A physical demonstration lets us test whether feedback maintains the intended state despite unequal devices and finite resolution. The following early experiments make different claims and should be read separately.
Massoud and Horiuchi built a head-direction circuit whose localized activity could persist after a cue and move with velocity input. It had 32 bump positions around a circle, a spacing of \(11.25^\circ\). This demonstrates a physical orientation representation with finite resolution. It does not establish an exact continuum of persistent states or a measured Brownian diffusion law.3
Giulioni and colleagues built a recurrent spiking circuit with low and high activity states. Brief stimulation could initiate activity lasting seconds despite millisecond circuit dynamics. Their measurements also examined noise-driven transitions and recovery after disturbance. This is bistability: two locally stable states under the same ongoing conditions. It supplies a physical working-memory example, but its two-state retention is a different task from retaining an arbitrary angle.4
The comparison gives a useful reading rule for current machines: determine what values the network distinguishes, then ask how long and how accurately it preserves them. Neuron count or nonvolatile weight storage cannot answer those questions alone.

title: 17  Neuromorphic chips choose where physics performs the calculation
text:
17.1 Digital and analog implementations expose different parts of the neural model
Suppose we want to study how a noisy network retains an angle. One machine can calculate every state update as arithmetic. Another can let capacitor voltages perform part of the dynamics. A third can use material conductances to multiply inputs by stored weights. The scientific choice is which physical effects we want to control, measure, or exploit. This chapter compares these implementations and then examines recent demonstrations of memory and learning.
The research snapshot is October 30, 2026. “State of the art” here means selected recent capabilities supported by primary papers, with older architecture papers supplying their physical explanation. It does not mean one machine leads every task. We distinguish measured chips, experiments partly run on a separate computer, and proposed hardware evaluated by simulation. A host computer is a separate general-purpose computer that controls an experiment or performs calculations assigned outside the neuromorphic chip.
Draft diagrams: These unreviewed generated images may contain missing labels, incorrect numbers or misleading relationships. Use the chapter text and sources as the reference.
A useful platform must make the variables of interest accessible. If the question concerns a specific noise law, a digital update may allow precise control of the injected noise. If the question concerns physical circuit variability, analog dynamics expose that variability directly. Interpreting either choice as a biological result requires a matched model and experiment. Hardware calibration adjusts circuit settings to make measured device responses match requested responses more closely.
The first two rows describe digital neural computation, while BrainScaleS-2 directly implements parts of the differential equations in analog circuitry. Its dynamics run roughly a thousand times faster than the biological model time. That acceleration makes long model intervals accessible quickly, but communication and measurement delays still occur in physical time.1
On-chip learning means that circuitry on the chip computes and applies some weight changes. It is distinct from loading previously trained weights. Loihi 2 offers programmable learning rules. SpiNNaker2’s 2026 technical preprint reports an on-chip learning implementation. BrainScaleS-2 combines local measurements with programmable processors that update weights. An experiment may still use weights trained beforehand or learning performed on a separate computer, so its learning setup must be checked.2

section: 17.2 Recent results improve temporal computation, adaptation, and device stability
text:
17.2 Recent results improve temporal computation, adaptation, and device stability
The following studies make progress on different parts of the memory problem. For each, ask what information persists and which physical component is responsible.
A useful input history on Loihi 2, 2025. Kleyko and colleagues implemented a stored history of recent inputs and functions of those inputs that include products. A trained readout uses these values to predict an output. This shows that changing chip state can supply useful information about recent inputs. It is not a measurement of indefinitely stable cue retention. Their pictured Hala Point system is much larger than the resources used in the experiment.3
Persistent spatial activity on SpiNNaker 2, September 2026. Aitsam and colleagues ran a 768-neuron recurrent sheet on one chip. A host computer processed the physical event camera’s output into a smoothed estimate of the target’s center and sent that position to the chip. The configured neural update used deterministic integer-weight dynamics, without an added stochastic neural-noise term. During an eight-second interval without input, the decoded activity center moved by at most half a cell. This establishes persistence for that interval, not a measured lifetime or a test of noise-driven diffusion. During tracking, recurrence reduced frame-to-frame jitter by 15% relative to the host-smoothed input, but added about 115 ms of lag and increased mean position error from 2.02 to 5.65 cells. The robot-guidance evaluation used a simulated robot, and its power figures were estimates. Longer-delay tests with controlled noise would help compare this implementation with the stochastic memory theory.4
Rapid adaptation using PCM, 2025. Ortner and colleagues used physical PCM weights for a recurrent spiking network that produced robotic-arm commands after a task-specific update. Earlier training adjusted the model for rapid adaptation to new tasks. The PCM units performed matrix-vector products. Other operations ran on a host computer. This locates the demonstrated advance in weight adaptation and mixed hardware computation. It does not show that PCM cells themselves sustained an autonomous recurrent activity pattern.5

Reduced material drift, online 2025 and in a 2026 issue. Wang and colleagues measured low resistance drift in a chromium-telluride phase-change material, CrTe\(_3\). Reduced drift can help a programmed conductance continue representing the intended weight. Their demonstration of several programmed resistance levels used laser programming and electrical readout. Electrical switching was a separate demonstration. Operation with several levels in nanoscale devices, performance beyond a million programming cycles, and variability across large arrays remained open. This is progress in a storage material, not a complete multilevel neuromorphic processor.6 
Better temporal state, faster adaptation, and more stable weights solve different problems, so progress in one does not establish the others. For the Burak comparison, the missing measurement is often how a decoded value changes during an input-free delay.

section: 17.3 Explicit slow memory is a current design choice, with distinct costs
text:
17.3 Explicit slow memory is a current design choice, with distinct costs
Fast spiking units can lose earlier inputs before a later decision needs them. One solution is to add a slower state that summarizes recent activity and sends input back to the fast units. Sun and colleagues’ 2026 dual-memory-pathway design takes this route. Their tested slow pathway uses a linear state based on a Legendre memory unit: several stored components summarize the shape of recent input over a sliding time window. It represents a recent input history, rather than a cue held unchanged on a continuous attractor. Its proposed digital hardware holds successive slow states in registers, small, fast digital storage locations, and other variables in SRAM. The hardware results came from post-layout simulations, which model a circuit after its physical layout has been designed. They were not measurements of a fabricated chip. The weights were trained before the evaluated tasks.7
A model with one stored number illustrates gradual forgetting without reproducing that richer input history. Let \(z_k\) be current input to a stored quantity \(m_k\):
\[ m_{k+1}=\alpha m_k+\beta z_k,\qquad 0<\alpha<1. \]
Here \(m_k\) is the stored state after update \(k\), \(z_k\) is the input at that update, \(\alpha\) is the retained fraction, and \(\beta\) converts input units into state units. For gradual forgetting in this example, \(0<\alpha<1\). After input stops, \(m_{k+n}=\alpha^n m_k\). The state remembers earlier input through its present value, while gradually forgetting it. This model illustrates slow storage. It is not the full equations or an independent performance test of Sun and colleagues’ architecture.

Example: the update interval determines the physical memory time.
If updates are separated by \(\Delta t\), equating \(\alpha^n\) with \(e^{-n\Delta t/\tau_m}\) gives \(\tau_m=-\Delta t/\ln\alpha\). With \(\Delta t=1\) ms and \(\alpha=0.999\), \(\tau_m\) is about 1 second. Executing the same updates a thousand times faster reduces that physical decay time to about 1 millisecond, unless the mapping between model time and wall time is changed. A number described as “slow” must be specified relative to other processes and the task clock.

Scaling a network also adds communication constraints. Ilmberger and Schemmel’s 2025 preprint measured communication in a four-chip BrainScaleS-2 prototype. The timing matters because its analog states continue changing while messages are transmitted. A small delay in wall time can be a substantial delay in accelerated model time.8
The comparison needs a specified task, permitted error, delay, and system boundary. Energy for a matrix operation omits state maintenance, communication, conversion, and host work when those are outside the measured unit. The next chapter turns these qualifications into an experiment that can compare the machines on the same memory question.

title: 18  Memory experiments must separate device error from network dynamics
text:
18.1 Repeated cue-and-delay trials separate drift from random spreading
The earlier stability comparison followed the response to one disturbance. A memory experiment instead repeats a cue and observes what happens as disturbances continue over time. After an angle cue, the estimate may be wrong because the state wandered, because unequal connections pull it toward another angle, or because the observer reads it poorly. One accuracy score combines these causes. This chapter first separates the mean motion from trial-to-trial spread, then relates that spread to circuit noise and finally asks what the output reveals about the state. The protocol and reduced models are proposed tools, not results already demonstrated on every platform in the previous chapter.
Draft diagrams: These unreviewed generated images may contain missing labels, incorrect numbers or misleading relationships. Use the chapter text and sources as the reference.
Begin with a circuit whose joint activity represents an angle. Choose a decoder on separate calibration data, then keep it fixed while testing retention. A decoder is a specified rule for estimating the represented quantity from observable circuit signals. A decoder given every internal state has a different task from a downstream neuron receiving only spikes.
Use the following sequence:
Record the decoded state immediately after each cue so that error in writing the value can be separated from error accumulated during retention. Report the number of repeated trials and uncertainty in the estimated drift and diffusion.
An active circuit has demonstrated useful memory only when its later signals distinguish the earlier cues at the required accuracy. High firing rate alone does not establish this. Nor does a small average error if positive and negative errors cancel.
For short intervals, a useful local model is
\[ d\theta=b(\theta)dt+\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dW_t. \]
Here \(\theta\) is the represented angle, \(b(\theta)\) is its systematic angular motion per unit time, and \(D(\theta)\) is half its local variance growth rate. The Brownian increment \(dW_t\) has mean zero and variance \(dt\); it represents the random disturbance accumulated during the short interval \(dt\). Let \(\Delta\theta=\theta(t+\Delta t)-\theta(t)\) be the angular change over lag \(\Delta t\). With nearly constant coefficients over that short lag, repeated trials near the same angle give \(\mathbb E[\Delta\theta]\simeq b\Delta t\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)\simeq2D\Delta t\). Correlated perturbations, preferred states, or boundaries can invalidate that short-lag fit. At long delays, report the distribution of angular errors around the circle. Values separated by a full turn represent the same angle, so a local unwrapped variance cannot be extended indefinitely as a measure of angular error.
The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the mean of the squared changes \(\mathbb E[(\Delta\theta)^2]\) over the chosen lag. It equals \(\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)+\mathbb E[\Delta\theta]^2\). Thus a growing MSD can include systematic motion as well as random spreading. Compare the mean displacement and its variance before interpreting an MSD slope as diffusion. The eye-drift measurements likewise require an explicit displacement convention and an estimate of measurement error.
Estimate readout noise before interpreting short-lag variance as motion of the stored value. Independent errors with constant variance in two position readings add a constant offset to the measured displacement variance.
The measurement path can also smooth or delay a signal, and noise can enter at different points along that path. For example, a circuit’s output filter smooths a changing voltage; a camera or actuator can introduce further delays. The eye study asks a related question about neural commands filtered by eye mechanics. Measure or model the filter and the observation noise separately before assigning the observed time scale to the memory state. The electronic analogy does not establish the biological mechanism.

title: 18  Memory experiments must separate device error from network dynamics
text:
Present a brief cue for angle \(\theta_0\), then remove it. Test many angles, including values between any suspected preferred positions.
Hold the connection weights fixed during each retention trial. Record the actual settings, temperature, update interval, and any imposed noise.
Repeat trials at several delays \(t\) and decode \(\hat\theta(t)\). Use a common reference for angular differences. Unwrapping tracks crossings of \(0^\circ/360^\circ\) by adding or subtracting full turns to continue the trajectory. Use it only when sampling is frequent enough to identify crossings reliably.
Report mean error and error variance separately as functions of cue and delay. Also report failures in which the activity pattern disappears or changes form.
Repeat with changed noise, calibration, or numerical precision, changing one factor at a time. Compare with the same model running in a numerical reference implementation.










Measurement check: readout noise can look like state motion
Suppose each position estimate contains independent, zero-mean measurement error with variance \(\sigma_m^2\). The difference of two estimates then adds \(2\sigma_m^2\) to displacement variance, even when the circuit does not move. For independent constant-\(D\) state motion, the measured short-lag displacement variance is \(2D\Delta t+2\sigma_m^2\). A nonzero intercept can reveal this contribution. Correlated readout errors, overlapping observation windows, or a state that changes during the readout require a fuller model. This is the same type of separation needed when interpreting the eye-drift measurements.

title: 18  Memory experiments must separate device error from network dynamics
section: 18.2 Physical parameters act through decay, bias, and noise projection
text:
18.2 Physical parameters act through decay, bias, and noise projection
A changed component affects memory through the circuit’s equations. Increasing a leak current can shorten a component time constant. Changing a recurrent weight can alter restoration or introduce a preferred angle. A fluctuating current can perturb many neurons, yet only part of the resulting activity change remains as a change of the remembered angle.
The projection derived in Part I makes the last statement precise under a specific model. Let the vector \(\mathbf r\) contain the network’s activity variables, with local dynamics \(d\mathbf r=\mathbf f(\mathbf r)dt+B\,d\mathbf W_t\). Here \(\mathbf f(\mathbf r)\) is the deterministic rate of change of the activity, \(d\mathbf W_t\) collects independent Brownian increments with covariance \(I\,dt\), and the matrix \(B\) maps those increments into the activity variables. Assume a smooth family \(\mathbf r_*(\theta)\) of steady states with one neutral memory direction and locally decaying directions, and disturbances small enough for a leading-order approximation. Let \(\boldsymbol\ell\) be the left neutral vector, the object called \(\mathbf v\) in Part I, normalized so that \(\boldsymbol\ell^T d\mathbf r_*/d\theta=1\). It converts an activity disturbance into its surviving angular displacement. Evaluating \(B\) and \(\boldsymbol\ell\) at that state, the leading local approximation gives
\[ D(\theta)=\tfrac12\boldsymbol\ell^TBB^T\boldsymbol\ell. \]
Noise matters through both its size and the directions in which it pushes the circuit. Large disturbances in rapidly corrected directions can matter less than small disturbances along the memory direction. In a general network the left neutral vector differs from the visible tangent to the family. Using the tangent alone can predict the wrong change in the remembered angle caused by a given activity disturbance. Curvature and state-dependent noise can also contribute drift beyond this local approximation.
Here \(B\) represents fluctuations that vary across time and trials, including noise deliberately added to a digital update or measured fluctuations in an analog circuit. A fixed device mismatch instead changes the deterministic dynamics \(\mathbf f\) and can create repeatable bias or preferred angles. It can also change which disturbances affect the remembered value by changing the return flow and noise sensitivity. If mismatch removes the family of steady states, the neutral-vector formula above is no longer directly applicable; any reduced description must be justified for the changed circuit. A configured deterministic neural rule has no stochastic term unless one is supplied; that statement does not make the physical digital chip free of timing variation or hardware errors.

Derivation: project circuit fluctuations onto the remembered angle
Write \(\delta\theta\simeq\boldsymbol\ell^T\delta\mathbf r\) in the local linear regime. For the neutral mode, \(\boldsymbol\ell^T\) times the linearized deterministic drift is zero. The stochastic increment is \(d\theta\simeq\boldsymbol\ell^TB\,d\mathbf W_t\). Since \(\operatorname{Cov}(d\mathbf W_t)=I\,dt\), its variance is \(\boldsymbol\ell^TBB^T\boldsymbol\ell\,dt\). Equating this to \(2D\,dt\) gives the displayed coefficient. The normalization ensures that the result measures angular displacement rather than an arbitrarily scaled activity coordinate. This calculation transfers only after the hardware’s local dynamics and noise assumptions have been checked.

The following changes suggest tests under the model assumptions above. In the table, \(B\) maps Brownian noise into the circuit activities, \(BB^T\) describes its covariance per unit time, and \(\mathbf f\) is the deterministic rate of change of those activities.




Table 18.1: Controlled changes and the memory measurements they motivate.

Example: a tighter distribution can hide a biased memory.
Consider two illustrative circuits after a one-second delay. Circuit A has zero mean angular error and variance \(4\) deg\(^2\). Circuit B has mean error \(3^\circ\) and variance \(1\) deg\(^2\), because it is attracted toward a preferred angle. Their mean squared errors are \(4\) and \(1+3^2=10\) deg\(^2\). Circuit B has less random spread but worse cue retention. Reporting only its smaller variance would hide the effect of pinning.

title: 18  Memory experiments must separate device error from network dynamics
section: 18.3 Matching time and readout is necessary to compare memory accuracy
text:
18.3 Matching time and readout is necessary to compare memory accuracy
The source papers supply different constraints on this hardware experiment.

Burak and Fiete (2012): compare diffusion with the information available in spikes under matched noise, dynamics, and observation assumptions. A processor that stores an exact internal angle and exposes it directly to the decoder has changed the readout problem.
Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022): a measured output can filter the internal command. Camera exposure, output smoothing, or a mechanical actuator can change the observed motion. Calibrate that path before assigning an output time scale to the memory circuit itself.



Mainali and colleagues (2025): patterns of firing across physical positions constrain a spatial representation. Reproducing field-size statistics does not by itself show that a network implemented in hardware retains position without input. Spatial structure and temporal persistence need separate tests.


These links concern the tested mechanisms, not a claim that a chip reproduces the animal systems. The synthesis chapter sets out the evidence supplied by the original papers.
To compare readout with Part I’s Fisher information, first specify the signal and observation duration. Fisher information measures how the distributions of those signals change with nearby values of the current state. An observer estimating the initial cue after a delay faces an additional uncertainty: the represented value may have moved since the cue. A precise estimate of the current bump does not by itself recover the earlier angle. For the neural model of Burak and Fiete, \(D\ge 1/(2\tau^2J)\), where \(D\) is the diffusion coefficient, \(J\) is the internal spike information rate, and \(\tau\) is the synaptic time constant. An electronic circuit needs matched noise and dynamics before the same bound can be tested.
Time conversion is especially important for accelerated hardware. If model time \(t_m=a t_p\), where \(t_p\) is physical time and \(a>1\) is the acceleration factor, let \(\Delta\theta\) be the angle change and \(D_m\) the diffusion coefficient per unit of model time. The diffusion law \(\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)=2D_m t_m\) becomes \(2(aD_m)t_p\). The physical-time coefficient is \(D_p=aD_m\), measured per physical second. This is a change of units for the same ideal trajectory. Physical communication delay, temperature drift, or limited readout speed can prevent a real device from obeying that ideal rescaling.
For an energy comparison, specify the cue distribution, delay, permitted decoding error, and failed-trial rate. Measure energy over writing, waiting, and reading, including required host processing and interfaces. Then report how error and energy change as delay increases. An operations-per-second or operations-per-watt figure alone cannot establish the cost of retaining a useful value.
The resulting research question is concrete: which part of the physical implementation limits the accuracy of a remembered quantity, and does changing that part improve retention under the same task and readout? That question turns von Neumann’s comparison into a test of contemporary neural and electronic memory mechanisms.

title: Part IV: Simulations connect model assumptions to measurable outcomes
text:
Network simulations test how random spikes move a stored value: To compare a simulated memory trace with Burak and Fiete’s (2012) theory, the numerical update and the measurement of the stored value must match the model. The foundation chapter explains the spike-update cycle, and the long-delay chapter interprets its diffusion tests. Here the additional task is to recover the published network settings, distinguish a numerical position measurement from the theoretical coordinate, and identify choices left open for an independent reproduction.
Eye simulations connect a noisy neural command to measured motion: A reproduction of Ben-Shushan et al. (2022) must distinguish the recording analysis from the simulated eye-control pathway. The circuit chapter explains why a noisy internal command is a possible source of drift. Here the added detail is how the published parameters, spike generator, update intervals, saved samples, and MATLAB files determine the numerical experiment, and which code or data gaps limit reproduction. The pathway below gives the mechanism needed to interpret those choices.
Random spatial maps test the statistics of place fields: To reproduce Mainali et al.’s (2025) place-field comparisons, we need the rules for generating and fitting model maps, and for measuring both model and recorded maps. The spatial-model chapter explains the statistical assumptions, and the tests chapter interprets the evidence. Here the additional detail is the Python map-generation procedure, filter and boundary conventions, fitted summaries, field detectors, and access to code and recordings. Position is the independent variable; each generated map is fixed during analysis, so these computations do not simulate a remembered position changing over time.
Reproduction depends on the model, numerical method, and measurement: A simulated eye trace can look convincing while answering the wrong question. It may use different spike statistics, a different muscle response, or a different definition of displacement from the experiment. Beyond the paper-specific methods in the preceding chapters, a reproduction needs checks that its software, resolution, and saved run record preserve the intended comparison. This chapter explains how to choose those checks and distinguish the authors’ program from an independent implementation or a smaller teaching model.

title: 19  Network simulations test how random spikes move a stored value
text:
19.1 A simulation renews the same synaptic state that the theory approximates
To compare a simulated memory trace with Burak and Fiete’s (2012) theory, the numerical update and the measurement of the stored value must match the model. The foundation chapter explains the spike-update cycle, and the long-delay chapter interprets its diffusion tests. Here the additional task is to recover the published network settings, distinguish a numerical position measurement from the theoretical coordinate, and identify choices left open for an independent reproduction.
Draft diagrams: These unreviewed generated images may contain missing labels, incorrect numbers or misleading relationships. Use the chapter text and sources as the reference.
The physical idea is continuing neural activity after a cue has ended. A spike briefly increases synaptic activation. That activation decays, but it also changes the rates at which other neurons fire. Recurrent connections can therefore renew the activity. Random event times disturb the pattern that represents the remembered value.
The computer stores each neuron’s synaptic activation \(s_i\). The total input \(g_i\) and firing rate \(r_i\) are calculated from it:
\[ g_i=\sum_j W_{ij}s_j+b_i,\qquad r_i=\phi(g_i). \]
Here \(W_{ij}\) is the connection from neuron \(j\) to neuron \(i\), \(b_i\) is a constant input, and \(\phi\) converts total input into a rate in spikes per second. In the paper’s normalization, each spike increases \(s_i\) by one and activation decays with time constant \(\tau\). The earlier neural mechanism and derivation explain these variables and the continuous-time equations.1
One short simulation step has a causal order:
The ring simulation uses the Euler update introduced in Chapter 1: approximate a variable’s change over a short interval by its current derivative times that interval. For decay alone, an interval \(h\) changes \(s_i\) to approximately \(s_i(1-h/\tau)\). Spike increments are added according to the event model. This finite step approximates the continuous dynamics, so its accuracy must be checked at the resolution needed for the reported statistic.
Each generated spike changes the recurrent inputs and can change the rates of later spikes. The theory explains when these interacting changes can be described by diffusion of one coordinate.
